UNITED STATES MARINE CORPS

                                                                                1 April 2025

FOREWORD

The requirement to balance traditional offensive and defensive tasks and tactics against enduring lessons
from recent operations made writing Marine Corps Warfighting Publication (MCWP) 3-01, Offensive and
Defensive Tactics, imperative. This publication comprehensively addresses the philosophy of tactics in
general and offensive and defensive tactics specifically, throughout the competition continuum. It does not
specifically discuss stabilization doctrine or tasks; although it does contain guidance for simultaneously
recognizing, executing, and transitioning between offense, defense, and stabilization activities.

MCWP 3-01 is the Marine Corps’ basic warfighting offensive and defensive tactics publication. It serves as
a common starting point for leaders and units to address the specific tactical problems that face them in a
globally contested environment, within multiple domains, across the competition continuum. This revision
reflects that Marines employ a tactical system of single battle that integrates and synchronizes warfighting
functions across all domains, focused on a thinking enemy, to offset disadvantage and create relative
advantage through the use of multidomain combined arms.

MCWP 3-01 is a compendium of best practices and common terms, not a dictate that must be rigidly
adhered to. Rather, it provides the basics of offensive and defensive tactics from the squad level to the
Marine division and points the reader to additional references for further study. This publication is intended
for the Marines, leaders, commanders, and staffs from the squad level to the Marine division as a
foundational document to assist in preparing and executing offensive and defensive tactics in any given
operational environment.

This publication supersedes MCWP 3-01, dated 20 September 2019.

Reviewed and approved this date.

                                                ROBERT M. HANCOCK
                                               Colonel, U.S. Marine Corps
                                      Director, Ground Combat Element Division
                                         Capabilities Development Directorate

                         Part I.
            Tactical Fundamentals

Part I introduces the role of Marine Corps tactics and discusses how the tactics taxonomy nests
within multidomain combined arms. This part discusses the art and science of tactics, the role of
tactics, and common tactical concepts and control measures that apply to offensive and defensive
operations as well as enabling activities.


---



---

                     CHAPTER 1.
                        TACTICS

According to Marine Corps Doctrine Publication (MCDP) 1, Warfighting, tactics refers to the
concepts and methods to accomplish a particular mission in either combat or other military
operations. In combat, tactics can be thought of as the art and science of winning engagements and
battles. It includes the use of firepower and maneuver; the integration of different arms; and the
immediate exploitation of success to defeat the enemy. To accomplish missions, commanders use
combat power (i.e., tactics), which is generated by combining elements of the Marine air-ground
task force (MAGTF). The tactical-level commander uses combat power in battles, engagements,
and small-unit actions. (See MCDP 1 and MCDP 1-3, Tactics, for more information.)

TACTICAL LEVEL OF WARFARE

The tactics and supporting techniques and procedures described in this publication are only
starting points for the Marine who must understand the difference between tactics, techniques, and
procedures. Tactics requires prudent judgment as well as adaptation to the unique circumstances
of a specific situation. Techniques and procedures are rote, established patterns, that once learned
can apply repeatedly to various situations. Tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTP) provide the
tactician with tools to use when developing the solution to a tactical problem. Marines use
combine existing TTP to solve problems, or they create new ones, as the situation requires. The
tactician determines a solution by mastering doctrine and TTP, tempered and honed by experience
gained through training and operations. The tactician uses creativity to develop solutions for
which the enemy is neither prepared nor able to cope.

The levels of warfare (i.e., strategic, operational, and tactical) link strategic objectives and tactical
actions. The tactical level of warfare is “the level of warfare at which forces plan and execute
battles and engagements to achieve military objectives” (The DoD Dictionary of Military and
Associated Terms, hereafter referred to as the DoD Dictionary). Activities at the tactical level focus
on arranging and maneuvering combat elements in the most effective relation to each other and to
the enemy. The strategic and operational levels of warfare provide context for tactical operations;
without tactical operations are reduced to a series of disconsnected and unfocused actions.

Engagement
An engagement is “a tactical conflict, usually between opposing lower echelon maneuver forces”
(DoD Dictionary). They are typically conducted at the Marine expeditionary brigade (MEB) or
regimental level and below. Engagements are usually short, executed in terms of minutes, hours,
or days. They can result from one side’s deliberate offensive movement against an opponent or
from a chance encounter between two opponents, such as a meeting engagement.


---

MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

    Battle
    A battle consists of a set of related engagements that lasts longer and involves larger forces than
    an engagement. Battles can affect the course of a campaign or major operation. For example, a
    battle take place when a Marine expeditionary force (MEF) fights for one or more significant
    objectives. Battles are usually operationally significant, if not operationally decisive.

    Levels of command, size of units, types of equipment, or types of forces or components are
    not associated with a particular level of warfare. National assets such as intelligence and
    communications satellites, previously considered principally in a strategic context, are an
    important adjunct to tactical operations. Commanders use strategic, operational, or tactical
    actions based on the potential effect or contribution they will make to achieving strategic,
    operational, or tactical objectives.

    Advances in technology in the information age have made information and the communication of
    information levers that have compressed the interrelationships between the levels of warfare.
    Commanders must envision a logical flow of operations across the levels and allocate resources
    and assign tasks to the appropriate commands. However, commanders at every level must be aware
    that in a world of high connectivity, which allows for constant and immediate communications, any
    single event can affect any or all levels of warfare. See Joint Publication (JP) 3-0, Joint Campaigns
    and Operations, for more information about the principles of joint operations.

   ART AND SCIENCE OF TACTICS

    The art (skillful wielding) and the science (proven practices and technologies) of tactics are two
    distinctly different yet inseparable constructs. A tactician is an individual devoted to mastering
    both. Commanders and leaders at all echelons must be tacticians to lead their Marines and Sailors
    in simultaneously conducting offensive, defensive, and stabilization activities.

    An operation is “a sequence of tactical actions with a common purpose or unifying theme” (DoD
    Dictionary). Tacticians use the art and science of tactics to maneuver and position formations.
    Maneuver is “employment of forces in the operational area, through movement in combination
    with fires and information, to achieve a position of advantage in respect to the enemy” (Marine
    Corps Supplement to the DoD Dictionary of Military and Associated Terms, hereafter referred to
    as the USMC Dictionary). Marines use maneuver tactics to gain and exploit positions of relative
    advantage to accomplish the mission.

    To successfully execute Marine Corps tactics, commanders must apply various tactical concepts.
    Key concepts include achieving a decision, gaining advantage, being faster than the enemy,
    adapting, cooperating with friendly forces, and exploiting success. Commanders use these
    concepts when planning and executing tactics. These are not stand-alone ideas; rather, Marines
    combine them to achieve a greater effect than they can accomplish using them individually.
    Commanders must know where and when to apply these concepts and which combinations to use
    in order to achieve the desired effect. See Chapter 2 and MCDP 1-3 for a detailed discussion of
    key Marine Corps tactical concepts.

                                                                         1-2


---

                                                                                  MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

Art of Tactics
An art, as opposed to a science, requires Marines to exercise intuitive faculties that cannot be
learned solely by study. Tacticians must temper their study and evolve their skill through various
relevant, practical experiences. The more experience the tactician gains, the greater is that
individual’s mastery of the art of tactics.

Tacticians use the art of tactics to solve tactical problems within the commander’s intent
by considering—

  • Types and forms of operations, forms of maneuver, methods, and tactical tasks.
  • Task organization of available forces, to include allocating scarce resources.
  • Arrangement and choice of control measures.
  • Operational tempo.
  • Risks the commander is willing to take.

These considerations represent a starting point for the tactician to create a unique solution to a
specific tactical problem. Although there are checklists for techniques and procedures, there are
no checklists for solving tactical problems. Therefore, tacticians must use their experience and
creativity, their staffs, and their subordinates to outthink their enemies.

When employing the art of tactics, Marines consider three interrelated aspects:

  • The creative and flexible tools.
  • Decision making in uncertain conditions and when faced with an intelligent enemy.
  • An understanding of the human element (i.e., the effects of combat on Marines and Sailors).

Creativity and Flexibility. Marines must provide the commander with creative and flexible tools,
such as TTP, training, organizations, and materiel. The infinite variations of any situation, the
changing mission factors of mission, enemy, terrain and weather, troops and support available–time
available (METT-T), and the independent will of the enemy demand creativity and flexibility from
the tactician.

Decision Making in Uncertain Conditions. Marines must recognize and operate within the
knowledge that tactical decision making takes place under conditions of uncertainty, in
time-constrained environments, and against opposing wills. Leaders must apply their judgment,
making the best use of the time and information available at the moment of decision and
avoiding the illusion of certainty. To establish control, leaders use mission-type orders and
direction to execute command and feedback into their decision-making process.

Understanding the Human Element. Success in combat depends on the human aspect of warfare as
much as it does on any numerical or technological factor. Marines must understand both the enemy
and friendly forces; this human element differentiates combat from problems they encounter during
training or in a classroom. Combat leaders seek to recognize and exploit fear and weakness in their
enemies while safeguarding friendly forces from similar effects. Tacticians accomplish this by
gaining and maintaining the initiative and dictating the tempo of continuous combat operations.

                                                                    1-3


---

MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

    Continuous combat operations against an intelligent enemy takes a toll on friendly forces,
    severely straining their physical and mental stamina, which can result in decreased vigilance,
    slowed perception, difficulty communicating, and an inability to concentrate or accomplish
    manual tasks. The tactician seeks to maximize these effects on the enemy while minimizing
    them on the friendly force by choosing tactics that dictate tempo and by exercising tactical
    patience—the art of developing the situation and timing decisions when conditions are favorable.
    The tactician must weigh the risk between pushing personnel beyond their limits to exploit
    success versus resting them to prevent the collapse of unit cohesion. See MCDP 1-3 for a more
    detailed discussion on developing the situation and timing and how it affects the human element.

    Science of Tactics
    The science of tactics requires Marines to understand the capabilities, techniques, and procedures
    of combat that can be measured and codified. The science of tactics includes measuring the
    physical capabilities of friendly and enemy organizations and systems, such as determining how
    long it takes a given organization (e.g., regimental landing team [RLT]) to move a certain
    distance. It also includes techniques and procedures used to accomplish specific tasks, such as the
    tactical term support by fire and the associated control graphic that compose the language of
    tactics. This publication focuses on the science of tactics—the techniques and procedures for
    employing various elements of the multi-domain combined arms (MDCA) team. See MCDP 1-3
    for a more detailed discussion on the science of tactics.

   HASTY VERSUS DELIBERATE OPERATIONS

    Most operations are conducted in either a hasty or deliberate manner. A hasty operation is
    conducted when the tactical situation requires the commander to use available forces and
    fragmentary orders (FRAGORDs) to perform actions with minimal preparation, trading planning
    and preparation time for speed of execution. The 1st Battalion, 1st Marine Regiment’s initial
    assault into Hue City in 1968 was a hasty operation conducted with available forces. A deliberate
    operation is conducted when the tactical situation allows the commander to develop and
    coordinate detailed plans and mission-specific rehearsals; task organize the force; and thoroughly
    prepare and synchronize shaping and sustaining actions.

    The 1st Battalion, 1st Marine Regiment’s initial assault into Hue City in 1968 illustrates hasty
    operations conducted with available forces. At the other end of the spectrum is a deliberate
    operation, such as the 1st Marine Division’s breach operation during the opening hours of
    Operation DESERT STORM in 1991. Although improved command and control (C2) systems
    provide leaders with greater situational awareness, facilitate decision making, and diminish the
    distinction between hasty and deliberate operations, commanders and their staff must determine
    which type of operation is most appropriate.

   OPERATIONAL CHOICES AND TRADEOFFS

    A commander’s decision to conduct a hasty or deliberate operation is based on the current
    knowledge of the enemy situation, an assessment of whether there are adequate available assets
    (to include time), and the ability to coordinate and synchronize those assets. Greater certainty is

                                                                         1-4


---

                                                                                  MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

necessary is for detailed planning and preparation, which is associated with deliberate or
complicated operations. Greater uncertainty, which typically accompanies crises or changes to a
situation, is often associated with hasty operations. Hasty operations require immediate action
with the available forces and information. A key skill for a commander—and part of the art of
tactics—is knowing when there is enough intelligence to make a decision within the higher
commander’s intent and constraints.

When commanders plan and prepare for an operation, they should use the least amount of time
necessary to ensure a reasonable chance of success. This allows friendly forces to act faster than the
enemy, permitting the rapid concentration of friendly strength against enemy vulnerabilities and
mitigating uncertainty in tactical operations. Although commanders must understand the possible
negative effects of reduced coordination, they must balance that risk against allowing the enemy
more time to change the situation, conduct preparations, and move additional units within supporting
range or distance. If the enemy can improve its disposition faster than the friendly force can, delays
in execution decrease the commander’s chances of success. Additionally, commanders should
provide subordinates the maximum time possible to conduct their own planning and preparations.

The fundamentals of maneuver warfare indicate it is typically better for commanders to act with
speed, audacity, and momentum when conducting military operations than to act with caution.
Bold decisions give the best promise of success; however, commanders must differentiate between
prudent risk and gambling. Prudent risk is a deliberate exposure to potential injury or loss when the
commander judges the outcome in terms of mission accomplishment as being worth the cost.
Commanders determine whether to exploit an opportunity by applying military judgment,
mitigating risk to an acceptable level, and determining whether the remaining risk is worth
accepting. The World War I decision to advance the Marines into Belleau Wood to stem the
German advance is an example of a justifiable, prudent risk. A gamble is conducting an operation
that can lead either to victory or to the complete destruction of one’s force. Rare situations can
arise when a gamble might be justified, such as when defeat is merely a matter of time and the only
chance for victory lies in an operation of great risk. Lieutenant Colonel Joshua Chamberlain’s
decision to direct a bayonet charge with what was left of the 20th Maine on the second day of the
Battle of Gettysburg is an example of a successful military gamble, as Union forces were able to
surprise and force the Confederates into a retreat despite being nearly out of ammunition.

When facing a less capable and less prepared enemy force, commanders can forego detailed
planning, extensive rehearsals, and significant changes in task organization. For example, an
attacking battalion landing team encountering enemy security outposts just moving into position
can conduct actions on contact to immediately destroy the outposts without losing momentum.
Against a larger and more prepared enemy however, the commander needs more preparation time
and a larger force to succeed. If the commander determines that the enemy forces cannot be
defeated with the available forces, the commander must determine what additional measures to
take to be successful.

RISK REDUCTION

Commanders encounter internal and external factors and influences that cast uncertainties
regarding whether and when they will achieve their objectives. The effect of this uncertainty
deviates from the expected. It can be positive, negative, or both, and can address, create, or result

                                                                    1-5


---

MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

in opportunities and threats. The decision to engage or not to engage an identified risk depends on
the commander’s risk threshold, which also guides the staff engaged in risk reduction. The
commander’s risk guidance is based on an assessment of negative and positive outcomes and
measured against their likelihood and potential impact.

Choices and the potential cost of those choices characterize operations. Commanders decide
whether they can accomplish their mission based on current intelligence of the enemy situation and
an assessment of the asset available (including time) and means to coordinate and synchronize
those assets. If those assets are unavailable, commanders take additional time to plan, resource, and
prepare for an operation, or they articulate where and how they will assume risk. When executing a
hasty operation, commanders should still operate within the framework of prudent risk.

Commanders reduce risk by acquiring information and intelligence within the context of the
time available to make decisions (see Table 1-1 for risk reduction factors). They use combat
information, which is unevaluated data that cannot be processed into tactical intelligence in time
to satisfy the tactical intelligence requirements. The key difference between combat information
and intelligence is the amount of planners have to analyze data. Acting on combat information
exposes friendly forces to risk, such as enemy deception, but also allows commander to exploit
fleeting opportunities. When the friendly forces act based on intelligence, they increase the
effectiveness of tactical operations and the efficient use of resources but risk surrendering
battlespace tempo to the enemy. As commanders receive combat information and intelligence,
they can determine whether hasty or deliberate operations will accomplish the mission..

Table 1-1. Risk Reduction Factors.

Less Information and Intelligence                More Information and Intelligence

More uncertainty and more risk to force.         Less uncertainty and less risk to force.

Commander employs—                               Commander employs—
• More reconnaissance and surveillance.          • Smaller reconnaissance and surveillance.
• Larger reserve.                                • Smaller reserve.
• More security.                                 • Fewer security formations.
• Reduced speed of operations.                   • Increased speed of operations.

Operates in a less distributed manner.           Operates in more distributed manners.

Commanders reduce risk through the methods they choose to employ their forces. Amid greater
uncertainty, friendly forces typically choose formations that prioritize force protection over speed
and create a large reserve capable of reacting to unforeseen events. Conversely, units with greater
certainty typically reduce risk by dispersing and distributing forces and by increasing operational
tempo. Although C2 systems and precision fires often provide Marine Corps forces an asymmetric
advantage over certain enemies, such advantages are often fleeting, with enemy forces quickly
reacting by camouflaging themselves (e.g., hiding among the population

Changes to task organization, mission, and priorities are part of an operation’s process.
Commanders, advised by their staffs, determine the optimal formation and organization for a
specific mission, and they continuously assess risk. When necessary, commanders make changes
and allocate resources to minimize risk. Every change has opportunities and risks, and
commanders balance the two to achieve their purpose.

                                            1-6


---

                                                                                  MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

FIGHTING AT A DISADVANTAGE

Offensive and defensive operations at the tactical level involve a constant struggle for advantage.
Against a peer competitor, commanders can expect limited air superiority and should not allow
this to dominate the decisions made and actions taken.

Although aviation is a central element of the MDCA tactical system, successful units recognize
that they cannot know when an enemy will contest the air domain nor allow friendly airflows to
dictate tactical success. They acknowledge that there will be times of distinct disadvantages, but
never willingly cede a space, and they contest perceived enemy advantages. They combine the
effects of capabilities across the other domains to not only mitigate disadvantage but also retain
freedom of maneuver, maintain tempo, and create periods of peak advantage.

Examples of fighting through disadvantage include—

  • Integrating air defenses, to include counter-unmanned aerial systems that challenge enemy
     air advantage.

  • Monitoring signals, systems, and platforms to provide warning of enemy air systems and
     identify gaps in enemy air coverage.

  • Conducting aggressive and unabated actions in space and the information environment to
     maintain pressure on the enemy, influence the timing and tempo of their operations, and take
     shaping actions to maximize periods when friendly units have the advantage.

  • Maintaining multi-layered sensing to feed the targeting process so action can be conducted as
     soon as assets become available.

  • Employing decoys as a standard action to complicate enemy targeting and slow their
     decision-making process.

  • Targeting enemy communications to disrupt command and control and degrade their
     targeting cycle.

SOLVING TACTICAL PROBLEMS

Marines solve tactical problems by gaining and maintaining the initiative—forcing the enemy to
react to friendly operations—at a time and place of their choosing. A commander should never
surrender the initiative once it is gained. The commander quickly builds momentum to by apply
available combat power while operating inside the enemy’s decision-making cycle, and mastering
the transitions from the defense to the offense and vice versa. These general principles allow the
commander to maximize friendly combat power and minimize enemy combat power by preventing
the enemy from fighting as a MDCA force. Commanders seize, retain, and exploit the initiative by—

  • Maneuvering more rapidly than the enemy to gain positional advantage (the place where the
     effects of fires are most destructive).

  • Employing firepower to facilitate and exploit positional advantage.

                                                                    1-7


---

MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

       • Sustaining subordinate forces before, during, and after engagement with the enemy.
       • Achieving and maintaining information superiority.
       • Planning beyond the initial operation and anticipating possible events.
       • Pressing the battle.
       • Accepting risk while leading Marines and Sailors and pushing systems to their limits.

    Tactical success—the end goal for all operations—is when the opposing enemy force can no
    longer achieve its tactical objectives or prevent friendly forces from accomplishing their mission.
    Decisive tactical success is when the enemy no longer has the means to oppose the friendly force,
    or when the enemy admits defeat and agrees to negotiated an end to hostilities. Historically, rapid,
    tactical success results in fewer friendly casualties and lowered resource expenditures. However,
    it could also weaken MDCA synchronization.

    Resolving tactical problems is a collective effort. Commanders must have full confidence in their
    subordinates’ mastery of the art and science of tactics. See MCDP 1 and MCDP 1-3 for more
    information on solving tactical problems.

   MULTI-DOMAIN COMBINED ARMS IN THE SERVICE TACTICAL SYSTEM

    The Marine Corps employs a tactical, single-battle system that integrates and synchronizes
    warfighting functions (see Appendix B) across all domains to offset disadvantage and create
    relative advantage by using multi-domain combined arms. Multi-domain combined arms integrate
    lethal and nonlethal fires in conjunction with maneuver to create effects that exploit windows of
    relative advantage by synchronizing capabilities across domains. Commanders use this integration
    to mitigate enemy advantages and create conditions that will enable them to defeat enemy forces,
    achieve objectives, and consolidate gains Marine Corps units use MDCA operations to impose
    multiple dilemmas on the enemy.

    All Marine Corps operations are MDCA operations because they integrate capabilities from all
    domains. At the tactical level of warfare, Marine Corps units provide the following capabilities:

       • Ground maneuver forces able to seize and hold terrain.
       • Surface-based indirect fires.
       • Air and missile defense.
       • Artillery and antiship missile attack.
       • Logistics.

    During offensive and defensive operations and stabilization tasks and activities, Marine Corps
    units also provide fixed- and rotary-wing aviation, unmanned aircraft systems (UAS), and
    satellite communications.

                                                                         1-8


---

                     CHAPTER 2.
                 COMMON TACTICAL
     CONCEPTS AND CONTROL MEASURES

MARINE CORPS OPERATIONS

Offensive operations are conducted to take the initiative from the enemy, gain freedom of action,
and generate effects to achieve objectives. Defensive operations are conducted to defeat an
enemy attack, gain time, economize forces, or develop conditions favorable to offensive and
stability operations. Stabilization activities are conducted to maintain or reestablish a safe and
secure environment and provide essential governmental services, emergency infrastructure
reconstruction, and humanitarian relief. Enabling activities connect offensive and defensive
operations with stabilization activities. On their own, they are not decisive, but they help set
conditions for the execution of all operations. They require either a deliberate planning effort or a
well-developed and understood standing operating procedures (SOP) to execute. Every operation
and activity have a mission that consists of a task and purpose.

Commanders conduct reconnaissance and security activities to help execute the various tasks and
actions associated with combat and stabilization activities. Enabling activities set the friendly
conditions required for mission accomplishment. Enabling activities do not directly accomplish
the commander’s end state and are not decisive on their own, but to the commander uses them to
conduct successful offensive and defensive operations and stabilization activities. For example, a
forward passage of lines might enable an attack to continue, allowing a new unit to pass through,
thereby maintaining momentum and keeping pressure on the threat. Enabling activities can also be
described or listed as key tasks during the execution of a mission.

Offensive and defensive operations arrange friendly forces by purpose. Purpose describes
friendly force goals with respect to the enemy force’s ability to achieve its objectives. An
objective is “the clearly defined, decisive, and attainable goal toward which an operation is
directed” (DoD Dictionary). Based on the purpose assigned, the commander selects a type
of offensive or defensive operation and any enabling activities required. All operations have
subsets called activities, methods, forms, and techniques. The variations organize forces as the
parent operation, with differing conditions and outcomes.


---

MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

   BATTLESPACE FRAMEWORKS

    The battlespace is, “the environment, factors, and conditions that must be understood to
    successfully apply combat power, protect the force, and/or complete the mission. It includes the
    physical environment (air, land, maritime, and space domains); the information environment
    (which includes cyberspace); the electromagnetic spectrum; and other factors. Included within
    these are friendly, enemy, adversary, and neutral entities contained within or having an effect on the
    operational areas, areas of interest, and areas of influence” (USMC Dictionary). Commanders use
    battlespace frameworks to enhance their understanding so they can best organize their forces in
    relation to one another and in time, space, event, and purpose. Battlespace frameworks provide
    commanders and their staffs with a means to ensure they consider all essential elements of military
    operations during the planning and execution phases. They are situation- and mission- dependent
    and vary in structure between units within the same operation. Commanders generally use either
    spatial- or purpose-based battlespace frameworks.

    Spatial-based battlespace frameworks consist of deep, close, and rear operations (see Figure 2-1)
    and are either contiguous or noncontiguous. Commanders typically use lines of operation with
    spatial-based battlespace frameworks. Purpose-based battlespace frameworks consist of decisive,
    supporting, and sustaining actions. Commanders typically use lines of effort with purpose-based
    battlespace frameworks. It is possible to blend the two types, and changes in situation and mission
    might mandate a transition between them. See MCDP 3 for further discussions of battlespace
    frameworks, areas of interest, influence, and operations, as well as contiguous and noncontiguous
    areas of operation (AOs). See Joint Publication (JP) 5-0, Joint Planning, for further information
    on lines of operation and lines of effort.

MEF Forward Boundary
               MEF Deep

MEF Close  Division Deep
           Division Close

            Division Rear

         MEF Rear
MEF Rear Boundary

           Figure 2-1. Spatial-Based Battlespace Framework Example.
                                              2-2


---

                                                                                  MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

Spatial-Based Battlespace Framework
Commanders use spatial-based battlespace frameworks to arrange operations and forces in terms
of time, space, and geography. Typically associated with aspects of traditional warfare, spatial-
based battlespace frameworks are useful when the tactical problem, mission, and situation is
primarily based on ground objectives, physical capabilities of the enemy, and the corresponding
deployment of friendly forces.

Deep Operations. Deep operations, as part of a battlespace framework, are “military actions
conducted against enemy capabilities that pose a potential threat to friendly forces. These military
actions are designed to isolate, shape, and dominate the battlespace and influence future
operations” (USMC Dictionary). Supporting efforts are typically associated with deep operations.
A supporting effort has “designated subordinate unit(s) whose mission is designed to directly
contribute to the success of the main effort” (USMC Dictionary). Deep operations can weaken
enemy capabilities, force an early culmination, or otherwise attack the enemy system so that
friendly forces can handle the remaining enemy forces when deep operations transition to part of
the close battle. Commanders conduct deep operations to seize the initiative, create windows of
opportunity for decisive action, restrict the enemy’s freedom of action, and disrupt the cohesion
and tempo of enemy operations. Deep operations might require commanders to coordinate and
integrate with national-level assets and joint forces.

Close Operations. Close operations, as part of a battlespace framework, are “military actions
conducted to project power decisively against enemy forces that pose an immediate or near-term
threat to the success of current battles or engagements. These military actions are conducted by
committed forces and their readily available tactical reserves, using maneuver and combined
arms” (USMC Dictionary). The main effort is typically associated with close operations. A main
effort is “the designated subordinate unit whose mission at a given point in time is most critical to
overall mission success. It is usually weighted with the preponderance of combat power and is
directed against a center of gravity through a critical vulnerability” (USMC Dictionary).
Commanders designate a main effort to prioritize resource allocation. The reserve can serve as the
decisive element of the battle. Marines conducting close operations require speed and mobility to
rapidly concentrate overwhelming combat power at the critical time and place. Close operations
are primarily conducted by MDCA forces from the ground combat element (GCE) and supported
by the MAGTF.

Rear Operations. Rear operations, as part of a battlespace framework, are “military actions
conducted to support and permit force sustainment and to provide security for such actions”
(USMC Dictionary). All MAGTF elements conduct rear operations, although they are typically
associated with supporting efforts. The MAGTF commander might need to provide commanders
in the rear area with additional capabilities, such as a tactical combat force, fire support assets, civil
affairs, and associated command and control. To minimize the logistical footprint, rear operation
commanders can use seabasing, host-nation support, and existing infrastructure. As the operation
progresses, the rear area’s geographic location, C2 structure, and the organization changes.

Purpose-Based Battlespace Framework
Commanders use purpose-based battlespace frameworks to arrange actions, forces, and
resources in terms of time, conditions, and effects. Associated with aspects of irregular warfare,
purpose-based battlespace frameworks are useful whenever the primacy of the tactical problem,

                                                                    2-3


---

MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

    mission, and situation is based on functions, activities, actions, and effects. Once AOs are
    assigned to subordinate units, the commander and staff assign broad tasks and purposes to
    subordinate units by designating decisive, shaping, and sustaining actions.

    Decisive Actions. Decisive actions include “any action the commander deems fundamental to
    achieving mission success” (USMC Dictionary). The designated main effort typically conducts
    the decisive action. Because multiple units can be engaged in the same decisive action,
    commanders must carefully delineate priorities between units. Because any particular action or
    series of actions conducted by friendly forces might prove decisive, commanders must remain
    prepared to exploit unexpected or unplanned opportunities. For example, strikes and raids
    associated with shaping operations might lead to a loss of will and an unexpected enemy
    withdrawal from the battlespace.

    Shaping Actions. Shaping actions are “the lethal and nonlethal activities conducted throughout the
    battlespace to attack an enemy capability or force to influence the enemy commander’s decision
    making” (USMC Dictionary). Shaping actions set conditions for the decisive action by affecting
    the enemy, indigenous populations, and institutions, and terrain. Shaping actions can be conducted
    throughout a unit’s AO and involve any combination of forces and capabilities. Shaping actions
    can be conducted before, during, or after the decisive action begins. Supporting efforts typically
    conduct shaping actions. Shaping actions can become decisive actions if friendly forces have
    unexpected success or opportunities.

    Sustaining Actions. Sustaining actions are “activities conducted to prepare and support friendly
    forces (e.g., planning, logistics, force protection) that promote unity of effort and extend
    operational reach” (USMC Dictionary). Sustaining actions differ from decisive and shaping
    actions because they are focused internally (on friendly forces) rather than externally (on the
    enemy, environment, or population). For example, logistical support, movement control,
    infrastructure development, terrain management, and anti-terrorism support measures supporting
    force protection are a part of mission accomplishment. Sustaining actions typically address
    important logistics and force protection actions essential to the success of decisive and shaping
    actions. Although the success of decisive and shaping actions might rely on sustaining actions,
    these actions cannot be decisive themselves.

   METT-T MISSION FACTORS

    The five METT-T mission factors describe the unique situation in which a tactician executes the art
    and science of tactics. Marines analyze the mission factors, which is critical to planning, execution,
    and assessment. The tactician considers these five factors, as well as civilian considerations, which
    are continuous and inherent for any operation. Their individual effects on an operation differ, but
    each mission factor must be considered during the commander’s visualization and design process.
    They can be a part of the science of tactics—such as terrain and weather effects on movement rates
    and fuel consumption, or they can be part of the art of tactics—such as the terrain and weather
    effects on morale.

                                                                         2-4


---

                                                                                  MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

BASIC TACTICAL CONCEPTS

There are basic tactical concepts, which are common to both offensive and defensive operations,
that commanders use along with the following to envision operations:

  • Their experience.
  • Principles of joint operations.
  • METT-T mission factors.
  • Operational design elements.
  • Warfighting functions.
  • Subordinate commander and staff estimates of supportability.
  • Input from other commanders.

The following alphabetical list discusses the basic tactical concepts.

Control Measures
Commanders issue control measures to subordinate commands to assign responsibilities,
coordinate fires and maneuver, and control operations. In general, all control measures should be
easily identifiable on the ground (i.e., terrain features). Examples include boundaries, objectives,
coordinating points, contact points, and direction of attack.

Decisive Engagement
A decisive engagement is an engagement in which a unit is considered fully committed and
cannot maneuver or extricate itself. Decisive engagement can be planned (e.g., a unit is expecting
to decisively engage the enemy) or it can be forced (e.g., a reconnaissance unit is compromised
and is forced to decisively engage the enemy). The unit’s mission usually drives the acceptance of
decisive engagement rather than the unit’s physical ability to extricate itself. For example, a unit
might become decisively engaged to hold key terrain, defeat a specific enemy force, or seize a
specific objective. Decisive engagement takes place from the perspective of the involved unit. The
senior headquarter’s guidance dictates which forces are committed or uncommitted. A committed
force is a force in contact with an enemy or deployed on a specific mission or course of action
(COA) that precludes their employment elsewhere. An uncommitted force is “a force that is not in
contact with an enemy and is not already deployed on a specific mission or course of action”
(USMC Dictionary).

Defeat in Detail
Commanders achieve defeat in detail by concentrating overwhelming combat power against
separate parts of a force rather than defeating the entire force at once. It might occur because of
enemy action, such as piecemeal commitment to the battle, which allows for defeat of each
portion as it arrives. Or it might occur because of friendly action, such as conducting operations to
individually isolate and then destroy portions of the enemy. A smaller force can use this technique
to achieve success against a larger enemy.

                                                                    2-5


---

MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

    Flanks
    Flanks are the right and left limits of a unit (see Figure 2-2). Stationary units are designated
    relative to the enemy’s actual or expected location. Moving units are defined by the direction of
    movement. The flanks’ level of vulnerability varies with its formation and position. An assailable
    flank is a flank that is exposed to attack or envelopment. In Figure 2-2 the flanks are assailable
    because the force can only bring limited combat power to bear to their right and left. Conversely,
    an attack on the flanks of the force in Figure 2-2 is risky for enemy forces because the friendly
    force need only turn right or left to bring its combat power to bear. Decisions about the
    vulnerability of friendly and enemy flanks are fundamentally decisions of mission, terrain,
    position, and orientation.

                                 Left Flank

Left Flank                                   Right Flank

            Right Flank

            Line Formation       Column Formation

                                          Figure 2-2. Flanks of a Stationary Unit.

Flanks can become vulnerable because of their mission, terrain, a weakness in their forces, their
physical position or formation, the opponent’s technical capability (e.g., the ability to conduct
vertical envelopment), or because of unprotected gaps between adjacent units. An attacking force
might accept risk to its flanks to bring combat power to bear at the point of decision. A flank
anchored on restrictive terrain may not be vulnerable to armored or mechanized forces but may
be vulnerable to foot mobile infantry forces. Sufficient room must exist for the attacking force to
maneuver for the flank to be assailable. A unit could mitigate the vulnerability of an assailable
flank by linking both flanks to other forces or by using various techniques, such as
supplementary positions.

A defensive position on the flank is a geographical location on a force’s flank where commanders
can place fires capabilities. An attacking commander maneuvers to occupy flanking positions
against a defending force to place destructive fires directly against enemy vulnerabilities. A
defending commander maneuvers to occupy flanking positions of a hostile route of advance for
the same reason. A flanking position that an advancing enemy can readily avoid has little value to
the defender unless the enemy is unaware that it is occupied.

                            2-6


---

                                                                                  MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

Maneuver
Maneuver is the movement of forces for the purpose of gaining an advantage over the enemy.
Maneuver is one of the six warfighting functions. Maneuver creates and exposes enemy
vulnerabilities to the massed effects of friendly combat power. A commander uses elements of
combat power to attain positional advantage over an enemy and be capable of applying those
massed effects.

Piecemeal Commitment
Piecemeal commitment is the immediate employment of units in combat as they become available
instead of waiting for larger aggregations of units to ensure mass. It is the unsynchronized
employment of available forces so that their combat power is not employed effectively. Piecemeal
commitment subjects the smaller committed forces to defeat in detail and prevents the massing
and synchronizing of combat power with follow-on maneuver and combat service support (CSS)
elements. Although generally negative, piecemeal commitment can be advantageous to maintain
momentum, to retain or exploit the initiative, or to reinforce a faltering operation, particularly if
the commitment of small units provides all the combat power needed to avert disaster. Search and
attack operations employ the piecemeal commitment of troops. See Chapter 4 for a discussion of
search and attack operations.

Reconstitution
Reconstitution comprises “those actions that commanders plan and implement to restore units
to a desired level of combat effectiveness commensurate with mission requirements and available
resources. Reconstitution operations include regeneration and reorganization” (USMC Dictionary).
Reorganization is “action taken to shift internal resources within a degraded unit to increase its
level of combat effectiveness” or, “in administration, the realignment of force structure” (USMC
Dictionary). Regeneration is the “significant replacement of personnel, equipment, and supplies in
an attempt to restore a unit to full operational capability as rapidly as possible” (USMC Dictionary).
The commander conducts reconstitution when one or more subordinate units become combat
ineffective, or when the commander can raise the combat effectiveness of a subordinate unit closer
to the desired level by shifting available resources. Besides typical logistic actions, reconstitution
can include—

  • Removing the unit from combat.
  • Assessing effectiveness with external assets.
  • Reestablishing a chain of command.
  • Training the unit for future operations.
  • Reestablishing unit cohesion.

Reconstitution transcends typical day-to-day logistic actions. However, it uses existing systems
and units to do so.

Reserve
The reserve primarily exists to reinforce success. The reserve is not an initially committed force
and thus does not typically have a full suite of force multipliers until it is committed. The
commander constitutes a reserve regardless of where within the range of military operations a
mission is conducted. The commander bases the reserve’s size on the level of uncertainty and risk

                                                                    2-7


---

MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

    in the current tactical situation. The reserve’s location depends on their most likely mission,
    time-distance requirements, and survivability considerations. A quick reaction force is an example
    of a reserve. A reserve’s primary tasks are to—

       • Conduct the decisive action.
       • Retain or regain the initiative.
       • Take advantage of unexpected success.
       • Counter tactical reverses that threaten the integrity of the friendly force’s operations.

    A commander should always retain a reserve, reconstituting one whenever possible once the
    original reserve is committed.

    Rules of Engagement
    Rules of engagement (ROE) are “directives issued by competent military authority that delineate
    the circumstances and limitations under which United States forces will initiate and/or continue
    combat engagement with other forces encountered” (DoD Dictionary). The level of the ROE’s
    permissiveness or restrictiveness affects the commander’s decision on how to conduct operations.
    For example, ROEs might limit a company conducting a flanking attack in terms of weapons
    systems they can use to isolate the objective, suppress enemy positions, and exploit success.
    Additionally, ROE might affect the commander’s decision to isolate and pursue the enemy or
    conduct pursuit by fire. Rules of engagement always recognize the right of self-defense and the
    commander’s right and obligation to protect assigned personnel. It is imperative that leaders not
    only know the ROE but have the ability to conceptualize them so that they can train their Marines
    to these standards as it relates to the desired end state to accomplish the mission.

    Tactical Mobility
    Mobility is “a quality or capability of military forces which permits them to move from place to
    place while retaining the ability to fulfill their primary mission” (DoD Dictionary). Exercising
    mobility in and around the enemy is tactical mobility, a function of the relationship between
    cross-country mobility, firepower, and force protection. Marines consider tactical mobility and the
    relative combat power of friendly and enemy forces when developing COAs. For example, armor
    units have good mobility, but poor tactical mobility in restrictive terrain, yet they have excellent
    mobility in open terrain unless the enemy can neutralize their protection and resist suppression.
    Similarly, foot-mobile infantry battalions move slowly, but have superior tactical mobility in
    restrictive terrain. In open terrain, such units move more quickly, but their vulnerability to enemy
    fires and maneuver makes their tactical mobility poor. Tactical mobility can be enhanced by route
    selection, movement techniques, and movement times.

   BASIC CONTROL MEASURES

    Commanders use control measures to help delineate responsibilities and coordinate fire and
    maneuver among various subordinate units. Although control measures are both permissive
    (allows something to happen) and restrictive (limits how something is done), commanders use
    them in a manner that provides the greatest possible freedom of action to subordinates,

                                                                         2-8


---

                                                            MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

establishing only those necessary to provide essential coordination and deconfliction between
units. Commanders remove restrictive control measures as soon as possible. Control measures can
be graphical, such as boundaries, or procedural, such as target engagement priorities.

Commanders use control measures to conduct and plan for current and future operations. The
commander adjusts control measures as necessary to maintain synchronization and ensure mission
accomplishment as the tactical situation evolves. Control measures help a commander balance the
friction inherent in military operations by reducing the chance of a collapse in tempo and
offensive action, which could negatively impact accomplishing the assigned mission.

Control measures apply to all forces at all echelons. A phase line or checkpoint established by
higher headquarters applies to the commander’s unit, and to subordinate units. Commanders
reference only the control measures established by the higher headquarters when making reports
to that headquarters. Commanders, choose to establish a standard naming convention for control
measures in the unit SOP. Examples of such naming conventions would be car model names for
phase lines and city names for objectives. See Table 2-1 for basic control measure symbols.
