Airspace Coordinating Measures
An airspace control plan is “the document approved by the joint force commander that provides
specific planning guidance and procedures for the airspace control system for the joint force
operational area” (DoD Dictionary). It contains airspace coordinating measures (ACMs), which
are “measures employed to facilitate the efficient use of airspace to accomplish missions and
simultaneously provide safeguards for friendly forces (DoD Dictionary). Commanders use airspace
coordinating measures for all methods of air support when conducting offensive and defensive
tactics. Airspace elements establish ACMs to accomplish one or more of the following functions:

  • Establish reserved airspace for specific airspace users.
  • Restrict the actions of some airspace users.
  • Create airspace in which units can use weapons with minimal risk of friendly fire incidents

     (death, injury, or property damage).
  • Control actions of specific airspace users.
  • Require airspace users to accomplish specific actions.

Joint Publication 3-52, Joint Airspace Control, provides additional information on each of the
following joint ACMs:

  • Coordinating altitude.
  • Low-level transit routes.
  • Minimum-risk routes.

                                                                   2-13


---

MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

       • Restricted operations areas.

       • Special use airspace.

       • High density airspace control zones.
       • Standard use Marine Corps aviation flight routes.

    Areas of Operations and Boundaries
    Areas of operation are a common control measure used whenever commanders have ground-based
    tactical tasks. A higher headquarters assigns subordinates an AO using boundaries. These
    commanders can, in turn, assign subordinates their own AOs, decentralizing execution while
    maximizing freedom of action. Depending on the METT-T, AOs might extend down to the
    company level. Not using an AO centralizes execution and limits the options of subordinates.
    Commanders typically centralize execution when mandated by METT-T. For example, an RLT
    commander might assign subordinate battalions battle positions in support of an RLT engagement
    area. Areas of operation typically change over the course of an operation. Factors that influence
    such change include—

       • Incorporating geopolitical constraints.

       • Achieving objectives.

       • Assuming a new task or mission.

       • Shifting to a new phase of the operation.

       • Anticipating exploitation and pursuit.
       • Assuming the main effort.

    When assigning an AO, commanders must consider the capabilities of subordinate units to control
    and manage the area. The staff may recommend battlespace refinements based on the analysis of
    the terrain and tasks as well as friendly and adversary center of gravity, capabilities, and limitations.
    Areas of operation that are greater than a unit’s area of influence should not be assigned. However,
    an area of influence is “an area inclusive of and extending beyond an operational area wherein a
    commander is capable of direct influence by maneuver, fire support, and information normally
    under the commander’s command or control” (DoD Dictionary). The area of interest may change
    based on the commander’s understanding of the situation. The extent of the area of influence may
    change based on changes in the amount of forces present, equipment capabilities and available, or
    rules of engagement. The commander’s AO may need to change based on the scope of the mission,
    the results of operations, operational reach, or to ensure sufficient battlespace to maneuver and
    protect his force. While ground combat units typically receive AOs, aviation and logistic units
    might also receive AOs if properly resourced. For example, a MAGTF might assign an air base
    and corresponding AO to the aviation combat element (ACE). The ACE would likely require
    augmentation of C2 assets and security forces. Units have the following responsibilities when
    assigned to an AO:

       • Terrain Management. The AO owner controls the battlespace to include assigning additional
          boundaries and AOs to subordinates. Even when higher headquarters assigns units to the AO,
          the owning unit still dictates final placement. This ensures the unit commander controlling the
          AO knows what units are in that area and where they are located.

       • Intelligence Collection. Commanders conduct intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance
         (ISR) activities within their AOs to maintain current and accurate operational pictures of their

                                                                        2-14


---

                                                                                  MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

     areas that they can share both within and external to their units to establish a common
     operational picture of those areas. See Chapter 13 for more information on reconnaissance
     and MCWP 2-10, Intelligence Operations, for more information on intelligence processes.

  • Civil-Military Operations. Ensuring that public order and safety exist within the unit’s AO are
     implied tasks for commanders during any operation.

  • Air and Ground Movement Control. Units cannot move across boundaries into another unit’s
     AO without receiving clearance from the unit owning the AO. The owning unit controls
     movement throughout the AO. The designation, maintenance, route security, and control of
     movement along routes within an AO are the responsibility of the owning unit unless the
     higher echelons’ coordinating instructions direct otherwise. Similarly, the ground maneuver
     commander manages the airspace below the coordinating altitude, using procedural control
     measures and positive control measures, to include air defense. The coordinating altitude is
     “an airspace coordinating measure that uses altitude to separate users and as the transition
     between different airspace control elements” (DoD Dictionary). Details regarding airspace
     control can be found in MCWP 3-20, Aviation Operations.

  • Clearance of Fires. Within their AO, the owning unit can employ any direct or indirect fire
     system without receiving further clearance from higher headquarters. Standard exceptions
     regarding cross-boundary effects and ROE apply.

  • Security. The security of all units operating within the AO is the responsibility of the owning
     commander. If the commander cannot or chooses not to provide security throughout the AO,
     all affected individuals and organizations are informed of when, where, and under what
     conditions the commander will not exercise this function. Each unit commander remains
     responsible for local unit security measures. See Chapter 14 for further information on
     security operations.

  • Personnel Recovery. Personnel recovery is “the sum of military, diplomatic, and civil efforts to
     prepare for and execute the recovery and reintegration of isolated personnel” (DoD Dictionary).
     The Marine Corps executes both ground-based personnel recovery and aircraft-based tactical
     recovery of aircraft and personnel (also referred to as TRAP). Tactical recovery of aircraft and
     personnel is “a Marine Corps mission performed by an assigned and briefed aircrew for the
     specific purpose of the recovery of personnel, equipment, and/or aircraft when the tactical
     situation precludes search and rescue assets from responding and when survivors and their
     location have been confirmed” (DoD Dictionary). The AO commander is responsible for
     recovering and returning isolated persons within that AO to friendly control.

  • Influence the Population. To influence the population is “to persuade the civil population
     within the area of operations to support or cooperate with operations by friendly forces, or, at a
     minimum, to accept the friendly force presence in the area of operations” (USMC Dictionary).
     For more information, see MCWP 8-10, Information.

Contiguous and Noncontiguous Areas of Operation. A contiguous AO is one in which all
subordinate command AOs share one or more boundary (see Figure 2-3). A noncontiguous AO
involves one or more subordinate AOs that do not share a boundary (see Figure 2-3). Higher
headquarters is responsible for the intervening area between noncontiguous AOs. The commander
can choose to organize the AO so that subordinate units have contiguous AOs, noncontiguous AOs,
or both. The AOs can be assigned within both spatial- and purpose-based battlespace frameworks.

                                                                   2-15


---

MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

Contiguous                                            Noncontiguous

            Figure 2-3. Areas of Operation.

Contiguous AOs have distinctive forward, lateral, and rear boundaries. A commander bases the
decision to establish contiguous AOs on METT-T analysis. Units with contiguous AOs are
typically within supporting distance of one another and may be within supporting range of direct
or indirect fires. Other reasons a commander establishes contiguous AOs include the following:

  • The AO is of limited size to accommodate the force.
  • Political boundaries or enemy disposition require concentration of force.
  • There is a risk of being defeated in detail by enemy forces.
  • The enemy situation is not clear.
  • Friendly force is significantly outnumbered.
  • Concentration of combat power along a single axis of advance, movement corridor, or against

     a single avenue of approach is required.

A noncontiguous AO does not have distinctive forward, rear, and lateral boundaries. Commanders
establish noncontiguous boundaries that enclose the entire area. Subordinate boundaries are
continuous and closely approximate the subordinate unit’s area of influence. For example, the
commander typically established a noncontiguous regimental boundary at the limit of observed
fires for the RLT’s security forces. Because noncontiguous boundaries must provide all-around
security, the commander typically cannot concentrate combat power on a single axis.
Additionally, commanders must account for the risk that comes with noncontiguous AOs because
the units are typically out of supporting range from each other.

The commander bases the decision to establish noncontiguous AOs on METT-T analysis.
Commanders establish noncontiguous AOs because—

  • Limited friendly forces must occupy, or control widely separated key terrain.
  • Subordinate units do not need to provide mutual support.
  • Dispersed enemy or population centers throughout the AO require a corresponding dispersal

     of friendly units.

                                                                   2-16


---

                                                                                  MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

Operations in areas not included in assigned noncontiguous AOs are the responsibility of the
common higher commander. Using these AOs requires innovative means to conduct logistic
operations, including aerial resupply. A commander has the following choices for establishing
ground lines of communications (LOCs) with subordinates who have noncontiguous AOs:

  • Assign subordinates the route security mission for each main supply route (MSR).
  • Assume risk by having CSS elements run convoys with only their organic self-defense

     capabilities, while assigning the mission of responding to enemy contacts beyond a convoy’s
     self-defense capability to subordinate units.
  • Assign a subordinate unit the mission of providing convoy security for each convoy. For
     example, the MAGTF could assign its military police the mission of providing convoy
     security for critical ground convoys.

Boundaries. A boundary is “a line that delineates surface areas for the purpose of facilitating
coordinating and deconflicting operations between adjacent units, formations, or areas” (DoD
Dictionary). Commanders use boundaries to define the limits of an AO and establish ground
forces’ responsibilities. The ACM control the vertical dimension. The commander bases the
boundaries of subordinate units on clearly defined terrain features. Commanders should not assign
boundaries that split responsibilities for roads, rivers, railways, or other transportation routes.
Additionally, responsibility for an avenue of approach and key terrain should also belong to only
one unit. The commander adjusts boundaries as necessary in response to the evolving tactical
situation. The commander is responsible for any areas not delegated to subordinates.

After characteristics of the terrain are accounted for within the context of the unit’s assigned
mission, existing political boundaries, such as city limits and provincial borders, are important
considerations in developing friendly unit graphical control measures and assigning subordinate
unit AOs. Military boundaries that conflict or do not align with existing political boundaries
require additional planning to deconflict, manage, or organize the use of indigenous capabilities.
However, during protracted operations within an AO, commanders should periodically adjust
subordinate unit AOs to avoid creating sanctuaries that an enemy could exploit.

The forward boundary in the direction of the enemy is the farthest limit of an organization’s
responsibility. Decisive or shaping actions directed against enemy forces beyond an echelon’s
forward boundary are the responsibility of the next higher headquarters. For example, if a division
assigns a forward boundary to a regiment, then the division conducts operations beyond the
regiment’s forward boundary. The higher echelon headquarters typically assigns the lower
echelon a forward boundary based on the higher echelon’s scheme of maneuver (SOM) and each
echelon’s ability to acquire and attack targets in their respective areas. Lateral boundaries span the
area from the unit’s rear boundary to their forward boundary. Similar to forward boundaries,
decisive or shaping actions directed against enemy forces beyond an echelon’s lateral boundary
are the responsibility of adjacent units or the next higher headquarters.

The area behind the rear boundary line of an AO, sector, or zone of action assigned to a
particular unit belongs to the next higher commander, and positioning of elements behind it
must be coordinated with that commander. The rear area, is where most of the unit’s logistic,
administrative, and CSS functions are conducted. Regardless of whether assigned or using a

                                                                   2-17


---

MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

    contiguous or noncontiguous AO, the rear area is generally the area opposite the direction of a
    unit’s focus on an enemy force. Because a unit’s combat power is generally focused forward or
    outward, units seek to defend their rear areas and exploit the enemy’s.

    Assembly Area
    An assembly area is “an area in which a command is assembled preparatory to further action”
    (USMC Dictionary). An ideal assembly area offers—

       • Concealment from air and ground observation.
       • Adequate entrances, exits, and internal routes.
       • Space for dispersion. Each assembly area is separated by enough distance from other

         assembly areas to preclude mutual interference.
       • Cover from direct fire.
       • Good drainage and soil conditions that can sustain unit vehicles and individual movement.
       • Terrain masking of electromagnetic signatures.
       • Terrain allowing observation of ground and air avenues into the assembly area.
       • Standoff distance outside the range of enemy medium indirect fires.

    The commander assigns each unit its own assembly area or, if necessary, subdivides an assembly
    area. All units and echelons can be assigned assembly areas. Since the assembly area of one unit is
    typically in the AO of another, assembly areas are treated as noncontiguous AOs. The unit
    occupying the assembly area has the same responsibilities there as in their AO.

    Assembly area site selection should be made relative to the concept of operations per the site’s
    ability to contribute to security, flexibility, and future operations. An assembly area site should
    enable units to quickly and smoothly move to subsequent positions by concealed routes. Smaller,
    lighter, and less tactically mobile units use assembly areas closer to the enemy than do larger,
    heavier, and more tactically mobile units.

    An assembly area must be large enough to accommodate the force occupying it. Because of
    dismounted infantry’s small signature, their assembly areas are typically smaller than those
    assigned to mechanized and motorized units and can be closer to enemy forces without risking
    detection. A mechanized and motorized unit’s tactical mobility allows them to occupy assembly
    areas at a greater distance from the line of departure than infantry units.

    There are three methods to organize an assembly area: a single area, part of a large assembly area,
    or dispersed. The biggest difference between the three methods is the amount of security required
    since every assembly area inherently conducts a perimeter defense.

    Single Assembly Area. The single area method configures a unit in a perimeter defense with
    maneuver units deployed along the entire perimeter. Command and control, sustainment, and any
    other supporting units are located within the interior of the assembly area.

                                                                        2-18


---

                                                                                  MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

Large Assembly. A unit can also occupy a portion of a larger assembly area. This typically takes
place when a subordinate formation occupies a portion of their higher headquarters’ assembly
area. With this method, a unit has boundaries with adjacent units and may only have a portion of
its assembly area focused on a perimeter.

Dispersed Assembly Area. A unit may use a dispersed method to assign assembly areas. In this
method, commanders assign subordinate units individual assembly areas. These subordinate units
maintain their own security. Similar to the single assembly area method, maneuver units occupy
perimeter assembly areas with command and control, sustainment, and other units located within
the interior.

Axis of Advance
An axis of advance is “a line of advance assigned for purposes of control (often a road, group of
roads, or a designated series of locations) extending in the direction of the enemy” (USMC
Dictionary). An axis of advance designates the general area through which the bulk of a unit’s
combat power must move. When developing the axis of advance, the commander also establishes
bypass criteria

Battle Handover Line
The battle handover line (BHL) is a designated phase line where responsibility transitions from
the stationary force to the moving force and vice versa (Army Doctrine Publication 3-90, Offense
and Defense). The common higher echelon commander of the two forces establishes the BHL
after consulting both commanders; however, the stationary commander determines the location of
the line. The BHL is forward of the FEBA in the defense or the FLOT in the offense. Commanders
establish a BHL where the direct fires of forward combat elements of the stationary unit can
effectively support the passing unit’s passage of lines. The area between the BHL and the
stationary force belongs to the stationary force commander. The stationary force commander can
employ security forces, obstacles, and fires in the area.

Battle Positions
A battle position is, “in ground operations, a defensive location oriented on an enemy avenue of
approach from which a unit may defend” (USMC Dictionary). See Chapter 8 for more information
on battle positions in the defense.

Checkpoint
A checkpoint is “a predetermined point on the ground used to control movement, tactical maneuver,
and orientation” (USMC Dictionary). Units can also use a checkpoint as a fire control measure in
lieu of a target reference point (TRP), which is the preferred control measure. Checkpoints are useful
for orientation. Units may use checkpoints to supplement or as substitutes for phase lines.

Contact Point
A contact point is, “in land warfare, a point on the terrain, easily identifiable, where two or more
units are required to make contact” (DoD Dictionary). Commanders use contact points to ensure
coordination between units or to coordinate linkups. See Chapter 23 for more information on
linkups. Contact points are established where phase lines intersect with lateral boundaries or on
identifiable terrain. The commander provides a date-time-group to indicate when to make
physical contact.

                                                                   2-19


---

MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

    Control Point
    In land warfare, a control point is “a position along a route of march at which personnel are
    stationed to give information and instruction for the regulation of supply or traffic” (DoD
    Dictionary). Commanders use control points to control, coordinate, deconflict, and affect the
    movement of pedestrian and vehicular traffic. Control points can be hasty or deliberate. They can
    be friendly, neutral, or hostile focused. For example, control points can regulate friendly forces,
    such as an ambulance control points, or provide force protection, such as an entry control point.
    They can be neutral focused, such as a deliberate vehicle control point that controls the movement
    of a population. Finally, they can be hostile focused, such as a hasty vehicle control point that
    seeks to interdict enemy movement or break-up friendly movement patterns. Control points are
    established at major road intersections, choke points, friendly position entry and exit points, and at
    any other place the commander deems appropriate to regulate movement. Deliberate control
    points receive a task and purpose similar to an obstacle and are assigned to an owning unit. Hasty
    control points are established on order with a specified date-time-group and duration.

    Direct Fire Control Measures
    Commanders create the greatest effect on the enemy by controlling the manner, method, and time
    to initiate, shift, and mass fires, and when to disengage by using control measures for their direct
    fires. They use direct fire control measures to control, coordinate, and deconflict their battlespace
    geometry. Commanders must understand the characteristics of weapon systems and available
    munitions (e.g., the danger to unprotected personnel when tanks fire discarding sabot ammunition
    over their heads or near them). Direct fire control measures defined in this publication include
    engagement areas, engagement criteria, engagement priorities, sectors of fire, TRPs, and trigger
    lines. Publications for the rifle squad and infantry platoon address other direct fire control
    measures, such as frontal, cross, or depth fire patterns and simultaneous, alternating, or observed
    techniques of fire.

    Engagement Area
    An engagement area is “an area where the commander intends to contain and destroy an enemy
    force with the effects of massed weapons and supporting systems” (USMC Dictionary). This
    includes organic firepower and supporting systems, such as close air support (CAS). The
    commander determines the engagement area’s size and shape by the relatively unobstructed line
    of sight from the weapon systems in their firing positions and the maximum range of those
    weapons. The commander designates engagement areas to cover each enemy avenue of approach
    into unit positions. The commander also can use them to designate known or suspected enemy
    locations. The commander arrays available forces and weapon systems into these areas in
    positions to concentrate overwhelming effects. The commander subdivides an engagement area
    into smaller engagement areas for subordinates using one or more TRPs or prominent terrain
    features. The commander assigns sectors of fires to subordinates in a way that prevents friendly
    fire incidents; however, responsibility for an avenue of approach or key terrain is never split.
    These sectors typically do not affect friendly maneuver. Commanders, of units up to battalion,
    generally use this control measure. For further discussion of engagement area development see
    Marine Corps Tactical Publication (MCTP) 3-34B, Combined Arms Countermobility Operations.

                                                                        2-20


---

                                                                                  MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

Engagement Criteria
Engagement criteria are those circumstances that allow engagement of an enemy force without a
specific command to do so. Examples are a point or line on the ground that an enemy crosses or an
event or action that an enemy takes. They can be restrictive or permissive. For example, a
company commander could tell the first platoon to wait until three enemy tanks reach a TRP
within their engagement area before initiating fire. Another example is a battalion commander
telling a company commander not to engage an approaching enemy unit until the enemy commits
themselves to an avenue of approach. The commander establishes engagement criteria in the
direct fire plan. Commanders and leaders of small tactical units use engagement criteria in
conjunction with engagement priorities and other direct fire control measures to mass fires and
control fire distribution.

Engagement Priority
Engagement priority is the designated sequence of attack for targets in order of importance
assigned to specific units, weapons, or weapon systems to facilitate the defeat of the enemy.
Engagement priorities are assigned based on the type or level of threat at different ranges to best
match friendly capabilities against threat vulnerabilities. Engagement priorities are situationally
dependent. The commander uses engagement priorities to distribute fires rapidly and effectively.
Subordinate elements can have different engagement priorities. For example, the commander
establishes engagement priorities so that light armored vehicles engage enemy infantry fighting
vehicles or armored personnel carriers, while anti-armor systems and any attached tanks engage
enemy tanks. Units typically engage the most dangerous targets first, followed by targets in depth
or specialized systems, such as engineer vehicles.

Fire Support Coordination Measures
In the same way control measures are used for direct fires to aid units in generating the greatest
effects on the enemy, fire support coordination measures (FSCMs) facilitate the rapid engagement
of targets while deconflicting battlespace geometry. Fire support coordination measures are either
permissive or restrictive. A unit’s boundaries are the most basic FSCM. The fire support
coordinator recommends FSCMs to the commander based on the commander’s guidance, location
of friendly forces, SOM, and anticipated enemy actions. Fire support coordination measures
discussed in this publication include battlefield coordination lines (BCLs), coordinated fire lines
(CFLs), fire support coordination lines (FSCLs), free-fire areas (also referred to as FFAs), kill
boxes, no-fire areas (NFAs), restrictive fire areas (RFAs), restrictive fire lines (RFLs), final
protective fires (FPFs) and fire support targets. See Chapter 8 for more information on FPF. See
MCWP 3-31, Marine Air-Ground Task Force Fires and Effects, for further information on FSCMs.

Permissive Fire Support Coordination Measures. The primary purpose of permissive measures is
to facilitate attacking targets. Once they are established, no further coordination is required to
engage targets affected by the measures. Permissive FSCMs include BCL, CFL, FSCL, free-fire
area, and kill box.

Battlefield Coordination Line. The BCL facilitates expeditious attacks, with surface indirect fires
and MAGTF aviation fires, between the BCL and the FSCL. Per JP 3-09, Joint Fire Support;
MCWP 3-31; and MCTP 3-10F, the BCL allows MAGTF aviation to strike targets without GCE
commander approval. An airspace coordination area will always overlie the area between the BCL
and the FSCL. Ground units can strike any targets beyond the BCL and short of the FSCL with

                                                                   2-21


---

MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

    artillery and rockets without coordination as long as those fires deconflict with established
    airspace coordination area overhead. The BCL location is graphically portrayed on fire support
    maps, charts, and overlays by a solid black lie with the letters “BCL” followed by the establishing
    headquarters in parentheses above the line and the effective date-time group below the line.
    The BCL facilitates expeditiously attacking surface targets of opportunity between the BCL and
    the FSCL. When a commander establishes a BCL, its primary purpose is to allow MAGTF
    aviation to attack surface targets without further approval from the commander in whose area the
    targets are located.

    Coordinated Fire Line. A CFL is “a line beyond which conventional surface-to-surface direct
    fire and indirect surface fire support means may fire at any time within the boundaries of the
    establishing headquarters without additional coordination but does not eliminate the responsibility
    to coordinate the airspace required to conduct the mission” (DoD Dictionary). The purpose of
    the CFL is to expedite the surface-to-surface attacks beyond the CFL without coordination with
    the ground commander in whose area the targets are located. Within the MAGTF, the GCE
    typically establishes the CFL, which can be simultaneously established at the division, regiment,
    and battalion levels. It is located as close as possible to the establishing unit, without interfering
    with maneuver forces, to open up the area beyond the CFL to fire support. A higher echelon can
    consolidate subordinate unit CFLs; however, any changes to the subordinate CFLs are coordinated
    with the subordinate headquarters.

    Fire Support Coordination Line. The FSCL is “a fire support coordination measure established by
    the land or amphibious force commander to support common objectives within an area of operation,
    beyond which all fires must be coordinated with affected commanders prior to engagement, and
    short of the line, all fires must be coordinated with the establishing commander prior to engagement”
    (DoD Dictionary). The primary use of the FSCL is to facilitate the expeditious attack on targets of
    opportunity beyond the coordinating measure. It provides a measure for coordination between
    ground elements and supporting forces without endangering friendly troops in the air or on the
    ground or requiring additional coordination with the establishing headquarters. The FSCL—

       • Facilitates attack on surface targets beyond it.

       • Provides ground commanders with sufficient control of aircraft short of it to ensure
          troop safety.

       • Maximizes employment of weapons where they are most efficient, and provides aviation
          commanders, air control agencies, and pilots with enough information to identify where
          control or coordination is required before aircraft can attack ground targets.

    An FSCL does not divide an AO by defining a boundary between subordinate unit AOs and the
    AO of the establishing headquarters. Supporting elements attacking targets beyond the FSCL
    must ensure that the attack will not produce adverse effects on, or to the rear of, the FSCL. Other
    than the FSCL, all air to ground and surface to surface attack operations are controlled by the
    appropriate commander.

    The commander designating an FSCL remains responsible for establishing the priority, effects, and
    timing of fires impacting beyond the FSCL. The FSCL should follow well-defined terrain features,
    easily identifiable from the air. When positioning the FSCL, commanders must consider the tactical
    situation. This includes the SOM or plan of defense, weather, terrain, type and source of aircraft,

                                                                        2-22


---

                                                                                  MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

and overall flexibility of maneuver and fire support. When establishing an FSCL, a key factor is the
range of the commander’s organic weapon systems. By establishing an FSCL close in, yet at
sufficient depth to not limit high tempo maneuver, land and amphibious force commanders ease the
coordination requirements for engagement operations within their AOs by forces not under their
control, such as naval surface fire support or air interdiction.

Free-Fire Area. A free-fire area is “a specific region into which any weapon system may fire
without additional coordination with the establishing headquarters” (DoD Dictionary). Usually, a
GCE or MAGTF command element establishes a free-fire area on easily recognizable terrain.

Kill Box. A kill box is “a three-dimensional permissive fire support coordination measure with an
associated airspace coordinating measure used to facilitate the integration of fires” (DoD
Dictionary). Commanders use kill boxes to facilitate air-to-ground and surface-to-surface
interdiction fires, allowing lethal attacks against surface targets without further coordination with
the establishing commander and without the requirement for terminal attack control.

There are two types of kill boxes: a blue kill box and a purple kill box. The purpose of a blue kill
box is to facilitate the attack on surface targets with air-to-surface munitions. The purpose of a
purple kill box is to facilitate the attack on surface targets with subsurface, surface-to-surface, and
air-to-surface munitions. The key difference is that with the purple kill box, the number of joint
weapon systems available to combine and maximize their effects without significant coordination
increases. Surface-to-surface direct fires are not restricted in either type.

See MCRP 3-31.4, Multi-Service Tactics, Techniques, and Procedures for Kill Box Planning and
Employment, for more information on kill boxes. See MIL-STD-2525 for additional examples of
kill box symbology.

Restrictive Fire Support Coordination Measure. Restrictive FSCMs safeguard friendly forces.
A restrictive FSCM imposes coordination requirements prior to the engagement of those targets
affected by the measure. Examples include an NFA, RFA, RFL, and fire support targets. See
MCWP 3-31 for more information on restrictive FSCMs.

No-Fire Area. An NFA is “an area designated by the appropriate commander into which fires or
their effects are prohibited” (DoD Dictionary). A commander uses an NFA to protect independently
operating elements (e.g., forward observers, support elements) and for humanitarian reasons such
as protecting concentrations of displaced civilians or cultural monuments. Exceptions to this rule
occur when the establishing headquarters temporarily approves fires within the NFA or when an
enemy force within an NFA engages a friendly force, and fires are deemed necessary to defend
friendly forces.

Restrictive Fire Area. An RFA is “a location in which specific restrictions are imposed and into
which fires that exceed those restrictions will not be delivered without coordination with the
establishing headquarters” (DoD Dictionary). Any ground-unit commander, typically at the
battalion level and above, can establish an RFA within the ground-unit commander’s own zone.
A company operating semi-independently can establish an RFA, as required. To facilitate rapidly
changing maneuver areas, on-call RFAs can be used. The RFA is activated and deactivated when
requested by the maneuvering unit or scheduled by time or event. Commanders can establish an
RFA on recognizable terrain or they can express it by grid coordinates or by radius from appoint.

                                                                   2-23


---

MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

    Restrictive Fire Line. An RFL is “a specific boundary established between converging, friendly
    surface forces that prohibits fires or their effects from crossing” (DoD Dictionary). The common
    commander of the converging forces establishes the RFL, which is usually located on easily
    recognizable terrain and closer to the stationary force.

    Fire-Support Targets. In the fire-support context, a target is an area designated and numbered for
    future firing (JP 3-60, Joint Targeting). There are control measures for point targets, circular
    targets, rectangular targets, and linear targets. The commander designates fire-support targets
    using a two letter and four digit code established in fire support doctrine. The commander may
    group two or more targets for simultaneous engagement. The commander may also attack
    individual targets and groups of targets in series or in a predetermined sequence. The fact that a
    series or group of targets has been designated does not preclude an attack on individual targets
    within the series or group. It also does not preclude an attack on one or more groups of targets
    within the series.

    Fire support targets are classified as either planned targets or targets of opportunity. Planned
    targets are those targets on which fires are prearranged, although the degree of this
    prearrangement may vary. Targets of opportunity are not planned in advance and are engaged as
    they present themselves in accordance with established engagement criteria and ROE.

    Individually planned fire support targets may be further subdivided into scheduled and on call fires.
    Scheduled targets are planned targets on which artillery and other fire support assets deliver their
    fires in accordance with a pre established timeline. On call targets are planned targets engaged in
    response to a request for fires rather than in accordance with an established timeline. An on call
    target requires less reaction time than does a target of opportunity. The degree of prearrangement
    for the on call target influences the reaction time from request to execution—the greater the
    prearrangement, the faster the reaction time. Priority targets are an example of on call targets that
    have short reaction times, since each priority target has a firing unit designated to execute at any
    given time. An example of a priority target is final protective fires (FPFs).

    Time-sensitive targets are not area targets designated and numbered for future firing. They are “a
    joint force commander-validated target or set of targets requiring immediate response because it
    is a highly lucrative, fleeting target of opportunity or it poses (or will soon pose) a danger to
    friendly forces” (DoD Dictionary). See MCWP 3-31 and MCTP 3-10F for more information on
    fire support and fire support targets.

    Forward Line of Own Troops and Forward Edge of the Battle Area
    The forward line of own troops (FLOT) is “a line that indicates the most forward positions of
    friendly forces in any kind of military operation at a specific time” (USMC Dictionary). The
    FLOT does not refer to small, long-range reconnaissance assets, observation posts, or stay-behind
    forces. Rather, the FLOT normally identifies the forward location of covering and screening
    forces. In the defense, it may be beyond, at, or short of the forward edge of the battle area (FEBA),
    depending on the tactical situation. The FEBA is “the foremost limits of a series of areas in which
    ground combat units are deployed to coordinate fire support, the positioning of forces, or the
    maneuver of units, excluding areas in which covering or screening forces are operating” (DoD

                                                                        2-24


---

                                                                                  MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

Dictionary). (Chapter 8 discusses the FEBA with other defensive control measures.) Friendly
forces forward of the FLOT may have a restrictive fire coordination measure, such as an RFA,
placed around them to preclude friendly fire incidents.

Handover Line
The handover line is “a control measure, preferably following easily defined terrain features, at
which responsibility for conducting combat operations is passed from one force to another”
(USMC Dictionary). In ground combat operations, a handover line is a predetermined location,
typically a phase line designated as a handover line where control of the battle is transferred to
the main battle force. The common higher commander of the two forces establishes the handover
line after consulting with both commanders. The stationary commander determines the location
of the line. The handover line is forward of the FEBA in the defense and the FLOT in the offense.
The commander establishes it where elements of the passing unit can be effectively supported
by the direct fires of the stationary unit until passage of lines is complete. (See Chapter 17 for
information about passage of lines). The area between the handover line and the stationary force
belongs to the stationary force commander. The stationary force commander might employ
security forces, obstacles, and fires in the area.

Line of Contact
The line of contact is, “a general trace delineating the location where two opposing forces are
engaged” (USMC Dictionary). Units develop their line of contact based on the maximum effective
range of the direct fire weapons systems, or the visual line of sight from known or estimated
enemy locations. The enemy side of the line of contact is designated using the abbreviation
“ENY.” The line of contact is a general trace delineating the location where friendly and enemy
forces are engaged. In a manner similar to the FLOT, it does not refer to ambushes, patrol
contacts, and other small unit tactical actions but rather delineates the general line of engagement
between significant ground forces. In the defense, a line of contact is often synonymous with the
FLOT. In the offense, a line of contact is often combined with the line of departure.

Probable Line of Contact. Planners can designate a phase line as a probable line of contact for
other forms of contact. For example, based on IPB and information collection, friendly forces can
depict the known of anticipated locations of enemy artillery assets and determine a probable line
of contact for enemy indirect fires.

Line of Departure
The line of departure is, “in land warfare, a line designated to coordinate the departure of attack
elements” (DoD Dictionary). See Chapter 3 for more information on the line of departure.

Linkup Point
A linkup point is an easily identifiable point on the ground where two forces conducting a linkup
operation meet. When used in conjunction with an infiltration, linkup points should be large
enough to provide cover, concealment, and room for all infiltrating elements to assemble. The
commander should position linkup points on defensible terrain located away from enemy troop
movement routes.

                                                                   2-25


---

MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

Main Battle Area
The MBA is “that portion of the battlespace in which the commander conducts close operations to
defeat the enemy. Normally, the main battle area extends rearward from the forward edge of the
battle area to the rear boundary of the command’s subordinate units” (USMC Dictionary). Within
a spatial-based battlespace framework, the MBA is where the commander conducts close
operations that accomplish the mission. See Chapter 8 for more information on the MBA.

Named Area of Interest
A named area of interest (NAI) is “a point or area along a particular avenue of approach through
which enemy activity is expected to occur. Activity or lack of activity within a named area of
interest will help to confirm or deny a particular enemy course of action” (USMC Dictionary).
Named areas of interest are usually selected to capture indications of enemy COAs but can also be
related to battlespace and environmental conditions. The NAI could be a person, group, or portion
of cyberspace. The commander tailors the shape of the NAI symbol to the actual area the
commander wants observed, rather than using a prescribed shape. It is possible to redesignate an
NAI as a targeted or target area of interest (TAI) on confirmation of enemy activity within the
area, allowing a commander to mass the effects of combat power on that area.  

Obstacle Control Measures
An obstacle is “any barrier designed or employed to disrupt, fix, turn, or block the movement, and
to impose additional losses in personnel, time, and equipment” (DoD Dictionary). Forces emplace
tactical and protective obstacles that reinforce existing terrain and obstructions and integrate them
with fires to shape engagements and affect the enemy’s ability to move or maneuver. Commanders
can emplace protective obstacles within 500 meters of their positions; however, higher
headquarters can provide restrictions on the types of obstacles subordinate commanders use.
Additionally, higher header quarters provides guidance and employment authority for obstacles
farther than 500 meters from subordinate positions. Commanders use the obstacle control to
ensure emplaced obstacles support the concept of operations and do not interfere with future
operations. Obstacle control measures are zones, belts, groups, and restrictions. Table 2-2
summarizes obstacle control measures. See Chapter 21 for a more detailed discussion on obstacles
and how they support countermobility. Also, see MCTP 3-34B for information on developing
engagement areas and achieving obstacle integration.

                                            2-26


---

                                                                                  MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

Phase Line
A phase line is “an easily identified feature in the operational area utilized for control and
coordination of military operations” (DoD Dictionary). A commander establishes phase lines to
control the maneuver of subordinate units. Phase lines are not boundaries unless designated as
such and do not establish any specific responsibilities between units, unless specified in the
operation order. When possible, the commander places them along easily recognizable terrain
features (e.g., roads, railroad tracks, rivers, ridgelines) to ensure easy identification. Some phase
lines have additional designations for specific purposes, such as a line of departure or a probable
line of deployment (PLD) (see Chapter 3). A disengagement line, which is a phase line, is
typically used in the defense (see Chapter 8).

Position Area
A position area is an area that is occupied, or will be occupied, by an artillery unit with their
elements disposed to provide artillery support. Commanders assign position areas for artillery
(PAAs) to manage terrain, deconflict maneuver, simplify battlefield geometry, and manage risk
(e.g., probable areas of enemy counterfires). Position areas are not AOs, and occupying artillery
units do not have the authority and responsibilities associated with AOs. For example, other units
can move through a PAA without clearing that movement with the artillery unit. Similarly, PAAs
do not constitute a rigid restrictive area for the artillery unit; they should be used as guides as
applicable for the mission, terrain, and tactical situation. See MCTP 3-10E, Artillery Operations,
for further information on PAAs.

Point of Departure
The point of departure is “a specific place where a unit will cross the line of departure” (USMC
Dictionary). Reconnaissance and security patrols commonly use a point of departure as a control
measure, particularly during limited-visibility conditions. Like a line of departure, it marks the
point where the unit transitions from movement to maneuver.

Radar Zone
Search zones prioritize the search pattern and provide the reaction posture of the radar system to
meet the maneuver commander’s intent. Each radar system can be programmed to store up to nine
different zones. There are four different types of zones used with the radar: the critical friendly
zone (CFZ), the call for fire zone, the artillery target intelligence zone, and the censor zone. These
zones are used with artillery target acquisition radar. For additional information on employing
these zones, see MCTP 3-10F, Fire Support Coordination in the Ground Combat Element, and
Marine Corps Reference Publication (MCRP) 3-10E.7, Tactics, Techniques, and Procedures for
Field Artillery Target Acquisition.

Rally Point
A rally point is “an easily identifiable point on the ground at which units can reassemble and
reorganize if they become dispersed” or, “a planned or hasty location where a separated flight
joins up” (USMC Dictionary). Forces conducting a patrol, convoy, or an infiltration commonly
use this control measure. An objective rally point (ORP) is a rally point located nearest the
objective where a unit makes final preparations prior to approaching the objective or where the
unit reassembles after completing actions on the objective. To serve both as a preparation point
and a rally point, the commander typically establishes the ORP far enough from the objective to
prevent the enemy from detecting the actions.

                                                                   2-27


---

MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

    Route
    A route is a prescribed course from a point of origin (start point) to a specific destination (release
    point); it could be a road or an axis of advance. Commanders use routes to manage maneuver and
    deconflict traffic. Routes can have different functions such as passing routes or MSRs. Commanders
    can further designate routes as open, supervised, dispatch, reserved, or prohibited. The commander
    can assign names, numbers, or alphanumeric designations to routes within an AO. For a detailed
    discussion on planning and executing routes, see MCRP 3-40F.7, Multi-Service Tactics, Techniques,
    and Procedures for Tactical Convoy Operations.

    Sector of Fire
    A sector of fire is “a defined area that is required to be covered by the fire of individual or
    crew-served weapons or the weapons of a unit” (USMC Dictionary). Battalions and smaller
    echelons primarily use this direct fire control measure. Each sector of fire can extend from a firing
    position to the maximum engagement range of the weapon, or it can be an enclosed area at a
    distance from the firing position. The commander should assign each subordinate unit or available
    weapon system a primary sector of fire and a secondary sector of fire to increase the capability of
    concentrating fire in certain areas. The primary sector of fire is that area in which the assigned
    unit, individual, or crew-served weapon team is initially responsible for engaging and destroying
    enemy targets in accordance with established priorities of engagement. Fire shifts to the secondary
    sector, on order, when there are no targets in the primary sector, or when the commander needs to
    cover the movement of another friendly element. This secondary sector of fire should correspond
    to another element’s primary sector of fire to obtain mutual support. Subordinate commanders
    may impose additional fire control measures as required.

    Support-by-Fire Position
    A support-by-fire position is the general position from which a unit conducts the tactical task of
    support by fire (see Appendix C). Commanders establish these positions to support the maneuver
    of another force by using direct fires to suppress or neutralize enemy positions capable of
    affecting the maneuver force. Support-by-fire positions are located within the enemy’s maximum
    friendly direct fire range, in a manner that prevents being masked by friendly maneuver, and
    properly deconflicted from other elements of battlespace geometry. Support-by-fire positions are
    often located on the flank of the assault force, elevated above the objective if possible. Typically,
    only company-sized units and below use support-by-fire positions. A support-by-fire position
    symbol designates the general location and direction from which the unit provides fires; it does
    not indicate a specific site.

    Target Area of Interest
    A TAI is “the geographical area where high-value targets can be acquired and engaged by friendly
    forces” (DoD Dictionary). Not all TAIs form part of the friendly COA; only TAIs associated with
    high priority targets are of interest to the staff. The staff identifies these TAIs during planning and
    wargaming. Target areas of interest interdict enemy forces by fire, maneuver, or jamming to
    reduce or deprive them of some capability. Whereas an engagement area is where a commander
    plans to use all available weapons to destroy an enemy force. Engagement areas plan for the use of
    all available weapons; TAIs might be engaged by a single weapon. The commander designates a
    TAI where friendly weapon systems can best attack high value and high-payoff targets. The unit

                                                                        2-28


---

                                                                                  MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

staff develops these TAIs during the planning process. The shape of a TAI reflects the type of
target and the weapon system intended to engage that target. A commander can designate a TAI
for any organic or supporting systems, including CAS.

Target Reference Point
A TRP is “an easily recognizable point on the ground (either natural or man-made) used to
initiate, distribute, and control fires” (USMC Dictionary). Once established, they also become
indirect fire targets designated by the fire support officer. Target reference points are used at the
regiment level and below. Marines use TRPs to identify sectors of fire and to distribute or
concentrate direct and indirect fires. Target reference points must be easily identifiable at all
visibility levels; they are typically terrain features, buildings, or markers emplaced by the owning
unit. Although associated with engagement areas, TRPs are useful in all types of offensive and
defensive actions—in the same manner as establishing targets in a fire support plan for an attack.
As in indirect fire targeting, TRPs are also established using a “top-down planning, bottom-up”
refinement methodology. As with indirect fire targeting, commanders and subordinates should
resist establishing too many TRPs, shifting direct and indirect fires off existing TRPs if necessary.
Target reference points are either designated per standard indirect target naming conventions or, if
not associated with an indirect fire target, by a numeric-only system.

Trigger Line
A trigger line is a phase line used to initiate a preplanned event. Trigger lines are often used to
initiate and mass fires into an engagement area or an objective at a predetermined range for all or
like weapon systems. They may signal the requirement to withdraw to another position. In the
offense, the crossing of a phase line might act like a trigger to execute preplanned fires. A trigger
line could indicate the requirement to engage certain types of enemy systems, such as enemy
breaching assets. Similar to phase lines, trigger lines are typically located on identifiable terrain
that crosses an engagement area, a direction of attack, or an axis of advance. The commander can
designate one trigger line for all weapon systems or separate trigger lines for each weapon or type
of weapon system. The commander can combine other control measures, such as engagement
criteria and priorities, with trigger lines, and can use a time-based or a geography-based fires
delivery methodology. Engagement criteria might be either time or event-driven, such as
establishing that a certain number or certain type of vehicle must cross the trigger line before
Marines initiate engagement. The commander might also initiate engagement by firing a personal
weapon or giving the oral command to fire.

The trigger line’s location varies based on METT-T requirements, with a special focus on
time-distance factors. For example, the distance an enemy force is likely to traverse in the
time it takes from when fires are requested to when they impact. By beginning with identifying
where the commander wants the effects of direct and indirect fires to be conducted, planners
can use the time to deliver those fires with the likely speed of the enemy to determine where
to the trigger line. Distance generally reflects the more rapid response.

Plans are built to be flexible, and commanders and planners should avoid using trigger lines to begin
long sequences of events; it is better to incorporate multiple trigger lines or other control measures,
such as TRPs. Similarly, the effects of fires should be considered when using trigger lines. Massed
fires in depth might create limited-visibility conditions that preclude the use of direct fires.

                                                                   2-29


---

                        PART II.
                    THE OFFENSE

Marines use offensive operations to defeat and destroy enemy forces as well as to seize terrain,
resources, and population centers. Part II describes the fundamentals of the offense and the four
offensive operations—movement to contact, attack, exploitation, and pursuit.


---



---

                     CHAPTER 3.
             OFFENSIVE OPERATIONS

The offense is the decisive form of warfare. Although other operations may cause great damage or
harm to the interests of an enemy, offensive operations provide the means to decisive victory.
Commanders conduct offensive operations to impose their will on the enemy by shattering the
enemy’s moral, mental, and physical cohesion.

When seizing, retaining, or exploiting the initiative, the commander is conducting offensive
operations. Even when conducting defensive operations or stabilization tasks and activities,
commanders apply offensive concepts. Offensive operations—

  • Destroy enemy forces and equipment.
  • Deceive and divert the enemy.
  • Deprive the enemy of resources.
  • Gain information.
  • Fix the enemy in place.
  • Seize key terrain.
  • Force an enemy decision.
  • Disrupt enemy actions or preparations.

The focus of offensive operations is the enemy, not seizing terrain. Although units can be tasked to
seize key objectives or terrain features, the operation’s goal is defeat of the enemy. Successful
offensive operations—

  • Avoid the enemy’s strength and attack their weakness by focusing combat power against the
     enemy’s critical vulnerabilities.

  • Isolate the enemy from their sources of support to include the population.
  • Strike the enemy from unexpected directions, disrupting their plans.
  • Exploit every advantage.
  • Overwhelm the ability of enemy decision makers to observe, orient, decide, and act.

CHARACTERISTICS OF THE OFFENSE

Offensive characteristics include—
  • Audacity.
  • Concentration.
  • Surprise.
  • Tempo.


---

MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

    Offensive operations capitalize on intelligence, allowing units to shape the battlespace, maneuver
    to gain a position of advantage, and generate a greater operational tempo than the enemy can
    match. Commanders initiate selective contact with enemy forces to shape their decisive operation.
    The decisive operation determines the outcome of the major operation, battle, or engagement.
    Commanders accept operational risk to maintain the initiative, dictate the terms of battle, and
    undertake COAs that—although difficult or unexpected—generate the maximum effects on the
    enemy. (See Chapter 2 for more on decisive operations.)

    Audacity
    Audacity refers to extraordinary boldness and courage. In military terms, audacity is the
    willingness of friendly forces to strike boldly and decisively amid uncertainty and operational
    risk to achieve decisive victory. Audacity can be a simple, daring plan, executed aggressively, or
    it can consist of direct, forceful, solutions to complex problems that commanders use to break
    stalemates and political impasses. Audacious commanders apply combat power, exploit sudden
    opportunities, and overcome impassable obstacles. They understand when and where to take
    risks and do not hesitate as they execute their plan. Commanders dispel uncertainty through
    action; they compensate for lack of information by seizing the initiative and pressing the fight.

    Concentration
    Concentration is massing combat power to generate overwhelming effects to achieve a single
    purpose. Commanders balance the necessity for concentrating forces to create effects with the
    need to disperse them to avoid creating targets for the enemy or giving away the element of
    surprise. Advances in ground and air mobility, target acquisition, and long-range precision fires
    enable attackers to rapidly concentrate effects. Command and control information systems can
    provide reliable, relevant information that assists commanders in determining when and where to
    concentrate forces to mass effects.

    Attacking units manipulate their own and the enemy’s force concentration by combining
    dispersion, aggregation, deception, and attacks. By dispersing, attackers stretch enemy defenses
    and deny targets to enemy fires. By rapidly massing forces along converging axes and
    synchronizing the effects of available supporting assets, attackers overwhelm enemy forces at the
    decisive point. After an attack, commanders prioritize exploitation and maintaining momentum
    while weighing the risks of keeping their forces concentrated despite potential enemy reactions.
    Should enemy forces threaten friendly forces, they may disperse again. Commanders adopt the
    posture that best suits the situation, protects the force, and sustains the momentum of the offense.

    The concentration of combat power to generate overwhelming effects includes—

       • Assembling ground forces.
       • Capitalizing on air superiority to deny the enemy the ability to detect or strike friendly forces

         from the air.
       • Using direct land, air, and maritime resources to delay, disrupt, or destroy enemy

         reconnaissance elements or capabilities.
       • Using rear security, information protection, and counterfire to protect friendly forces as

         they concentrate.

                                                                         3-2


---

                                                                                  MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

Surprise
In the offense, units achieve surprise by attacking the enemy at a time or place the enemy does
not expect or in a manner for which the enemy is unprepared. To achieve surprise, one must
estimate the enemy commander’s intent and deny that commander the ability to gain thorough
and timely situational understanding. Commanders use unpredictability and boldness to gain
surprise. The nature, direction, timing, and force of the attack also help achieve surprise. Surprise
delays enemy reactions, overloads and confuses the enemy commander’s C2 systems, induces
psychological shock among enemy soldiers and leaders, and reduces the coherence of the
defense. Surprise diminishes enemy combat power, which enables friendly forces to exploit
enemy paralysis and hesitancy.

Tactical surprise is fleeting and difficult to achieve. Modern surveillance and warning systems,
readily available commercial imagery products, and the global news cycle make achieving
surprise more difficult. Nonetheless, units can achieve surprise by recognizing and reacting to
opportunity, and by operating in a way the enemy does not expect. To achieve surprise, units often
must by accept operational risk, demonstrate a willingness to endure hardship; using and
warfighting doctrine and mission-type orders help generate flexibility and adaptability. Marines
use bad weather, seemingly impassable terrain, feints, demonstrations, and false communications
to lead the enemy into inaccurate perceptions. They use sudden, violent, and unanticipated attacks
to paralyze the enemy and shape the environment for the main effort’s decisive action.

Friendly forces can achieve surprise through unexpected changes in tempo, such as moving
slowly or creating a perception of unpreparedness before rapidly accelerating operations.
Commanders can conceal the concentration of their forces, masking activity that might reveal the
direction or timing of an attack, and then use superior mobility to achieve rapid massing of combat
power. Finally, friendly forces use advantages and capabilities such as air assault and amphibious
raids, special operations forces (referred to as SOF), information and cyberspace actions, and
naval strikes and joint fires to create gaps in the enemy’s defenses that enable surprise.

Tempo
In military terms, tempo is “the relative speed and rhythm of military operations over time with
respect to the enemy” (USMC Dictionary). In the offense, commanders seek to dictate the tempo
of operations to maintain dominance, momentum, and initiative, thereby increasing combat
power. Commanders increase tempo to prevent the enemy’s recovery from the initial assault.
Faster tempos—

  • Degrade the enemy’s situational awareness and ability to make timely, relevant decisions.
  • Deny the enemy a chance to rest.
  • Disrupt the enemy’s plans.
  • Destroy the enemy’s ability to effectively react.

Commanders make the rapid and timely decisions necessary in a high-tempo environment by
empowering subordinates through mission-type orders, staff processes that focus on effective
command and control, and by accepting uncertainty.

                                                                    3-3


---

MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

    Dictating tempo acknowledges that offensive operations require rapidity, violence of action, and
    coordination and synchronization of combat power and logistics to effect concentration at
    decision points, maintain the offense, and avoid culminating points. Commanders dictate when to
    attack and when to alter tempo to reconstitute, reorganize or conduct reliefs in place (RIPs).
    Effective staff processes, efficient logistic procedures, and prior planning are critical to
    maintaining the ability to conduct operations without ceding the initiative to the enemy.

   FUNDAMENTALS OF OFFENSIVE OPERATIONS

    The Marine Corps warfighting philosophy is offensive in nature. It focuses on the enemy and uses
    tempo to seize the initiative and degrade the enemy’s ability to resist. To be decisive in offensive
    operations, the attacking force weights the main effort. The fundamentals of offensive action,
    which have evolved from the time-proven application of the joint warfighting principles, include
    the following:

       • Orient on the enemy.
       • Gain and maintain contact.
       • Develop the situation.
       • Concentrate superior firepower at the decisive time and place.
       • Achieve surprise.
       • Exploit known enemy weaknesses.
       • Seize and control key terrain.
       • Gain and retain the initiative.
       • Neutralize the enemy’s ability to react.
       • Advance by fire and maneuver.
       • Maintain momentum.
       • Act quickly.
       • Exploit success.
       • Be adaptable.
       • Be aggressive.
       • Provide security for the force.

   TYPES OF OFFENSIVE OPERATIONS

    The four types of offense are movement to contact, attack, exploitation, and pursuit. Table 3-1
    contains the planning symbols associated with movement to contact, exploitation, and pursuit.
    There are numerous methods to conduct and execute these types of offensive operations—such as
    the different ways to conduct an attack; there is no limit on how commanders and Marines
    approach tactical problems, or how they execute these offensive operations.

                                                                         3-4


---

                          MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

Table 3-1. Offensive Operations and their Planning Symbols.

Operations                Planning Symbol

Movement to Contact

Exploitation

Pursuit                   P

                              NOTE
                              Attack does not have a planning symbol. Unless a commander deems it is
                              necessary to constrain subordinates, the default type is an attack; graphic
                              control measures such as an axis of advance or direction of attack can be
                              used to convey the commander’s intent. Additionally, exploitations and
                              pursuits are generally a branch or sequel to a successful attack.

Movement to Contact
Movement to contact is employed to develop the situation and establish or regain contact with the
enemy. It is one of the most used types of offense because of its almost universal utility.
Commanders conduct a movement to contact when the enemy situation is vague, whether trying
to locate the enemy, regain contact with the enemy, or preserve tactical flexibility. A movement to
contact also forces the enemy troops to reveal themselves for further friendly force targeting or
operations. Even when the enemy situation is known, commanders often use movement to contact
methods as a means of force protection in their approach or when conducting exploitations and
pursuits. Forces executing a movement to contact seek to make contact with the smallest friendly
force feasible to avoid decisive engagement and enable decisive action by a main effort. Once
contact is made with an enemy force, the commander has five options: attack, defend, bypass,
delay, or withdraw. There are two methods of movement to contact—the approach march and the
search and attack (see Chapter 4).

Attack
An attack is characterized by coordinated movement, supported by fire, conducted to defeat,
destroy, or capture the enemy, or seize and/or secure terrain. Attacks can be either decisive or
shaping actions and hasty or deliberate. The methods of attack are:

  • Spoiling.

  • Counterattack.

  • Reconnaissance in Force.

  • Raid.
  • Ambush.

Units use multiple attack methods to increase effects.

                     3-5


---

MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

    An attack differs from a movement to contact because, even in a hastily conducted attack, the
    commander knows part of the enemy’s disposition. This knowledge enables the commander to
    better synchronize the attack and employ combat power more effectively than in a movement to
    contact. If an attack is successful, the enemy is no longer willing or able to offer effectual
    resistance. Chapter 5 discusses the attack and methods of attack in further detail.

    Exploitation
    Exploitation, which follows a successful attack, is designed to disorganize the enemy in depth
    and extend to the initial success of the attack by preventing the enemy from disengaging,
    withdrawing, and reestablishing an effective defense. Whether conducting hasty or deliberate
    operations, commanders plan to exploit the success of every attack without losing momentum or
    the initiative. The attacking element or a reserve element can conduct exploitation activities.
    Exploitation places necessary, but immense, demands on Marines’ endurance and equipment.
    Chapter 6 discusses exploitation.

    Pursuit
    A pursuit is designed to catch or cut off a hostile force attempting to escape, with the aim of
    destroying it. A pursuit typically follows a successful exploitation. However, any type of offense
    can transition into a pursuit if enemy resistance is diminished, and they flee the battlefield.
    Because the conditions necessary to conduct a pursuit are not predictable, pursuits are difficult to
    plan. Commanders and staffs must recognize and exploit “catastrophic success.” A pursuit entails
    rapid movement and decentralized control. Like exploitation, it places great demands on the
    endurance of Marines and equipment to take advantage of the opportunity to defeat the enemy.
    Chapter 7 discusses the pursuit.

   PHASES OF THE OFFENSE

    Phasing of offensive operations depends on how the commander decides to solve the tactical
    problem. A commander can use any or all of the following five phases in an offensive operation:

       • Gain and maintain enemy contact.
       • Disrupt the enemy.
       • Fix the enemy.
       • Maneuver.
       • Follow through.

    Typically, the first three phases are shaping actions, while the maneuver phase is the decisive
    action. Follow through is usually a sequel or a branch based on the current situation. It can consist
    of transition to other types of offense operations such as exploitation, or it can transition to
    defensive operations or stabilization tasks and activities.

                                                                         3-6


---

                                                            MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

number necessary to complete the mission while providing subordinate units with the flexibility to
respond to changes. See Figure 3-1 for a graphic depiction of common offensive control measures.
The following paragraphs discuss those control measures common only to offensive operations
(see Table 3-2). For more information on basic control measures, see Chapter 2.
