Assault Position
An assault position is “that position between the line of departure and the objective in an attack
from which forces assault the objective. Ideally, it is the last covered and concealed position
before reaching the objective (primarily used by dismounted infantry)” (USMC Dictionary).
Momentum in an assault is critical; therefore, any time a unit spends in an assault position should

                                                3-7


---

MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

    be minimal. Final preparations before the assault include ensuring the readiness of personnel,
    weapons, and special equipment, and the reorganizing the plan after combat losses. Assault
    positions are often located near to either a final coordination line (FCL) or a PLD.

    Assault Time
    The assault time is the assigned time to attack the initial objectives throughout the geographical
    scope of the operation. Local commanders usually establish the assault time to coordinate and
    synchronize the actions of the assault with the effects generated by other units on the enemy, such
    as final mortar fires or increased rate of fire from support-by-fire positions.

    Assembly Area
    A tactical assembly area is “an area that is generally out of the reach of light artillery and the
    location where units make final preparations (pre-combat checks and inspections) and rest, prior
    to moving to the line of departure” (DoD Dictionary). Tactical assembly areas are positioned
    where enemy contact is likely and where planners anticipate commitment of a unit into combat.
    Units that typically occupy a tactical assembly area include—

       • Units designated as tactical reserves.
       • Units completing a rearward passage of lines.
       • Units conducting tactical movement (temporary).
       • Units undergoing reconstitution.

    Units in tactical assembly areas are typically preparing to execute a forward passage of lines
    followed by offensive operations or have been assigned a reserve mission by their higher
    commander. See Chapter 2 for more information on assembly areas.

    Attack-by-Fire Position
    An attack-by-fire position designates the general position from which a unit conducts the tactical
    task of attack by fire (see Appendix C). A commander typically employs an attack by fire when
    the mission does not require or support close combat and occupation of a geographical objective
    by another friendly force. The attack-by-fire position enables subordinate units to accomplish the
    attack-by-fire task while deconflicting battlespace geometry. The attack-by-fire position only
    indicates the general location to be occupied, not the specific site. Attack-by-fire positions are
    rarely applicable to units larger than company size.

    Attack Position
    An attack position is “the last position occupied by the assault echelon before crossing the line of
    departure” (DoD Dictionary). However, an attack position is not an assembly area. An attack
    position facilitates the deployment and last-minute coordination of the attacking force before it
    crosses the line of departure. It is located on the friendly side of the line of departure and offers
    cover and concealment for the attacking force. The battalion level and below primarily use the
    attack position. Whenever possible, units move through the attack position without stopping. An
    attacking unit might occupy an attack position for a various reasons; for example, when the unit is
    waiting for specific results from preparation fires, or when it is necessary to conduct additional
    coordination, such as a forward passage of lines. If the attacking unit occupies the attack position,

                                                                         3-8


---

                                                                                  MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

it stays there for the shortest amount of time possible to avoid losing momentum or providing the
enemy a target. If required to loiter in the attack position, the attacking unit immediately assumes
a defensive posture.

Axis of Advance
During offensive operations, higher headquarters can establish bypass criteria, which are control
measures that specify the conditions and size under which friendly units should avoid contact with
the enemy. There are three primary reasons a commander uses an axis of advance:

  • To direct the bypass of locations that could delay the progress of the advancing force, such as
     known contaminated areas.

  • To indicate that the force is not required to clear the area as they advance, only the assigned
     axis in accordance with specified bypass criteria.

  • To indicate the need to move rapidly (e.g., an exploitation or pursuit).

Direction of Attack
The direction of attack is a specific direction or assigned route a force uses and does not deviate
from when attacking. It is a restrictive control measure. A direction of attack maximizes control
over subordinate unit movement, and commanders often use it during night attacks, infiltrations,
and when attacking in limited visibility. The commander establishes a direction of attack through
various means, such as TRPs, checkpoints, and way points. When using a direction of attack, the
commander designates a point of departure and a release point.

Final Coordination Line
The FCL is “a line used to coordinate the ceasing and shifting of supporting fires and the final
deployment of the assault echelon in preparation for launching an assault against an enemy
position” (USMC Dictionary). Prior to crossing the FCL, planners make final adjustments to
supporting fires to reflect the tactical situation rather than the planned situation. An FCL should be
easily recognizable on the ground and is often associated with an assault position. The FCL is not
an FSCM.

Limit of Advance
The limit of advance (LOA) is “an easily recognized terrain feature beyond which attacking
elements will not advance” (USMC Dictionary). Limits of advance are restrictive control
measures. Because LOAs prevent units from exploiting success, commanders only use them if
they do not want units to conduct an exploitation or pursuit. A commander might employ an LOA
to prevent overextending the attacking force or to mitigate battlespace geometry (e.g., preventing
the maneuver element from advancing into isolation fires). A commander usually selects a
recognizable, linear terrain feature on the far side of the objective, perpendicular to the direction
of attack, as the LOA. Commanders position LOAs far enough beyond the objective so it can be
defended by friendly forces. A forward boundary is always a limit of advance because the unit
cannot act or move beyond the forward boundary. However, an LOA is not always a forward
boundary because there are other reasons to hold a unit physically short of a forward boundary.

                                                                    3-9


---

MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

    Line of Departure
    The line of departure is a restrictive control measure used to synchronize and coordinate the actions
    of the attacking and supporting forces to create the greatest concentration of effects on the enemy at
    the point of decision. It is not intended to serve as a preparatory position—commanders designate
    an attack position for that purpose, if required. Rather, units employ combat formations and cross
    the line of departure at the time of attack, allowing other attacking and supporting elements to
    synchronize and execute their assignments in support of maneuver. Generally, the line of departure
    is perpendicular to the direction the attacking force will take on their way to the objective. The
    commander analyzes friendly actions such as rates of movement, the enemy situation, and terrain
    before designating a line of departure. Friendly forces control the line of departure to prevent
    enemy interference with maneuver units. The line of departure should provide cover for maneuver
    units deploying into and crossing the line. When a unit already in contact is the attacking unit, the
    line of departure is also the line of contact.

    Objective
    In offensive operations, objectives are either terrain- or force-oriented. Terrain objectives should
    place the enemy at a disadvantage and facilitate further actions against them. Force-oriented
    objectives should disrupt, degrade, or destroy specific enemy elements to achieve the commander’s
    purpose. Commanders might use both types of objectives in the same operation—for example,
    seizing a key crossroad to prevent the enemy’s withdrawal (i.e., terrain-oriented) and enable their
    destruction (i.e., force-oriented). The commander typically assigns subordinate commanders only
    their final objectives but can assign intermediate objectives as necessary.

    Probable Line of Deployment
    A PLD is “an easily recognized line selected on the ground where attacking units deploy in assault
    formation prior to beginning an attack” (USMC Dictionary). It is usually a linear terrain feature
    perpendicular to the direction of attack and recognizable under limited-visibility conditions.
    Commanders use a PLD when a unit does not cross the line of departure in assault formation. The
    commander should establish the PLD outside the range where the enemy can place the attacking
    force under effective direct fire.

    Time of Attack
    The time of attack, often referred to as H-hour, is “the hour at which the attack is to be launched. If
    a line of departure is prescribed, it is the hour at which the line is to be crossed by the leading
    elements of the attack” (USMC Dictionary). However, it can also designate the time to implement
    preliminary phases of the operation, such as strikes or an air assault phase. Commanders and their
    staffs use the time of attack to coordinate shaping actions within the attack.

             NOTE: In amphibious operations, H-hour is the time at which the first waterborne
             wave of an amphibious assault lands on a beach.

    The headquarters planning the offensive operations specifies the term’s exact meaning. When
    determining time of attack, the commander considers the time subordinate units require to—

       • Conduct necessary reconnaissance, prepare plans, and issue orders.
       • Synchronize plans between all subordinate units.

                                                                        3-10


---

                                                                                  MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

  • Complete attack preparations, such as pre combat inspections.
  • Move to the line of departure or point of departure.

An assault time’s scope differs from a time of attack. A time of attack begins with crossing the line
of departure and synchronizes all the actions necessary for units to conduct the assault; the time of
attack is usually preplanned and typically does not change.

Zone and Sector
A zone is an operational area assigned to a unit in the offense that only has rear and lateral
boundaries (Field Manual [FM] 3-0, Operations). The non-bounded side of a zone is open toward
enemy forces. A higher-echelon headquarters uses fire support coordination and maneuver control
measures such as a limit of advance and a coordinated fire line to synchronize its deep operations
with those of a subordinate unit. Zones allow higher headquarters to adjust deep operations
without having to change unit boundaries. This gives greater flexibility to the higher headquarters
for controlling deep operations, allowing subordinate units to focus on close and rear operations.
A zone is best for front-line units executing high-tempo offensive operations characterized by
direct fire contact with the enemy and a fluid forward line of troops. Units treat everything behind
the forward line of troops as an AO with the associated nine responsibilities. Zones can be further
subdivided as needed.

A sector is an operational area assigned to a unit in the defense that has rear and lateral
boundaries with interlocking fires (FM 3-0). The non-bounded side is open toward the enemy.
A higher-echelon headquarters uses fire support coordination and maneuver control measures
such as battle positions and trigger lines to synchronize subordinate units. Higher headquarters
are responsible for synchronizing operations forward of the main battle and security areas or
coordinated fire line. Units use sectors to synchronize and coordinate engagement areas and
allow for mutually supporting fields of fire, which do not require coordination between adjacent
units. Units treat everything behind the forward line of troops as an AO with the associated nine
responsibilities. Sectors can be further subdivided as needed.

FORMS OF CONTACT

Contact is an interaction between two forces. There are three possible types of interactions:

  • Both forces are in contact with each other.
  • A friendly force is in contact with an enemy force, while the enemy force is not in contact

     with the friendly force.
  • A friendly force is out of contact with an enemy force; however, the enemy force is in contact

     with the friendly force.

                                                                   3-11


---

MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

    Leaders account for how to defend or mitigate against the enemy using these forms of contact.
    They also make plans on how to use these forms of contact against the enemy. Units use all the
    available capabilities to conduct various forms of contact. The 10 forms of contact are—

       • Direct. Interactions from ground-based, line of sight weapons systems (including small arms,
         tank main guns, and antitank missiles).

       • Indirect. Interactions from non-line of sight weapons systems (including cannon artillery,
          mortars, and rockets).

       • Non-Hostile. Neutral interactions that may degrade military operations (including civilians on
          the battlefield, nongovernmental organizations, or neutral forces).

       • Obstacle. Interactions from natural and man-made obstacles (including rivers and minefields).
       • Chemical, Biological, Radiological, and Nuclear (CBRN). Interactions from friendly, enemy,

         and civilian CBRN effects (including chemical attacks, nuclear attacks, industrial accidents,
         and toxic or hazardous).
       • Aerial. Interactions from air-based combat platforms (including attack helicopters, armed
         UAS, and fixed-wing aircraft).
       • Visual. Interaction from acquisition via the human eye, optical, or electro-optical systems
         (including ground reconnaissance, telescopic, thermal, and infrared sights on weapons and
         sensor platforms such as UAS and satellites).
       • Electromagnetic. Interactions via systems used to acquire, degrade, or destroy using select
          portions of the electromagnetic spectrum (including radar systems, jamming, cyberspace, and
          electromagnetic pulse).
       • Influence. Interactions through the information dimension intended to shape the perceptions,
         behaviors, and decision making of people relative to a policy or military objective (including
         through social media, telecommunications, human interaction, and other forms of
         communication and contact).
       • Audio. Interaction from acquisition via the human ear, auditory, artillery sound
         ranging (aural and stopwatch), sonar, microphone sensors, and optoacoustic means
         (e.g., laser-based transducers).

    The forms of contact describe the method of interaction that identifies the location or activity of a
    force. The forms of contact also—

       • Quickly describe to others what is happening.
       • Describe the method of engagement.
       • Provide an understanding of a force’s capabilities and ranges.
       • Can trigger additional actions, typically in the form of battle drills.

    An exception to these forms of contact are interactions with friendly or neutral civilians, military
    forces, or nongovernmental organizations. This interaction is categorized as a non-hostile form
    of contact.

                                                                        3-12


---

                                                                                  MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

Whenever a force gain contact with another force, the gaining force can impede the freedom of
action of that other force while enhancing their own freedom of action. For example, after gaining
visual contact on an enemy force, friendly forces can maneuver—out of enemy contact—to a
position to best destroy the enemy force. Ideally, when friendly forces engage enemy forces, they
use as many different forms of contact as possible to create a dilemma for the enemy and allow the
friendly force to accomplish its mission.

Visual contact allows one force to gain understanding of another other force with or without the
other force’s knowledge. When units conduct direct, indirect, and aerial forms of contact, they use
visual contact. When using CBRN, obstacle, non-hostile, electromagnetic, influencing, or audio
forms of contact, units should still visually confirm what is happening. For example, an animal
could trigger an electronic ground sensor and a unit must confirm with visual contact whether the
ground sensor was activated by enemy forces or by an animal.

When commanders direct friendly forces to gain and maintain contact, units decide which form or
forms of contact is best to use for the situation. The unit must understand where the enemy force is
what it is trying to do, while minimizing the forms of contact the enemy conducts on friendly forces.

Friendly forces should assume that the enemy always has them under some form of visual,
electromagnetic, or influence contact. The proliferation of communication capabilities results in
an increasing ability of friendly, neutral, and adversarial actors to influence one another. Relevant
actors increasingly use social media in the battlespace to influence other actors’ perceptions.
Therefore, leaders should encourage disciplined actions that will help mitigate enemy contact,
such as masking, deception, electromagnetic spectrum discipline, and camouflage.

ACTIONS ON CONTACT

Actions on contact is a process used to help leaders understand what is happening and to take
action. Actions on contact is not intended to generate a rigid, lockstep response to the enemy.
Rather, the goal is to provide an orderly framework that enables leaders to apply sound decision
making and timely actions to complete the operation.

Actions on contact are applicable to all operations. They are applicable to a squad coming into
direct fire contact with an enemy during a movement to contact, a rifle company observing enemy
in the defense, a communications element ambushed by the enemy, or a division in the attack. This
framework enables leaders to quickly assess a situation as it develops and what actions, if any, they
need to take. Actions on contact are—

  • React.
  • Develop the situation.
  • Choose an action.
  • Execute and report.

Once a friendly force makes contact with the enemy, they conduct actions on contact regardless of
whether the enemy has detected their presence. Actions on contact are not to be confused with the
battle drill of “react to contact,” which is a trained response, requires minimal orders to accomplish,

                                                                   3-13


---

MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

    and is initiated by an enemy action. Actions on contact can also start with a unit reacting to contact,
    which simultaneously starts the actions on contact process for different echelons.

    Typically, a unit’s SOP dictates specific actions, to include battle drills and reports, depending on the
    type of contact. Additionally, the mission variables, commander’s intent and guidance, and scheme
    of maneuver guide the actions individual units take when they make contact with enemy forces.

    Leaders understand that at different echelons, actions on contact require different amounts of
    time to conduct with the primary variable being the time it takes to develop the situation. At the
    company-level and below, units can quickly develop the situation and choose an action to execute.
    Battalions and higher might need to execute the rapid response planning process (known as R2P2)
    or a deliberate Marine Corps Planning Process (MCPP) session to synchronize their echelon to a
    new action. Leaders balance the need to conduct their actions on contact with the need to maintain
    momentum. See MCWP 5-10, Marine Corps Planning Process, for more information.

    React
    One of the tenets of maneuver warfare is to make contact with the smallest element possible. This
    element is the one that reacts to contact while the rest of the force begins conducting actions on
    contact at different tempos. If the enemy initiates contact, the friendly element in contact conducts
    the react-to-contact the unit practiced in their battle drill. Any unengaged portion monitors the
    situation and prepares to either support the portion of the unit in contact or continue the mission.
    Simultaneously, the unit in contact reports the contact to their higher headquarters. If friendly
    forces make contact first without the enemy being aware, they pause to determine whether they
    have been detected. If they have not been detected, they move to a location where they will not be
    observed and continue the actions on contact process

    Develop the Situation
    The unit in contact develops the situation to define the threat. This helps to develop the situation
    and provides more maneuver space to execute further actions. As the situation develops and the
    enemy force’s dispositions, strength, and intentions become clearer, the unit in contact submits
    additional reports. Significant reporting data includes—

       • Size, activity, location, composition, and orientation of the enemy force.
       • Effects of obstacles and terrain.
       • Enemy capabilities.
       • Probable enemy intentions.
       • Methods of gaining positional advantage over the enemy.
       • Friendly situations (location, strength, and capabilities).
       • Possible friendly actions to achieve the specified end state.

    Lower echelons, such as companies and below, require less time to develop the situation.
    Regiments and divisions will take longer to develop the situation and determine whether the
    enemy is acting according to the plan before the commander can make an informed decision.

                                                                        3-14


---

                                                                                  MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

Choose an Action
After the unit makes contact, its leaders gather information to make an assessment based on their
understanding of the enemy and friendly forces’ composition and disposition and chooses an
action consistent with the higher echelon commander’s intent and within the unit’s capabilities.

These actions typically are—

  • Attack.
  • Bypass.
  • Defend.
  • Delay.
  • Withdraw.

If the unit in contact encounters reinforcing obstacles, its Marines will either bypass them or
conduct a hasty breach using organic resources. For obstacles not covered by fire, the unit can
either seek to bypass or create lanes to support its maneuver or the maneuver of a supported unit.

Circumstances might dictate that the action requires a higher commander’s approval, such as
when action—

  • Requires additional resources.
  • Is not within the commander’s intent.
  • Sets conditions for the higher echelon to continue.
  • Changes their higher echelon’s scheme of maneuver.

Execute and Report
After the unit selects an action—and receives higher echelon approval, if necessary—they begin
conducting the actions. The unit initiates direct and indirect fires to gain the initiative when
engaging enemy forces. If the action is to attack, the unit in contact immediately attacks if it has
sufficient, immediately available combat power to overwhelm the enemy force. If the action is to
defend or withdraw, the unit in contact does so while maintaining contact and continuing to gain
as much information as possible about the enemy forces disposition and positions. If the action is
to bypass the enemy, the unit in contact maintains contact and continues their mission. Unless
specifically directed by their higher headquarters to break contact, the unit in contact maintains
contact regardless of the chosen action. Reporting to the next higher echelon is required to ensure
the unit’s actions are consistent with the commander’s intent.

FORMS OF MANEUVER

Maneuver is the “employment of forces in the operational area, through movement in combination
with fires and information, to achieve a position of advantage in respect to the enemy” (USMC
Dictionary). The Marine Corps employs six forms of maneuver:

  • Frontal Attack.
  • Flanking Attack.

                                                                   3-15


---

MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

       • Envelopment.
       • Turning Movement.
       • Infiltration.
       • Penetration.

    Planners use the six forms of maneuver to develop offensive COAs and synchronize the
    warfighting functions. Different levels of command combine the forms of maneuver differently
    (e.g., a company might conduct a flanking attack when executing their portion of the parent
    battalion’s envelopment). Although higher commanders rarely specify forms of maneuver, their
    guidance and intent, along with the mission and any implied tasks, might impose constraints such
    as time, security, and direction of attack that narrow a subordinate commander’s options. Key
    factors such as the terrain, adjacent unit’s actions, and enemy dispositions and likely reactions also
    affect the choice of maneuver. A single operation can contain several forms of maneuver, such as
    a frontal attack to clear a security area, penetration to create a gap in enemy defenses, and
    envelopments to defeat the rest of the enemy force.

    Frontal Attack
    A frontal attack is “an offensive maneuver in which the main action is directed against the front of
    the enemy forces” (USMC Dictionary). Figure 3-2 depicts a frontal attack. A commander might
    use a frontal attack as a shaping action in conjunction with other forms of maneuver such as
    applying pressure along a wider front to enable a penetration as the decisive action or to fix an
    enemy force in support of an envelopment. Since a frontal attack often pits strength against
    strength, frontal attacks without significant combat power advantages over the enemy are rarely
    decisive and often unwarranted. A commander might use a frontal attack to—

       • Rapidly overrun a weak enemy force.
       • Clear enemy security forces.
       • Overwhelm a shattered enemy during an exploitation or pursuit.
       • Fix enemy forces in place as part of a shaping action.
       • Conduct a reconnaissance in force.

    Force Organization. Because frontal attacks generally result when friendly forces seek to quickly
    overwhelm a weak enemy or as part of a more deliberate shaping effort, there is no unique force
    organization associated with this form of maneuver. However, the force can expect to use security,
    main body, and reserve elements. Security elements conduct tasks such as locating the enemy and
    providing support by fire. Main body elements conduct attacks by fire or assaults. A reserve
    conducts the decisive action or exploits success.

    Control Measures. When conducting a frontal attack, units might use minimal control measures
    (i.e., an AO defined by unit boundaries and objective). Other control measures include—

       • Attack positions.
       • Lines of departure.
       • Phase lines.

                                                                        3-16


---

                                                                                  MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

  • Assault positions.
  • LOAs.
  • Direction of attack or axis of advance for maneuver units.

                                           Figure 3-2. Frontal Attack Example.
Planning a Frontal Attack. When planning a frontal attack against a weaker enemy, planners focus
on maintaining tempo. Planners seek to rapidly deploy assault formation, execute the assault, and
conduct force consolidation and reorganization. At the battalion level and below, units often use
battle drills to accomplish these actions. When a unit conducts a frontal attack as part of a shaping
action, the primary planning objective is how to fix or disrupt the enemy force while mitigating
the risk of losing personnel and equipment. A unit might conduct a frontal attack by executing a
feint or demonstration or using attack by fire (direct or indirect).
Executing a Frontal Attack. The unit conducting a frontal attack advances on a broad front,
typically with their subordinate ground maneuver elements abreast (except for the reserve). This
clears the enemy’s security area of enemy security forces and intelligence, reconnaissance,
surveillance, and target acquisition assets while advancing the friendly force into the enemy’s main
defenses. Once the unit makes enemy contact, the attacking force’s subordinate elements rapidly
develop the situation and report enemy dispositions to the commander, so the commander can
direct the exploitation of enemy weaknesses. The attacking force fixes enemy forces in their current
locations and seeks to gain positional advantage to destroy the enemy using fire and movement.
If the attacking unit discovers a gap in the enemy’s defenses, the commander seeks to exploit that
weakness and disrupt the integrity of the enemy’s defense. After assessing the situation and
ensuring it is not a trap, the commander can employ the reserve to exploit the opportunity. The
commander synchronizes the exploitation with the actions of other maneuver and support
elements to prevent possible enemy counterattacks from isolating and destroying the reserve and
other exploitation elements. If a unit conducting a frontal attack can no longer advance, it adopts a

                                                                   3-17


---

MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

    defensive posture. The commander might require the unit to assist the forward passage of lines of
    other units. The unit continues to perform reconnaissance of enemy positions to locate gaps or
    assailable flanks.

    Flanking Attack
    A flanking attack is “an offensive maneuver directed at the flank of an enemy” (USMC
    Dictionary) (see Figure 3-3). Commanders use this form of maneuver to place friendly combat
    power against an enemy’s flank, defeating the enemy while minimizing the effect of the enemy’s
    frontally oriented combat power. Forces attack the flank using fires or by a successful penetration.
    Usually, a supporting effort engages and fixes the enemy by combining fires and maneuver while
    the main effort maneuvers to attack the enemy’s flank. Units often use this form of maneuver in
    hastily conducted attacks or as a battle drill in meeting engagements.

                                                                                                                            1
                                                             2

                                                                                                                       A
                                                           B

              1 Shaping element A action diverts enemy attention.
              2 Flanking element B attacks enemy flank.

                                               Figure 3-3. Flanking Attack Example.

    Envelopment
    Envelopment, also called a single envelopment, is “an offensive maneuver in which the main
    attacking force passes around or over the enemy’s principal defensive positions to secure objectives
    to the enemy’s rear” (USMC Dictionary). Commanders use envelopments to seize terrain, destroy
    specific enemy forces, interdict enemy withdrawal routes, and deliver a psychological shock to the
    enemy. The main effort focuses on attacking beyond an assailable flank. By doing so, friendly
    forces avoid the enemy’s strength (i.e., the enemy’s front) where the effects of enemy fires and
    obstacles are the greatest, while gaining a position of advantage. If no assailable flank is available,
    the attacking force might attempt to create one by conducting a penetration.

    The primary difference between an envelopment and a flanking attack is the friendly force’s depth
    relative to the enemy’s positions. An envelopment is a flanking attack delivered beyond the
    enemy’s flank and into the enemy’s rear area, but short of the depth associated with a turning
    movement. There are also varying levels of effort in terms of force to space ratios; logistics; and
    command and control between flanking attacks, envelopments, and turning movements. The
    flanking attack is the simplest in these terms and is most likely executed by battalions and below.
    Envelopments are typically conducted at the RLT and division level, whereas turning movements
    are conducted at the division level and above. The four methods of envelopment are—

       • Single envelopment.
       • Double envelopment.

                                                                        3-18


---

                                       MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

  • Vertical envelopment.
  • Encirclement.

A single envelopment is a variation of envelopment where a force attacks along one flank of an
enemy force. A single envelopment is generally easier to control and does not require a significant
number of forces. See Figure 3-4 for an example of a single envelopment.

A double envelopment is “an offensive maneuver designed to force the enemy to fight in two or
more directions simultaneously to meet the converging axis of the attack” (USMC Dictionary).
A double envelopment is a variation of envelopment where forces simultaneously attack along
both flanks of an enemy force. A force seeking to execute a double envelopment must also have
a substantial mobility advantage over defending forces. A unit performs a double envelopment
by conducting a frontal attack to fix enemy forces in place while enveloping both of the enemy
force’s flanks. A double envelopment generally requires more forces than a single envelopment
and is more difficult to control. See Figure 3-4 for an example of a double envelopment.

          Objective Area                                   Objective Area

             1 Fixing element A fixes enemy in place.
             2 Enveloping element(s) B outflanks enemy and arrives at objective.

                          Figure 3-4. Envelopments.

A vertical envelopment is “a tactical maneuver in which troops that are air-dropped, air-landed,
or inserted via air assault, attack the rear and flanks of a force, in effect cutting off or encircling
the force” (USMC Dictionary). A force seeking to execute a vertical envelopment requires
the necessary vertical lift capability and indirect fire assets to suppress enemy air defense
capability. Because of the forces required, typically only divisions can conduct double and
vertical envelopments, as these organizations have the resources and capability to control these
envelopments. For more information on vertical envelopments, see Chapter 18.

Encirclement is where one force loses its freedom of maneuver because an opposing force is able
to isolate it by controlling all ground lines of communications and reinforcement. An encirclement
restricts the enemy's freedom of maneuver by controlling all ground routes of evacuation and
reinforcement. A unit can conduct offensive encirclements designed to isolate an enemy force;
conversely, the enemy could encircle the friendly force, thereby isolating the friendly force.

                              3-19


---

MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

    Encirclements occur because combat operations are chaotic, intense, and highly destructive,
    extending across large areas containing relatively few units as each side maneuvers against the
    other to obtain positional advantage.

    A unit performs an encirclement or double envelopment by fixing the enemy in place while going
    around or over both hostile flanks. Because of the forces required, typically only divisions and
    larger organizations have the resources to execute double envelopments and encirclements. For a
    detailed discussion on encirclement operations, see Chapter 19.

    Force Organization. The force conducting a single envelopment must perform two primary tasks:
    fix the enemy force in its current location and conduct the envelopment. Security, support, and
    fixing elements perform supporting effort tasks such as reconnaissance, security, frontal attacks,
    attacks by fire, and support by fire. Enveloping elements act as the main effort by attacking
    terrain- or force-oriented objectives beyond the enemy flank. A reserve element is prepared to
    exploit success or defeat enemy counterattacks. Commanders executing double envelopments
    determine which of the two envelopments will accomplish the mission and make that force the
    main effort. Security, support, and fixing elements conducting supporting efforts for both
    envelopments are prioritized accordingly. The key shaping action necessary for success is fixing
    the enemy, and commanders must be prepared to accept risk to ensure its success.

    Control Measures. The commander, at a minimum, establishes boundaries to designate AOs
    for each element participating in the envelopment. The commander also designates phase lines;
    support-by-fire and attack-by-fire positions; contact points; and direct fire and fire support
    coordination measures, such as an RFL or boundary between converging forces, and any other
    control measures necessary to control the envelopment.

    Planning an Envelopment. The commander seeks to maneuver the enveloping element around or
    over the enemy’s main defenses to secure objectives on the enemy’s flank or rear. From those
    objectives, the enveloping element can use its positional advantage to employ superior combat
    power against a defending enemy oriented in the wrong direction. To do so, the commander must
    be aware of the enemy’s positions and their ability to react. For example, if the enemy has strong,
    mobile counterattack forces, the commander must mitigate their ability to affect the fight. Using
    branches and sequels, the commander plans how to exploit the envelopment’s success—for
    example, deciding whether to seek encirclement or transition to pursuit.

    The commander plans for the enveloping element to remain within supporting distance of the
    fixing element. (If an enveloping element is going outside supporting distance, it is more likely
    conducting a turning movement, not an envelopment). Similarly, the commander must ensure the
    enveloping element has adequate short-term sustainment, as LOCs between the rear area and the
    enveloping element are likely to be intermittent in the early stages of an envelopment. An LOC is
    “a route, either land, water, and/or air, that connects an operating military force with a base of
    operations and along which supplies and military forces move” (USMC Dictionary).

                                                                        3-20


---

                                                                                  MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

Executing an Envelopment. Marines execute envelopments by combining surprise, overwhelming
combat power, superior tactical mobility, air and information superiority, and fixing the bulk of
the enemy in their positions. The commander uses ISR assets to find enemy flanks and determine
enemy dispositions, guide the enveloping force, and provide continuous intelligence collection to
identify changes in enemy COAs throughout the execution of the envelopment.

After the fixing element identifies an assailable flank, or creates a flank by a penetration, they pin
the enemy in place. The enveloping element then exploits the situation, rapidly moving before the
enemy can react. Speed and violence of execution are important as the enemy typically seeks to
mitigate envelopments through planning, alternative defensive positions, counterattack elements,
or reserves. Friendly forces also use ground and air shaping efforts to isolate the battlespace and
prevent the enemy from countering the enveloping element.

The enemy might attempt to counter an envelopment by extending their flank, interdicting the
enveloping force’s LOC to cut them off from the support of the fixing force, or conducting a
frontal counterattack. When facing a flank extension, the enveloping force typically attacks
through the weakened extension rather than attempting to maneuver around the extended flank,
as doing so slows momentum and risks losing support from the fixing force. When facing the
temporary interdiction of their LOC, the enveloping element maintains the initiative and dictates
tempo by selecting objectives vital to the enemy and their short-term self-sustainment. If
confronted with a frontal counterattack, the fixing element defends itself or conducts a delay
while the enveloping force continues the envelopment.

After enveloping one flank—which places the enemy at a disadvantage—the commander might
choose to establish favorable conditions for passing to a double envelopment by using reserves, or
the commander might exploit success by generating additional combat power along the same axis.
Alternatively, the commander can destroy or defeat the enveloped enemy force in place or
transition to another type of operation, such as exploitation or pursuit.

Turning Movement
A turning movement is a “form of offensive maneuver in which the attacking force passes around
or over the enemy’s principal defensive positions to secure objectives deep in the enemy’s rear”
(USMC Dictionary) (see Figure 3-5). It is typically geography based. Commanders frequently
transition to this form of offensive maneuver as part of an exploitation or pursuit. A turning
movement differs from envelopment in two ways. First, a force executing a turning movement
does not engage the enemy in the enemy’s current locations but seeks their displacement. Second,
the force executing the turning movement typically relies on external support—such as aerial
resupply or the amphibious task force (for amphibious turning movement). Division levels and
above generally execute turning movements.

Force Organization. The commander directing a turning movement organizes available resources
to conduct three main tasks: conduct the turning movement (typically the decisive action),
conduct shaping actions, and conduct reserve operations. Although METT-T determines the
exact composition of these turning, shaping, and reserve elements, each must be able to execute
semi-independent operations across the warfighting functions. In particular, the commander must
organize and resource the turning force to execute operations independent of the main body for
extended periods of time.

                                                                   3-21


---

AMCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

                                                                          Objective Area

                                                                                             3

                                                               2

                                                                               C

                                   1 Shaping element A action diverts enemy attention.
                                   2 Turning element B outflanks enemy and arrives at objective.
                                   3 Enemy force moves (turns) out of position to pursue turning element.
                                   3 Reserve element C advances to exploit the turning elements success.

                                                   Figure 3-5. Turning Movement.

    The commander task-organizes the shaping elements and reserve elements to ensure the turning
    force’s success. Shaping elements conduct operations such as attacks, feints, and demonstrations
    designed to divert the enemy’s attention or draw resources away from the turning force’s AO. The
    reserve element prepares to exploit the turning element and shaping element’s success or counter
    unexpected enemy actions.
    Control Measures. The commander uses boundaries to establish AOs for units executing the
    turning movement. They can also use additional control measures, such as phase lines,
    contact points, objectives, LOAs, and direct fire and fire support coordination measures to
    synchronize operations.
    Planning a Turning Movement. Planners must determine three key factors when planning a
    turning movement:

       • Critical terrain that threatens the enemy’s survival, displaces them, and exposes them to defeat.
       • Which way the turning force should maneuver to the objective and the planning associated

          with that movement (e.g., movement, staging, loading assault support assets).
       • How long the turning force will operate before a linkup or relief takes place and how to

          sustain the force during that time.

    In addition, the commander conducting a turning movement also considers—
       • Exploitation and pursuit branches and sequels for shaping, turning, and reserve element.
       • Defensive operations by the turning force.

                                                                        3-22


---

                                                                                  MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

  • Linkups between the turning force and the main body.
  • Retrograde operations for the turning force.

All forces executing a turning movement must consider logistics planning, which is critical to the
maneuver itself and the exploitation of success. From maneuvering and sustaining the turning
force to avoiding culmination during pursuit, this form of maneuver not only requires significant
sustainment planning, but also the willingness of commanders to accept risk to personnel and
equipment to prevent the enemy’s escape. Logistic planners recognize that standard supporting
distances and responsibilities might not be applicable to this movement, and they adjust their
plans to use available resources. Because excessive supplies and equipment can slow operational
tempo, units carry only what is required to meet their immediate needs. Staffs establish and
maintain required supply levels in the objective area by phasing supplies on an accompanying,
follow-up (automatic and on-call), and routine basis. Ammunition and petroleum, oils, and
lubricants (POL) typically constitute the major tonnage items.

Executing a Turning Movement. The shaping and reserve elements focus on moving the turning
element to the objective area, with sufficient combat power and CSS to accomplish the mission.
Whenever possible, the turning force maneuvers without encountering the enemy. Techniques to
accomplish this include outflanking the enemy or using assault support and amphibious means to
avoid the enemy’s positions. Shaping elements support this effort by executing attacks to fix the
enemy, using feints and demonstrations to divert their attention, and applying the information
warfighting function to create and exploit information advantages in pursuit of mission objectives,
thereby corrupting the enemy’s decision-making processes. Reserve elements prepare to exploit
the turning elements successes, exploit unexpected opportunities created by the shaping element,
or reinforce shaping actions that enable the successful maneuver of the turning force.

When threatened with a turning movement, an enemy commander that has not prepared a COA
for a turning movement is in a dilemma as the original plan for defense is dissembled. First,
enemy forces must move from their original positions to meet the threat presented by the turning
force. Often enemy forces must commit available reserves against this new threat, which exposes
their reserves to friendly fires. After the turning movement, enemy forces must engage the
friendly force on ground that they have not chosen or prepared. The other option for enemy forces
is to continue to hold the terrain they occupy at the risk of becoming enveloped and potentially
encircled by friendly forces. Whenever possible, units conducting a turning movement try to reach
the terrain-oriented objective that compels enemy forces to reposition prior to encountering them.
Friendly forces finding their way into the enemy force’s rear area to rapidly exploit the situation
seek to achieve their objectives before the enemy can react. Rapid movement is essential to
prevent enemy forces from occupying previously prepared positions in the enemy force’s rear.

The maneuver of the turning element is what causes enemy forces to leave their positions. A
turning element typically conducts most of its operations outside the supporting range of the
diversion element and possibly outside its supporting distance. The turning element must contain
sufficient maneuver, functional, and multifunctional capabilities to operate independently for a
specified period. Units organize the reserve to exploit success by using either the turning element
or the diversion element.

                                                                   3-23


---

MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

    Infiltration
    An infiltration is “the movement through or into an area or territory occupied by either friendly or
    enemy troops or organizations. The movement is made, either by small groups or by individuals at
    extended or irregular intervals. When used in connection with the enemy, it implies that contact is
    avoided” (USMC Dictionary).

    Marines conduct infiltration by land, water, air, or by any combination of these means. Moving
    and assembling forces covertly through enemy positions takes a considerable amount of time.
    To successfully infiltrate an area, the force must avoid detection and engagement. Because this
    requirement limits the size and strength of the infiltrating force—and infiltrated forces alone can
    rarely defeat an enemy force—infiltration is typically used in conjunction with and in support of
    other offensive maneuvers. The commander orders an infiltration to move all or a portion of a unit
    through gaps in the enemy’s defenses to—

       • Reconnoiter enemy positions and surveil NAIs and TAIs.
       • Attack enemy held positions from an unexpected direction.
       • Support the main effort by isolating the battlespace and occupying support-by-fire positions.
       • Secure key terrain or interdict enemy LOCs.
       • Conduct ambushes and raids to disrupt the enemy’s rear area.
       • Conduct a covert breach of reinforcing obstacles.

    Special operations forces and infantry units up to regimental size typically conduct an infiltration.
    However, smaller units can do so, particularly against an enemy force that is dispersed over a wide
    area. The reverse of infiltration is exfiltration (for more information regarding exfiltration, see
    Appendix C).

    Force Organization. Typically, to be successful, the infiltrating force must avoid detection at least
    until they reach an ORP. The infiltrating unit commander organizes the main body into one or
    more infiltrating elements. The elements’ size is based on METT-T and mission requirements.
    Larger elements require greater gaps in the enemy’s defenses; the loss of one large element can
    endanger the mission, but they also increase the commander’s control, speed the execution of the
    infiltration, and provide responsive combat power. Conversely, smaller elements are harder to
    detect, require smaller gaps in the enemy defenses; the discovery or loss of one or two smaller
    elements is unlikely to endanger the mission. However, smaller elements are more difficult to
    control, require more control measures, and slow the infiltration.

    Each infiltration element organizes itself as if conducting an approach march type of movement to
    contact using security elements and a main body (see Chapter 4 for more information about
    movement to contact). In general, each infiltration element is responsible for local security and
    reconnaissance. Larger infiltration elements have increased security requirements, such as using
    an advanced guard, flank security, and rear guards. In some instances, and if resources allow, the
    commander might employ security forces along infiltration routes to conduct screen and guard
    missions for the infiltration elements (see Chapter 14).

                                                                        3-24


---

                                                                                  MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

Control Measures. Control measures for an infiltration include, at a minimum, an AO for the
infiltrating unit, one or more infiltration lanes with start points and release points (or a direction
or axis of attack), a line of departure or point of departure, linkup, and rally points, one or more
geographic or force-oriented objectives, and an LOA. The commander can impose other measures
to control the infiltration including checkpoints, phase lines, and assault positions. If it is not
necessary for the entire infiltrating unit to reassemble to accomplish its mission, the force may use
numerous smaller objectives to accomplish its purpose with the appropriate control measures for
each infiltrating element moving to its assigned objective.

An infiltration lane is a control measure that commanders use to coordinate forward and lateral
movement of infiltrating units and fix fire planning responsibilities. The commander selects
infiltration lanes that avoid the enemy, provide cover and concealment, and facilitate navigation.
Each unit assigned an infiltration lane picks their own routes within the lane and switches routes
as necessary. The left and right limits of the infiltration lane act as lateral boundaries for the unit
conducting the infiltration. Attacks by rotary or fixed wing aircraft, indirect fires, or munitions
effects that impact the lane must be coordinated with the infiltrating unit. Commanders typically
assign a single infiltration lane to company size units (although they can use more) and two or
more to larger organizations (i.e., battalion and above).

Planning an Infiltration. Planning for infiltration requires units to conduct three tasks: conducting
the infiltration, conducting follow-on actions after the infiltration is complete, and conducting
linkup and relief procedures after they accomplish the mission. Planners consider three key factors
when planning an infiltration:

  • Intelligence on the positions of the enemy. Without this intelligence, the infiltration form of
     maneuver becomes little more than a high-risk, time consuming, probing of the enemy.

  • Integrating supporting fires and information. Operations security (OPSEC), ruses, tactical
     deception, and similar information functions assist the infiltrating force in avoiding an enemy
     force, minimizing direct contact, and maximizing surprise. Units can use ground- and air-
     delivered fires to assist in tactical deception, support feints and demonstrations, and fix the
     enemy in their positions.

  • Command and control to include deconflicting communications among multiple units on
     multiple lanes; handling contingencies; synchronizing and coordinating follow-on activities;
     and conducting linkups and reliefs.

After identifying gaps or weaknesses in the enemy’s defensive positions, the commander assigns
minimum control measures to subordinate units such as AOs, infiltration lanes, and objectives.
Commanders select infiltration objectives based on the effects they want to generate, not
necessarily the relative position of the enemy. Commanders use single or multiple infiltration
lanes, depending on the size of the infiltrating force, terrain they will travel, amount of detailed
information on enemy dispositions, available time, and the number of possible lanes. Single
infiltration lanes—

  • Facilitate navigation, control, and reassembly.
  • Require the existence or creation of only one gap in the enemy’s position.
  • Reduce the area for which detailed intelligence is required.

                                                                   3-25


---

MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

    Multiple infiltration lanes—

       • Increase difficulty with maintaining control.
       • Require the existence or creation of more gaps in the enemy’s security area.
       • Reduce the possibility of compromising the entire force.

    Each subordinate unit commander picks one or more routes within their lane and establishes
    additional contact points, rally points, assault positions, and other control measures as necessary.
    Routes should provide cover and concealment while avoiding known enemy and civilian locations
    and traffic routes. Multiple routes within infiltration lanes should be far enough apart to prevent
    elements from seeing one another, but close enough that elements can swiftly move from one to
    another. Depending on METT-T, infiltration element commanders also determine the movement
    method they will employ on the routes within assigned lanes—as a whole unit, smaller elements,
    or two person teams.

    When planning for the infiltration’s movement portion, units create contingency plans for the
    following situations:

       • A lead element makes contact, but the trail elements have not started infiltrating.
       • A lead element infiltrates successfully but compromises one or more trailing elements.
       • A compromised linkup point.

    Additionally, units should identify abort criteria.

    After planning for the infiltration, planners address mission accomplishment, post-mission
    activities (e.g., linkups, relief), and sustainment. The method the infiltration force uses to linkup
    with other friendly forces is a function of the larger plan. Planners should consider the following:

       • Is the infiltration a supporting effort or the decisive action?
       • Is the linkup dependent upon success elsewhere?
       • What are the contingencies if the plan should fail?

    The answers to these questions assist logistic planning by determining what the infiltration force
    must carry, when and how they might be resupplied, and how they should execute logistic
    functions such as casualty evacuation during the operation.

    Conducting an Infiltration. Reconnaissance and security operations continue throughout the
    infiltration operations, enabling infiltration elements to maintain situational awareness of enemy
    locations and reactions. When the conditions are set by supporting efforts, the infiltrating force
    departs from the assembly area in their infiltration elements, which move to their respective start
    points, through their assigned infiltration lanes, to a release point. If infiltration elements conduct
    their movement in smaller units (e.g., a company moving by platoons) then the unit uses a series
    of linkup points to reassemble. Infiltration elements use redundant navigation methods and report
    progress and statuses to their higher headquarters.

                                                                        3-26


---

                                                                                  MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

Larger infiltration elements use an approach march technique with advance guard, main body,
flank security, and rear-guard units. The distance between these elements varies depending on
METT-T. For example, a narrow infiltration lane might require the unit to accept risk by forgoing
or bringing in their flank security. Infiltration elements should remain within supporting distance
of each other, and the main body should avoid having decisive engagement forced upon it. Upon
exiting the infiltration lanes, elements move to one or more ORPs to consolidate combat power,
refine the plan, and conduct any last minute coordination prior to continuing the mission. The
infiltration force then conducts those tasks needed to accomplish their mission.

A commander might need to abort an infiltration operation if the situation changes so drastically
during the infiltration that the infiltrating force is no longer capable of accomplishing their
mission. Examples of changes that might trigger such an action include—

  • Significant portions of the infiltrating force’s combat power are lost through navigation
     errors, enemy action, accidents, or maintenance failures.

  • Movement or significant reinforcement of a force oriented objective.
  • Detection of the infiltration by the enemy.
  • Changes in the tactical situation that render the mission unfeasible, such as the initiation of an

     enemy attack.

Penetration
A penetration is “a form of maneuver in which an attacking force seeks to rupture enemy defenses
on a narrow front to disrupt the defensive system” (USMC Dictionary). The exploiting force uses
this form of maneuver to destroy the enemy’s defense, subsequently isolating the enemy and
enabling defeat in detail. A successful penetration maneuver begins in the enemy’s security area
and passes through their main defensive positions into their rear operational area. A commander
uses this maneuver when there is no assailable flank, envelopment is impractical or will take too
much time, or enemy defenses are overextended and have exploitable weak spots. Penetrations
often require the commander to conduct breaching operations.

Organization of Forces. To penetrate a well-organized position, units requires overwhelming
combat power at the point of penetration and the resources to maintain local combat superiority
to maintain momentum and tempo. The initial penetration is weighted to ensure its success;
commanders are willing to accept risk in follow-on penetrations to do so. At a minimum,
penetrations use breach, support, and assault elements. Commanders should designate these
elements for each defensive position the force is required to penetrate. Commanders can
designate security and reserve elements to conduct reconnaissance, isolate the area of
penetration, manage expected or unexpected contingencies, and prevent the enemy from
interfering with the main effort—typically the assault element.

Control Measures. To control and synchronize the attack, a commander assigns, as a minimum—

  • An AO to every maneuver unit.
  • A line of departure or line of contact.
  • Time of attack or time of assault.
  • Phase lines.

                                                                   3-27


---

MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

       • Objectives.
       • An LOA or handover line.

    Planners establish narrow lateral boundaries for the main effort to focus overwhelming combat
    power at the point of penetration. The commander positions the LOA beyond the enemy’s main
    defensive position to provide maneuver room to complete the breach. The commander uses a
    handover line instead of an LOA if follow-and-assume forces are already designated to conduct a
    forward passage of lines (see Chapter 17). If the operation results in opportunities to exploit
    success and pursue weakened enemy, the commander adjusts existing boundaries to accommodate
    the new situation. At the small-unit level, commanders add additional control measures such as
    breaching points, lanes, checkpoints, support-by-fire positions, PLDs, attack and assault positions.
    Commanders can also designate either an axis of advance or direction of attack to further control
    maneuver and mass combat power at the point of decision.

    Planning a Penetration. Marines execute penetration maneuvers to systematically paralyze and
    overwhelm the enemy at the point of penetration, but only when that penetration can be exploited.
    In addition to analyzing likely penetration points, planners must also analyze the terrain beyond
    them to ensure maneuver elements can proceed from the breach to a decisive objective.

    The depth of the enemy position and the relative strength of attacking echelons determine the
    width of the penetration. Available artillery, air support, information capabilities, and other force
    multipliers helps add to the commander’s relative combat power at the point of decision. A wider
    gap enables a greater friendly force movement into the enemy rear area while making it more
    difficult for the enemy to close the gap. A deeper penetration eases the task of rolling up newly
    created enemy flanks exposed by the breach while making it more difficult for the enemy to
    restore their defense by withdrawal.

    Like a frontal attack, a penetration aims at the strength of the enemy defense (though boundaries
    between enemy units often offer weak points). A frontal attack may support a penetration.
    Consequently, planning centers on accomplishing the systematic defeat of the enemy’s defense in
    the area of the penetration. The commander’s plan for the penetration usually consists of the
    following four phases:

       • Isolate the area of penetration.
       • Breach the enemy’s main defensive positions.
       • Widen the breach to secure the flanks.
       • Seize the objective and exploi the success of the penetration.

    Isolating the area of penetration means denying the enemy’s ability to affect the fight. Isolation
    includes conducting information activities to disrupt and mislead enemy decision making, using
    ruses and OPSEC to mask friendly troop movements, fires to prevent support and physical
    reinforcement, and actions to inhibit the enemy’s use of supporting arms.

    Planners create detailed, synchronized plans to suppress and destroy enemy elements that can
    affect the breach, to include if and where to commit engineering forces. Planners must also
    address how to phase initial assault elements through the breach to secure the far side and expand
    the penetration, and how to rapidly push combat power through the breach, creating a gap for

                                                                        3-28


---

                                                                                   MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

further exploitation. Units often create multiple breach points to ensure this movement is
effectively conducted (to include back breaching) and to provide redundancy to the movement
plan. (See MCTP 3-34B for more information on breaches and breaching.) Command and control
of this portion of the penetration is critical and commanders should rely on secondary and tertiary
means of signals and communications, so combat power moves rapidly into and through the point
of penetration.

The final phase of the plan (seize the objective and exploit the success of the penetration) requires
detailed coordination and synchronization. Units must lift or shift isolation fires as needed to prevent
the enemy from interdicting the penetration point. Units typically conduct battle handovers and
forward passage of lines, and CSS must phase forward. Finally, equipment and personnel casualties
retrograde through the same movement channels inuse by elements moving forward. In this phase,
planners ensure friendly forces are far enough forward to enable displace or destroy the enemy’s rear
forces. The gap must be held open, diverging combat power to roll up enemy flanks risks allowing
the enemy to successfully withdraw and reconstitute the defense.

Executing a Penetration. The following paragraphs discuss the four phases of executing a
penetration maneuver (see Figure 3-6).

        Objective Area                                                                Objective Area

                                                                                            B

                                                                                               5

     1             2                                                               A        C

              B                                                                          6
