        C

1 Support element A delivers suppressive and destructive fire to enemy positions.  4 Breach element B continues to objective.
2 Breach element B penetrates enemy's main line of resistance.                     5 Assault element C seizes and destroys enemy positions.
3 Assault element (follow-and-support element) C trails breach element.            6 Reserve element D reinforces and secures the breach flanks.

                        Figure 3-6. Penetration.

Isolate the Area of Penetration. Support elements conduct shaping actions to set the conditions for
a successful breach, which marks the beginning of the penetration. Such support includes creating
information advantages, which starts before the operation and continues throughout the maneuver.
Supporting arms deliver fires in the vicinity of the breach site fix enemy reserves, and interdict
movement routes into the penetration area. Feints, demonstrations, and frontal attacks reinforce
information effects and fix the enemy in their positions. Finally, depending on METT-T, other
forms of maneuver, such as infiltration and vertical envelopment, deliver supporting efforts
directly into the enemy’s rear operational area to further isolate the area.

Breach the Enemy’s Main Defensive Positions. Once the support elements sets the conditions, the
commander commits the breach element on a relatively narrow front focusing combat power on the
penetration point and close-in objectives that support it. Support elements deliver suppressive and
destructive fires to enable the maneuver of the breach and assault elements. The assault element

                        3-29


---

MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

    moves rapidly through breaches to secure the breach site and the immediate area before continuing
    forward. Other support elements, or the reserve element, with follow-and-support missions, trail
    the assault element. See Appendix C for more information on follow-and-support and follow-and-
    assume tactical tasks.

    The commander monitors operations, ensuring that supporting efforts coordinate and synchronize
    their actions with the progress of the breach and assault elements (e.g., shifting fires, electromagnetic
    warfare, information activities); continue to disrupt enemy reactions; and move forward to occupy
    other support positions. The commander also ensures follow-on units are prepared to immediately
    move forward and reinforce or exploit the breach. The intelligence staff tracks reports and battle
    damage assessments to help the commander determine whether subordinate forces are penetrating
    the enemy’s main defensive positions and not just the enemy’s security area.

    Widen the Breach to Secure the Flanks. Upon penetrating the main defenses, friendly
    forces begin to widen the breach by conducting shallow envelopments or attacks by fire to
    hold it open and progressively widen its flanks. This task typically falls to supporting elements,
    trailing the assault element, tasked with follow-and-support missions. If commanders choose to
    commit the reserve for this task, they either accept risk or reconstitute the reserve element from
    another part of the force. The actions of supporting arms continue to be closely coordinated
    to simultaneously maintain isolation of the penetration area, support the assault element, and
    support follow-and-support elements and their missions. Additional supporting efforts, such as
    combat engineers, are committed forward to assist in improving lanes and to provide mobility
    and countermobility support to elements widening and securing the flanks.

    Seize the Objective and Exploit Success. The assault element conducts the decisive action by
    seizing the objectives that destroy the continuity of the enemy’s defense. Objectives can be
    geographic, force-oriented, or both. The commander commits other follow-and-support elements
    to enable the assault element to continue their maneuver. If the distance from the point of
    penetration to the objective is too great for the initial assault element to continue, or unexpected
    enemy actions demand it, the commander uses follow-and-assume elements to pass forward,
    become the new main effort, and continue the assault. Coordination and synchronization remain
    critical to phase exploitation units forward, shift supporting arms, and counter enemy actions.

   COMMON OFFENSIVE PLANNING CONSIDERATIONS

    Accurate and lethal weapons, increased tactical mobility, ever-present sensors, and a complex
    operational environment all characterize contemporary MDCA warfare. Units have a higher
    probability of tactical success when they can visualize the battlespace, understand the implications
    of existing friendly and enemy dispositions, and take effective action. The planning considerations
    for the offense also apply to the defense with situationally appropriate modifications.

    Only a determined offense with a high tempo and conducted to great depth, can destroy the enemy
    force. The attacker’s principal advantage is that it possesses the initiative. Maintaining the initiative
    enables units to engage the enemy at the time and in a manner of their choosing. Attacking units
    have the time and opportunity to develop a plan and to concentrate the effects of subordinate forces

                                                                        3-30


---

                                                                                  MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

and combat enablers to create conditions for success. Units strike the enemy in unexpected ways at
unexpected times and places. They rapidly and violently execute these attacks, which are
unpredictable and seek to disorient enemy forces.

Attacking units maintain tempo by rapidly following up on attacks to keep enemy forces off-balance
and to deny them the ability to recover. Friendly forces develop flexible plans that allow them to
take advantage of opportunities to maintain the initiative and dictate operational tempo. Because
offensive operations are intense and have a high tempo, units take proactive measures to prevent
culmination prior to accomplishing their assigned mission. Friendly operations must be fast enough
to prevent effective counteraction; therefore, attacking units change their means and methods before
enemy forces can adapt and respond.

Command and Control
Synchronizing the seven warfighting functions through planning and preparation prior to
execution increases a unit’s effectiveness. However, the fluid nature of combat requires leaders to
orchestrate the actions of subordinates during the execution phase. Leaders determine where they
can best affect the flow of operations and influence critical events by redirecting the effects of
committed forces, changing priorities of support, or employing echelon reserves. To effectively
redirect, units should be well forward in the echelon’s formation, usually with the force designated
to conduct the main effort or at a location where a key decision or task must be accomplished to
enable the success of the main effort. Examples of key tasks or decisions can include executing a
forward passage of lines or a wet-gap crossing. Once the unit conducting the main effort makes
contact with the enemy, friendly forces quickly move to where they best can assess the situation
and continue the offensive operation.

At battalion and above, units anticipate requirements to shift the main effort during an offense to
press the battle and keep enemy forces off balance. They develop decision points to support these
changes using both human and technical means to validate decision points.

In addition to assigning objectives and identifying decision points, leaders at all echelons consider
how to exploit advantages that arise during operations and how to seize intermediate and final
objectives. Leaders exploit success by aggressively executing the plan, taking advantage of
subordinate unit’s initiative, and employing other units. The echelon reserve also provides a
flexible capability to exploit unforeseen advantages.

Units maintain communications and comprehensive throughput of information among all units.
They plan how to position and reposition command and control systems to help control operations.
Units plan how to expand the communications coverage to accommodate increased distances and
enemy efforts to deny and degrade friendly communications systems. Units provide for redundant
communication means.

A unit maintains its common operating picture throughout an operation. For a common operating
picture to aid a unit in maintaining situational awareness, the unit requires timely and frequent
updates of relevant information. All echelons report information on the disposition and activities
of friendly and enemy forces.

                                                                   3-31


---

MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

    Maneuver
    Although inherent to all military operations, the concept of the offense is inextricably linked to
    maneuver. To attack one must maneuver against the enemy—regardless of their relative
    mobility—to strike blows that cause damage and create defeat. Maneuver is combined with fires
    to avoid enemy strengths and create or exploit enemy gaps. Commanders use maneuver to achieve
    surprise and create greater effects than the force would otherwise accomplish. Security forces and
    information activities mask maneuver, other supporting efforts shape the battlespace for the
    success of maneuver, and the main effort delivers the decisive action through maneuver. Finally,
    maneuver combined with fires enables friendly forces to successfully close with, shock, and
    destroy or defeat the enemy through close combat. Close combat, which encompasses all actions
    that place friendly forces in a direct fire fight with the enemy, is supported by direct and indirect
    fires and other assets. Close combat can also include hand-to-hand combat with the enemy.

    Two planning factors of offensive maneuver are objective type and relative mobility. Objective
    type is critical because it addresses the purpose of maneuver. (Is the objective a key piece of
    terrain or an enemy force?) If a unit is maneuvering against terrain that can provide an advantage
    over the enemy, its forces are only relevant to friendly forces if they are moving, reaching, and
    seizing the objective. Friendly forces may even choose to bypass them or force them to withdraw.

    Relative mobility is the friendly force's mobility compared to the enemy (i.e., are friendly units
    more or less mobile than the enemy?). For example, mounted forces in armored vehicles are more
    mobile than dismounted enemy forces.

    Combat Formations. Units conducting ground movement use combat formations in the presence
    of the enemy or when contact with an enemy is likely or intended. As it relates to ground
    operations, a combat formation is an ordered arrangement of forces for a specific purpose and
    describes the general configuration of the formation. A commander can use seven different
    combat formations depending on METT-T:

       • Column.
       • Line.
       • Echelon (left or right).
       • Box.
       • Diamond.
       • Wedge.
       • Vee.

    Combat formations allow a unit to move on the battlefield in a posture suited to the mission and
    commander’s intent. Planners weigh terrain characteristics, movement methods, and visibility to
    determine the arrangement and location of the unit’s personnel and vehicles within a given
    formation. A unit might employ a series of combat formations during an operation; each has its
    advantages and disadvantages. Subordinate units within a combat formation can also employ their
    own combat formations, consistent with their situation. When choosing formations and moving
    between them, commanders consider the advantages and disadvantages of each as they apply to
    command and control, maintenance, firepower orientation, ability to mass fires, and flexibility.

                                                                        3-32


---

                                                                                  MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

All combat formations use one or more of the three movement techniques: traveling, traveling
overwatch, and bounding overwatch. Chapter 15 describes these three movement techniques. By
designating the combat formation, the commander—

  • Establishes the geographic relationship between units.
  • Indicates probable friendly reactions to enemy contact.
  • Indicates the level of security desired.
  • Establishes the preponderant orientation of subordinate weapon systems.
  • Postures friendly forces for attack or defense.
Column. In a column formation, elements are placed one behind another. The unit moves in
column formation when the commander does not anticipate enemy contact, the objective is
distant, and speed and control are critical. Figure 3-7 depicts a column formation. When present,
the fire support units’ location within the column reflects the column’s length and the range fans
of those fire support systems. Usually, the lead element uses a traveling overwatch technique
while the following units are in traveling formation. The trailing element moves at variable speeds
and may pause for short periods to overwatch the lead element. Employing a column formation—
  • Provides the best formation to move large forces quickly, particularly with limited routes or in

     limited visibility.
  • Limits enemy contact to a small part of the total force while facilitating control and reaction

     to that contact.
  • Provides a base for easy transition to other formations.
  • Works in restricted terrain.

                                              Figure 3-7. Column Formation.
A disadvantage is that most of the column’s firepower can only be immediately applied from the
column’s flanks. The length of the column can negatively impact control. Additionally, there is a
potential for inadvertently bypassing enemy units or positions and exposing the unit’s flanks and
rear or running head-on into an enemy deployed perpendicular to the column.

                                                                   3-33


---

MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

    Line. In a line formation, the unit’s subordinate ground maneuver elements move abreast of each
    other (see Figure 3-8). A commander employs this formation when assaulting an objective because
    it concentrates firepower to the front in the direction of movement. A line formation also—

       • Facilitates speed and shock in closing with an enemy.
       • Enables the coverage of wide frontages.
       • Facilitates the occupation of attack-by-fire or support-by-fire positions.

                                                     Figure 3-8. Line Formation.
    The disadvantages of using a line formation include the following:

       • Provides less flexibility of maneuver than other formations because it does not distribute units
         in depth.

       • Linear deployment allows a unit deployed on-line to bring only limited firepower to bear on
         either flank.

       • Provides limited or no reserve.
       • Limits overwatch forces.
       • Limits control of a unit using a line formation in restricted terrain or in limited visibility.
    Echelon. In an echelon formation (see Figure 3-9), commanders arrange subordinate elements on
    an angle to the left (echelon left) or to the right (echelon right) of the direction of attack. This
    formation provides for firepower forward and to the flank of the direction of the echelon and
    facilitates control in open areas. Echelons enables forces not in contact with the enemy to
    maneuver against known enemy forces. It provides minimal security to the opposite flank of the
    direction of the echeloning. Units operating on the flank of a larger formation commonly use this
    formation. The primary disadvantages of the echelon formation are that it is more difficult for
    commanders to maintain control in restricted terrain or in limited visibility, and there is a lack of
    firepower available on the opposite side the echelon.

                                                                        3-34


---

              MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

Echelon Left  Echelon Right

Figure 3-9. Echelon Left and Echelon Right.

Box. In a box formation, commanders arrange subordinate elements in a square. It is a flexible
formation that provides equal firepower in all directions. Commanders typically use this
formation when they know the enemy’s location. With this formation, half the force could be
decisively engaged at the same time, limiting the combat power available to maneuver. The box
formation arranges the unit with two forward and two trail maneuver elements (see Figure 3-10).
A unit with only three maneuver elements, cannot adopt the box formation unless it is reinforced.
The subordinate elements usually move in a column formation with flank security. Commanders
with general knowledge about the enemy often use it when executing an approach march,
exploitation, or pursuit. Employing a box formation—

• Enables the unit to quickly and easily change to any other formation.
• Facilitates rapid movement, yet still provides all around security.
• Provides firepower to the front and flanks.
• Facilitates control.

The primary disadvantages are that it requires sufficient maneuver space for dispersion and
multiple routes. At the battalion and company level, enemy units could converge on one element
at a time as the other elements’ direct fires are masked by other friendly forces.

Figure 3-10. Box Formation Example.
                    3-35


---

MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

    Diamond. A diamond formation is a variation of the box formation with one maneuver unit
    leading, maneuver units positioned on each flank, and the remaining maneuver unit to the rear
    (see Figure 3-11). In this formation, subordinate elements usually move in a column formation
    with flank security. It is most effective during approach marches, exploitations, or pursuits when
    the commander has only general knowledge about the enemy. Employing a diamond formation—

       • Enables the commander to maneuver either left or right immediately, without first
         repositioning, regardless of which subordinate element makes contact with the enemy. This is
         the chief advantage of and the difference between a diamond and a box formation.

       • Facilitates making enemy contact with the smallest possible force yet still provides
         all-around security.

       • Provides firepower to the front and flanks.
       • Changes easily and quickly to another formation.
       • Facilitates speed of movement while remaining easy to control.
       • Provides an uncommitted force for use as a reserve.
    The primary disadvantages of this formation are that it requires—
       • Sufficient space for dispersion laterally and in depth.
       • Four subordinate maneuver elements.
       • Multiple available routes.

                                                  Figure 3-11. Diamond Formation.
    Wedge. Commanders use the wedge formation to arrange forces to attack an enemy appearing to the
    front and flanks (see Figure 3-12). A unit with only three subordinate maneuver elements can adopt
    the wedge formation. The commander uses the wedge when contact with the enemy is possible or
    expected, but the enemy’s location and dispositions are vague. It is the preferred formation for an
    approach march because initial contact is usually with only one unit, leaving the others free to

                                                                        3-36


---

                                                                                  MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

maneuver and develop the situation. Within the wedge, subordinate units employ the formation best
suited to the terrain, visibility, and likelihood of contact. Employing a wedge formation—

  • Provides maximum fire power forward and allows a large portion of the unit’s firepower to be
     used on the flanks.

  • Enables units to rapidly cross open terrain.
  • Facilitates control.
  • Enables rapid changes in the force’s orientation.
  • Facilitates rapid change to other formations.

                                              Figure 3-12. Wedge Formation.
The primary disadvantages to the wedge formation are that it—

  • Requires sufficient space for dispersion laterally and in depth.
  • Requires the availability of multiple routes.
  • Lacks ease of control in restricted terrain or limited visibility.
Vee. The vee formation disposes the unit with two maneuver elements abreast and one or more
units trailing (see Figure 3-13). This arrangement is well suited for an advance against a known
threat to the front. The commander might use this formation when expecting enemy contact and
the enemy’s location and disposition are known. Employing a vee formation—
  • Provides maximum firepower forward and good firepower to the flanks, but the firepower on

     the flanks is less than that provided by the wedge.
  • Facilitates continued maneuver after contact is made and a rapid transition to the assault.
  • Enables units to quickly change to other formations.
The primary disadvantages to this formation are that it—
  • Makes changing the direction of movement (e.g., 90 degree turn) more difficult than a wedge.
  • Makes control in restricted terrain and limited-visibility conditions difficult.
  • Requires sufficient space for dispersion laterally and in depth.

                                                                   3-37


---

MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

                                                     Figure 3-13. Vee Formation.
    Limited-Visibility Operations. Typically, limited visibility presents significant control problems
    when conducting offensive operations. However, the force with the capability and training to
    operate effectively in limited visibility can achieve significant advantages over the force that
    cannot operate in these conditions. For limited-visibility conditions to be an opportunity
    rather than a disadvantage, commanders must ensure they train to fight and operate in these
    conditions—to include phasing from daylight to night operations.
    Regardless of technology, units conducting operations in limited visibility or adverse weather
    require increased planning and preparation. Planners develop significant redundancies in control
    methods such as terrain associated reference points, route marking, guides, or GPS [Global
    Positioning System] waypoints to guard against failure or degradation of night vision.
    Additionally, the commander develops GO/NO GO criteria and decision points about using
    illumination. Despite technology, limited-visibility operations degrade the capabilities of
    individuals and units. Cognitive abilities degrade more rapidly than physical strength and
    endurance. Night vision devices degrade the user’s depth perception. Ideally, planning should
    include recuperation time for units conducting a night attack before being committed to other
    operations. While always a consideration, the fighting load of Marines conducting night
    operations should be limited.
    Assured Mobility. Assured mobility is “a framework—of processes, actions, and capabilities—that
    assures the ability of a force to deploy, move, and maneuver where and when desired, without
    interruption or delay, to achieve the mission” (USMC Dictionary). When planning offensive
    operations, commanders and staffs apply the following assured mobility fundamentals:

       • Predict potential obstacles to mobility by analyzing enemy TTP, capabilities, and likely
          countermeasures; the effects of terrain; and civil considerations in terms of vehicular traffic,
          dislocated civilians, etc.

       • Detect the location of avenues of approach, natural and man-made obstacles, and enemy
          obstacle resource capabilities.

       • Prevent negative effects on friendly mobility through shaping actions such as eliminating
          enemy countermobility capabilities, preparing to mitigate natural obstacles, and destroying

                                                                        3-38


---

                                                                                  MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

     terrorist networks implanting improvised explosive devices and mines. Prevent also includes
     denying the enemy the ability to disrupt or destroy friendly mobility capabilities—such as
     protecting breaching assets until they must be committed.
  • Avoid likely impediments to mobility, whether in terms of enemy action, natural features,
     friendly shortfalls, or combinations of all three—even if this results in the selection of less
     favorable, but unexpected routes.
  • Neutralize obstacles and impediments as soon as possible to allow unrestricted movement of
     forces. The TTP available to do this are a factor of METT-T, ROE, and the type of military
     operation being conducted. For example, how one mitigates an urban minefield in a major
     combat operation will be different from mitigating that same urban minefield in a
     peacekeeping operation.
  • Protect by implementing survivability and other force protection measures that will prevent
     observation of friendly forces and degrade or eliminate the effects of enemy actions. This can
     include actions from creating new routes that allow forces to move unobserved and
     unmolested, to the employment of mine rollers, to the use of electronic warfare systems to
     disrupt improvised explosive devices.

For more information on assured mobility, see MCTP 3-34A, Combined Arms Mobility.

Mobility. In the offense, units rely on mobility to concentrate combat power, conduct shaping
operations, exploit success, and pursue a retreating enemy. Mobility enables friendly forces to
achieve surprise by passing through or over terrain thought impassable, or by creating new routes
to allow units to mass undetected by the enemy. Mobility allows friendly forces to retain momentum
and dictate tempo by passing quickly and efficiently through natural and man-made obstacles.
Mobility operations are “those combined arms activities that mitigate the effects of natural and
man-made obstacles to enable freedom of movement and maneuver” (USMC Dictionary). Mobility
operations include six primary tasks:

  • Conduct breaching.
  • Conduct clearing (areas and routes).
  • Conduct gap crossing.
  • Construct and maintain combat roads and trails.
  • Construct and maintain forward airfields and landing zones (LZs).
  • Conduct traffic management and control.

Maintaining momentum in the offense often requires breaching operations. Ideally, obstacles are
bypassed. If necessary, the preferred method of conducting breaching operations is employing a
hasty breach, which avoids the loss of time and momentum associated with deliberate breaches. A
hasty breach is the rapid creation of lanes through minefields, barriers, fortifications, or enemy
obstacles by any expedient method when the time factor does not permit detailed reconnaissance,
deliberate breaching, or bypassing the obstacle. Commanders ensure that maneuver forces have
the means to conduct hasty breaches.

                                                                   3-39


---

MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

    A deliberate breach is “the systematically planned and executed creation of a lane or clear route
    through a barrier, obstacle, or fortification” (USMC Dictionary). The fundamentals of assured
    mobility allow commanders to determine likely breach sites, and if unavoidable, how to best
    shape and conduct efficient deliberate breaches. Breaching operations use a reverse planning
    sequence from the objective back to the assembly area. For more information on breaching, see
    MCTP 3-34A.

    Units conduct clearing operations to eliminate enemy obstacles or residual obstacles within an
    assigned area or along a specified route. A clearing operation is “an operation designed to clear or
    neutralize all mines and obstacles from a route or area” (DoD Dictionary). Typically, an MDCA
    force built around an engineer-based clearing force conducts clearing operations. Units can
    conduct clearing operations as a single mission to open or reopen a route or area or on a recurring
    basis to support efforts to defeat a sustained threat to a critical route. For more information on
    clearing operations, see MCTP 3-34A.

    Rivers and other gaps remain major obstacles despite advances in technology and aviation
    support. Wet gap crossings are among the most critical, complex, and vulnerable of military
    operations. Similar to breaches, hasty crossings are preferred to maintain momentum and limit the
    amount of defensive preparation time available to the enemy. The size of the gap, as well as the
    enemy and friendly situations, dictate the specific TTP units use to conduct the crossing.
    Deliberate gap crossings typically require augmentation of amphibious and engineering assets.
    For more information on gap crossings, see MCTP 3-34A. See Chapter 22 for more information
    on mobility.

    Countermobility. Commanders use countermobility operations to enable economy of force
    operations, isolate the battlespace, and provide security. Countermobility operations are “those
    combined arms activities that use or enhance the effects of natural and man-made obstacles to
    deny enemy freedom of movement and maneuver” (USCM Dictionary). Units create obstacles to
    provide security to flanks and deny the enemy counterattack routes as friendly forces advance into
    the enemy’s defense. Similarly, units use obstacles to provide force protection for consolidation
    and reorganization after a successful offensive operation. Countermobility enables economy of
    force—smaller forces able to defend larger areas—allowing units to mass combat power for
    offensive action elsewhere. Finally, they help isolate the battlespace, preventing reinforcement
    and withdrawal and dividing the enemy’s defense into portions for defeat in detail. Although
    countermobility operations have significant utility in the offense, commanders ensure that
    conducting countermobility does not hinder offensive maneuver. Countermobility includes four
    primary tasks:

       • Site obstacles.
       • Construct, emplace, or detonate obstacles.
       • Mark, report, and record obstacles.
       • Maintain obstacle integration.

    During the planning phase, planners identify avenues of approach that offer natural flank protection
    to an attacking force are identified, such as rivers or ridgelines. Obstacles are sited and constructed,
    bridges destroyed, and minefields emplaced to interdict roads, trails, and avenues of approach.

                                                                        3-40


---

                                                                                  MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

Units can use natural terrain features such as swamps, canals, lakes, forests, and escarpments to
quickly reinforce flank security. To maintain momentum, Marines conducting countermobility
operations in the offense focus on rapid emplacement and flexibility. Engineer support must keep
pace with advancing maneuver forces and be prepared to emplace obstacles alongside them.
Planners ensure that mobility operations are properly prioritized, and that engineers receive both
the resources and planning guidance necessary to make decisions that support the commander’s
plan during execution. Siting, construction, and emplacement planning consider blocking enemy
avenues of approach and withdrawal, containing bypassed enemy forces, and isolating the
battlespace from reinforcement. Depending on METT-T and the ROE, commanders can use aircraft
or artillery to emplace minefields containing scatterable munitions. These scatterable munitions can
be tailored to remain active for a selected length of time before they self-deactivate or self-destruct.
Minefields containing scatterable munitions might be unmarked munitions because some mines
may lie outside the intended boundary of the minefield. Obstacles must be marked, reported, and
recorded, and properly integrated with maneuver. Chapter 8 addresses integrating countermobility
into the defense. See Chapter 21 and MCTP 3-34B for a more information on countermobility.

Fires
Fires is “the use of weapon systems or other actions to create specific lethal or nonlethal effects on
a target” (DoD Dictionary). Fire support is “fires that directly support land, maritime, amphibious,
space, cyberspace, and special operations forces to engage enemy forces, combat formations, and
facilities in pursuit of tactical and operational objectives” (DoD Dictionary). Commanders and
staffs use the targeting process to select and prioritize targets, and weaponeer to those targets to
support the offensive SOM. The four fire support tasks are—

  • Supporting forces in contact.
  • Supporting the commander’s concept of the operation.
  • Integrating fire support with the SOM.
  • Sustaining fire support.

Commanders use organic, lethal and nonlethal fires to create numerous options for generating
lethal and nonlethal effects to gain and maintain fire superiority, which enables maneuver. The
commander uses long-range fire support systems (e.g., artillery and air support) and short-range
fire support systems (e.g., mortars) to engage the enemy throughout the battlespace. Fire support
planning, which results in a fire support plan, is a continuous, concurrent cycle of analyzing the
enemy and friendly situation; conducting targeting; tasking and allocating fire support assets;
scheduling fires; and coordinating execution to integrate fire support with the SOM and maximize
combat power. It relies upon top-down planning and bottom-up refinement. Fire support planning
answers the question, “How will fires support the SOM?” In the offense, the SOM typically
includes of the following:

  • Gain and maintain enemy contact.
  • Disrupt the enemy.
  • Fix the enemy.
  • Maneuver.
  • Follow through.

                                                                   3-41


---

MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

    In support of the SOM, the staff determines—

       • What types of targets to attack.
       • How to acquire and track targets.
       • When to attack targets.
       • What fire support assets are available to attack targets.
       • How to coordinate the attacks.
       • How to integrate with information for the purpose of creating and exploiting information

         advantages in pursuit of mission objectives.
       • What defines success.

    When planning offensive fires, fire support planners consider—

       • Assigning priority of fires to the main effort.
       • Planning fires to disrupt the enemy's capability to conduct command and control.
       • Planning fires on critical points in movement and on known or suspected enemy direct

         fire positions.
       • Planning priority targets.
       • Planning fires to support the momentum of the supported unit (e.g., screens, suppressive

         fires on bypassed enemy defenses or obstacle clearing).
       • Planning fires on likely assembly areas.
       • Planning fires on the objective, on gaps, and beyond the objective to exploit success.
       • Preventing the enemy’s withdrawal from, or reinforcement of, the objective.
       • Creating a gap in the enemy’s defenses or causing them to react where they become

         vulnerable (e.g., fires to disrupt their direct fire weapons to facilitate maneuver of the
         supported unit).
       • Attacking enemy indirect fire assets to keep them from firing on friendly forces as
         they advance.
       • Planning fires on flanks and crossings of exposed areas, such as smoke and air- and
         artillery-delivered scatterable munitions.
       • Ensuring fire support assets are positioned and supplied to provide continuous support
         during the attack.
       • Creating fire support control measures as close to maneuver elements as possible to
         maximize fire support to maneuver, shape the battlespace, and engage targets of opportunity.

    As the attacking force moves forward, they use preparatory fires suppress, neutralize, or destroy
    enemy positions, thereby shaping the battlespace to create conditions favorable to maneuver.
    Planners weigh the probable effects of preparatory fires against the potential advantages of
    achieving surprise, particularly in limited-visibility conditions. Whether the commander chooses
    to make an assault without using preparatory fires, they still plan fires to use if necessary.

                                                                        3-42


---

                                                                                  MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

Quick-Fire Support Planning. Commanders use quick fire support planning to respond to
immediate threats using the available fire support assets. During quick-fire support, when
time does not permit detailed evaluation of targets and fire planning, the supported unit’s FSC
has authority to plan supporting arms fires. The effective assignment of joint forward observers
and target acquisition assets to quick fire or exclusive nets also provides responsive fires.
Quick-fire nets allow the lead observers to associate directly with specific field artillery or
mortar fire units. These kinds of communication arrangements enhance responsiveness through
streamlined net structures and focused priorities. Communications planning should also include
the need for communication nets for the clearing of targets for rotary- and fixed-wing attacks.
See MCTP 3-10F for more information on quick-fire plans and nets in fire support planning.

Air and Missile Defense Planning. The GCE’s primary means of air defense is the employment of
passive air defense measures and the ACE’s execution of antiair operations in accordance with the
joint force air component commander. Passive air defense measures are an essential and inherent
part of air and missile defense planning at all levels. If an enemy attacks a unit’s aerial systems in
assembly areas, attack positions, or while moving, the unit disperses and conducts small-arms air
defense. Enemy air threats consist of UAS and rotary- and fixed-wing aircraft. As part of the air
defense plan, the GCE accounts for, and supports, the deployment of various radar systems and the
presence and maneuver of light antiair defense units. The commander at each echelon establishes
air defense priorities based on the concept of operations, SOM, air situation, and the air defense
priorities established by higher headquarters. If the commander has air defense systems directly
supporting the attack, their coverage is generally weighted toward the unit’s decisive action and
establishes a protective corridor over the terrain traversed by the subordinate unit or units
conducting the decisive action. Command and control of all air defense assets requires complete
and timely communications to ensure the correct weapon status for the protection of friendly air
support assets. See MCTP 10-10B, Multi-Service Tactics, Techniques, and Procedures for Air and
Missile Defense (AMD), for more information.

Information Activities
Marines apply the information warfighting function to create and exploit information advantages
in pursuit of mission objectives. To do this, Marines consider and integrate the information
warfighting function with the other functions to achieve focus and unity of effort in operations.
Marines apply the warfighting function to create and exploit three information advantages:

  • Systems Overmatch. Systems overmatch refers to the technical advantage of one side over
     another, yielding fires, intelligence, maneuver, logistics, force protection, or C2 advantages.

  • Prevailing Narrative. A prevailing narrative influences public opinion or perception, yielding
     trust, credibility, or believability advantages.

  • Force Resiliency. From an information perspective, resiliency embeds a Marine or unit’s
     ability to resist, counter, and prevail against enemy and adversary reconnaissance,
     technical disruptions, and foreign malign activity such as misinformation, disinformation,
     and propaganda.

Information serves a vital role in every activity Marines undertake. It is fundamental to
intelligence, command and control, situational understanding, decision making, etc. The Marine
Corps uses the term information environment to refer to the global competitive space that spans
the warfighting domains, where all operations depend on information. It includes information

                                                                   3-43


---

MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

    itself and all relevant social, cultural, psychological, technical, and physical factors that affect the
    employment of forces and bear on the decisions of commanders. Information is inseparable from
    the physical environment, allowing commanders to plan and conduct operations in all warfighting
    domains to create or exploit information advantages. The inseparable nature of information from
    the operational environment allows a commander to plan and conduct operations to leverage the
    power of information by using the following four functions of information:

       • Information Generation. All deliberate and coordinated activities undertaken to gain and
         maintain access to the information environment; build awareness of information-based
         threats, vulnerabilities, and opportunities; hold opponent systems at risk; and create the
         necessary information to plan and conduct operations.

       • Information Preservation. All deliberate and coordinated activities undertaken to protect and
          defend the information, systems, and networks used to facilitate planning and friendly
          operations against internal and external threats.

       • Information Denial. All deliberate and coordinated activities undertaken to deny, disrupt,
         degrade, or destroy the information needed by the opponent to understand the situation, make
         decisions, or act in a coordinated fashion.

       • Information Projection. All deliberate and coordinated activities undertaken to communicate,
         transmit, or deliver information of any type to inform, influence, or deceive an observer or
         targeted system.

    The role of information in the offense is to enable the commander to successfully maneuver and
    mass combat power at the point of decision. Information is integrated with fires and maneuver to
    accomplish this purpose. Marines use various information activities to support of this goal, such
    as using tactical deception (TAC-D) to induce enemy action or inaction, electromagnetic warfare
    attacks to disrupt enemy C2 networks at critical moments in the battle, or to mitigate interference
    in military operations. Marines conduct information activities by integrating, coordinating, and
    synchronizing the following information capabilities:

       • Tactical Deception. Tactical deception is a friendly activity that causes enemy commanders to
          take action or cause inaction that is detrimental to their objectives. It creates windows of
          opportunity by causing the target to react or falsely interpret friendly operations. See Chapter
          20 for a detailed discussion of TAC-D.

       • Electromagnetic Warfare. Electromagnetic warfare uses offensive and defensive TTP to
          shape, disrupt, and exploit an enemy or adversary such as disrupting or destroying enemy C2
          networks, disrupting improvised explosive devices, assisting military deception activities,
          disrupting enemy air defense systems, protecting friendly C2 networks, etc.

       • Operational Security. Operational security contributes to the offense by denying enemy or
          adversary access to information, which slows the enemy’s or adversary’s decision-making
          cycle, thereby providing opportunity for friendly forces to attain objectives.

       • Military Information Support. Military information support aids the offense by undermining
         the enemy’s will to resist, increasing the acceptance of friendly forces in occupied territory,
         increasing the element of surprise, encouraging the noninterference by civilians with military
         operations, and increasing the psychological effect of military deception activities on enemy
         leaders and forces.

                                                                        3-44


---

                                                                                  MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

  • Cyberspace Actions. Cyberspace actions are planned in conjunction with electromagnetic
     warfare using both offensive and defense cyberspace operations to attack, deceive, degrade,
     disrupt, deny, exploit, and defend electromagnetic information and infrastructure.

  • Physical Attack. Physical attack is applying combat power to physically neutralize or destroy
     enemy forces, equipment, installations, and networks associated with their C2 system. Since
     the enemy can recover, units typically conduct physical attack at a particular moment or to
     generate an effect for a certain time.

  • Physical Security. Physical security consists of friendly actions taken to prevent or mitigate
     an enemy’s attempt to conduct physical attacks against friendly C2 forces, equipment,
     installations, and networks.

  • Information Assurance. Information assurance uses information security and computer
     security to protect friendly information—and the credibility and accuracy of that
     information—from enemy attack or influence.

  • Controlling Electromagnetic Emissions and Frequency Hopping. Controlling electromagnetic
     emissions and frequency hopping ensures units protect their command, control,
     communications, computers, intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance systems.

  • Counterintelligence. Counterintelligence is the intelligence function focused on force
     protection—identifying and counteracting enemy attempts at espionage, sabotage,
     subversion, or terrorism.

  • Communication Strategy and Operations. Marine Corps communication strategy and
     operations (also referred to as COMMSTRAT) communicates and engages domestic and
     foreign publics to build understanding, credibility, and trust. Because of legal considerations
     regarding communication strategies and operations, the plan must have an awareness of all
     information activities, integrate with those that it is appropriate to integrate with, and avoid
     compromising others. Communication strategies and operations also provides commanders
     operational imagery and supports information activities, with visual information. For more
     information, see MCTP 3-30F, Marine Corps Public Affairs, and MCTP 3-32A, Marine
     Air-Ground Task Force Combat Camera.

  • Civil-Military Actions. Civil-military operations include any activity of the command
     concerned with the relationships between the force and the civil authorities and people in the
     unit’s AO. They primarily focus on enabling military operations by mitigating issues with the
     civil populace. Civil-military operations is the responsibility of commanders at all levels,
     regardless of whether they receive civil affairs personnel or other enablers. For more
     information, see MCTP 3-03A, Marine Air-Ground Task Force Civil-Military Operations.

  • Defense Support to Public Diplomacy. Defense support to public diplomacy consists of
     activities and measures taken by Department of Defense (DoD) components to support and
     facilitate the United States (US) Government’s public diplomacy efforts. Much of the
     operational-level information activity conducted in any theater is directly linked to public
     diplomacy objectives. Defense support to public diplomacy requires coordination among US
     Government departments and agencies, and all DoD components.

See MCWP 8-10, Information in Marine Corps Operations, for more information.

                                                                   3-45


---

MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

    Intelligence
    Commanders use the intelligence preparation of the battlespace (IPB) process to understand, and
    design the framework to solve the tactical problem. A continuous process that begins even before
    mission receipt, the commander uses available ISR assets to study the terrain and confirm or deny
    the enemy’s strengths, dispositions, and likely intentions, particularly where and in what strength
    the enemy will defend. Indications of an obstacle’s location and composition and the positioning of
    engineer assets may be key in determining where and when the enemy will defend. Additionally,
    units use ISR assets to collect information about the civilian population in the AO to confirm or
    deny their numbers, locations, and likely intentions—particularly the likelihood of civilians staying
    or fleeing combat area.

    Intelligence and operations officers, in coordination with the rest of the staff, develop a synchronized
    and integrated intelligence collection plan that satisfies the commander’s decision, maneuver,
    targeting, and information requirements. A commander’s information requirements are dictated by
    METT-T, but commonly include—

       • Analysis of key terrain, observation and fields of fire, cover and concealment, obstacles,
         avenues of approach (also referred to as KOCOA). See MCTP 2-10B, MAGTF Intelligence
         Production and Analysis.

       • Locations, composition, equipment, strengths, and weaknesses of the defending enemy force,
         to include high priority targets and enemy ISR capabilities.

       • Intervisibility lines, lines-of-sight, enemy direct-fire weapon range fans.
       • Locations and range fans of enemy indirect fire weapon systems and units.
       • Effects of weather and terrain on current and projected operations.
       • Numbers, routes, and directions of movement of dislocated civilians.
       • Likely actions and reactions of civilians and third-party actors.
       • Withdrawal routes for enemy forces.
       • Anticipated timetable schedules for the enemy’s most likely COA and other probable COAs.
       • Locations of—

           Obstacles.
           Possible enemy assembly areas.
           Gaps and assailable flanks.
           Areas for friendly and enemy air assault operations.
           Enemy air defense gun and missile units.
           Enemy information assets and units.
           Enemy logistic assets.
          Enemy C2 and intelligence nodes and ISR systems and the frequencies used by the

            information systems linking these systems.

    If friendly ISR assets cannot answer the commander’s information requirements, the echelon
    intelligence staff can send a request for information to higher and adjacent units, the commander
    can commit additional resources, or the commander can decide to execute the offensive operation
    with the current information.

                                                                        3-46


---

                                                                                  MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

Logistics
In offensive operations, tactical commanders use logistics to maintain the momentum through
force sustainment. Pausing for resupply or other services risks ceding the initiative to the enemy.
Further, commanders should take advantage of windows of opportunity and launch offensive
operations with minimum advance warning time. Therefore, logistic commanders and planners
must remain closely integrated throughout the operations process (i.e., plan, execute, assess) with
their ground counterparts to be aware of these potential opportunities and likely actions to exploit
them. A key to successful offensive operations is the ability to anticipate the requirement to push
support forward, specifically regarding ammunition, fuel, replacements, and water. The
commanders of logistic elements must act, rather than react, to support requirements.

Logistic elements conduct CSS and the logistic functions as far forward, and as close to maneuver
units as possible, to maintain momentum and tempo. Units use preplanned and preconfigured
packages of essential times—such as POL and ammunition—to help maintain the offensive
movement and tempo, for short-duration offensive operations such as raids, or to support
distributed operations. The commander works with logistic officers and elements to—

  • Analyze the unit’s basic load.
  • Identify specific and critical items necessary to the operation.
  • Evaluate contingency requirements.
  • Determine sustainment requirements.

Attacking units cross-load supplies and critical resources to prevent their destruction in the event
they lose a single vehicle or system. The commander considers the likelihood that logistic
preparations for the offense will be detected by enemy forces and plans for that risk accordingly.

The availability of adequate supplies and transportation to sustain the operation becomes more
critical as it progresses, particularly in situations where maneuver elements are widely dispersed.
Whether foot-mobile or vehicle-mounted, supply LOCs become strained, and requirements for
repair and replacement of weapon systems increase. The CSS elements in direct support of
maneuver units must task-organize and be as mobile—regardless of terrain—as the forces they
support. They can do so by using aerial resupply and forward logistics bases.

Maintenance assets move as far forward as the tactical situation allows to repair inoperable and
damaged equipment and return it to battle as quickly as possible. Crews continue to perform
preventive maintenance checks and services as modified for the climate and terrain in which they
find themselves. The expedient execution of battle damage repair by maintenance crews and
recovery teams is critical to sustaining offensive operations. Battle damage repair restores the
minimum essential combat capabilities required to support a specific combat mission or to enable
the equipment to self-recover.

General engineering are those engineering capabilities and activities, other than combat
engineering, that modify, maintain, or protect the physical environment. General engineering
encompasses a wide spectrum of activities, including horizontal and vertical construction,
explosive ordnance disposal, hygiene services (i.e., showers and laundry), engineering
reconnaissance, bulk water production, and bulk fuel storage. To support sustained offensive
operations, the GCE's combat engineer battalions posses organic capabilities to perform limited

                                                                   3-47


---

MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

    general engineering tasks. This can include providing mobile electric power to meet the needs of
    the regimental and battalion headquarters. Most general engineering requirements will need to be
    planned for and provided by the LCE as offensive operations allow.

    The offense consumes more resources than other operations, and it can generate significantly
    greater casualties in a short period of time. As with other logistic functional areas, the means of
    triaging and evacuating casualties is pushed as far forward as possible. Logistic planners
    anticipate greater health service support requirements with offensive operations and coordinate
    and synchronize additional medical support and augmentation. These include—

       • Coordinating and synchronizing additional medical support or augmentation, such as medical
         evacuation support, forward resuscitative surgical intervention provided by forward
         resuscitative and surgical detachments, combat support and field hospitals, casualty collection
         points, ambulance exchange points, and established Class VIII resupply.

       • Quickly locating and evacuating injured personnel from the battlefield.
       • Providing effective tactical combat casualty care and emergency medical treatment for

         injured personnel.
       • Transporting casualties to medical treatment facilities at the next higher role of care.
       • Using casualty evacuation considerations (CASEVAC) assets when the number of casualties

         overwhelms the medical evacuation system’s capacity.
       • Accurately triaging and rapidly conducting medical evacuations of injured personnel to

         medical treatment facilities at the next higher role of care.
       • Planning CASEVAC routes (ground and air) along with contingencies during times of

         hazardous trafficability.
       • Designating casualty evacuation capability within their formations because CASEVAC

         capacity is rarely sufficient.

    Health services planning, in terms of evacuation routes and ambulance exchange points, becomes
    more important depending on the type of offensive operation and enemy capabilities. A penetration
    conducted in an urban environment will most likely preclude aerial casualty evacuation at, or near,
    the point of injury. Similarly, the vulnerability of LOCs in an envelopment may preclude ground
    casualty evacuation. In any event, planners must coordinate and integrate CASEVAC and treatment
    plans across the warfighting functions.

    The LCE provides other services to the GCE, however, manpower restrictions mandate that the
    committed LCE support be located in the LCE rear area. Services are subdivided into two
    components: command support and combat service support services. Commanders are responsible
    for the health, welfare, and morale of the personnel in their command. These services include the
    following: personnel administration; religious ministry; billeting; financial management; food
    service support; and morale, welfare, and recreation (MWR). Whereas, combat service support
    services are primarily provided by the LCE, which provides services including operational
    contract support, postal, legal, mortuary affairs, security support, civil-military operations, and
    hygiene and waste management. Because of the geographic separation of these services from the

                                                                        3-48


---

                                                                                  MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

LCE and the GCE during offensive operations, commanders will need to plan for a phased support
that delivers these capabilities when offensive action permits. See MCTP 3-40B, Tactical-Level
Logistics, for more information.

Force Protection
Force protection includes those measures commanders take to preserve their force’s potential so
that it can be applied at the appropriate time and place. In the offense, commanders might face
challenges with protecting their force because units must mass combat power while conducting
maneuvers that can expose them to the enemy. To increase force protection, units try to maintain
greater momentum and tempo than the enemy. This denies the enemy a chance to plan, prepare,
and execute an effective response to friendly actions.

To safely mass the force at the point of decision, commanders consider—

  • Using multiple routes.
  • Dispersing forces.
  • Destroying isolated forces in piecemeal.
  • Scheduling rotation and relief of forces before they culminate.
  • Using terrain wisely.
  • Integrating force protection with information capabilities (e.g., OPSEC, communication

     strategies and operations, information assurance, counterintelligence).
  • Using units to execute personnel recovery according to METT-T.
  • Mitigating friendly fire through the use of confirmation briefs, rehearsals, and briefbacks,

     maintaining situational awareness across the force, and the elements of battlespace geometry.
  • Ensuring rear area security is properly tasked, organized, led, and resourced.
  • Using passive (camouflage, cover, concealment, counter-improvised explosive device

     awareness) and active (engineering assets) survivability activities. For more discussion about
     survivability see Chapter 8 and MCTP 3-34C, Survivability Operations.
  • Employing proper CBRN postures and preparedness.

TRANSITIONS

Tactical units execute missions using various tasks and actions associated with the offense and
defense and stabilization activities. As discussed in Chapter 2, units can employ different tasks at
different times depending on mission and situation. Transitions, in this case, take place when there
is a change to either the mission, the environment, the AO, unit task organization or function,
enemy’s actions or TTP, or some combination of these factors.

Offensive operations cease with the realization of victory and an end to hostilities, when a
commander receives a change in mission (e.g., being ordered to conduct security operations for
another element), or when the force reaches a culminating point. A culminating point is “the
point at which a force no longer has the capability to continue its form of operations, offense or
defense” (DoD Dictionary). In offensive operations this takes place when the strength shifts

                                                                   3-49


---

MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

    from the attacking force to their opponent. The culminating point takes place because of
    operational reasons, logistic reasons, or some combination of the two. Operational reasons
    include encountering heavily defended areas that cannot be bypassed, the enemy receiving
    reinforcements, or the enemy experiencing success with a counterattack. Logistic reasons
    include physical exhaustion, casualties, equipment losses, and expenditures that outstrip CSS.

    Units can regain offensive momentum, but often only after difficult fighting or following an
    operational pause, which is “a temporary halt in operations” (DoD Dictionary). An operational
    pause in offensive operations might be forced by a culminating point. Conversely, a commander
    might plan an operational pause to replenish combat power. Planning operational pauses requires
    careful phasing, expeditious sustaining actions, and operations to maintain pressure on the enemy
    and deceive them as to the nature and length of the pause.

    Transition to Defensive-Oriented Operations
    A unit transitions from the offense to the defense because they are ordered to do so, have planned
    to do so after a phase or objective is met, or are forced to do so by a culminating point or enemy
    action. Of these scenarios, the worst is having the defense forced upon the commander because it
    invites substantial risk as the force must significantly alter their posture and focus suddenly and
    unexpectedly. Units are spread out and might be weakened, defensive measures are hasty, and
    personnel may find themselves fighting on unfavorable and desperate terms. Consequently,
    commanders either plan to transition to the defense or seek to anticipate likely culmination points
    so they have the freedom to choose when and where to halt the attack, and have time to plan the
    defense, minimize vulnerability to attack, and facilitate a return to offensive operations. As the
    unit transitions from the offense to the defense, the commander—

       • Maintains contact and surveillance of the enemy.
       • Establishes a security area, security forces, and local security measures.
       • Redeploys artillery assets to ensure the support of security forces.
       • Redeploys forces to support future offensive actions.
       • Maintains or regains contact with adjacent units in a contiguous AO and ensures that units

         remain capable of mutual support in a noncontiguous AO.
       • Transitions the engineer effort by shifting the emphasis from mobility to countermobility

         and survivability.
       • Consolidates, reorganizes, and requests logistic support for defensive operations, and seeks to

         maximize opportunities for reconstitution of the force.
       • Explains the rationale for transitioning from the offense to the unit’s personnel.

    A commander can use two basic techniques when transitioning to a defensive operation, regardless
    of the defense (i.e., area, mobile, retrograde, and counterlanding) the commander plans to conduct.
    (See Chapter 8 for more information on the defense.) The first technique is for the leading elements
    to commit forces and push forward, claiming enough ground to establish a security area anchored
    on defensible terrain. The main force moves forward or rearward as necessary to occupy key terrain
    and institutes hasty defensive operations that progress towards deliberate operations as time and
    resources allow. The disadvantage of this technique is that if the force is facing a culminating point

                                                                        3-50


---

                                                                                  MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

or unexpected change in the situation, they probably lack the combat power necessary to push
forward and create a proper security area—thus leaving the main body exposed to decisive
enemy actions.

The second technique is to establish a security area along the unit’s current position, moving the
main body rearward to defensible terrain. The security force thins out and the remaining force
deploys to organize the defense. The disadvantage of this technique is that unless the main body
falls far enough back to create a deep security area, enemy forces be able to accurately template
the forward trace of friendly units and engage with artillery and other fire support systems,
complicating defensive preparations and causing personnel and equipment casualties.

Civil considerations are inherent to all operations; transitioning from offense to defense often
requires units to focus on stabilization tasks and activities, which includes increased civil
considerations for the commander. Transitioning to defensive operations often creates a lull
where civilian populations seek aid, flee from the area, or if hostile, interfere with friendly
activities. The commander should consider how to minimize effects of the civilian population on
military activities while still providing protection measures associated with international law.

Transition to Stabilization Activities
Units transition from offensive related tasks to stabilization activities because of changes in
mission or the situation, or at when hostilities end. If the latter, this transition should be the
execution of previous planning efforts—the stabilization activities needed to support a transition
to civil authority cannot be afterthoughts. Ideally, all the unit’s efforts to date have been about
setting the conditions to successfully transition to stabilization activities and eventual withdrawal.
It follows that setting these transition conditions have significant impact on the planning and
execution of the combat actions leading up to them. As the unit transitions from offensive tasks to
stabilization activities, the commander—

  • Maintains contact and surveillance of any remaining enemy or hostile elements.
  • Maintains the combat power necessary to conduct security operations.
  • Establishes AOs, either contiguous or noncontiguous, for subordinate forces.
  • Prepares to transition some or all combat support units to other roles such as provisional

     infantry, mobility support, or critical infrastructure reconstruction.
  • Conducts command and control and task reorganization to support stabilization activities

     functions to include adding and integrating new functions and enablers.
  • Seeks to integrate operations with proper civil authority, whether an occupational

     government, international organization, or host-nation authority.
  • Consolidates, reorganizes, and requests logistic support for stabilization activities, and seeks

     to maximize opportunities for reconstitution of the force.
  • Readdresses risk assessment assumptions and ROE.
  • Conducts necessary training and reorientation of the unit’s personnel to combat complacency

     and reinforce the shift in emphasis from the offense to stabilization activities.

                     CHAPTER 4.
             MOVEMENT TO CONTACT

Movement to contact is used to develop the situation and establish or regain contact with
the enemy. It is type of offensive activity is applicable across the range of military operations.
Commanders conduct a movement to contact to create favorable conditions for subsequent tactical
tasks, such as forcing the enemy to reveal themselves. A commander conducts a movement to
contact when the tactical situation is not clear or when the enemy has broken contact. A properly
executed movement to contact develops the combat situation and maintains the commander’s
freedom of action after contact is gained. This flexibility is essential to maintaining the initiative.
All tactical concepts, control measures, and planning considerations introduced in Chapters 2 and 3
apply to the conduct of a movement to contact. The attack preparation considerations introduced in
Chapter 5 also apply.

A movement to contact employs purposeful and aggressive movement, decentralized control, and
the hasty deployment of MDCA formations from the march to develop the situation for further
action. Two methods of movement to contact are approach march and search and attack. The
fundamentals of a movement to contact are—

  • Focus all efforts on finding the enemy and forcing them to reveal themselves. Make initial
     contact with the smallest force possible to develop the situation and avoid decisive engagement
     of the main body until a time of the commander’s choosing.

  • Task-organize and use movement formations that enable the force to rapidly deploy and
     attack in any direction.

  • Keep subordinate forces within supporting distances to facilitate a flexible response.
  • Maintain contact regardless of the COA adopted once contact is gained.

Close air support, air interdiction, and antiair operations are essential to the success of large-scale
movements to contact. Local air superiority or, at minimum, air parity is also vital to the
operation’s success.

Current intelligence collection capabilities often preclude the need for large units, such as
regiments and divisions, to conduct movements to contact for purposes of finding the enemy. But
finding the enemy in general terms and locating them in specific terms that allow them to be
targeted are often very different propositions. Further, apparent certainty can be quickly degraded
by an enemy’s use of complex terrain (e.g., jungle, urban, extensive forests), OPSEC, and
information activities. The more capable an enemy, the more likely they can disrupt intelligence
collection. Regardless, locating the enemy is only one aspect of a movement to contact.
Movement to contact remains the preferred way to gain and maintain contact with the enemy,
develop the situation as enemy dispositions are discovered, and mitigate risk if the enemy is
contacted during movement.


---

MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

    A primary threat to friendly force movement, which a movement to contact mitigates, is a
    meeting engagement. A meeting engagement “is a combat action that occurs when a moving
    force, incompletely deployed for battle, engages an enemy at an unexpected time and place”
    (USMC Dictionary). In a meeting engagement, the force that reacts first to the unexpected
    contact generally gains an advantage over their enemy—seizing the initiative is imperative.
    Platoon levels and below promptly conduct battle drills, and standard actions on contact for
    larger units can give initiative to the friendly force.

   APPROACH MARCH

    An approach march is the “advance of a combat unit when direct contact with the enemy is
    imminent. Troops are fully or partially deployed. The approach march ends when ground contact
    with the enemy is made or when the attack position is occupied” (USMC Dictionary). A commander
    uses this method of movement to contact when the enemy is operating in larger, organized elements
    whose locations might be generally—but not specifically—known, when seeking to gain or regain
    contact with the enemy and develop specific information on their disposition, or when contact is
    possible and security is more important than speed (e.g., conducting an exploitation or moving from
    the line of departure to the assault position). All units at the platoon level and above can conduct an
    approach march using any ground movement.

    Commanders conduct shaping operations to support subordinate maneuver elements conducting
    approach marches. Such operations might include targeting known and suspected enemy
    positions, isolating the battlespace, attacking enemy reserves, and conducting information
    activities. Subordinate commanders receive support (e.g., fire support, enablers, logistic support)
    to seize the initiative upon contact with the enemy.

    Force Organization
    At a minimum, units conducting movement to contact using an approach march have a forward
    security force—either a covering force or an advance guard—and a main body. However,
    subordinate units within the main body might use advanced guards to operate behind the covering
    force as shown in Figure 4-1. Commanders can add flank and rear security elements, particularly
    when their rear forces or flanks are not protected by adjacent or following units but in advance of
    their individual columns, to provide specific support and protection to that column.

    The main body can consist of one or more columns. Security elements may receive screen or
    guard missions. Resourcing of the forward security force, flank, and rear security elements is
    dependent upon METT-T. Chapter 14 discusses security operations such as screen and guard.

    Security Forces. All security elements of an approach march have two primary purposes. The first
    is to protect the main body against surprise; the second is to prevent the main body from becoming
    decisively engaged by the enemy until the commander decides to do so. Forward security
    elements have two additional purposes. They make contact with the enemy to develop the
    situation and they are responsible for mobility and countermobility operations in support of the
    main body.

                                                                         4-2


---

             MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

             Covering Force

             Advance Guard

     Left    Main Body                Right
Flank Guard                       Flank Guard

                        Security
