         and focus on mission accomplishment.

       • Attackers will seek to exploit unit boundaries. Commanders mitigate this by selecting
         boundaries that do not increase coordination issues and ensuring subordinate units’ defensive
         plans align with the higher plan and are coordinated and rehearsed. Commanders also ensure
         that subordinate commanders physically meet with adjacent, supporting, and supported units.
         Coordination includes intelligence collection plans, location and composition of security
         forces, obstacle plans, fire plans, information plans, and air defense coverage areas. If

                                                                         8-8


---

                                                                                  MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

     physically tied in, units strengthen their boundaries by integrating them (e.g., at the boundary,
     one squad of Company A is positioned in Company B’s AO and vice versa).
  • Command posts in the defense tend to be more static than in the offense and can expect to be
     actively targeted by the enemy. Commanders and staffs seek to balance the needs of
     command and control with survivability and plan for displacement and redundancy.
     Commanders place themselves at points of friction and where their influence will produce the
     greatest effect.

Maneuver
Maneuver is an inherent part of any defense and provides units with flexibility and the ability to
shape the defensive battle. Typically, the defender uses maneuver to disrupt and delay enemy
forces as they pass through the security area, act decisively against them in the MBA, limit their
ability to exploit any successes, and create opportunities for exploitation and a transition to the
offense after defeating them.

Security. The security area begins at the FEBA and extends as far to the front and flanks as
security forces are deployed, typically to the forward boundary of the AO. Forces in the security
area conduct reconnaissance to furnish information about the enemy and to delay, deceive, and
disrupt the enemy. Units conduct operations in the security area to confuse the enemy about the
location and nature of the commander’s defensive plan, prevent the enemy from observing
preparations and positions, and keep the enemy from delivering observed fire on the positions.
Conducted aggressively and effectively, friendly actions in the security area offset the attackers’
inherent initiative in choosing the time and place to attack by forcing the attackers to deploy
prematurely and disrupting their tempo and formations.

Beginning as the enemy approaches the security area, the defending force acts against the depth of
the enemy’s formation in both time and space throughout the attack. If practical and acceptable,
commanders do not cede the security area to the enemy, but rather use it as maneuver space in
which to continue to conduct operations against the attacker. Failing that, supporting arms, the
ACE, and information activities continue to range the depth of the enemy, seeking to destroy or
disrupt the employment of key units and assets, such as artillery and reserves.

Commanders at all echelons counter enemy ground reconnaissance activities through active and
passive measures. From divisions pushing forward independent units to conduct cover operations,
to a platoon pushing forward a listening post, commanders must not permit enemy ISR assets to
determine the precise location and strength of defensive positions, obstacles, engagement areas,
and reserves. While typically associated with the security area, security operations are conducted
throughout the battlespace, including rear areas, to destroy enemy reconnaissance efforts. Units
implement OPSEC and other force protection measures to deny the enemy information about
friendly dispositions. See Chapter 14 for more information on security operations.

Use of Terrain. While the attacker seeks to dictate tempo and the time and place of engagement,
the defender typically—even when time is constrained—can choose and occupy the terrain they
will defend. The terrain chosen should optimize the defending force’s capabilities while
minimizing and mitigating those of the attacker. An infantry force defending against an armored
threat will seek restrictive terrain that eliminates enemy’s mobility and firepower advantages
while maximizing the infantry’s survivability and maneuverability prospects. Similarly, defenders

                                                                    8-9


---

MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

    seek terrain that offers cover and concealment for themselves while compelling the attacker to
    cross large open spaces. Beyond merely choosing suitable terrain, the defender uses the time
    available to add reinforcing obstacles to existing terrain to restrict the attackers’ maneuver
    options. In a similar manner, the defensive force may seek to deny terrain to the enemy in one area
    to force the attacker into terrain more favorable to the defender. See MCTP 3-34B for information
    on reinforcing obstacles.

    The defending commander selects terrain that allows massing friendly combat power but
    compels the enemy to choose formations or deployment methods that lead to piecemeal
    commitment. Commanders accomplish this by analyzing likely avenues of approach, and then
    using obstacles and defensive techniques to create conditions that disrupt and delay the enemy
    while maximizing the employment of defensive capabilities (e.g., antitank missiles). This allows
    an outnumbered defender to create favorable force ratios and employ force multipliers, such as
    information activities and indirect fires on terms of advantage. Terrain features that favor
    defensive operations include—

       • A series of parallel ridges across the line of hostile advance.
       • Unfordable streams, swamps, lakes, and other obstacles on the front and flanks.
       • High ground with good observation and long range fields of fire.
       • Concealed movement routes immediately behind defensive positions.
       • Limited road network in front of the line of contact to confine the enemy to predictable

         avenues of approach.
       • A good road network behind the line of contact that allows forces to reposition as the

         battle progresses.

    Mass and Concentration. Forces seek to deliver overwhelming combat power at the point of
    decision. Using maneuver in the defense allows the defender to rapidly shift combat power,
    conduct economy of force operations, and employ a reserve when and where needed. The decisive
    action in the defense is typically enemy oriented because—

       • A key purpose of any defense is to retake the initiative and return to offensive operations.
       • Even if the defensive mission is terrain-oriented, the defender must defeat the enemy force to

          successfully protect or retain that terrain.

    In an area defense, commanders choose where to defeat the enemy and build engagement areas
    that concentrate combat power at that point. In a mobile defense, commanders also choose where
    to defeat the enemy and use the reserve to deliver the decisive action. Even during a retrograde,
    commanders choose key points where they can concentrate combat power to disrupt and delay
    enemy advances or pursuit.

    In the defense, there are numerous ways to mass combat power and generate the desired effects.
    As discussed above, using fires, air support, and information activities throughout the depth of the
    enemy’s advance sets the conditions for decisive action in the close battle. Similarly, a commander
    may begin employing weapon systems at their maximum range, bringing an ever-increasing
    volume of firepower as the enemy advances—for example, heavy antitank weapons begin firing,
    then medium antitank weapons as the range closes, and then light antitank weapons. These types

                                                                        8-10


---

                                                                                  MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

of techniques seek to disrupt, delay, attrite, and, if possible, defeat the enemy as far forward of
friendly defensive positions as possible. They are generally applied against enemy forces of
similar or larger size than the defender. The major disadvantage is that these techniques disclose
friendly positions early, risking their destruction.

Conversely, defenders may use surprise to mass combat power at the point of decision. While
commanders still seek to shape the battle in the security area, they use “massed surprise”
fires—the equivalent of a defensive ambush—in the close battle. This method synchronizes
the simultaneous delivery of indirect-, direct-, and air-delivered fires, and information activities
(e.g., electromagnetic warfare) at once and at a relatively close range. This type of technique is
generally applied when the main effort of the defense is a counterattack and the unit seeks to
shock and stun the enemy with effective fires prior to delivering the attack. It is also ideal when
facing isolated enemy units, when using a reverse-slope defense, or where the enemy is less
capable or smaller than the defender. The major disadvantages are the difficulties in synchronizing
fires in larger formations and the danger that the enemy’s attack’s mass and momentum could
carry them into friendly positions anyway.

Force Capabilities. The type of defense a commander chooses, and the employment of maneuver
in that defense, is based on the nature of the enemy and the type of friendly forces available.
Commanders with amphibious assault vehicles should select a defensive SOM that increases their
tactical mobility and protection. Combat vehicles provide defending forces with the ability to
maneuver, occupy static protective positions, and then return immediately to maneuver. They are
ideal for conducting security operations, executing counterattacks, and operating in challenging
environments such as CBRN.

Dismounted infantry forces facing a large force seek to base their defenses on close terrain and
prepared fighting positions to maximize their advantages in relative mobility and short-range
infantry and antiarmor weapons. Commanders can conduct vertical envelopments to exploit
exploiting the mobility of this method to rapidly shift combat power, occupy a blocking position,
conduct rear area security (e.g., react to an enemy vertical envelopment), reinforce flanks, and
reinforce encircled friendly forces. See Chapter 18 and MCTP 3-01B, Air Assault Operations, for
more information on vertical envelopments.

The speed, mobility, and versatility that the ACE brings to the defense can be crucial in offsetting
many of the attackers’ advantages. Beyond those tasks often associated with CAS, the ACE can
execute screening operations to the front and on the flanks of the defender, range and conduct
attacks throughout the depth of the enemy’s assault, and cover obstacles by observation and fire in
the security area. In addition to typical assault support roles, the ACE can counter the enemy’s
ability to conduct vertical envelopments, close gaps in the defensive plan before the arrival of
maneuver forces and disrupt or delay enemy attempts to exploit success. The role of the ACE
beyond delivering fires in support of maneuver should not be overlooked in defensive planning.
Commanders must be cognizant of the limited assets and support times of aviation fires platforms
to augment the defensive plans of ground units. Units employ direct air support in preparation to
shape the fight as far out in front of the defense as possible, while rotary-wing or fixed-wing CAS
is employed at decisive times in the close tactical fight.

                                                                   8-11


---

MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

    Assured Mobility. In the defense, all three aspects of assured mobility—mobility, countermobility,
    and survivability—are present. All demand attention, but with limited time, limited engineering
    assets, and limits on resources, the commander must establish priorities among the three.
    Commanders should coordinate closely with the LCE to determine what is possible and balance
    that against the defensive tactics they choose to use. A dismounted infantry force operating in
    restrictive terrain against an armored enemy is likely to prioritize countermobility and
    survivability tasks. A commander choosing to use a mobile defense in which the reserve
    will conduct a counterattack as the decisive action is likely to prioritize mobility operations.
    Regardless, the defense places a heavy demand on assured mobility considerations and on Class
    IV and V materials. See MCTP 3-34A, MCTP 3-34B, and MCTP 3-34C for more information
    and details on employing assured mobility concepts.

    Mobility. Mobility actions include creating, improving, and maintaining routes to support logistic
    activities, the rapid movement of combat power within the defensive plan, and the maneuver of
    the reserve. Routes must support the movement of combat and tactical support vehicles. Since the
    enemy will likely target these routes, critical tasks for engineers include creating bypasses and
    alternate routes as well as positioning themselves to support mobility requirements during the
    conduct of the defense. The priority of mobility support is given to routes used by counterattacking
    forces and then routes used by maneuver forces displacing to subsequent positions. Other mobility
    actions include coordinating gaps in obstacles and, at higher levels, creating LZs and tactical landing
    strips to support the defensive plan.

    Countermobility. Countermobility efforts focus on denying mobility to the enemy and are
    balanced against likely, future friendly mobility needs. Destroying a bridge may deny the enemy
    an avenue of approach, but it also may eliminate counterattack opportunities and complicate
    future offensive maneuver. Countermobility activities seek to integrate reinforcing obstacles with
    existing obstacles and terrain to create a greater effect. Tasks include—

       • Supporting the commander’s shaping and decisive actions by halting, delaying, and
          disrupting enemy movement.

       • Canalizing the enemy into engagement areas.
       • Denying avenues of approach.

    To do this, Marines use obstacles to create block, turn, disrupt, and fix effects. Obstacles are
    integrated into observation and fire plans, are concealed whenever possible, and receive priority
    focus from counterreconnaissance and security activities.

    Because the effects that countermobility actions might generate on future mobility, and because
    of the nature of countermobility resources (e.g., scatterable munitions), obstacle emplacement
    is tightly controlled. Commanders designate the unit responsible for establishing and securing
    each obstacle. They could retain execution authority for some obstacles or restrict the use of some
    obstacles to allow other battlespace activities to take place. The commander allows subordinate
    commanders some flexibility in selecting the exact obstacle positions. However, all units must
    know which gaps or lanes—through obstacles and crossing sites—to keep open for movements,
    as well as the firing and self destruct times of scatterable munitions to prevent delays in
    movement. Commanders must be specific and clear in their orders for executing reserve obstacles
    and closing lanes.

                                                                        8-12


---

                                                                                  MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

Defensive improvement is continuous. Given time and resources, the defending force constructs
additional obstacle systems in depth, paying special attention to assailable flanks and rear. The
rear is particularly vulnerable if there are noncontiguous AOs or nontraditional threats. Obstacle
systems can provide additional protection from enemy attacks by forcing the enemy to spend time
and resources to breach or bypass them. The defending commander tries to predict enemy points
of breach based on terrain and probable enemy objectives. The defending force develops the
means to counter enemy breach attempts, such as coordinated fires, and reestablishes obstacles by
using scatterable munitions or other techniques. Forcing the enemy to breach an obstacle can be a
technique used to make the enemy vulnerable to destruction.

Tactical and protective obstacles are constructed primarily at company level and below. Small-unit
commanders ensure that observation and fires cover all obstacles to hinder breaching. Deliberate
protective obstacles are common around fixed sites. Protective obstacles are a key component of
survivability actions. They are tied in with FPFs and provide the friendly force with close in
protection. Commanders at all echelons track defensive preparations, such as establishing Class IV
and V supply points and start or completion times of obstacle belts and groups. The commander
and staff plan how the unit will restore obstacles the enemy has breached. Units use artillery, air, or
ground systems to reestablish minefields. See Chapter 21 and MCTP 3-34B for more information
on obstacles and obstacle integration.

Limited Visibility. The attacking forces’ ability to create limited-visibility conditions—including
thermal neutralizing smoke—and the smoke and dust associated with a battle requires defending
units to rapidly modify their defense to one that is effective during limited visibility. Therefore,
defenders simultaneously plan for daylight and limited-visibility operations. Whether the attack
comes during the day, during the night, or spans the two, the defending force is unlikely to be able
to adjust their positions. For example, defenders may choose to position themselves closer to
avenues of approach that are more conducive to limited-visibility operations. The enemy will likely
take advantage of limited-visibility conditions to attack, conduct reconnaissance operations,
breach, or reduce defensive obstacles, conduct infiltrations, or advance closer to friendly positions.

Defending units can expect enemy forces to take advantage of limited-visibility conditions to—

  • Conduct reconnaissance operations to locate the defending force’s weapons, defensive
     obstacles, and positions.

  • Breach or reduce defensive obstacles.
  • Move elements through gaps caused by reduced weapon ranges.

While Marine Corps units have significant night vision capabilities, limitations on fields of view
and depth perception place some restrictions on their utility in the defense. Limited-visibility
conditions generate psychological effects on the defender and attacker. These conditions affect
defensive maneuver in the same manner as they affect offensive maneuver—requiring tighter
formations, increasing cross-country navigation difficulties, and slowing movement rates. To
overcome potential limited-visibility problems, defensive planning considers the following:

  • Focusing long-range detection equipment, such as radar, sensors, and thermal-imaging
     devices, on well-defined avenues of approach. Employing multiple means in the same area of
     interest improves the likelihood of detection.

  • Employing combat power along terrain features the enemy is likely to use for orientation in
     the darkness, such as wood lines and water courses.

                                                                   8-13


---

MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

       • Increasing the numbers of infantry, scouts, observation posts, combat patrols, etc., deployed
         forward and between defensive positions to detect and slow enemy movement (particularly
         enemy infiltration attempts) and protect obstacles against enemy breaching attempts.

       • Employing obstacles and early warning devices to slow the advancing enemy and
         alert defenders.

       • Rehearsing displacement and movement plans. Defending units moving over rehearsed routes
         should be able to move faster than an enemy force moving through unfamiliar terrain.

       • Planning for illumination on or behind likely engagement areas to silhouette enemy forces
         while leaving defenders in shadows and darkness.

       • Ensuring that any adjustments to the defense for limited-visibility conditions are completely
         reversed by daylight and vice versa.

    When the friendly units have superior night-vision technology, commanders can use smoke and
    bispectral (blocking visible and infrared light) obscuration. While using smoke as a redundant
    targeting mark is a conventional use, other uses include denying the enemy the ability to
    determine and target friendly positions or use their target-acquisition optics and impairing the
    enemy’s ability to navigate and maintain formations. As with all smoke and thermal obscurants,
    proper placement is critical to avoid generating limited-visibility effects against friendly forces.
    See MCTP 3-10E for more information on using smoke as an obscurant.

    Enemy Vertical Envelopment. Some potential enemies plan to use airborne and air assault units, in
    various numbers and sizes, against defending US and allied forces. Defeating these enemies
    begins with the MAGTF taking steps to counter them before they launch and during their
    movement to the drop zone (DZ) or LZ. Ground combat element and rear area security
    commanders, when faced with a potential vertical envelopment, rely on IPB to determine, and
    prioritize each potential DZ or LZ. They establish systematic surveillance of these areas to warn
    of enemy attempts to insert forces. Units assigned to defend potential landing sites position
    themselves at the most likely points of enemy entry, develop positions at other sites, and rehearse
    movement and occupation tasks. Weapons are positioned to maximize the coverage of DZs and
    LZs while minimizing battlespace geometry issues. Defenders develop fire support plans that
    make use of conventional munitions and scatterable munitions. Engineers place obstacles on sites
    of potential enemy vertical envelopment, and commanders consider using countermobility
    operations along the routes the enemy will most likely use to depart their DZs and LZs.

    If enemy forces successfully execute a vertical envelopment, the defensive response must contain
    and counterattack the enemy force before they can become organized and reinforce. The MAGTF
    isolates the enemy by helping to reestablish air superiority while indirect fires and CAS fix and
    disrupt the enemy in place. Security forces gain and maintain contact, developing and shaping the
    situation for deploying the main effort. The main body, if not already in position, deploys to
    contain and fix enemy forces, and then executes offensive operations to defeat them. If the enemy
    is successful in consolidating and reinforcing, the defensive priority shifts to containing the enemy
    and creating the conditions for eventual offensive action. If an enemy vertical envelopment is a
    likely COA, commanders must consider how they will shape their battlespace and organize and
    resource subordinate units, considering that vertical envelopment will likely be conducted in
    conjunction with other offensive actions. It is probably beyond the capability of units at the
    regiment-level and below to defend against both a ground assault and a vertical envelopment.

                                                                        8-14


---

                                                                                  MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

Fires
In the defense, units use the fires warfighting function to neutralize, suppress, or destroy enemy
forces; to delay or disrupt the enemy’s ability to execute a given COA; and to enhance the effects
of massed direct fires. Fires and information activities support the commander’s decisive and
shaping actions.

Indirect Fires and Joint Fires. Defending commanders combine information activities with
indirect fires and CAS to shape the battle and support the main effort. The defensive SOM uses
fires and air support to execute the single-battle construct. Not only do they conduct shaping
actions as the enemy advances, but even as the battle moves into the MBA, indirect fires and air
support continue to target and defeat critical enemy assets, reserves, and follow-on forces
throughout the battlespace, conducting simultaneous actions that defeat the attacker’s bid for
victory while contributing to the defender’s main effort. Indirect, joint, and air-delivered fires
enable units to generate effects across the entire enemy force at once—not just provide sequential
responses to their advance.

Indirect fires have the greatest effects on the enemy when they are synchronized with air-delivered
fires, direct fires, and the defensive SOM. Such integration must take place from the beginning of
planning. To accomplish this, the defending force ensures that all elements of the fire support
chain—from joint fire observers to naval gunfire liaison officers—understand the commander’s
intent for fires and the defensive SOM. The force distributes fire support assets throughout the
AO, closely linking weapons systems with redundant target acquisition means (e.g., UAS, ground
reconnaissance assets). Fire support control measures are permissive and placed as close to
friendly positions as possible to facilitate engagement. High-payoff targets and high-value targets
along with their engagement priorities are determined through the lens of the single battle.

Air- and ground-delivered fires contribute significantly to the commander’s shaping actions
because of their range and flexibility. Commanders use fire support assets to disrupt the enemy’s
preparations, such as attacking likely enemy assembly areas, logistic hubs, and interdicting
enemy movement. Fires support friendly reconnaissance and counterreconnaissance efforts and
high-payoff targets are attacked continuously and as early as possible.

Commanders use counterfires against enemy fire support assets as shaping actions, and the timing
of counterfires requires consideration. The advantages of engaging in the counterfire battle early
usually outweigh the risks to the defending force, particularly when the defender has superior fire
support. However, when commanders are forced to balance limited fire support resources against
other shaping requirements or are concerned about the survivability of those assets, they may
choose to delay counterfires until the enemy enters the MBA. Having friendly fire support assets
that can rapidly shoot and move and effective counterreconnaissance efforts are other important
considerations in counterfire timing.

The commander and staff plan fires to support counterreconnaissance activities and the security
force. These fires should assist in destroying enemy reconnaissance assets, deceiving the
enemy regarding the location of the MBA, and supporting the security force commander’s
SOM—specifically supporting canalization, disruption, delay, and the security force’s withdrawal

                                                                   8-15


---

MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

    criteria and plan. The latter, to include battle handover to units in the MBA, requires detailed
    consideration and rehearsal. To deconflict battlespace geometry, commanders use NFAs over
    reconnaissance and security force elements.

    Indirect, joint, and air-delivered fire planning for the close battle in the MBA focus on disrupting
    the enemy’s attack (e.g., breaking tempo, fragmenting MDCA efforts), preventing the enemy from
    massing combat power, and creating vulnerabilities for the main effort to exploit. Commanders
    accomplish this by integrating fire support with direct fires and achieving MDCA effects at critical
    points, such as choke points, obstacles, and engagement areas. Fires in the MBA support rearward
    passage of lines for the security force, and forward passage of lines for reserves. Fire support assets
    can close obstacle gaps and fortify breached obstacles. Other fire planning considers—

       • Suppressing enemy direct and indirect fire systems and air defense assets to support friendly
         defensive maneuver, particularly counterattacks, disengagements, and repositioning.

       • Isolating enemy forces that have penetrated the defensive area from their reserves and
         follow-on forces.

       • Allowing for flexibility in reallocating and reprioritizing fire support assets and targets to
         respond to the enemy’s main effort, counter unexpected enemy actions or success, and
         support friendly exploitation of opportunities.

    Air and Missile Defense. As in the offense, the GCE’s primary means of air defense are passive air
    defense measures and the ACE’s execution of antiair operations in accordance with the joint force
    air component commander’s counterair plans. The goal of such plans is to develop an environment
    in which the defender can operate unimpeded by interference from enemy air, missile, or UAS
    threats. When conducting an area defense, commanders can easily integrate the defensive SOM
    with air defense planning, usually prioritizing the main effort. When conducting mobile or
    retrograde defenses in the presence of an enemy air threat, commanders must choose if and when to
    prioritize air defense coverage of supporting effort, main effort, and reserves.

    The GCE’s active antiair measures employ small arms and are most effective against unmanned
    aircraft or enemy rotary-wing aircraft. However, the GCE’s primary contributions to antiair
    operations are passive air defense measures. The two types of passive air defense are attack
    avoidance and damage-limiting measures; both rely on cover, concealment, and deception.

    Attack avoidance focuses on not being seen and, therefore, not targeted by enemy air threats.
    Avoiding aerial observation requires the same skills and principles as avoiding ground
    observation—hiding, blending, and disguising positions by selecting advantageous positions,
    exercising camouflage discipline, and constructing material to augment existing concealment.
    Damage-limiting measures of passive air defense are similar to those used to protect against
    indirect fire threats—dispersion, protective construction, and cover. See MCTP 3-01A, Scouting
    and Patrolling, for more information on camouflage and concealment, and see MCTP 10-10B for
    more information on air defense.

                                                                        8-16


---

                                                                                  MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

Information Activities
The information activities and planning considerations for the defense are similar to those
discussed in Chapter 3. The commander and staff still analyze and determine those decision
makers, whether individuals, groups, or populations, that require influence to support the
defensive SOM. Depending on the defensive action, information activities range from degrading
enemy C2 capabilities to directing the movement of civilians to evacuation centers.

Commanders still ensure the control of electromagnetic emissions and frequency hopping.
However, where possible, they use closed fiber-optic systems to protect communications,
computers, and other intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance systems.

Commander’s may find discernibly different relationships among local populations when
conducting offensive maneuver or maintaining a defense. These relationships can be driven by
numerous factors, to include history, culture, recent actions, and politics. This issue is more than
one of military expediency—such as keeping dislocated civilians off routes critical to military
operations or relinquishing some of the territory of friendly populations—it is also an issue of
politics and emotion. These considerations might constrain available COAs. For example, the
military may not be allowed to trade space (and the friendly population associated with it) for
time. Regardless of whether such constraints exist, commanders must synchronize their
information capabilities to support defensive COAs that maximize the probability of success
while minimizing or mitigating the effects on the friendly populace.

Intelligence
During planning, the commander and staff use the IPB process and implement an intelligence
collection plan to learn and understand the terrain, identify probable enemy objectives and
approaches, and develop appropriate NAIs and TAIs. (See MCRP 2-10B.1 for a detailed
discussion of terrain analysis.) Commanders study how the enemy tends to operate, to include
patterns they may have established. Commanders consider enemy capabilities, such as their ability
to conduct air attacks or infiltrate forces behind friendly units, and the presence of follow-on
enemy forces capable of continuing or exploiting attacks. Commanders also consider enemy
vulnerabilities to friendly actions such as counterattacks, interdiction, information activities, and
canalization by obstacles.

The commander’s IPB and intelligence collections should plan to identify as many of the
following requirements as early as possible:

  • Locations, dispositions, composition, equipment, strengths, and weaknesses of the advancing
     enemy force.

  • Location of critical enemy capabilities—C2 nodes; engineer units and assets; indirect fire
     weapon systems and artillery control and counterbattery assets; air defense units; information
     assets; and logistic resources and units.

  • Likely enemy operational points of interest—reconnaissance objectives or goals, possible
     assembly areas, potential air assault or airborne areas, staging areas for follow-on forces,
     withdrawal and reinforcement routes.

  • Potential enemy weaknesses, including timetables for most likely COAs, gaps between
     enemy formations, assailable flanks, and other enemy vulnerabilities.

                                                                   8-17


---

MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

       • Civil considerations—locations, numbers, and intentions of civilian populations, to include
         likely routes and directions of movement for dislocated persons.

       • Weather and terrain effects on current and projected operations.

    Because commanders must “see” the enemy throughout defensive operations, commanders ensure
    that their intelligence collection plan will survive contact with the enemy so they can acquire
    needed information. This requires establishing redundancy among ISR resources and providing
    for their resupply and reconstitution.

    Logistics
    Force sustainment in the defense priorities for the defending force are typically obtaining
    ammunition and the materials needed to construct obstacles and defensive positions. Commanders
    ensure that their logistic officers and supporting logistic units understand the commander’s intent,
    the defensive SOM, and branches and sequels—particularly rapid transitions to offensive
    operations. To both limit the risk to CSS units and increase logistic responsiveness, the
    commander considers stockpiling and caching critical supply items within the security area and
    MBA—including destruction plans, if necessary, to deny their use to the enemy. Commanders
    can apply this concept to maintenance as well—using well-supplied, forward-positioned,
    multifunctional maintenance contact teams to minimize the risk to logistic units while enabling
    the quick repair and return of many types of equipment without the need for evacuation.

    Supply. Units err on the side of maintaining full stocks of supply items in case enemy actions
    disrupt resupply. They conduct resupply during times when an enemy attack is least likely. This
    might or might not be during limited-visibility conditions, depending on enemy capabilities.
    Although logistic commanders are responsible for the defense of their units, defending
    commanders often use camouflage or smoke to aid resupply and reduce the chances of detection.

    The defending force must not underestimate the transportation, manpower, and lead times
    associated with supplying construction materials for defensive preparations and for constructing
    those positions and obstacles. Planners may have to factor logistic limitations and strong points
    into their defensive SOM. If a commander must retain critical terrain and a strong point is not
    logistically feasible, then the commander develops other defensive types and methods to
    accomplish the mission.

    Medical Support. Defending forces generally receive more rapid and responsive medical support
    than attacking forces because their relatively static position allows more time to prepare for
    casualties. Medical planning includes preparing for robust use of ambulances and ambulance
    exchange points to quickly evacuate casualties to places of safety. Depending on the nature of the
    enemy threat (e.g., a significant air defense capability that hinders air evacuation), higher levels of
    trauma care may be pushed forward to stabilize patients before further evacuation to definitive
    care is possible. Commanders consider building in “reserve” capacity to allow for rapid response
    to mass casualties—such as extra, pre-staged ambulances.

    Security. Placing and moving logistic resources in the defense requires balancing responsive
    support and exposure to risk. Commanders include CSS units into the defensive plan, factoring
    in placement, rear area terrain management, movement planning, and traffic control. Ideally,
    commanders seek to maximize CSS capabilities of units while minimizing their security

                                                                        8-18


---

                                                                                  MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

requirements. A combat logistics battalion that is spending most of its time in self-defense will
not have the time or resources to efficiently exercise their functions. Conversely, trying to
create a risk-free environment for that battalion requires assigning combat power away from the
defense or positioning the battalion too far away from potential threats to be effective.

Logistics security requirements vary with types of defenses as follows:

  • Because area defense security attempts to check or limit enemy advances in terms of terrain,
     logistic functions may be placed closer to the FEBA (remaining deconflicted from the
     movement requirements of maneuver units).

  • A mobile defense uses terrain as maneuver space; commanders must simultaneously protect
     logistic functions from enemy penetration and support an active, maneuver-based defense.
     This requires task organizing and pushing specific logistic functions forward in direct support
     of maneuver elements, while emplacing higher-echelon support deeper into the rear area.

  • Retrograde defense strives to provide maneuver units with the maximum resupply and
     support possible before an operation commences, and then falls steadily back on safeguarded
     logistic units far to the rear in new, planned defensive positions. In a manner similar to the
     way some artillery batteries provide fire support while others displace, CSS units can displace
     rearward in echelon with maneuver forces, providing continuous support though accepting
     greater risk. For more information on tactical logistics, see MCTP 3-40B.

Health Services. Planning for health services in the defense in terms of evacuation routes and
ambulance exchange points varies with different types of defensive operations and enemy
capabilities. An area defense conducted in an urban environment most likely precludes aerial
casualty evacuation at or near the point of injury. Similarly, the vulnerability of LOCs in an
envelopment might preclude ground casualty evacuation. Planners must coordinate and integrate
CASEVAC with casualty collection points and treatment plans across the warfighting functions.

When designating a casualty collection point, the unit commander determines whether medical
personnel will be at the casualty collection points, considering the risk versus the availability of
personnel. Medical personnel might not be available to staff these points; therefore, combat
lifesavers and ambulatory patients might be required to perform self-aid, buddy aid, or combat life
support. The casualty collection points should be identified on operational overlays and planned
by phase for operations. The casualty collection point planning considerations include site
security, proximity to the landing zone, cover and concealment, and access to evacuation routes.
Leaders should provide guidance on aid and litter teams, distribution of casualty equipment, and
proper avoidance of choke points. Medical personnel are responsible for activity inside the
casualty collection point and the supported unit leaders are responsible for activity outside the
casualty collection points.

To establish the tactical casualty flow, leaders must be able to answer the following questions:

  • Where will the casualties evacuation site be located?
  • Will ground, air, or water assets conduct evacuation to the casualty collection point?
  • How will evacuation be conducted to the casualty collection points?
  • What are the distances and travel times?

                                                                   8-19


---

MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

       • Would casualties be able to make it that far? If not, what parts of the plan need to be corrected?
       • Who will evacuate the casualties (CASEVAC or MEDEVAC)?
       • Are medical assets positioned to ensure continuity of care?

    For more information on tactical casualty treatment, see MCTP 3-40B.

    Force Protection
    Unit survivability is critical in any defensive operation. Force protection preserves subordinate
    unit capabilities. Commanders remain attuned to changes in enemy tactics and adapt force and
    individual protective measures accordingly. In the defense, commanders consider—

       • Conducting personnel recovery in accordance with METT-T. Commanders ensure there are
         reasonable plans—such as designating rally points—for units and personnel to execute
         unassisted recovery operations in chaotic and rapidly changing ground situations.

       • Integrating the elements of battlespace geometry into the defense SOM to avoid friendly fire
         incidents—particularly during counterattacks and mobile and retrograde types of defenses.

       • Conducting operational security from information protection to counterreconnaissance and
         from camouflage to antiterrorism.

       • Mitigating and operating in a CBRN environment within the METT-T construct.
       • Adhering to general safety guidelines, to include conducting daily battle rhythm activities in

         limited-visibility conditions and during construction of defensive positions.
       • Allowing for explosive ordnance disposal, with a special emphasis on force awareness of the

         quantities and locations of unexploded munitions in and around defensive positions as a result
         of enemy indirect fire.

    Survivability. Mobility in the defense focuses on enabling units to move rapidly between positions
    and engage the enemy from those positions. Defensive planning must strive for maximum
    survivability, making every attempt to mitigate enemy detection and safeguard the Marines.
    This is particularly true of units assigned terrain-focused missions. Beyond the construction of
    rudimentary individual- and single-weapon fighting positions, the defense primarily relies on
    engineer support. In defensive planning, commanders must carefully consider engineering
    priorities—to include construction and material limitations—in prioritizing not only among
    mobility, countermobility, and survivability tasks, but within those tasks as well. A battalion
    commander’s priorities could be overcoming an obstacle in an engagement area, supporting the
    battle position of the main effort overlooking that engagement area, or improving the route for a
    counterattack force, addressing other positions and other obstacles only if time permits.

    Survivability tasks include using engineer equipment to assist in preparing and constructing
    trenches, command post shelters, as well as radar, artillery, and combat vehicle fighting
    positions. They address protecting supply stocks against blast, shrapnel, incendiaries, and CBRN
    contamination. Commanders provide guidance on the level of protection, such as hull defilade
    or overhead cover, system priorities, and early use of specialized engineer systems that can
    construct survivable positions. Commanders also address standards, such as overhead protection
    against 82 mm mortars, while engineers advise the commander on the costs in terms of time and
    material to meet those standards. The commander’s priority in engineer survivability planning

                                                                        8-20


---

                                                                                  MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

during defensive operations is determining the most appropriate locations and standards for the
construction of survivable positions. MCTP 3-34C provides additional information about
constructing and maintaining survivable positions.

In accordance with METT-T, units can conduct survivability moves between their primary,
alternate, and supplementary positions. A survivability move involves rapidly displacing a unit,
command post, or facility in response to direct and indirect fires, the approach of an enemy unit, a
natural phenomenon, or as a proactive measure based on intelligence, meteorological data, and
risk analysis of enemy capabilities and intentions (including weapons of mass destruction).

DEFENSIVE FORMS

Commanders arrange and employ forces to solve the tactical problem. The defensive forms
provide commanders with the tools they need, in the combinations they see fit, to execute an area,
mobile, retrograde defense, or counterlanding. Each defensive form—sector, battle position,
strong point, linear, perimeter, and reverse slope—has its own purpose and unique considerations.

Sector Defense
Commanders incorporate sectors into their defensive SOM when they want to provide subordinate
commanders maximum latitude to accomplish assigned tasks. For instance, a battalion
commander might task a company with delaying the enemy and then provide them a defensive
sector in which to generate that effect. The designated unit’s company commander might choose
to use a combination of ambushes and battle positions within the assigned sector to create the
delay. The extent of the assigned sector is based on METT-T but should be no larger than what the
unit can influence. Sectors are not the same as AOs because units assigned sectors have none of
the responsibilities associated with AOs. For this reason, defensive sectors are typically assigned
only to company-sized units or smaller.

Battle Position Defense
As discussed earlier in this chapter, battle positions are both a defensive method and an intent
graphic that depicts the location and general orientation of a defending force. Commanders
employ this defensive form when their defensive SOM requires the force, or a portion of the force,
to orient relative to terrain. For example, a company may occupy a battle position to disrupt, delay,
or block enemy movement along an avenue of approach to set the conditions for the rest of the
battalion to counterattack. Or that same company might occupy a battle positions as the battalion’s
main effort to concentrate fires in an engagement area. Commanders employing battle positions as
part of their SOM must consider the time and material necessary to prepare them.

Strong Point Defense
Commanders establish a strong point when the mission requires retaining terrain indefinitely and
when it is possible that the defending force may be isolated for periods of time by enemy action.
The physical position of a strong point is considered a technique of battle position, but its unique
purpose makes it a valuable tool when the defending force must maintain control of key terrain.
Strong points are labor and material intensive, requiring significant investment in engineering
resources and support. They may be linked together to form fortified areas, or they may serve as
the anchor for a mobile defense.

                                                                   8-21


---

MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

    Linear Defense
    Commanders use the linear defensive form in conjunction with linear obstacles (e.g., ridgelines,
    rivers, valleys), either with or without man-made obstacle augmentation. Although the linear
    defensive form may be incorporated into any type of defense, it is typically associated with area
    defenses because the commander accepts less risk by not allowing the enemy to cross the obstacle.
    Forces conducting this defensive method either defend along or behind the obstacle depending on
    the larger defensive SOM.

    An area defense is typically used to defend forward along a linear obstacle. Security forces
    conduct shaping actions forward of the obstacle, conducting a rearward passage of lines while
    units in the MBA use the linear form to conduct the decisive action. Any enemy attempts to
    penetrate or seize a bridgehead should be isolated and counterattacked. A bridgehead is, “an area
    of ground held or to be gained on the enemy’s side of an obstacle” (USMC Dictionary). A mobile
    defense is typically used to defend behind a linear obstacle. The commander tasks minimal forces
    to conduct the linear form. They act as a fixing force, using the obstacle to help them delay,
    disrupt, and canalize the enemy advance, leaving the enemy vulnerable to a counterattack by the
    main effort. The commander may counterattack penetrations or bridgeheads quickly or may lure
    the enemy further into the defensive battlespace to generate greater destruction.

    Because it is extremely difficult to deploy in strength along the entire length of a linear obstacle,
    the defending force must conduct economy of force measures in some areas. Consequently, the
    linear form is most effective when used in conjunction with others forms. For example,
    commanders might use sector defensive forms in the security area to disrupt and attrite the enemy,
    the linear form to fix the enemy, and a defense in depth to contain and eliminate penetrations.
    Failure to work in these types of defenses leaves the defending force vulnerable to enemy
    penetrations or bridgeheads the defending force cannot contain.

    Perimeter Defense
    The perimeter defensive form is a tool applied to all military operations. In terms of the defense, it
    is useful in all three defense types and can be used in conjunction with any of the defensive forms.
    A perimeter defense orients in all directions. It is usually employed by battalions or smaller,
    though it can also be employed by larger units executing base security functions. Commanders
    employ the perimeter defensive method in the following situations:

       • When holding key terrain (e.g., a strong point) or protecting important assets.
       • When providing for immediate self-protection or when bypassed by advancing enemy forces.
       • When the defensive SOM does not tie in adjacent units physically.

    A primary characteristic of a perimeter defense is a secure inner area with most of the combat
    power located on the perimeter. The security area is maintained through aggressive patrolling and
    security operations. Another characteristic is the ease of access for resupply operations. The
    commander coordinates direct and indirect fire plans to prevent friendly fire with neighboring
    units and noncombatants. Usually, the reserve centrally locates to react to a penetration of the
    perimeter at any point.

                                                                        8-22


---

                                                                                  MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

Perimeters vary in shape depending on the terrain and situation. If the commander determines the
most probable direction of enemy attack, the part of the perimeter covering that approach may be
reinforced with additional resources. The perimeter shape conforms to the terrain features that
best use friendly observation and fields of fire. Commanders can increase the effectiveness of the
perimeter by tying it into a natural obstacle, such as a river, which allows defending units to
concentrate their combat power in more threatened areas.

Force Organization. The characteristics of the defense apply to the perimeter defensive method in
the same manner as any other type or method of defense. Units using this defensive method have
security, main battle, and rear areas. They seek to shape operations in the security area and provide
depth and mutual support within the MBA—the perimeter. The commander uses security forces,
MBA forces, and a reserve. Depending on METT-T, the defending force either employs all their
combat power in one of two techniques.

In the first technique, commanders place all subordinate units in positions along the perimeter (see
Figure 8-1). The perimeter is divided into subordinate unit AOs with boundaries and contact
points. Each subordinate unit provides their own security force for patrolling and other security
operations. The commander either constitutes a reserve in the center or uses the least engaged
unit. This force organization maximizes combat power on the perimeter, reduces the possibility of
friendly fire incidents within the perimeter, and creates depth through in the security area. Risks in
this technique include a disjointed effort in the security area and ineffective reactions to enemy
penetrations of the perimeter.

In the second technique, commanders seek to create greater depth in the defense by employing
inner and outer perimeters (see Figure 8-1). For example, the regimental commander can assign
each battalion an AO, and direct them to employ their companies in a “two up, one back”
technique that creates an inner and outer perimeter and provides depth within the position itself.
The inner perimeter provides the reserve, the outer perimeter the main effort, and the regiment’s
third battalion can serve as the security force.

Perimeter Defense        Inner and Outer Perimeter Defense

Figure 8-1. Perimeter Defense Techniques.

                   8-23


---

MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

    Control Measures. The commander in a perimeter defense designates the trace of the perimeter,
    battle positions, contact points, and lateral and forward boundaries. The commander can use
    engagemnent areas, TRPs, FPFs, and principal direction of fire as fire control measures. The
    commander designates checkpoints, contact points, passage points, and passage routes for use by
    supporting efforts conducting reconnaissance and security operations.

    Planning a Perimeter Defense. Defending commanders face four significant decisions when
    planning perimeter positions. First, placing the position where it enables units to accomplish the
    mission. Second, determining the most likely enemy COAs, as the enemy is unlikely to attack from
    all directions at once. Third, creating the position making the best use of the terrain available.
    Fourth, locating the position where resupply is possible. For example, a commander tasked with
    defending a critical highway junction might have the unit establish a perimeter defense on high
    ground overlooking the junction. The position allows the junction to be controlled by fire while the
    high ground offers the best terrain available and provides a relatively secure LZ for resupply.

    Commanders forming a perimeter do not merely cede the security area to the enemy. The success
    of a perimeter defense primarily relies on the defensive depth, early warning, and shaping space
    the security area offers. At a minimum, commanders typically employ their organic
    reconnaissance assets, such as the scout-sniper platoon, to provide early warning and
    counterreconnaissance and to disrupt enemy plans (e.g., emplacing mortars). Commanders may
    augment this effort with sensors, target acquisition radar systems, aerial surveillance, squad-size
    or smaller observation posts, ambushes along likely avenues of approach, and aggressive
    patrolling. Commanders may also choose to create independent security forces that operate
    outside of the perimeter to deny advantageous terrain to the enemy and create the conditions
    necessary for the main effort’s decisive action.

    When planning the defensive SOM, commanders and staff account for the terrain, internal tactical
    mobility, and likely enemy COAs. In open terrain, defending forces can cover physical gaps in the
    perimeter with fires. In restrictive terrain, defending forces compensate for restricted fields of fire
    and observation by narrowing frontages, shrinking the size of the perimeter, and physically
    linking adjacent units. This may require commanders to organize their forces with all combat
    power forward.

    The commander considers tactical mobility requirements internal to the position to enable the
    rapid movement of forces and the reserve (particularly when using inner and outer perimeters), to
    create depth within the perimeter, and to enable the execution of basic logistic functions free from
    enemy observation and interference. This is particularly applicable to units employing combat
    vehicles that need to consider the creation of alternate, supplementary, and hide positions.

    The defending force decides upon the most likely enemy COAs to create a defensive SOM and
    allocate combat power accordingly. While the perimeter defensive method provides for all-around
    security, the defender accepts significant risk by trying to defend everywhere equally. The force
    uses METT-T to determine likely enemy actions, counter them, and seek opportunities for
    offensive action. Accordingly, commanders integrate obstacles with fires and observation and seek
    to enable enough space within the perimeter for defensive maneuver, such as alternate positions for
    antiarmor weapons and proper placement for the reserve. Fire support planning is typical of the
    defense. If the defending force is isolated, commanders seek to use external fire support assets

                                                                        8-24


---

                                                                                  MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

before internal resources. Defensive positions within the perimeter are placed to decrease the
ability of the enemy to simultaneously suppress them with the same fires (i.e., forcing the enemy to
split their forces to deal with friendly positions vice allowing them to mass combat power).

Executing a Perimeter Defense. The defending force begins the defensive fight by executing
shaping actions in the security area. Depending on resources that are available, the defender works
to defeat enemy reconnaissance efforts, disrupt enemy movement, and deny the enemy’s use of
likely support-by-fire and assault positions. As the attack progresses, reconnaissance and security
assets use supporting arms and the commander employs information activities to further break up
enemy formations and tempo.

Attacks against the perimeter can consist of anything from enemy long range sniper, mortar, and
rocket fire attacks to suicide demolition squads and attacks by enemy ground and air forces.
Regardless, friendly supporting arms, antiarmor, and crew-served weapons leverage natural and
reinforcing obstacles to engage the enemy at long ranges. If the attack comes within small-arms
range, other weapons on the perimeter engage the enemy and FPFs are used, if required. Friendly
forces maneuver within the perimeter, using other positions to increase their chances of surviving,
limit enemy options, and counter threats. Should the enemy penetrate the perimeter, the reserve
blocks the penetration or counterattacks to restore the primary defensive positions. If the
commander uses an unengaged force to constitute a new reserve, the commander must retain
sufficient forces to defend the vacated sector, unless the situation forces the commander to assume
that degree of risk.

After successfully defending the perimeter, the unit pursues withdrawing enemy forces, as able,
either physically or through fires. If defending forces do not transition to the offense, they
immediately begin to reconstitute the defense and reestablish the security area. The staff modifies
the defensive SOM as much as practicable to present the enemy a different tactical problem
should they choose to attack again.

Reverse Slope Defense
The reverse slope defensive form is used in conjunction with other defensive forms when the
commander wishes to mask the main defensive positions from enemy observation and fires.
Defenders at the battalion level and below typically use this form when the enemy has a
qualitative or quantitative advantage that makes a forward slope defense untenable, when
defenders seek to use surprise in conjunction with the decisive action, or both. Additional
considerations include the following:

  • The crest and forward slope offer little or no cover and concealment, was lost, or was not seized.
  • Friendly units on the flanks can adequately cover the forward slope.
  • The defending force is in contact with the enemy and is forced to assume a hasty defense.

A successful reverse slope defense relies upon denying the enemy the topographical crest.
Although the defender may not occupy the crest in strength, controlling the crest by fire is
essential for success. The goal is to force enemy forces to try and cross the exposed crest while
denying them effective use of their supporting arms against a defender located on the reverse and
counter slopes. Firing from covered and concealed positions in these areas, using obstacles to
maximize effects, and having the ability to maneuver that a forward slope defense would deny

                                                                   8-25


---

MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

them, the defending force maintains a distinct advantage over enemy forces exposed on the
topographical crest. Enemy forces that do push forward of the crest remain exposed, disoriented,
and canalized into unfamiliar terrain, kill zones, and engagement areas.

Commanders choosing to use the reverse slope defensive method accept risk in limiting their
observation and ability to engage the enemy forward of the topographical crest. Often, the best
terrain to employ obstacles and create engagement areas is forward and once security forces
withdraw, the enemy is largely unimpeded in conducting maneuver and preparations for their
assault. Commanders must also consider that surprise is one fundamental advantage of this
defensive method, and once the enemy overcomes that effect, the defending force may be at a
considerable disadvantage. Finally, a reverse slope defense allows the enemy the advantage of
attacking downhill. See Figure 8-2 for slope components.

       Topographical Crest

       Forward Slope        Reverse Slope   Counter Slope

                Forward        Reverse
            Military Crest  Military Crest

Enemy

                                              Figure 8-2. Slope Components.

Force Organization. When executing the reverse slope defensive form, the commander uses the
security, MBA forces, and reserve forces associated with the defense. The security force executes
reconnaissance tasks, placing elements where they can observe the forward slope, the terrain
forward of it, and likely enemy avenues of approach. Other security elements attack enemy
reconnaissance assets, delay the enemy, disorganize the enemy’s attack, and deceive the enemy
regarding the exact location of the main defense. The defending force can source assets from the
reserve to occupy observation posts near or forward of the topographical crest to provide long
range observation of the enemy’s flanks and front.

The MBA forces position themselves to mass fires on enemy forces attempting to cross the
topographical crest. The MBA forces capitalize on the characteristics of the defense, maneuver,
terrain, and multiple positions to prevent the enemy from penetrating or effectively targeting
friendly positions. Figure 8-3 depicts the use of an oblique defilade to ensure coverage of the
crest. The force in the MBA assists the security force in maintaining observation and fires over the
forward slope as long as possible to disrupt enemy attempts to seize and push beyond the
topographical crest. Whenever possible, commanders use other maneuver elements to support
units in reverse slope positions by placing them where they can observe and generate effects on
the forward slope.

The reserve counterattacks enemy penetrations, maneuvers against exposed enemy flanks, and can
serve as the decisive action of the defense. Depending on METT-T and acceptable risk, the
defending force can employ the reserve in limited attacks across the topographical crest to disrupt
enemy forces on the forward slope. Commanders might place the reserve on the counter slope to
support the main battle force by fire or by maneuver, if the terrain allows.

                                                                   8-26


---

                                                                                  MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

                                               Figure 8-3. Oblique Defilade.
Control Measures. Defensive control measures introduced in previous chapters apply equally to
the reverse slope defense. Units establish engagement areas and obstacles on the reverse slope.
The topographical crest usually marks the far edge of the engagement area. The defending force
must dominate the topographic crest by fires to prevent the enemy from successfully engaging it.
Executing a Reverse Slope Defense. As with any impending attack, friendly security forces try to
observe and disrupt enemy preparations while at the same time deny the enemy’s the ability to do
the same. As the enemy advances, security forces use any combination of maneuver and
observation to disrupt, delay, and canalize the enemy through fires and combat. Security force
commanders endeavor to operate in a manner that does not disclose the main defensive positions
and make a determined effort to leave forces in place to observe the forward slope.
As the enemy advance reaches the forward slope, the security force or the main battle forces
establish observation of the enemy and use indirect fires to delay, disrupt, and attrite the enemy. If
it aligns with the METT-T, commanders use the forward slope positions to provide cover while
they withdraw to engage the enemy deep and as a tactical ruse to further mislead the enemy as to
the location of the main defensive positions. As the enemy nears the topographical crest,
commanders use integrated obstacles and direct and indirect fires to prevent enemy occupation
and use of the crest. Observers use indirect fires on the forward slope to further break up the
enemy’s momentum and attempts to recover and reorganize.
As the enemy attack stalls and hesitates on the topographical crest, commanders might choose to
employ the reserve. The reserve can: provide additional fires from the counter slope to support the
main effort; maneuver to enemy flanks and attack by fire; or counterattack and expel the enemy
from the crest. Commanders may also use the reserve to prolong the effectiveness of the reverse
slope defense, using the reserve to counter enemy attempts to bypass the defense.

TRANSITIONS

Units conduct transitions when—
  • The mission changes.
  • The enemy’s actions or TTP change.

                                                                   8-27


---

MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

       • Additional functions are added to a unit.
       • The environment changes (e.g., urban to rural).
       • The AO changes.
       • Task organization changes.

    Successful defensive operations transition to offensive operations or stabilization activities.
    Unsuccessful defenses transition to other types of defenses, such as a retrograde.

    Transition to Offensive Operations
    A unit transitions from the defense to the offense because they are ordered to do so, have planned
    to do so after some defensive criteria is met, or unexpected events present an opportunity to do so.
    Ideally, commanders consider a transition to the offense as part of their defensive planning,
    anticipating when and where the enemy will reach a culminating point or become vulnerable to
    offensive action. Although they must guard against enemy deception, Marines look for indicators
    of such conditions, to include the following:

       • Enemy forces begin to transition to the defense.
       • Enemy forces suffer heavy losses.
       • Enemy forces are committed piecemeal in continued enemy attacks.
       • Enemy reserve forces are identified among attacking forces.
       • Examination of captured or killed enemy personnel and captured or destroyed enemy

         equipment and supplies shows that the enemy force is unable to adequately sustain itself.
       • The tempo of enemy operations decreases.
       • Local counterattacks meet with unexpected success.

    To successfully transition to the offense after achieving initial success, the friendly force must
    establish momentum and capitalize on both the psychological boost that friendly forces receive,
    and the despair and confusion enemy forces endure. Although there will be an inevitable pause
    during the transition, commanders must minimize transition time to prevent the enemy from
    establishing an effective defense. Commanders achieve this by pushing security forces forward
    during the transition to maintain contact with and pressure on the enemy and avoid enemy
    deception operations. Simultaneously, commanders redeploy and reorganize for the attack with
    actions such as moving fire support assets forward and transitioning engineer priorities from
    countermobility and survivability to mobility.

    Commanders also plan to transition their logistic effort, shifting focus from supporting the defense
    of a known location to supporting advance and maneuver (e.g., shifting from stockpiling
    construction materials to pushing fuel forward). Planning for the transition from defense to
    offense also enables CSS assets to take advantage of the time available to conduct tasks such as
    deferred equipment maintenance and medical treatment that further aid the offense.

    Units can use two basic techniques when transitioning to the offense. The first and generally
    preferred technique is to attack using forces not previously committed to the defense. These forces
    may come from the reserve, be pulled from units not in contact, or be formed with reinforcements.
    These previously uncommitted forces are likely well-organized, rested, and in a position to plan

                                                                        8-28


---

                                                                                  MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

and prepare, and combat ready for offensive action. Their use mitigates delays that can occur
when the main battle force is still decisively engaged. When employing these units, the
commander will have to adopt economy of force operations or temporarily abandon AOs and
accept risk to generate sufficient combat power.

The second technique is to transition to offensive operations using the currently defending
forces. This technique generally has the advantage of being more rapidly executed and thus be
more likely to catch the enemy by surprise. The speed gained by this type of execution results
from not having to conduct an approach or tactical road march from reserve assembly areas or, in
the case of reinforcements, move from other AOs and reception, staging, organization, and
integration locations. Speed also results from not having to conduct a forward passage of lines
(see Chapter 17). The primary disadvantage of this technique is that forces suffering from
exhaustion may have to be replaced if the operation is not expected to culminate quickly.

Transition to Stabilization Activities
Civil considerations are inherent to all military operations. Just as a force conducting offensive
operations must plan to interact with a potentially hostile population, forces conducting defensive
operations can expect to deal with friendly civilians seeking aid or trying to flee the area. Beyond
this, however, are situations when stabilization activities become a unit’s primary focus of effort.

Units change their focus of effort from defensive to stabilization activities when the mission
changes (e.g., ordered to conduct rear area security), the situation changes, or hostilities end (e.g.,
friendly territory is successfully retained). If the latter, this transition should be accomplished per
previous planning efforts—stabilization activities that support transition to civil authority cannot
be afterthoughts. It follows that setting these transition conditions can significantly affect the
planning and execution of the preceding defensive operations. As the unit transitions from the
defense to stabilization activities, the commander—

  • Maintains contact and surveillance of any remaining enemy or hostile elements.
  • Maintains the combat power necessary to conduct security operations.
  • Establishes either contiguous or noncontiguous AOs for subordinate forces.
  • Prepares to transition some or all combat support units to other roles such as provisional

     infantry, mobility operations, or critical infrastructure reconstruction.
  • Conducts command and control and task reorganization to support stabilization activities to

     include adding and integrating new functions and enablers.
  • Where possible, integrates operations with proper civil authority, whether an occupational

     government, international organization, or host-nation authority.
  • Consolidates, reorganizes, and requests logistic support for stabilization activities, and seeks

     to maximize opportunities for reconstitution of the force.
  • Readdresses risk assessment assumptions and ROE.
  • Conducts necessary training and reorientation of the unit’s personnel to combat complacency

     and reinforce the shift in emphasis from the defense to stabilization activities.

                                                                   8-29


---



---

                     CHAPTER 9.
                   AREA DEFENSE

An area defense capitalizes on the strength inherent in closely integrated defensive organization
on the ground. Conducting an area defense helps consolidate and reconstitute forces necessary to
transition to offense operations or stabilization activities. Commanders may assign subordinate
units area defense missions as part of a larger type of defense.

The purpose of all defenses is to defeat the enemy and transition to the offense. All defenses use
terrain to their advantage. The area defense, however, focuses on retaining, denying, or clearing
specified terrain. A friendly force conducts, or is directed to conduct, an area defense when—

  • Terrain limits maneuver space, restricting the movement of the defending force but also
     affording natural lines of resistance and limiting the enemy to a few, well-defined avenues
     of approach.

  • The reserve is unavailable or is constrained by terrain, lack of mobility, or enemy
     air superiority.

  • The forces available are less mobile than the enemy and when the depth of the AO
     is limited.

  • There is enough time to organize the position and terrain allows for mutual support.
  • Employing precision weapons or weapons of mass destruction by the enemy is possible.
  • Conducting force protection while transitioning from the offense or stabilization activities.

The two methods of area defense are defense in depth and forward defense. Both demonstrate that
area defenses are not merely static, but also employ all characteristics of the defense including
maneuver. Static actions in the area defense usually consist of fires from prepared positions.
Maneuver actions include repositioning units between prepared positions (or forward operating
bases), counterattacks to enemy penetrations, and spoiling attacks to disrupt an enemy attack (see
Chapter 5).

FORCE ORGANIZATION

Regardless of whether commanders choose a spatial- or purpose-based battlespace framework,
they organize the force into security, MBA, and reserve forces to execute the defensive SOM (see
Figure 9-1). See Chapter 2 for discussion of battlespace frameworks.


---

MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

Security Area

Main Battle Area                                 Reserve
         Rear Area

                                Figure 9-1. Organization of Forces for an Area Defense.

Security Forces
Security forces in the area defense conduct the reconnaissance, counterreconnaissance, and
security tasks discussed in Chapters 8, 13, and 14. With the area defense’s focus on terrain, the
security force adds depth to the overall defensive effort and provides the ability to interrupt enemy
preparations through spoiling attacks and using supporting arms and defensive actions to delay,
disrupt, and attrite their advance. Ideally, the security force’s actions compel the enemy to conduct
a movement to contact. The commander places a high priority on quickly identifying and
attacking the enemy’s main effort. Commanders may assign screen, guard, or cover missions
depending on METT-T and the resources available (see Chapter 14). While commanders must
balance combat power requirements between the security force and MBA forces, they ensure that
the security force has, at a minimum, the resources necessary to provide early warning of enemy
action and to protect themselves from unexpected enemy contact. Commanders must convey the
