acceptable risk to the security force or the disengagement criteria in quantifiable terms, such as
friendly strength levels, time, or event. Assigning a force to conduct rear area security is a
decision based on METT-T, the size of the unit’s rear area, and available combat power.

Main Battle Area Forces
The MBA is where the main force executes the decisive action. Main battle forces consist of the
main and necessary supporting forces who will be executing the defensive SOM—halting and
defeating or destroying the enemy. In the area defense, the commander and staff build the MBA
force around key terrain and high-payoff targets, using fires from mutually supporting, prepared
positions supplemented with counterattack and force repositioning to retain terrain. The main effort
in the area defense often involves close combat given the priority regarding terrain retention.

Reserve
In the area defense, the force plans to succeed without using the reserve. The reserve is primarily
created to exploit opportunities, seize the initiative from the enemy, counter unexpected enemy
actions, or restore the integrity of the area defense against enemy success.

                                            9-2


---

                                                                                  MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

Examples include—

  • Reinforcing the defense of committed forces, such as extending their flanks to
     prevent envelopment.

  • Relieving depleted units and providing for continuous operations.
  • Reacting to threats directed against the friendly force’s rear area.
  • Covering a retrograde movement.

It might be difficult for commanders executing an area defense to constitute a reserve given the
demands on combat power that terrain retention entails and because attackers will seek to
overmatch combat power against defenders. While tempting to either forgo establishing a reserve
(company commanders and below form reserves based on METT-T) or use the “least engaged
unit,” these options end up being self-defeating because they rob commanders of crucial
flexibility. In the area defense, commanders can resolve this by placing their most mobile assets in
reserve. This provides the reserve with the mobility needed to perform their mission and enables
commanders to accept risk elsewhere in the battlespace because they have a force that can rapidly
respond to enemy threats.

Other alternatives include using security forces as a reserve once they retrograde back through
friendly lines, although commanders must then accept considerable risk to the security force
mission (i.e., security forces must withdraw in time to reconstitute themselves as a reserve) and
the reserve mission (i.e., enemy action may significantly degrade security forces rendering them
ineffective). Another option is to divide the reserve into smaller units spread throughout the
battlespace. This is effective when terrain significantly affects the reserve’s mobility; however, it
creates risk in that it becomes difficult to mass the reserve if necessary. Finally, commanders
accept prudent risk and place the reserve where they feel the reserve is most likely needed. This is
also effective when terrain affects reserve mobility and when commanders need the impact of the
entire reserve if committed. This last option is similar to others in that, in restrictive terrain, the
reserve is unable to rapidly respond to opportunity or crisis elsewhere.

CONTROL MEASURES

Commanders organize an area defense by, at a minimum, using boundaries and AOs to establish
security, main battle, and rear areas and assign responsibilities to subordinate units. When
possible, the boundaries of the security force coincide with those of the MBA force. The security
area should be deep enough to require the enemy to displace its combat support and CSS assets
(e.g., artillery and maintenance units) forward to carry the attack into the MBA. This makes those
assets vulnerable to friendly maneuver and supporting arms. Other area defense control measures
include engagement areas, the FEBA, handover lines, strong points, TRPs, NAIs, TAIs, and other
fire-coordination control measures. Chapters 2 and 8 define these control measures.

Commanders ensure the plans of their subordinates support the overall defense and are
deconflicted from each other by using control measures such as contact points and phase lines.
Commanders are responsible for overall battlespace geometry and movement planning between
the positions of subordinate units—particularly when planning passage of lines for security forces
and reserves. See Chapter 17 for information on rearward and forward passages of lines.

                                                                    9-3


---

MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

   PLANNING AN AREA DEFENSE

    The primary factor when planning an area defense is terrain—the nature of the terrain, its
    centrality, the balance of forces that dictates its use; area defense is a terrain-driven mission. In
    planning, the staff determines how to integrate available forces, fires, and obstacles with the
    existing terrain to isolate and defeat the enemy. The second factor is gaining the time necessary to
    prepare a coherent, coordinated, and effective defense that enables selected defensive positions to
    defeat the enemy by fire, absorb the enemy attack, and launch local counterattacks. Once dug,
    defensive positions cannot be moved. Without proper time to prepare, the unit risks committing to
    a faulty defensive SOM. See Chapter 8 for general defensive planning considerations.

    One key to addressing terrain and time is that selected defensive positions can provide mutual
    support and concentrate fires to build depth in the security and MBAs, create maneuver within
    the defense, and take full advantage of the terrain. Commanders also consider whether the unit
    will eventually be able to transition to some sort of offensive operation—remaining static in an
    area defense over time provides the enemy opportunity to better prepare and eventually
    overwhelm the defender.

    Commanders assigning the defensive mission define the area to defend. The ideal area defense is
    one in which effective mutual support exists throughout the breadth and depth of the defender’s
    tactical positions. This allows commanders to use multiple defensive methods, such as sectors and
    battle positions, and increase flexibility. However, commanders assigned the defense over broad
    fronts often must conduct noncontiguous operations. Commanders assigned shallow AOs
    experience reduced flexibility and must fight well forward.

    Therefore, commanders planning an area defense may be given, or may choose between, the two
    methods of area defense. The two methods are not exclusionary; part of a unit may conduct a
    forward defense while another part conducts a defense in depth. Commanders choose the defense
    in depth when the mission and METT-T enable the defending force to allow terrain and space to
    absorb the momentum of the enemy attack. Commanders choose a forward defense when the
    mission and METT-T do not allow for significant enemy penetration into the defensive area.

    Defense in Depth
    The defense in depth method is typically the preferred option. Forces using this method absorb the
    momentum of the enemy’s attack by forcing the enemy to attack repeatedly through mutually
    supporting positions arranged in depth. Figure 9-2 depicts a defense in depth with units deployed
    in noncontiguous AOs with enemy avenues of approach. Along with the general considerations
    for an area defense, commanders select the defense in depth method when the—

       • Mission is not restrictive and allows the unit to fight throughout the depth of the battlespace.
       • Terrain does not favor a defense well forward, and there is more easily defendable terrain

         deeper within the AO.
       • AO is deep compared to its breadth, and there is significant depth available.
       • Cover and concealment on or near the FEBA are limited.
       • Enemy has greater combat power than the defender.
       • Enemy has precision munitions or is likely to use weapons of mass destruction.

                                                                         9-4


---

                                                                                  MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

The use of the defense in depth requires the use of significant engineer and other resources
dedicated to survivability and countermobility. But the depth of the defense gives the friendly
force’s fire support assets time to deliver destructive effects throughout the battlespace and affords
the defending force multiple opportunities to concentrate overwhelming combat power against the
attacking enemy. The defense in depth also provides more reaction time for the defending force to
respond to the attack. Between the time the security forces provide their first warning and the time
the enemy commits to a COA, the staff is able to receive and process continuous information on
the attacker’s intentions and capabilities and respond accordingly, reducing the risk of an enemy
force penetrating the defense from an unexpected direction.

                                         Figure 9-2. Defense-in-Depth Example.

Forward Defense
When using the forward defense method of the area defense, commanders concentrate significant
portions of their available combat power into engagement areas along the FEBA. The intent is to
prevent significant enemy penetration into the defensive area. Commanders conducting a forward
defense fight to retain these positions along the FEBA and violently counterattack any enemy
penetration. Commanders accept risk in that, if the enemy penetrates the defense, the lack of depth
may enable the enemy to rapidly exploit success. In general, commanders execute the forward
defense when terrain must be retained for political, military, economic, or other reasons. In addition
to the general considerations for using an area defense, commanders select the forward defense
method when—

  • The best defensive positions are located along the FEBA.
  • Natural obstacles are located near the FEBA.
  • There is natural engagement areas near the FEBA.
  • Cover and concealment in the rear portion of the AO are limited.

                                                                    9-5


---

MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

    Logistic Considerations
    In addition to the typical logistic considerations for the defense discussed in Chapter 8, there are
    two that commanders must plan for in the area defense. The first is that area defenses require
    prepared defensive positions that demand significant construction time and material support. The
    second is that because area defenses are tied to terrain—and may take place in restrictive terrain
    where mobility is a concern—logistic functions may be pushed forward to enable rapid CSS.
    Therefore, logistic planners must ensure they do not place so many supplies and assets forward
    that they become vulnerable to destruction or capture should the enemy advance.

   PREPARING AN AREA DEFENSE

    When assigned or transitioning to a defensive mission, the commander employs the elements of
    design in considering the tactical problem and providing the staff with initial planning guidance for
    problem framing. If not immediately, then early in the planning process the commander will make
    the decision to employ an area defense. This early decision enables all MAGTF elements to begin
    planning and preparing for the mission—involving tasks such as obtaining and pre-positioning
    ammunition and barrier material.

    While a defending force may execute the area defense in a hasty or deliberate manner, effective
    area defenses require the maximum available amount of time. Consequently, initial preparations
    after the commander’s decision to execute an area defense involve significant reconnaissance and
    security efforts to acquire information that helps refine planning and preparation and to conduct
    shaping actions that increases preparation time. Available ISR assets are used to answer the
    commander’s critical information requirements. Within the force’s capability, OPSEC guidelines,
    and METT-T, security forces and supporting arms are employed to delay and disrupt enemy attack
    preparations by targeting and attacking them. If a commander determines that it is likely the
    enemy will attack before the defending force is prepared, the commander might have to commit
    substantial forces to security operations or conduct a spoiling attack—particularly if conducting
    deliberate operations.

    Upon receiving their warning orders, defending units conduct reconnaissance, whether a simple
    map reconnaissance or a more detailed leader’s reconnaissance on the ground of their assigned
    defensive areas and positions. As soon as practical, units establish their security areas and then
    occupy their defensive positions. Once security is established, units may begin to receive and
    pre-position supplies such as construction and barrier materials. Units rely on their SOPs and
    METT-T to establish and refine their defensive priorities of work. Those priorities might be—

       • Establishing local security and deploying a security force.
       • Identifying engagement areas where the commander wants to engage and destroy the enemy.
       • Conducting fire support planning, such as determining preplanned targets, TRPs, trigger

         lines, and FPFs to support the engagement areas.
       • Positioning key weapon systems to engage the enemy in the engagement areas and

         developing range cards and sector sketches.
       • Positioning observers to see both targets and trigger lines.

                                                                         9-6


---

                                                                                  MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

  • Positioning obstacle groups to support the effects generated by various weapon systems.
  • Designating and clearing fields of fire.
  • Preparing primary fighting positions based on the anticipated fighting conditions, such as the

     time of day and weather conditions.
  • Emplacing obstacles and surveying indirect fire targets to support those obstacles.
  • Providing concealment and camouflage for fighting and survivability positions as they

     are constructed.
  • Positioning CFZs over friendly positions by establishing sensor coverage and quick-fire links

     between the sensor and shooter. These CFZs are planned by the supporting artillery unit based
     on commander’s guidance and an assessment of the available radar positioning and
     operational capabilities.
  • Installing night and limited-visibility aids, such as thermal hot spots and chemical lights
     on TRPs.
  • Updating range cards and sector sketches as required.
  • Preparing alternate fighting positions.
  • Designating and preparing supplementary positions.
  • Designating hide positions and rehearsing movements to and from fighting positions. (Units
     may place their combat and tactical vehicles in hide positions at any time while preparing the
     defensive position.)
  • Positioning the reserve.
  • Establishing contact points with any adjacent units so that the defensive efforts of both units
     can be tied together.
  • Deconflicting the plans and fires of adjacent units.
  • Emplacing communications assets to support the unit’s primary, alternate, contingency, and
     emergency communications for each primary, supplementary, and alternate positions.
  • Improving mobility on counterattack routes and other routes to be used by the reserve.
  • Pre-stocking ammunition in revetments or bunkers where it can survive the enemy’s
     preparatory fires.
  • Rehearsing movements under daylight and limited-visibility conditions to include forward
     and rearward passage of lines.
  • Establishing sleep and rest plans.
  • Continuing to improve the defense.

Just as reconnaissance and security activities begin even as planning and preparation continue, so
do OPSEC and counterreconnaissance activities. Commanders employ camouflage, tactical ruses,
deception, and smoke to confuse and deceive enemy reconnaissance assets. Units quickly establish
wire communications among various subordinate elements to reduce their electromagnetic
signature. The conduct and evidence of preparation and rehearsals are mitigated by hiding or
camouflaging spoil from digging, as well as by altering when individual units conduct rehearsals
and how they conduct them (e.g., mounted units moving by foot instead of by vehicle, or by only

                                                                    9-7


---

MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

    one vehicle per platoon). Since the location, composition, and movement of the reserve are critical
    elements of information for the enemy, commanders work diligently to camouflage, conceal, and
    avoid detection of their reserve.

    As time and resources allow, the defending unit improves communication routes throughout their
    defensive positions to ease movement of supplies and forces, particularly the reserve. The
    leadership rehearses the plan using MDCA. Individual elements rehearse how to move from their
    hide positions to their primary positions and how they will occupy alternate and supplementary
    positions to continue to engage the enemy if the enemy’s attack progresses into the unit’s
    defensive positions. These rehearsals establish the time necessary to conduct these movements
    under different environmental conditions. Commanders modify their existing plans based on the
    results of rehearsals and changes in METT-T.

    Commanders include logistic leadership in the maneuver rehearsal to verify that routes for support
    do not cross or conflict with routes used by reserve forces or other maneuver elements.
    Commanders should balance the use of ammunition caches against the defending unit’s ability to
    guard them. Also, commanders should ensure that alternate supply routes are adequate to
    accommodate contingency plans and that units can effectively switch to alternate MSRs.

   EXECUTING AN AREA DEFENSE

    The successful area defense relies on actions in the security area to disrupt and attrite the enemy, and
    static, mutually supporting defensive positions arranged in depth that concentrate combat power to
    fix and defeat the enemy. The reserve is used to reinforce these efforts, exploit opportunity, or defeat
    unexpected enemy actions. Commanders use alternate and supplementary positions and local
    counterattacks to add further depth and flexibility to the defense.

    The phasing of defensive operations depends on how the commander decides to solve the tactical
    problem. In general, and subject to the needs of the commander and the mission, units conduct
    offensive operations in five phases:

       • Gain and maintain enemy contact.
       • Disrupt the enemy.
       • Fix the enemy.
       • Maneuver.
       • Follow through and counterattack.

    The first three phases listed are almost always shaping actions. Depending on the circumstances,
    either of the last two phases may be the decisive action.

    Gain and Maintain Enemy Contact
    Depending on METT-T and planning considerations, the commander may or may not have
    assigned the security force to conduct both reconnaissance and security tasks. Regardless, as
    operations begin, the initial focus of friendly forces in the security area and beyond is to win the
    reconnaissance and counterreconnaissance fight. This fight begins immediately, even as

                                                                         9-8


---

                                                                                  MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

preparations and planning continue elsewhere in the AO. Friendly ISR assets employ stealth,
supporting arms, technical means, and standoff to gain and maintain contact and observation of
the enemy. At the same time, security and aviation forces search for and destroy enemy
reconnaissance elements to conceal the defending force’s dispositions, capabilities, and intent.
Doing so forces the enemy to attack with limited information—making them susceptible to
deception and canalization—and fight on ground of the defensive commander’s choosing.

As the enemy prepares to attack, friendly reconnaissance efforts identify enemy assembly areas,
units and capabilities, C2 nodes, and critical assets such as breaching resources. The staff uses this
information to modify the defensive SOM, finalize planning and preparation, and take advantage
of opportunities. As the enemy’s attack begins, reconnaissance focuses on identifying enemy units
committed to the attack and their capabilities; the enemy’s intent and direction of attack; locations
of supporting arms, air defense assets, and command and control; and the depth and nature of
follow-on forces. As more information becomes available and multiple source reporting increases
its reliability, the commander and staff use the information, experience, and military judgment to
address decision points and determine when the enemy commits to a COA.

The single-battle construct underscores the significance of gaining and maintaining contact with
the enemy throughout a military engagement. Even as the enemy attack presses through the
security area and into the MBA, designated reconnaissance and security forces remain forward,
providing continuous information on enemy actions and enabling the commander and staff to
support the main effort by executing precision engagement against enemy C2 and logistic nodes
and identifying enemy flanks for counterattack. In the planning phase, the commander and staff
determine which elements remain forward and under what conditions, and their displacement
criteria. The commander retrogrades reconnaissance assets with the security force, replacing them
with technical means of ISR depending on METT-T and if the resources are available.

Disrupt the Enemy
The defending force begins disrupting the enemy as soon as possible after gaining and
maintaining contact. This is not a “phase” of the battle as much as an ongoing activity that takes
place throughout planning and preparation and into execution. At a minimum, the defending
forces employ supporting arms and information activities against enemy critical vulnerabilities.
During this time, commanders may choose to commit combat power to spoiling attacks, feints,
and demonstrations to further delay and disrupt—and perhaps even dissuade—enemy attack
preparations. If commanders do so, they do so with the planning and execution considerations
discussed in Chapters 3 and 5. Additional considerations include when and how to phase forces
conducting these types of activities back into the defensive SOM.

As the enemy’s attack enters the security area, the security force conducts activities designed to
gain information, disrupt the enemy forces’ tempo and formations, limit their options, and ideally,
compel them to conduct a movement to contact against a prepared defense. The security force
employs fire support and information capabilities to disrupt enemy forces’ decision-making
process and their ability to coordinate and synchronize actions. Using ambushes, limited
counterattacks, battle positions, and other defensive methods, the security force compels enemy
forces’ to repeatedly deploy, breaks up their formations, disrupts their ability to mass combat
power, and neutralizes their initiative. Once the process of disrupting the attacking enemy begins,
it continues throughout the defensive operation.

                                                                    9-9


---

MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

    As the battle in the security area unfolds, there are three possible outcomes. First, the security
    force could experience unexpected success, so severely disrupting and degrading enemy forces
    that they either retreat or become effectively fixed. Both reactions would present the commander
    with an opportunity to conduct offensive action with the commitment of the reserve and security
    forces. Second, the security force could accomplish its mission, delaying and disrupting enemy
    forces and setting them up for defeat by the main effort in the MBA. Third, the security force
    might fail its mission, allowing the enemy attack to advance into the MBA. In this case, the
    commander still expects to win in the MBA, but employs the reserves against the enemy in ways
    that directly support the main effort.

    Aside from the case of unexpected success, when the security force accomplishes its mission or
    reaches its displacement criteria, the security force (including reconnaissance elements), or
    designated elements of, conducts a rearward passage of lines and battle handover with main battle
    forces. The displacement and retrograde is conducted as quickly as possible to minimize the
    security force’s vulnerability to enemy fire, using multiple passage points, gaps, or lanes along the
    FEBA. Engineer assets close obstacle lanes as the security force completes its retrograde while
    maintenance and recovery assets position themselves to rapidly remove vehicle casualties from
    passage lanes.

    Depending on enemy pressure, the security force’s withdrawal can take place in mass or in
    sequence. The employment of fires, smoke, and information activities helps the security force
    break contact and facilitates the passage of lines. Combat support and CSS elements of the
    security force leave the security area early to avoid hampering the movement of maneuver forces.
    Transfer of responsibility between the security force and MBA forces occurs forward of the FEBA
    at the handover line. (See Chapter 17 for more information on passage of lines.) If forces are left
    in the security area to continue shaping and disruption actions, the commander must ensure fires
    and maneuver are deconflicted between the security areas and the MBAs.

    As the security force complete the battle handover they prepare for their subsequent tasks. The
    nature of those tasks depends on the defensive SOM. When the defending force is critically short of
    combat power, the security force can move immediately to pre-designated positions within the
    MBA, such as those associated with flank security, or they may immediately form the reserve. In
    both cases, a lack of resources could force the commander to accept the risk associated with
    employing a disorganized and potentially degraded force in such significant roles. Most often, the
    security forces move to an assembly area that allows them to reconstitute and reorganize prior to
    executing their subsequent tasks and follow-on missions. The presence of security forces in the
    assembly area allows the commander to immediately employ the existing reserve if desired, relying
    on the security forces to become the new reserve as they reassemble, resupply, and reorganize.
    However, it may be some time before security forces are ready for commitment.

    Fix the Enemy
    In the area defense, the friendly force begins to fix the enemy with shaping actions that delay,
    disrupt, and attrite the main enemy forces, isolate them from support, and disrupt follow-on
    forces. The friendly force completes fixing the enemy using obstacles and defensive positions in
    the MBA that pin the enemy in one or more engagement areas for destruction. The main effort
    defeats the enemy in these engagement areas either by fires, by counterattack, or both.

                                                                        9-10


---

                                                                                  MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

As the security force hands over the battle to the MBA force, direct and indirect fires and
information activities synchronize to continue the disruption and attrition begun in the security
area. Through fixed defensive positions and obstacles that use turn, disrupt, and block effects to
canalize the enemy, Marines remove the enemy’s options for maneuver while breaking up their
main force into isolated segments incapable of maintaining mutual support. Friendly supporting
efforts occupy these defensive positions and associated engagement areas, displace between them
when required, and conduct local counterattacks to set the conditions necessary for the main
effort’s success. The commander can employ the reserve to prevent the enemy from executing an
unexpected COA. Concurrently, forces remaining in the security area employ supporting arms and
maneuver to continue to attack and disrupt enemy command and control, follow-on forces, and
logistic resources.

Maneuver
As the enemy attack approaches the MBA, friendly forces prepare to execute the decisive action.
In the area defense, the decisive action is typically the massing of combat power in an engagement
area against the enemy main body. The defender uses the strength of prepared positions,
camouflage, concealment, and hide positions to offset attempts by the attacker to suppress and
neutralize friendly positions. The defender’s main effort uses a combination of obstacles and
massed fires to defeat the enemy while supporting efforts in the main battle and security areas
continue to attack and disrupt enemy follow-on forces, command and control, and logistics.

If the decision has not already been made, as the enemy advances deeper into the MBA the
defending commander selects a COA based on the enemy’s perceived intent. The enemy seeks to
place overwhelming combat power against what is perceived as weaknesses in the defense (a
general attacker-to-defender ratio of three-to-one could easily become a local six-to-one ratio or
higher), and the defensive SOM hinges on placing the main effort and combat power in a position
to restore a more favorable force ratio. Consequently, if the enemy is taking unexpected actions or
if friendly shaping efforts fail to compel the enemy to maneuver in the desired manner, the
commander considers committing the reserve to restore the situation, execute branch plans, and
displace the main effort to supplementary and subsequent positions. When committing the reserve
to reinforce a position or restore the situation, the defending forces must deconflict traffic priorities,
establish control measures, delineate command relationships, and mitigate battlespace geometry.

As the enemy commits its main effort, defending forces continue to execute the SOM. Gaps
between defensive positions are kept under surveillance, covered by fire, or when necessary,
covered by displacing units. Units respond to enemy penetrations in their battle positions and
sectors with local counterattacks or by repositioning to alternate positions. A unit does not
abandon a position unless it is in accordance with the defensive SOM or a higher commander
grants permission to do so. Enemy gains that threaten the overall integrity of the defense cannot be
allowed to consolidate. The friendly unit destroys enemy forces by committing the reserve
directly against them or at exposed flanks that isolate the enemy penetrations for later defeat. The
security force completes its reorganization and resupply and becomes available as a reconstituted
reserve. The defensive force continues to attack the enemy throughout the depth of the AO.

                                                                   9-11


---

MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

    With the enemy main body fixed, the defensive main effort executes its mission, massing combat
    power to defeat the enemy. The main effort may execute local counterattacks to enhance the
    destructive effects of fires and information activities on the enemy. In general, the lowest
    possible echelons conduct these local counterattacks, though commanders remain wary of
    piecemeal commitment.

    The maneuver phase in the MBA culminates in one of three ways. First, the defensive effort is
    successful, and the commander must determine how to best exploit the enemy’s defeat. Second,
    the defensive effort reaches a stalemate, and the commander must determine how to best adjust to
    the new enemy advance or how to restore the original defense through reinforcement and
    counterattacks by higher units. Third, the defensive effort fails, and the commander must
    determine whether the situation can be stabilized and if not, how to transition to retrograde
    activities. Only the commander who ordered the defense can designate a new FEBA and authorize
    a retrograde operation.

    Follow Through and Counterattack
    If the defense is successful, the commander counterattacks with the reserve and other available
    forces to maximize the damage inflicted by either attacking the enemy remaining in the MBA or
    pursuing a retreating enemy. Depending on METT-T, the commander uses this counterattack to
    restore the defense, transition the defending force to offensive operations, or establish security and
    cover the passage forward of other forces committed to the offense by higher command. The
    commander does not counterattack as an automatic response to an enemy penetration, nor does the
    commander commit the reserve solely because the enemy has reached a particular phase line or
    other location—a counterattack is an instrument used to support the main effort and the defensive
    SOM. The defending force relies on prior planning to best carry out a counterattack and to seize
    the initiative and tempo before the enemy has time to recover. The enemy is vulnerable
    immediately after the failure of an attack because—

       • Defensive preparations are hasty.
       • Enemy forces are dispersed, extended in depth, weakened, and not organized for defense.
       • Enemy attacks rarely culminate on ground ideally suited for defense.
       • Physical fatigue and the psychological effects of defeat can heighten vulnerability to attack.

    Local counterattacks are designed to restore the defense; a broader action is designed to wrest the
    initiative from enemy forces and then defeat them. If the commander commits to wresting the
    initiative away from the enemy and transitioning to the offense, friendly forces must set the
    conditions necessary for success by establishing favorable, relative combat power.

    If the defensive battle leads to a stalemate with both forces left in contact, the defending force
    commander seeks to retain the initiative and set the conditions for the next encounter. Since the
    area defense focuses on terrain retention from prepared positions, the defending force relies on the
    construction and depth of its defenses and maintains their positions. To reorganize and assault
    again, the commander uses repairs and improvement of defensive positions; tactical shifts in
    positions to confuse the enemy; attacks against enemy command and control, fire support, and
    logistic resources; and follow-on units to neutralize the enemy’s efforts. Because there is
    considerable risk in moving out of prepared positions while still in contact with the enemy, the

                                                                        9-12


---

                                                                                  MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

defending force only considers major shifts to the SOM when METT-T indicates a significant
change in the enemy’s posture. For example, the arrival of fresh enemy forces and their ability to
generate high force ratios could require a unit to change to the defensive SOM.
Because an area defense focuses on terrain retention, the commander has only limited options if the
defending unit is unable to maintain the integrity of its defense. Only the commander ordering the
defense can authorize a retrograde, and permission may only come if the force risks destruction.
However, contingency planning for a retrograde should be part of the defensive plan since a
retrograde, already a risky operation, becomes very dangerous if conducted ad hoc—the difference
between a retreat and a route. Chapter 11 addresses retrograde in detail.

                                                                   9-13


---



---

                    CHAPTER 10.
                  MOBILE DEFENSE

The mobile defense destroys the attacking enemy through maneuver and offensive action (see
Figure 10-1). The commander retains most of the available combat power in a reserve as the main
effort—a major counterattack. The commander commits the minimum possible combat power to
the security and MBA forces to shape the enemy’s advance and set the conditions for the
counterattack. In the mobile defense, terrain is only retained relative to its value in defeating the
enemy through maneuver and offensive action. This is what distinguishes it from the area defense,
where the focus is on retaining terrain and then denying the enemy that terrain by fixing them in a
series of interlocking positions and destroying them, primarily by fires.

                                          Figure 10-1. Mobile Defense Example.
Commanders choose to use the mobile defense when their mobility is equal or greater than that of
the enemy, when they are free to use terrain as maneuver space, or when the depth of the assigned
AO allows for a battle of fire and maneuver. Defenders can conduct a mobile defense in any
environment. Additional conditions suited to conducting a mobile defense are—

  • The assigned defensive frontage is too great for an effective area defense.
  • Time and resources for preparing defensive positions are limited.
  • Sufficient direct, indirect, and aviation fires are available to support the rapid concentration of

     combat power.


---

MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

       • The defender seeks security from weapons of mass destruction through maneuver and
         dispersion of forces.

       • The mission does not require denying the enemy specific terrain.
       • The AO lacks well defined, or many, avenues of approach.
       • The commander deliberately seeks to use a defensive battle to quickly transition back to

         the offense.

    Commanders conducting a mobile defense accept enemy penetration into their AO and use
    shaping actions, obstacles, local counterattacks, and even battle positions to control such
    penetrations, deceive the enemy as to the nature of the defense, and create conditions for the main
    effort counterattack. However, the attacker controls the initiative and determines the time and
    place to attack. Risks associated with the mobile defense are—

       • Supporting efforts in the security area and MBA may be isolated and defeated because of
         unexpected enemy actions or under resourcing in favor of the main effort.

       • A mobile defense conducted in a noncontiguous AO provides the enemy with substantial
         maneuver space that can prove difficult to effectively counter.

       • The enemy may interdict, delay, or disrupt the reserve’s ability to strike at the decisive point.
       • The enemy may successfully defeat shaping actions, entering areas not anticipated by the

         defensive commander and gaining significant momentum as it enters the MBA.
       • The defending force may not gain an accurate picture of the enemy’s intent and dispositions

         until it is too late to effectively react.
       • The decentralized operations required by the mobile defense increase the potential for

         friendly fire incidents.

   FORCE ORGANIZATION

    The mobile defense uses security, fixing, and reserve elements—the reserve, acting as the main
    effort, may consist of one-half to two-thirds to the defender’s combat power (see Figure 10-2).
    While the mobile defense may be executed at any level, it is typically employed at the regiment
    and above given the combat power requirements necessary to resource it.

    The security and fixing elements receive the minimum amount of combat power necessary to
    accomplish their missions. The security element conducts those tasks typically associated with the
    security area—reconnaissance, counterreconnaissance, and shaping actions in the face of an enemy
    advance (the commander could create a separate reconnaissance force). The fixing element acts
    across the MBA to create the conditions necessary for the commitment of the reserve—shaping or
    containing the enemy advance by turning, blocking, and delaying the attacking enemy force. The
    fixing element executes its portion of the battle by combining elements of an area defense with
    defensive methods associated with delaying actions. The reserve is the defender’s main effort. The
    reserve delivers the decisive action when the effects generated by the security and fixing forces
    make the enemy vulnerable to offensive action and defeat. The reserve is the commander’s bid for

                                                                        10-2


---

                                                                                  MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

success and must have more combat power and mobility than the force it seeks to defeat. For this
reason, the reserve contains most available combat power and relies on the security and fixing
elements to reduce the enemy force to a manageable level.

                                                                              Fixing Element

                                                                                                      Reserve Element

                                                                                                    Security Element

                               Figure 10-2. Organization of Forces for a Mobile Defense.
Resourcing a reserve in a mobile defense is difficult and requires the defending unit to assume risk.
The commander’s most critical decisions are when, where, and under what conditions to commit
the reserve. The commander usually accompanies the reserve to be placed at the point of friction so
they can resolve any issues that may delay or impede the reserve’s decisive employment.

CONTROL MEASURES

The minimum control measures necessary to execute the mobile defense are the AOs of the
security and fixing forces and the reserve’s line of departure or line of contact, objective, LOA,
and axis of advance or AO. Additional control measures for the security and fixing forces depend
on the defensive SOM and may include battle positions, phase lines, engagement areas, TRPs, and
FPFs. The commander may designate attack-by-fire and support-by-fire positions, passage points,
contact points, and passage lanes to support the reserve. Because the mobile defense combines
elements of the defense and the offense, those basic control measures discussed in Chapters 2, 3,
5, and 8 may apply. The commander and staff may have to determine and transmit these control
measures rapidly while units move to take advantage of an opportunity to commit the reserve in a
decisive counterattack.

                                                                   10-3


---

MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

   PLANNING A MOBILE DEFENSE

    The two fundamental planning concerns in the mobile defense are creating the conditions to
    successfully commit the reserve and committing the reserve. The following paragraphs address
    specific planning considerations by warfighting function for the mobile defense in addition to
    those addressed in Chapter 8.

    Maneuver
    A mobile defense is only viable if friendly forces have equal or greater mobility than that of the
    enemy. The friendly force gains and maintains relative mobility advantages over the enemy by
    having the necessary resources (e.g., vehicle and assault support) or by limiting the enemy’s
    mobility using obstacles, attrition, and suppression. Most of the unit’s countermobility assets
    support the fixing force while most of the mobility assets support the reserve. Situational obstacles
    provide a tremendous advantage to the defender during a mobile defense because they enable
    economy-of-force measures. The defender uses situational obstacles to exploit enemy
    vulnerabilities, exploit success, separate enemy follow on forces, and provide flank protection.

    As part of planning, the commander and staff determine the follow-on tasks and mission of the
    security force once the enemy passes through the security area. After conducting shaping actions to
    disrupt and delay the enemy, the security force—or elements of it—may withdraw back through the
    fixing force and reconstitute as an available maneuver force or may remain in the security area
    continuing to disrupt and harass the enemy’s reserve, follow-on forces, logistic elements, and C2
    assets. The amount of combat power available to the commander is a key element to this decision;
    however, the commander must remember that the security force will be returning from actively
    engaging the enemy and may remain unavailable for some time until reconstituted and reorganized.

    While civil considerations are basic to all operations, the status and movement of civilians are
    critical considerations during the mobile defense because of the reliance on maneuver and tempo.
    In the area defense, with the focus on terrain retention, civil considerations apply primarily to the
    rear area. In the mobile defense, civilian attempts to avoid advancing enemy formations and
    locations where combat could have immediate and negative impacts on the ground maneuver of
    defending units, unless steps are taken to account for their presence and provide them alternative
    routes. Ideally, host-nation civilian or military organizations will provide civilian traffic regulation
    and immediate essential services along designated civilian evacuation routes. However, if the host
    nation cannot perform these tasks, the defending unit will have to perform them.

    Fires and the Information
    The planning for fires and information activities in the mobile defense entail offensive and
    defensive considerations. Fire support assets and information capabilities must support the
    shaping actions of the security and fixing forces. They must support the security force’s actions to
    disrupt, delay, and break the enemy’s tempo and cover the withdrawal of security forces and
    reconnaissance assets. Fire support assets and information capabilities must also support the
    fixing force’s SOM that will likely entail displacement between positions, use of battle positions
    and engagement areas, while still maintaining the ability to effect enemy follow-on forces, C2
    nodes, and logistics resource in the deep area.

                                                                        10-4


---

                                                                                  MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

Conversely, the placement of fire support assets, the employment of aviation, and the use of
information activities must support the rapid shift to the offense as the reserve is committed. It is
unlikely that the battle handover between the fixing force and the reserve will be final or
complete. Some of the fixing elements will likely still be engaged throughout the MBA while the
commander may still have requirements for shaping actions in the security area and deeper. The
fire support and information plans must account for these various phases and requirements,
prioritize support, carefully determine placement and the movement of assets, and deconflict
battlespace geometry. The MDCA rehearsal is a priority that should be conducted even during
hasty operations.

Logistics
Like fire support and information planners, logisticians must consider how to support a defense
that is characterized by a deep AO, considerable dispersion of forces, and constant displacement
of those defensive forces. Logisticians must compare these requirements against the offensive
demands of the reserve as they commit to the attack. Designating the reserve as the main effort
prioritizes logistic planning—just as the commander accepts risk elsewhere to provide sufficient
combat power to the reserve, so to do logisticians accept risk to other parts of the force to
maximize support to the reserve.

Combat service support provided to the security element is minimal and in accordance with
general logistic planning considerations contained in Chapter 8. Logisticians attach critical
logistic elements (e.g., maintenance) to the security element, pre-position limited essential
supplies, and rely on the security element to self-haul the supplies they need to operate. The fixing
element relies on similar measures, stockpiling supplies in known defensive positions and along
movement routes. Equipment and personnel casualty evacuation, likely to be substantial in the
fixing element, is executed along predetermined routes and phased according to how the
engagement proceeds. Determining which routes and ambulance exchange points are active and
when will be an important function of information management. However, the fixing element
does receive material support and resource priority for countermobility activities.

The focus of the logistic effort is to enable the main effort success. Logistics planning is like that
of any attack. As the engagement unfolds, commanders must carefully weigh any changes to the
logistic plan that risk weakening the reserve.

PREPARING A MOBILE DEFENSE

The priority of work in preparing the mobile defense is given to the defensive positions, routes,
and countermobility requirements of the fixing element—these must be in place if the defending
force hopes to create the conditions in which the counterattack can succeed. This is closely
followed by route improvement for the reserve to speed and support their attack when committed.
Simultaneously, the defending force aggressively employs ISR assets to track enemy positions,
preparations, and indicators of intent. The security elements deploys and begins
counterreconnaissance operations.

                                                                   10-5


---

MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

    The reserve assembles in one or more areas depending on the width of the AO, the terrain, enemy
    capabilities, and the commander’s intent. Before the enemy attack begins, the reserve may deploy
    some or all its reserve elements forward in the MBA to—

       • Deceive the enemy regarding the purpose of the force.
       • Occupy dummy battle positions.
       • Create a false impression of unit boundaries.
       • Conduct reconnaissance of routes between the reserve’s assembly areas and

         potential objectives.

   EXECUTING A MOBILE DEFENSE

    This publication divides the execution of a mobile defense into the five phases, introduced and
    described in Chapters 3 and 9. These phases are—

       • Gain and maintain enemy contact.
       • Disrupt the enemy.
       • Fix the enemy.
       • Maneuver.
       • Follow through.

    The first three phases listed are usually shaping actions within a mobile defense. The maneuver
    phase is typically the mobile defense’s decisive action, while the follow-through phase is usually a
    branch or sequel operation.

    Gain and Maintain Enemy Contact
    Even before the defending unit begins to prepare and occupy the defense, reconnaissance
    elements—either independent of or subordinate to the security element—move forward, gain
    contact with the enemy, and focus on discovering the enemy’s strength and capabilities, locations,
    and intent. The commander tasks other ISR assets to determine the location of follow-on
    elements, critical assets, command and control, and enemy reserves. Determining the enemy’s
    intent and when they commit to a COA is critical information for the staff and enables adjustments
    to the defensive SOM and changes to the plan.

    Simultaneously, the security elements moves forward and establishes the security area to conduct
    its assigned mission of screen, guard, or cover depending on resourcing. The security element
    focuses on impeding the enemy’s ability to conduct reconnaissance and observe friendly
    preparations. Information activities during this period support the security element by jamming
    enemy communications, deceiving the enemy regarding the nature of the defense, and introducing
    hesitation into the enemy’s C2 decision and planning processes.

                                                                        10-6


---

                                                                                  MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

Disrupt the Enemy
The commander could decide to disrupt enemy preparations by executing spoiling attacks, feints,
and demonstrations in conjunction with information activities and fires. If the commander decides
to preserve combat power for use elsewhere, Marines can still disrupt enemy preparations through
supporting arms and information activities. These two elements of fires continue to support delaying
and disrupting the enemy as the enemy begins its advance into and through the security area.

Security elements engage the enemy forces as they penetrate the security area. In conjunction with
ISR assets, they seek to determine or confirm the enemy’s main effort and selected COA. The
security element conducts shaping actions designed to disrupt and delay the enemy’s advance
using fires coordinated with ambushes, local counterattacks, battle positions, and obstacles. Fires
and information activities provide support to the security element’s fight while continuing to
engage the enemy in the deep area, targeting enemy C2 assets and interdicting enemy reserves and
follow-on elements.

As the enemy advance continues through the security area and into the MBA, the security element
executes one of two actions. They may use the AO as maneuver space and remain in the security
area, supporting the actions of the fixing element in the MBA by continuing to disrupt and harass
the enemy’s reserve elements, follow-on element, C2 assets, and logistic resources. The security
element may withdraw from the security area, passing through the fixing element to reconstitute
and reorganize in the rear to become another maneuver asset.

Fix the Enemy
The commander and staff monitor the fight in the security area, and as the enemy enters the MBA,
makes any necessary changes to the plan to either take advantage of security element successes or
mitigate failures. If not already evident, the defending commander and staff determines the
enemy’s main effort and intended COA and adjusts the defensive plan as needed. The fixing
element begins to engage the enemy to generate the conditions necessary to commit the main
effort. The defending force uses the entire AO to allow the enemy to advance and become
vulnerable to the decisive action. The various supporting efforts that comprise the fixing element
use combinations of different defensive methods (e.g., battle positions, sectors, strong points) to
canalize, delay, disrupt, and attrite the enemy’s advance. Fires and information activities support
the defensive SOM by reinforcing the efforts of the fixing element, deceiving the enemy as to the
nature of the defense, and by disrupting the enemy’s ability to command and control.

The fixing element retains terrain only when—and only for the time necessary—they are
supporting the defensive SOM, such as when blocking one avenue of approach to compel the
enemy to use another. Fixing elements withdraw and reposition as necessary, not only to continue
to engage the enemy, but also as tactical ruses to encourage enemy advances along the preferred
routes. The fixing element uses obstacles to reinforce its operations, also making use of prepared
routes to efficiently and effectively conduct displacements, maneuver, and local counterattacks to
shape the enemy’s attack.

Any reserve elements placed forward to assist in tactical ruses and deception retrograde to the
reserve’s assembly area as the enemy enters the MBA. If left forward the security element—or
elements that remained in place—continues to support the fixing element’s efforts by harassing,
disrupting, and destroying enemy resources and units in the security area. If withdrawn, the

                                                                   10-7


---

MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

    security element becomes an additional reserve that can assist the fixing element in the event of
    unexpected enemy actions or success. Because the success of the mobile defense depends upon
    the striking power of the reserve, the commander only considers pulling elements from the reserve
    when the fixing element is threatened with defeat. But even in this case, the commander’s best
    choice would be to accommodate the new situation and commit the entire reserve to new
    objectives. The enemy cannot be strong everywhere, and what appears to be failure can still be
    translated into success by aggressive, offensive action at the right place.

    Maneuver
    Throughout the battle, ISR assets and combat reporting provide the commander and staff with the
    situational awareness and understanding necessary to initiate the reserve’s movement and attack.
    The defending commander and commander of the reserve remain collocated to facilitate
    communication and understanding. As the fixing force’s fight in the MBA unfolds, the
    commander’s staff makes changes to the reserve’s force-oriented objectives (or terrain-oriented if
    needed to provide orientation) based on the new situation. As critical events trigger planned
    decision points and the combat power of the reserve becomes overwhelming relative to the targeted
    enemy force, the reserve departs the assembly area and begins its attack (see Figure 10-3).

Figure 10-3. Mobile Defense Before and After Committing the Reserve.

The reserve executes the counterattack rapidly and violently, avoiding piecemeal commitment and
employing all combat power necessary to ensure success. The security and fixing forces continue
to conduct shaping actions designed to delay the enemy’s response to the attack and thwart or
disrupt attempts to react. Continued defensive actions and local counterattacks by supporting
efforts present the enemy commander with multiple problems and dilemmas that support the
reserve’s decisive action.

The reserve conducts the attack in accordance with those considerations and TTP associated with
offensive operations (see Chapter 5). When committed against a force-oriented objective, the
reserve typically executes the approach-march method of a movement to contact. The reserve
commander might use follow-and-support and follow-and-assume forces (a withdrawn and
reconstituted security force may serve in one of these roles). Relying on the presence and actions
of the fixing and security forces, speed and momentum, and supporting arms for security, the

                                                   10-8


---

                                                                                  MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

reserve commander accepts risk and attacks rapidly and aggressively. The reserve capitalizes on
the psychological and physical paralysis and hesitation the enemy will feel from a sudden,
massive assault and the forced transition from attacker to defender.

Engineers travel well forward to enhance the reserve’s mobility. A competent enemy will be aware
of threats to their flank and conduct countermobility actions to mitigate those threats. The reserve’s
obstacle-clearing detachment searches for existing obstacles and clears the route as much as
possible. Follow-on combat or general engineers expand breach lanes, improve trafficability, and
may improve expedient bridges or replace them with more durable structures. As able, combat
engineers with fixing forces transition their focus from countermobility to mobility operations (e.g.,
reopening passage lanes through friendly obstacles to support maneuver).

Follow Through
In a successful area defense, local counterattacks restore the defense. Prior planning, preparation,
and usually outside force commitment are required to transition the success of the area defense
into an offense. In a mobile defense, success translates much easier, much more quickly, and much
more effectively because of the reserve’s combat power. As the reserve overwhelms the enemy’s
attack, the commander considers the options for exploitation and pursuit (see Chapters 6 and 7). A
reconstituted and reorganized security force often provides the commander with a readily
available force to compel the enemy into a defensive posture. In those cases where a higher
commander ordered the mobile defense as a means to return to the offense, other forces will be
poised to pass through the reserve and continue the attack.

If the mobile defense ends in a stalemate with both forces left in contact (e.g., the attacker
successfully withdraws under pressure from the reserve), the defending force commander seeks to
retain the initiative and set the conditions for the next encounter. The defending force maintains
pressure on the enemy using supporting arms, information activities, and attacks against limited
objectives. The defending commander faces difficult choices if forced to restore the defense. The
mobile defense is predicated on maneuver, surprise, and offensive action. It will be difficult to
replicate these against a renewed attack by the enemy who will be appropriately wary and
prepared. If the same conditions continue to exist that led to the choice of a mobile defense in the
first place, the commander must significantly change the defensive SOM to present the enemy a
new tactical problem. Other options include requesting reinforcements, changing the type of
defense, or maneuvering to defend on different ground.

If unable to maintain the integrity of the mobile defense, the defending unit retrogrades. Only the
commander ordering the defense can authorize a retrograde and permission may only come if the
force risks destruction. However, contingency planning for a retrograde should be part of the
general defensive plan since a retrograde, already a risky operation, becomes very dangerous if
conducted in an ad hoc manner—the difference between a retreat and a rout. Given the nature of
the mobile defense, the blending of enemy and friendly forces, and the relative lack of prepared
positions, retrograde operations will be difficult. The contingency planning conducted for the
retrograde should be thorough to successfully execute a withdrawal. Chapter 11 addresses
retrograde in detail.

                                                                   10-9


---



---

                    CHAPTER 11.
                    RETROGRADE

The enemy may force retrograde activities or a friendly force may execute them voluntarily. In
either case, the higher commander of the force executing the activity must approve the retrograde.
Retrograde activities are transitional; they are not considered in isolation. There are three core
methods for conducting a retrograde: a delay, withdrawal, or retirement. There are two unique,
associated methods—denial and stay-behind.

There are two primary reasons a force conducts a retrograde. The first is to disengage from
operations to preserve the force or avoid combat under undesirable conditions. The second is to
reposition forces to create a more favorable environment in which to resume operations. Both
reasons are fundamentally tied to changing existing circumstances to create a more advantageous
situation. The following other advantages are fundamentally associated with one of the two
primary reasons:

  • Gain time without fighting a decisive engagement.
  • Resist, exhaust, and damage an enemy in situations that do not favor an area or mobile defense.
  • Draw the enemy into an unfavorable situation or extend the enemy’s LOCs.
  • Conform to movements of other friendly troops.
  • Simplify logistics by shortening LOCs.
  • Position the force where they can safely conduct reconstitution.
  • Adjust the defensive scheme, such as to secure more favorable terrain.
  • Deceive the enemy.

In each core retrograde method, a force moves to the rear, using combinations of combat
formations and marches. (Chapter 3 discusses combat formations; Chapter 15 discusses troop
movement.) The commander may use all three methods singularly or in combination with other
offensive or defensive operations. Designating main, supporting, and sustaining efforts in the
retrograde is based on determining which action allows the force to change existing circumstances
to more favorable ones. It is often associated with the actions of the security force or reserve.

Retrogrades can negatively affect the attitude of a unit more than any other type of activity
because it may be viewed as a defeat. A commander must not allow retrograde operations to
reduce or destroy unit morale because a retrograde demands discipline and aggressiveness. The
commander’s personal involvement, focused task and purpose, proper planning, and efficient
execution will help counter any negative effects of the operation on unit morale. After completing
a retrograde, the commander can reconstitute the force.


---

MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

   DELAY

    A delay is a planned method of retrograde in which a force under pressure trades space for time
    by slowing the enemy’s momentum and inflicting maximum damage on the enemy without, in
    principle, becoming decisively engaged. A delay wears down the enemy so that friendly forces
    can regain the initiative through offensive action, buy time to establish an effective defense, or
    determine enemy intentions as part of a security operation. Typically, in a delay, inflicting
    casualties on the enemy is secondary to gaining time. For example, a flank security force
    conducts a delay to provide time for the main body to reorient and establish a viable defense.
    Commanders might execute delays when they do not have enough combat power to effectively
    attack or defend. Units might conduct delays when ordered to do so as part of a shaping action or
    economy of force effort.

    The delaying force generally seeks to avoid decisive engagement, but its ability to do so is based
    on the amount of time they seek to delay the enemy and the importance of the delay to the overall
    situation. Conducting a delay as a shaping action is different than conducting a delay to support a
    parent unit’s ability to complete a retrograde across a river. The delaying force's ability to trade
    space for time requires depth within the AO. The amount of depth required depends on several
    factors, including the following:

       • Amount of required time to be gained and degree of acceptable risk.
       • Relative combat power and mobility of friendly and enemy forces.
       • Nature of the terrain and the ability to shape the AO with obstacles and fires.

    Ordinarily, the greater the available depth, the lower the risk involved to the delaying force and the
    greater the chance for success. A delay succeeds by forcing the enemy to repeatedly deploy its
    force, fight through a series of defensive positions, and consolidate and reorganize before
    continuing its advance. To succeed, the delaying force must pose a significant enough threat to
    force the enemy to repeatedly deploy and maneuver vice merely bypass. Delaying forces displace
    to subsequent positions before the enemy can decisively engage them in their current positions.
    Determining the length of time a delaying force can remain in a position without having to
    become decisively engaged is primarily a function of relative combat power and METT-T.

    Force Organization
    Units of all sizes conduct delays. The delaying force organizes into a main body, a security force,
    and a reserve. The security force usually conducts a screen forward of the initial delay positions.
    The main body, which contains most of the delaying force’s combat power, employs one of the
    two forms of delay—delay from subsequent or alternate positions. When using subsequent
    positions, the main body deploys as a complete unit. When using alternate positions, the main
    body divides into two, roughly equal parts and occupies sets of positions. (See Chapter 8 for more
    information on the types of positions.) The commander uses the reserve to contain enemy
    penetrations between positions, to reinforce fires into an engagement area, or to help a unit
    disengage from the enemy. These missions require that the reserve has the mobility and strength to
    strike with such force that an enemy has no option but to react to it.

                                                                        11-2


---

                                                         MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

Control Measures
The minimum control measures for a delay consist of an AO with associated boundaries,
coordination or contact points, and passage points or lanes. Additional control measures consist
of those typically associated with the defense (e.g., phase lines, battle positions, trigger lines,
disengagement lines) depending on the defensive SOM (see Chapter 8). The commander
designates contact points in front of, between, and behind units to assist coordination, ensure
continuity of the delay, and draw attention to enemy avenues of approach into unit flanks.
Chapter 17 addresses passage points and passage of lines.

The defending commander or the delaying force commander can use one or more delay lines. A
delay line is a phase line, forward of which the enemy must be delayed for a specified time or until
a specified event. Designating delay lines imposes a high degree of risk on the delaying unit. The
delaying unit must do everything in its power—including accepting decisive engagement—to
prevent the enemy from crossing that line before the time indicated. A delay line may also be
event driven. For example, a commander can order a delaying unit to prevent penetration of the
delay line until supporting engineers finish constructing a rearward obstacle belt.

Forms of Delay
The two forms of delay are from subsequent and alternate positions. The delaying force and the
subordinate elements can employ the forms of delay separately or in combination. For example,
the individual elements of the main body might use alternate positions when conducting the main
body’s larger execution of a subsequent position form of delay. The form a commander chooses is
driven by available combat power, the nature of the terrain, and the amount of time associated
with the delay (see Table 11-1). The more limited the combat power in relationship to the size of
the AO, and the less time the enemy must be delayed, the more likely a commander will keep the
main body together as a single element, using subsequent positions. Conversely, the greater the
amount of combat power available relative to the size of the AO, and the greater the length of time
required to delay the enemy, the more likely a commander will divide the main body into two or
more elements using alternate positions.

The defending force uses a delay from subsequent positions when the assigned AO is so wide
that available forces cannot occupy more than a single set of positions (see Figure 11-1). This tier
might be one set of mutually supporting battle positions occupied by the entire main body along a
single avenue of approach. The tier could consist of a set of battle positions, each along a different

    main body is committed forward and retrogrades from one tier back to the next. The risk a

    The preferred form of delay is from alternate positions (see Figure 11-2), where two or more

    Alternate positions are typically used when the delaying force operates on a narrow front. A delay
    from alternate positions is particularly useful on the most dangerous avenues of approach because
    it offers greater security than a delay from subsequent positions. However, it requires more forces
    and continuous maneuver coordination. Additionally, the delaying forces risk losing contact with
    the enemy between delay positions.
