Planning a Delay
A successful delay includes all the planning factors for the defense discussed in Chapter 8. Beyond
these, the delaying force commander and staff must plan for decentralized execution and dispersal
of friendly forces, the requirement to maintain a mobility advantage over the attacker, operating on
extended frontages and in proximity to the enemy, and the complications that may come when the
delaying force is acting as the rear guard—such as casualty and equipment evacuation, closing
obstacle lanes, etc. Subordinate commanders must have the flexibility to take immediate action to
inflict maximum destruction on the enemy and retain the integrity of their forces.

                                                                   11-5


---

MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

    The delaying force’s mission is central to all other planning. When tasking forces to conduct a
    delay, the commander provides them with specific guidance on the following:

       • Is the delay time or event driven?
       • What is the level of acceptable risk to the delay force?
       • How much freedom of maneuver does the delay force have?

    This guidance enables the delaying force commander to determine how to create the required
    effect. The commander can develop a framework to determine how best to arrange obstacles and
    forces to delay the enemy. Obstacles covered by fires in choke points force the enemy to deploy
    and create the conditions necessary for a breach. After delaying forces execute the breach, they
    regroup on the other side before resuming their advance. Engaging the lead elements of an enemy
    column may force them to deploy, but inflicting casualties will force them to consolidate and
    evacuate equipment and personnel, resulting in a delay. For these reasons, the task to delay is
    typically given to battalions and is rarely given to units below the company level. Companies and
    below usually receive defend tasks coupled with displacement criteria—for example, “destroy
    four vehicles and then conduct a displacement to position X.”

    In general, when force preservation is critical, commanders provide the force with broad tasks and
    purposes and the freedom of maneuver to accomplish them. This is most evident when a force
    conducts a delay as part of a shaping action in support of an area or mobile defense. In this case,
    the delay is part of a larger series of shaping actions and the commander likely has subsequent
    tasks for the delaying force. The delaying force delays the enemy as long as possible while
    avoiding decisive engagement, displaces upon meeting some criteria such as the enemy reaching a
    disengagement line, and then retrogrades for follow-on missions.

    Conversely, a delaying force given a specific task and purpose, defined battle positions and
    control measures (e.g., delay lines), is indicative of mission accomplishment taking precedence
    over force preservation. In this case, the success of the delay could be crucial to other critical
    events occurring, such as enabling the friendly main body to escape over a bridge over a major
    river. The delaying force accepts the risks associated with decisive engagement to provide the
    defending commander either a specific amount of time or to delay until a particular event takes
    place. The delaying forces do not displace until either the mission is accomplished, they are
    ordered to displace, or they are overwhelmed.

    The delaying force commander plans to operate in an ISR-scarce environment, particularly when
    conducting the delay in support of a retrograde (when conducting a delay in the security area of an
    area or mobile defense, it is likely the higher commander will leave ISR assets forward). The
    commander ordering the delay considers the how to echelon organic and supporting ISR systems
    rearward while still partially covering the AO during the delay. The delay force’s intelligence
    priorities are to detect the enemy forces’ advance and determine their intent and likely COAs. This
    enables the delaying force commander or staff to adjust the SOM if necessary to effectively
    employ forces. The ISR assets focus on detecting enemy attempts to bypass or envelop the flanks
    or strike the rear of the delaying force. The ISR assets also focus on detecting any enemy attempts
    to cut off the delay force through airborne, air assault, and attack aviation units.

                                                                        11-6


---

                                                                                  MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

Despite the difficulties associated with coordinating an operation across multiple avenues of
approach without becoming decisively engaged, commanders do not attempt to direct the details
of the fight—doing so risks losing the flexibility and rapid reaction inherent in maneuver warfare.
Rather, commanders rely on control measures, triggers, information feedback, and their judgment
and that of their subordinates to conduct command and control. Defensive commanders consider
assigning delays to their more experienced and capable subordinates.

A delay typically consists of multiple displacements that force the enemy to deploy over and over
against potential threats. The defending and delaying force commanders develop displacement
criteria—first for the entire delaying force, and then for subordinate elements of the delay force.
The mobility of both the enemy and the friendly force provides the baseline consideration for
realistic displacement criteria. An infantry force operating in complex terrain engages the enemy
at shorter ranges, displaces more often, and displaces shorter distances than an armored force in
open terrain. After considering relative mobility, other considerations for displacement criteria
include the terrain; the combat power available to the delaying force in terms of maneuver units,
engineering support, and fires; and the effects the delaying force must generate on the enemy.

Once disengagement criteria are set, subordinate units consider how to execute this difficult
evolution in the face of the enemy. Disengagement plans include the following:

  • A maneuver plan for tactical elements after disengagement—who moves along which route
     and when?

  • Fires and information activities to cover the disengagement by suppressing and disrupting the
     enemy (e.g., smoke, aviation delivered fires, tactical deception).

  • Adequate control and FSCMs such as FSCLs, handover lines, start times, and contact
     and passage points if moving back through friendly lines (executing a delay from
     alternate positions).

  • The earliest time for command posts, combat support, and CSS elements to move.
  • Designation of units responsible for closing lanes through obstacles and executing

     reserve obstacles.

The delaying force commander and staff uses the IPB process and METT-T to identify ground and
air avenues for enemy attacks and friendly counterattacks. Using AOs or sector defensive
methods, each likely enemy avenue of approach is assigned to one subordinate unit. The
commander either accepts risk by not covering unlikely routes or covers other avenues with ISR
assets. The cross coordination between units on different avenues of approach is critical, not only
for battlespace geometry issues, but to ensure that units do not get cut off when one or the other
withdraws or displaces. The commander and staff help mitigate this, if necessary, by assigning
initial and subsequent delay positions along the avenues of approach and any other control
measures (e.g., phase lines, trigger lines) to ensure coordination and synchronization across units.

Executing a delay calls for creativity in tactical problem solving. Commanders should not
underestimate the ability of the ACE to not only support delays but conduct them as well. Using
reconnaissance abilities and available firepower, elements of the ACE can create considerable
delays among enemy forces, to include spoiling attacks and counterattacks depending on enemy
air defense capabilities and the availability of friendly supporting arms to suppress them. In

                                                                   11-7


---

MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

    addition, air assault support can provide the delaying force commander increased options in
    rapidly displacing and repositioning maneuver units, logistic resources, and reconnaissance assets.
    Having the ability to engage the enemy with maneuver units and aerial delivered fires, withdraw
    ground forces to an LZ, and move them to another position to again engage the enemy provides
    significant mobility advantages to ground forces (see MCTP 3-01B).

    Similarly, defending commanders consider assigning delay missions to their most mobile forces.
    Motorized and mechanized units provide superior tactical mobility in most terrain—even
    restrictive terrain since, in the case of the defense, the defender has the advantage of selecting and
    improving the ground on which to conduct the delay. In cases where terrain or resources dictate
    committing dismounted forces to a delay mission, the defending commander still provides some
    sort of motorized or mechanized resource they can use to constitute a reserve that can rapidly
    intervene to extract elements of the force from unfavorable positions.

    Beyond methods of movement, the delaying force also creates greater mobility than the enemy
    by using engineering, fire support, and information resources. The priority of effort is
    countermobility—bridges prepared for demolition, obstacles covered by massed fires, and
    information measures that degrade and disrupt enemy command and control. Second to the
    countermobility effort is mobility activities, such as improving routes between delay positions and
    establishing traffic control plans to properly prioritize combat, combat support, and CSS element
    displacement. The delaying force should be able to construct numerous obstacles and deliver long
    range fires that continually force the enemy to deploy into assault formations, delaying their
    movement. The only exception to this is when the delaying force is conducting shaping actions in
    support of an area or mobile defense, vice retrograde. In these cases, the engineering assets and fire
    support available will be a function of the needs of the larger defensive operation. Finally, the
    delaying force addresses survivability by relying on organic means (e.g., digging individual fighting
    positions), coupled with well-chosen terrain (e.g., using the reverse side of a slope to provide hull
    defilade), using covered and concealed egress routes, and avoiding decisive engagement.

    While critical to the delaying force, the extended frontages and ranges common to retrograde
    operations make providing and massing fires difficult. Therefore, units assigned to delay in support
    of a retrograde often have more than the usual allocation of fire support assets. The robust
    employment of the ACE is critical in providing this support and helping offset risk to towed
    artillery systems being overrun by a mobile enemy. The overall defending commander balances this
    risk against anticipated requirements for subsequent operations. The exception to this is when a
    delaying force is conducting shaping actions for an area or mobile defense. In these cases, the
    combat power available to the delaying force will likely be subordinate to the larger defensive plan.

    Logistic planning entails many of the same concerns as that of fires planning—balancing the need
    for the delaying force to accomplish their mission against the risk of logistic assets being overrun
    by a mobile enemy. Complicating the delaying force’s mission is that personnel and equipment
    casualties will have to be evacuated, requiring careful consideration of priorities and disciplined
    execution. Combat service support organizations should plan to echelon their assets throughout
    the AO, allowing the delaying forces to fall back on support, which then signals CSS elements to
    echelon rearward. The presence of CSS elements operating along the same movement routes as
    C2, combat, and combat support units heightens the need for traffic control, availability of
    alternate routes, and prioritization planning.

                                                                        11-8


---

                                                                                  MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

Prepare a Delay
The general defensive preparations outlined in Chapter 8 also apply when conducting a delay.
Resources—including the time available—determine the extent of preparations. The delaying
force commander assigns the highest priority to reconnaissance—gaining and maintaining contact
with the enemy is fundamental to delaying their advance. Simultaneously, preparing positions is a
priority for the force. Except in the rare circumstance where the delaying force will accomplish
their mission from just one set of positions, preparing subsequent positions receives a higher
priority than it would in either an area or mobile defense. Engineers base their priorities of work
on the defensive SOM—the positions closest to the enemy may only support shaping actions that
allow the defending force to create the delay effect elsewhere. It is not always possible to
complete all preparations before starting the delay operation. Consequently, delaying units
continue to prepare and adapt plans as the situation develops.

Units use battle positions in the delay as in any other defense. The difference is not in task and
purpose—battle positions in the delay focus on an avenue of approach—but in preparation. In
other types of defenses, a battle position is likely the primary fighting position from which a unit
will accomplish their task and purpose, whereas any given battle position in a delay is just one of
numerous positions. Although a delay SOM also has its supporting and main efforts, general
position preparation places more emphasis on reconnaissance, flank and rear security, and
preparing routes for displacing than it does on protective obstacles, FPFs, and ammunition
stockpiling. In the delay, battle positions are sometimes referred to as delay positions.

While rehearsals are important in any military operation, the delay operation’s requirement to
repeatedly engage the enemy and displace rearward to do it again, coupled with branches and
sequels that could include local counterattacks and commitment of the reserve to exploit
unexpected opportunities, make rehearsals paramount. At a minimum, the commander and
subordinates execute an MDCA rehearsal that focuses on timing, triggers, and employing
multidomain combined arms. Small units and crews should practice moving to their various
positions in daylight and limited-visibility conditions.

Execute a Delay
The security force deploys well forward to gain and maintain contact with the enemy, executing
reconnaissance and security tasks (particularly when other ISR resources are scarce). The security
force seeks and destroys enemy reconnaissance elements, rendering the enemy unable to collect
information which will lead to confusion for the enemy and forcing its forces to hesitate and move
more cautiously. As the enemy’s advance guard enters the security area, the security force disrupts
and delays it without becoming decisively engaged, seeking to determine the enemy’s intent and
COA. Supporting arms and information activities engage and influence the approaching enemy as
far forward of the delay positions as possible.

As the enemy approaches, the security force moves by bounds back toward and through main
body positions, keeping the enemy under observation until the handover with the main body is
complete. They avoid compromising friendly positions by moving through the delay element’s
flanks of, avoiding friendly engagement areas and TRPs unless terrain and the tactical situation
make it necessary. Depending on the SOM, the security forces either halt and reorganize behind
the main body for follow-on tasks or continue their withdrawal back to and through the main
defensive lines where they begin reconstitution and await the rest of the delaying force.

                                                                   11-9


---

MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

    As the security force hands over the battle to the main body, the delaying force commander makes
    any final decisions or adjustments to the SOM based on enemy actions and their apparent intent.
    The main body executes the SOM using either alternate positions, subsequent positions, or a
    combination of both. Actions by the main body include ambushes, local counterattacks,
    employment of supporting arms and information activities, battle positions, and at higher levels,
    use of area and mobile defenses within assigned AOs (e.g., the main effort for a regiment
    conducting a delay might be the area defense of a subordinate battalion).

    The delay force preserves the force’s freedom of maneuver by engaging the enemy with sufficient
    force to temporarily stop the enemy’s advance. Unless the mission demands it, the delaying force
    avoids decisive engagement. The delaying force uses obstacles, fires, information activities, and
    defensive positions in depth to slow and canalize the enemy while exploiting its own mobility to
    confuse and defeat the enemy. Once a delay starts, units rapidly displace between positions.
    Whenever possible, friendly forces grasp any fleeting opportunity to seize the initiative, even if
    only temporarily. Doing so avoids passive defensive patterns that favor the enemy and rob the
    attacker of tempo and momentum. The delaying force may conduct strong counterattacks from
    unexpected directions to temporarily confuse and force the enemy commander to direct unplanned
    actions or commit enemy reserves and follow-on forces.

    The delaying force commander uses the single battle approach so the delaying force can
    continually and simultaneously engage the enemy throughout the AO. All manner of fires and
    information activities are waged throughout the delay and across the enemy force. Depending on
    the nature of the enemy’s air defense capabilities and the friendly force’s ability to suppress them,
    the ACE conducts a range of activities to attack, disrupt, and delay the enemy throughout the
    battlespace. Fires and information activities assist delaying forces by—

       • Introducing confusion into enemy decision-making processes and execution by degrading
         their ability to move, communicate, and conduct reconnaissance.

       • Suppressing enemy overwatch, support-by-fire, and attack-by-fire positions.
       • Supporting the disengagement and displacement of maneuver forces through fires,

         obscuration, closing breaches and lanes, and emplacing reinforcing obstacles.
       • Destroying high payoff targets.
       • Supporting limited counterattacks.

    The aggregate effect of all these actions, however, remains focused on massing the combat power
    of the delaying force.

    Within individual positions, subordinate commanders rely primarily on massed, surprise fires to
    create maximum damage and disruption to the enemy force. As enemy forces recover, reorganize,
    and begin to maneuver against the delaying force, the friendly force continues to direct destructive
    fires against them, tracking their actions and the progress of the engagement against displacement
    criteria. When the displacement criteria are met, or the delaying element risks decisive engagement
    or destruction, the element displaces under displacement fires using terrain and cover and
    concealed routes to break contact. Supporting arms fires target the vacated positions after the
    friendly force departs.

                                                                       11-10


---

                                                                                  MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

The delaying force remains flexible as the battle unfolds. Elements having unexpected success
may still have to withdraw depending on the effectiveness of the delay elsewhere. The
commander shifts combat power, to include the reserve, to allow threatened elements to disengage
or to counter unexpected enemy moves (e.g., bypassing a delay position). If retained in the AO,
the withdrawn security force becomes the new reserve. Whenever possible, retrograding elements
of the main body pass to the flanks of positions rather than through them.

Throughout the operation, friendly forces fall back on logistic support. Combat service support
elements remain one step ahead of the delay force’s retrograde movement using maintenance
contact teams and stockpiles of critical supplies to meet the immediate needs of elements in
contact. Support priorities are Casualty and equipment evacuation, ammunition, and petroleum
products. Maintenance operations prioritize evacuation over repair.

Terminating a Delay
A delay terminates when one of the following occurs:

  • The delaying force conducts a rearward passage of lines and battle handover with the
     defending force.

  • The defending force experiences unexpected success and becomes the basis for an area or
     mobile defense on appropriate terrain.

  • The defending force experiences unexpected success and becomes the basis for a transition to
     the offense.

Regardless, the outcome of the delaying force’s actions should be accounted for in the senior
commander’s main plan or in appropriate branches and sequels.

WITHDRAWAL

A withdrawal is a planned method of retrograde in which a force in contact disengages from an
enemy force and moves in a direction away from the enemy. It consists of two forms: under
pressure or not under pressure. Subordinate units may withdraw without the entire force
withdrawing. Withdrawals may be used in conjunction with other methods of retrograde—a delay
may cover a withdrawal and a withdrawal may precede a retirement. Ideally, commanders seek to
withdraw not under enemy pressure, though this is not always possible when an aggressive enemy
becomes aware of a friendly force’s withdrawal or intent to withdraw. A unit withdraws to an
assembly area or a new defensive position.

Withdrawals are inherently dangerous because they involve moving units to the rear and away
from what is usually a stronger enemy force. The heavier the previous fighting and the closer the
contact with the enemy, the more difficult the withdrawal. Therefore, OPSEC is extremely
important since competent enemy forces will attempt to exploit the withdrawal, using all available
capabilities to try to turn the friendly force’s withdrawal into a rout (OPSEC can be very difficult
within a civilian population that is likely migrating rearwards as well). The attacking enemy may
have ground and air superiority and continuously attempt to pursue, encircle, and destroy the
withdrawing force. The attacking enemy will try to use a combination of direct pressure,
enveloping forces, and fires to isolate the withdrawing friendly force for later destruction.

                                                                  11-11


---

MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

    Force Organization
    The commander typically organizes the withdrawing unit into a security force, a main body, and a
    reserve. On occasion, commanders may employ stay-behind forces. Unless there is sufficient
    planning time for the withdrawal, or circumstances dictate rapid changes (e.g., preventing an
    encirclement), commanders avoid changing or creating new task organizations to avoid
    complicating the operation.

    The security force maintains contact with the enemy, simulates the continued presence of the main
    body, and covers the main body’s withdrawal. To accomplish these tasks, the security force
    usually receives additional combat power and combat support, often serving as the main effort of
    the withdrawing force. The commander may create additional security forces to protect the flanks
    of the main body and to lead rearward movement, preventing enemy attempts to cut off or block it.

    When withdrawing, particularly under pressure, the commander generally finds it difficult to
    resource a reserve but makes every effort to do so. The reserve provides the withdrawal force the
    flexibility to respond to unexpected enemy actions, extricate encircled or heavily engaged forces,
    and take advantage of enemy mistakes to conduct local counterattacks that disrupt and delay the
    enemy. The main body of the withdrawing force consists of all elements remaining after the
    commander resources the security force and the reserve.

    Control Measures
    The withdrawing force must balance the requirement to move combat power away from the enemy
    for a follow-on purpose with its need for self-protection. The commander’ staff must closely
    coordinate and deconflict the rearward movement of combat, combat support, and CSS units while
    retaining the ability to generate decisive combat power at key times and places. Like a delay, the
    minimum control measures for a withdrawal consist of an AO with associated boundaries,
    coordination or contact points, and passage points or lanes. Additional control measures consist of
    those typically associated with the defense (e.g., phase lines, battle positions, handover lines, trigger
    lines, disengagement lines), depending on the defensive SOM. See Chapters 2 and 8 for more
    information on control measures.

    Forms of Withdrawal
    The two forms of withdrawal are withdrawal under or not under enemy pressure. In addition, a
    withdrawal can be assisted or unassisted. Assistance that the withdrawing force could receive
    from another force consists of support such as additional security and occupation of choke points
    and key terrain along withdrawal routes, management of movement and traffic control, fires,
    information activities, and logistics.

    The most preferred form is to conduct a withdrawal not under enemy pressure. This provides the
    commander the simplest tactical problem, the easiest coordination requirements, and the most time
    to plan, execute, and establish new, more favorable positions. The commander can accept prudent
    risks, such as ordering the main body to move by road march instead of in tactical formations. The
    commander and staff also have time to properly plan for stay-behind forces if necessary. This is the
    least likely method when already in contact with a capable and competent enemy.

                                                                       11-12


---

                                                                                  MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

The least preferred form is to conduct a withdrawal under enemy pressure. This form forces the
commander to weigh and balance force preservation against subsequent missions in the context of
the level and nature of the enemy pressure. Will the force have to fight its way clear of the enemy
every step of the way? How much might they lose doing so? Is the requirement to preserve the
main body for follow-on missions so great as to warrant risking the destruction of the security
force? A withdrawal under enemy pressure generally indicates a compressed decision and
planning cycle that entails risk that the commander will seek to offset through the assistance of
outside forces.

Planning a Withdrawal
Planning and coordinating a withdrawal is very similar to that of a delay. In both cases, the
commander and staff begin design and problem framing with the assumption that the enemy will
attempt to interfere with the withdrawal. Unlike a delay, where the lack of enemy action could
mean the delay force stays in place, in the withdrawal, the friendly force is still leaving.
Accordingly, the withdrawing commander and staff plans for enemy interference and develops
decision points and triggers that allow the force to transition to a “not under pressure” withdrawal
if enemy interference does not manifest. Further, the friendly force avoids any premature actions
that would indicate to the enemy that a withdrawal was being contemplated. Regardless of
whether the withdrawal is under pressure, the friendly force plans to—

  • Break away deliberately from the enemy.

  • Create a situation where the main body can displace rapidly, free of enemy interference.
  • Retain sufficient combat power and logistic resources to support security forces throughout

     the operation.

In creating the SOM for a withdrawal, the commander and staff decide whether the entire force
will attempt to withdraw simultaneously or by phases. While a simultaneous withdrawal allows
for a rapid and deliberate break from the enemy, the variables of METT-T, lack of sufficient
routes, and compliance of the enemy often do not allow for it. Therefore, the friendly force
typically conducts the operation in phases, determining an order of withdrawal-by-element that
balances speed of movement against the force’s overall ability to protect itself.

The first factor the commander and staff consider is follow-on missions. Why is the force
withdrawing in the first place and what must they be able to do once the withdrawal is complete?
This helps determine and prioritize what combat power and resources are needed to successfully
complete the withdrawal. The second consideration is how far the force must withdraw and what
lies between them and the withdrawal position? The staff analyzes the availability of transportation
assets and routes, how many combat support and CSS elements must also withdraw, and how their
movement and the movement of the maneuver elements of the main body can be phased. The third
consideration is how hard the enemy will press the withdrawing force. These three factors enable
the commander and staff to make three interrelated key decisions: when to start the movement of
selected combat, combat support, and CSS elements; when forward elements should start thinning
out; and when the security force should begin its disengagement operations.

The security force—specifically the rear, as opposed to flanks or forward security force—is
usually the main effort in either creating or preparing to create the space the main body needs to
withdraw successfully. The first consideration for security force planning is whether a security

                                                                  11-13


---

MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

    area exists between friendly and enemy forces. The existence of a security area increases the main
    body’s ability to break contact. An enemy in close contact with friendly forces is more likely to
    see through deceptions and recognize the indicators of a withdrawal. A security area makes such
    knowledge of friendly positions and actions less likely. Commanders create an autonomous
    security force when a security area exists, such as a regiment designating one battalion to serve as
    the security force. This simplifies command and control, and OPSEC is little affected. When no
    security area exists or enemy and friendly forces are in close contact, commanders mitigate
    OPSEC concerns by creating an ad-hoc security force under a designated commander. In this case,
    each battalion in the withdrawing regiment would leave a company forward, continuing expected
    and known routines to simulate the presence of the main body.

    Assigned tasks and resources determine whether the entire security force, or just portions of them,
    simulate the presence of the main body. Elements left in contact with the enemy employ
    information activities and techniques to deceive the enemy until it is too late for them to react.
    Regardless of how successful deception is, the security force commanders must expect to have to
    fight to provide the withdrawing force the time they need. Consequently, they develop
    disengagement criteria and instructions, while also ensuring that recovery, evacuation, and
    transportation assets are in place to aid disengagement and speed rearward movement.

    Determining when and how to begin rearward movement begins with selecting times and
    conditions when the enemy cannot observe the activity, to include through electronic emissions and
    enemy or neutral satellites. If possible, habituating the enemy to the conduct of friendly activities
    during limited-visibility conditions—for example, routinely conducting resupply at night will
    likely inure the enemy to the sounds of withdrawing vehicles at night. Security is most critical in
    the early stages of the operation when most combat support and CSS elements begin displacing.

    The primary decision a commander must make is how to both support the withdrawing elements
    and minimize the loss of logistic resources to enemy action. By concealing supplies along
    movement routes, CSS units can simplify support requirements and reduce the enemy’s ability to
    interfere with logistic operations. This allows logistic units to withdraw earlier than they
    otherwise could. The commander carefully considers whether to place supplies in caches. Once
    cached, supplies are difficult to recover if the operation does not go as planned. Other than
    medical items, the withdrawing unit evacuates or destroys all supplies that they are unable to
    evacuate to prevent capture. The commander establishes destruction criteria, which is time or
    event driven, for each class of supply.

    Preparing a Withdrawal
    The withdrawing force dispatches forces and resources (e.g., advance parties and engineers) to
    prepare the new positions for occupation. The commander institutes the deception and associated
    information plans. In accordance with these activities and OPSEC guidance, CSS elements begin
    phasing functions rearward. If using caches to support the withdrawing force, they begin deploying
    them. Other nonessential activities across the warfighting functions phase rearward as well.

    Planning for the withdrawing force’s follow-on mission continues and the commander and staff
    modifies the withdrawal as necessary to support it. In an unassisted withdrawal, the withdrawing
    units establish their own security force and reserve. They reconnoiter and secure the routes they
    will use during rearward movement while sustaining themselves during the withdrawal. When

                                                                       11-14


---

                                                                                  MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

conducting an assisted withdrawal, withdrawing commanders determine their shortfalls or risks
and seek to mitigate them by employing assisting forces or resources. As preparations begin, the
commander makes initial liaison with the assisting forces, brings them into the planning process,
determines tasks, and, as required, moves the assisting elements forward for employment.

Executing a Withdrawal
The security force is formed either based on a single unit or an ad-hoc blend from the
forward-most units. They begin functioning as the rear guard, executing assigned tasks such
as counterreconnaissance, tactical deception, delay as required, and limited offensive methods
such as spoiling attacks or feints. Elements to conduct flank and forward security (direction of
movement) begin their tasks if the SOM mandates. The command forms and locates its reserve
in positions—generally to the rear in close support of the security forces—that enables the force
to reinforce and assist the security forces by extricating heavily engaged elements and take
advantage of opportunities to use offensive action (e.g., counterattacks) to prevent enemy
interference with the withdrawal. In an assisted withdrawal, those forces and resources so
assigned begin their missions to provide security, aid movement, and support other activities.

On order, the main body uses limited-visibility conditions, smoke, and deception to move rapidly
rearward on multiple routes to intermediate or final positions. They may use multiple intermediate
positions to phase and coordinate movement while enhancing protection. If under enemy pressure,
the least engaged units retrograde first, while the security force and reserve act to support the
movement of more heavily engaged units. Movement is disciplined and traffic management
centralized even in the face of enemy pressure—units move along designated routes at given
times. Designated combat support units maintain their positions to offer indirect fires, mobility,
and countermobility support to the withdrawing force, while the rest move with CSS elements to
their new positions. Remaining combat support units use various techniques to echelon rearward
while providing support to the security, main body, and reserve forces. (See Chapter 15 for more
information on movement techniques.) The ACE uses aerial delivered fires in the close and deep
areas to prevent or disrupt enemy interference with the operation and employs assault support
assets as required for the security, main body, and reserve forces.

After the main body withdraws to a safe distance, the security force begins its rearward movement.
If using a DLIC, that detachment remains in contact until a designated time or event. Even if
the enemy does not pursue the withdrawing force, the security force continues to act as the rear
guard unless the commander assigns that mission to another element. If not pursued by the enemy,
the security force can transition to more effective and speedy means of movement, such as a
march column.

If the security element and reserve cannot prevent the enemy from closing on the main body, the
commander commits some of or all the main body to delay or defend and prevent the enemy from
further interfering with the withdrawal. In this event, the actions of the main body focus on
creating the conditions that enable the retrograde to resume at the earliest possible moment. The
enemy endeavors to fix friendly forces for their envelopment and destruction, and the commander
disrupts these attempts by using alternate routes to avoid enemy attacks and employing a forward
security element to hold open checkpoints or fight through enemy blocks.

                                                                  11-15


---

MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

    Terminating a Withdrawal
    Once the withdrawing force successfully disengages from the enemy, it executes one of three
    options. Its forces either withdraw to new positions that are part of the overall defense or they
    conduct a rearward passage of lines and occupy assembly areas for subsequent missions. In these
    two cases, they conduct reconstitution tasks and activities to rapidly regain effectiveness. Or, in
    the third case, once beyond the influence of enemy action, the withdrawing force transitions to a
    retirement and continues its rearward movement and next mission.

   RETIREMENT

    A retirement is a planned method of retrograde in which a force out of contact moves away from
    the enemy. Units conduct the retirement method to reposition forces for future operations or to
    accommodate the current concept of operations. A retiring unit organizes for combat, but it does
    not anticipate interference from enemy ground forces. The retiring unit has either successfully
    completed a withdrawal or, more likely, its security is being provided by another unit. Still, since
    the enemy could employ unconventional forces, vertical envelopment, air strikes, or long range
    fires to interdict the retiring unit, commanders plan for enemy actions and organize the unit to
    fight in self defense.

    Units conduct retirements as tactical road marches where security and speed are the most
    important considerations. If the force is transitioning from a withdrawal, the retirement begins
    when the security force completes its disengagement and can organize into a march formation.
    The retiring unit generally moves toward an assembly area, which should support the preparations
    for the unit’s next mission. Routes used by the retiring force should support speedy and efficient
    movement but should also allow for effective defensive measures if required. One high-speed
    route may best support fast movement, but two, slower, parallel routes might also support fairly
    rapid retrograde while providing more defensive options to respond to enemy actions.

    Force Organization
    The commander usually designates security elements and a main body in a retirement (see
    Figure 11-3). Elements of the force organize into march columns—the formation and number
    of columns vary depending upon the number of available routes and the potential for enemy
    interference. The commander typically moves major elements to the rear simultaneously.
    However, a limited road network or a flank threat could require the unit to echelon its movement
    in terms of time and ground locations.

    The factors of METT-T dictate the size and composition of the security forces. The primary
    security concern will be to the rear. Rear security acts to protect the rearmost columns from
    surprise, disruption, and attack. They also oversee stragglers and equipment evacuation.
    Commanders may establish flank security if necessary and typically establish an advanced guard
    augmented by a combat engineer detachment to focus on mobility actions. In a manner similar to
    delay and withdrawal, the commander can use single units to conduct these security tasks or could
    require each march column to provide its own forward, flank, and rear security.

                                                                       11-16


---

                                                                                  MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

The main body organizes in a manner opposite that of an approach march (see Chapter 4). Combat
support and CSS units precede combat forces. When necessary, main body elements can reinforce
the rear guard or any other security element. Commanders rely on the ACE and the organic fire
support systems of the security forces to provide the first source of fire support. Combat support
units within the main body can always be pulled and re-tasked if necessary. Information activities
in support of the retirement are the responsibility of the overall commander of the retiring unit.

Control Measures
The control measures used in a retirement are the same as those used in a delay and a withdrawal.
As in a withdrawal, thorough planning and strict adherence to routes and movement times
facilitate an orderly retirement. The commander controls movement using movement times,
routes, and checkpoints. See Chapters 2 and 3 for movement control measures.

Planning and Execution of a Retirement
Units executing retirements try to begin them from some state of stability. Transitioning directly
from the withdrawal to retirement without allotting time to reestablish command and control,
resupply, and reorganization is avoided if possible. Once an element assumes a march formation,
it is prepared to initiate the retirement. The initial action is to move combat support, CSS units,
and CSS resources to the rear. During the initial phase, the force retires in multiple small columns.
As the distance from the enemy increases, smaller columns can consolidate into larger ones for
ease of movement control. Where the force begins retirement, the factors of METT-T, and the
availability and status of road nets influence the commander’s decision regarding the size of
various columns and when they might consolidate.

Commanders generally place engineer assets with the advanced guard to support mobility
requirements, from road and bridge repair to route clearance. If there is a countermobility
requirement, other engineer resources may travel with flank and rear security elements. Traffic
management and equipment evacuation are planning priorities. The lack of an enemy presence
does not lessen the requirement for smooth, efficient, and rapid execution. The retiring force still
uses limited-visibility conditions, satellite observation windows, and deception to complicate
enemy attempts to gain information on or influence the force.

                                                                  11-17


---

MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

    Just as with a delay and withdrawal, the command must anticipate and plan for the effects
    retrograde movements will have on logistic support for the operation, particularly about
    maintenance, resupply, and equipment and casualty evacuation. Retirements increase the demand
    for transportation assets and MSR space. This results in greater demand for effective route
    management, consumption of Class III (and possibly Class V) supplies, and pre-positioned
    services and supplies. The amount and location of caches depends upon the nature of the
    retirement—if the area is being abandoned, then commanders must prevent the buildup of
    unnecessary resources and develop comprehensive plans for the complete evacuation of
    supporting functions. The commander establishes maintenance, recovery, and evacuation
    priorities and destruction criteria for inoperable equipment.

    During a retirement, CSS units echelon their movements to maintain adequate support to the
    committed force—priority of support goes to the rear guard, which is likely falling back through a
    logistic gap created by the needs of the main body. Friendly forces keep MSRs open and
    decontaminated as necessary. Logistic units maintain maximum dispersion consistent with control
    and local security. Their goal is to provide uninterrupted support and maximum protection during
    the time it takes to conduct the retirement operation. Recovery and evacuation vehicles position
    themselves at critical locations to keep disabled vehicles from blocking movement routes. By
    echeloning support, the amount of time each CSS unit spends moving is reduced—time that
    prevents them from performing their primary support tasks. High priority assets may require
    added protection to prevent their loss or capture.

   UNIQUE RETROGRADE SITUATIONS

    Conditions that require conducting denial measures and stay-behind operations can arise during
    retrograde operations. These two methods of retrograde have their own unique planning and
    execution considerations.

    Denial Measures
    A denial measure is “an action to hinder or deny the enemy the use of territory, personnel, or
    facilities, to include destruction, removal, contamination, or erection of obstruction” (DoD
    Dictionary). Denial measures are not countermobility activities. Denial measures limit the
    enemy’s benefits of occupying an area; countermobility limits the enemy’s maneuver. There are
    times when an enemy unit will capture, or threaten to capture, friendly equipment and supplies,
    most often during retrograde. This may or may not be associated with the purpose of the enemy
    forces’ operation, and captured supplies (e.g., POL) could ease their logistic burden, increasing
    the efficiency of their operations. The fundamental reason to conduct denial measures is to avoid
    providing the enemy any assistance. The principles of denial include the following:

       • Destroy military equipment and supplies when friendly forces cannot prevent them from
         falling into enemy hands.

       • Responsibility for conducting denial measures rests with the user of the equipment and supplies.
       • If practical, denial measures should not preclude their later use by friendly forces (e.g., hiding

         vice destroying).
       • It is unlawful to deliberately destroy medical equipment and supplies or make food and water

         unfit for consumption.

                                                                       11-18


---

                                                                                  MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

A unit’s military equipment and supplies could expand to include military installations and any
civilian equipment and supplies used by the friendly force. Under the law of war, the destruction
of civilian property is only permitted when required by immediate military necessity. Determining
whether there is sufficient necessity to justify destruction is a complex decision that requires
considering moral, political, and legal considerations. Additionally, civil instability caused by
destroying civilian property, material, and equipment could have adverse effects on friendly
operations. The commander involves the staff judge advocate and civil affairs staff officer when
planning denial measures.

The commander who orders denial measures must consider the potential value military equipment
and supplies would have to an enemy when determining the priorities and the extent of the denial.
High priorities for denial measures include—

  • Classified equipment, material, and documents.
  • POL.
  • Sophisticated weapon systems or electronic equipment.
  • Heavy weapons and associated ammunition.
  • Communications equipment.
  • Bridging equipment, rafts, and ferries.
  • Air, sea, and land transport systems.

The commander issues detailed instructions to deny military equipment and supplies to prevent the
enemy from using them. Denial must also prevent an enemy from repairing a system through the
cannibalization of several systems. The unit must destroy the same parts in each type of system.

The commander and staff ensure that executing the denial plan does not adversely affect the unit’s
future operations. This includes carefully considering the force’s demolition policy in relation to
the purpose of the rearward movement and the contemplated subsequent actions of the force.
Widespread demolitions during a retrograde may become a greater hindrance to a friendly force
moving back into the area than to the enemy during the friendly retrograde. For example,
destroying the transportation infrastructure increases friendly logistic difficulties once the area is
recaptured. Removing or destroying militarily significant supplies and equipment (e.g., fuel,
obstacle materials, rail cars) from an area requires friendly forces to bring similar assets with them
when they reoccupy the area.

Units can expand denial actions to prevent the enemy from exploiting resources (e.g., fuel,
minerals, the indigenous population), routes of communication (e.g., river locks, railroad switching
yards, road interchanges, and bridges), and facilities (e.g., telephone exchanges, radio and
television stations, the industrial plants of a region). The defending force can assist civil authorities
in evacuating the civilian population. The defending force either removes the resources, supplies,
and facilities from the area being abandoned to the enemy or destroys them in place.

Total denial measures can produce long term political, economic, military, and environmental
effects. Total denial measures have operational, and possibly strategic, level impact. Total denial
measures consume large quantities of transportation and engineer resources and require
considerable time to plan and execute. Limited or partial denial measures are particularly suitable

                                                                  11-19


---

MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

    if the defending force expects to regain control of the area within a short time. The removal or
    destruction of only a few key components can reduce a facility to limited utility, yet it allows for
    the facility’s quick restoration of all functions once it is returned to friendly control. While limited
    denial measures may not affect the advance of properly supported enemy combat formations that
    have cross country mobility, they can seriously impede an enemy’s road bound, and rail bound
    logistic efforts if executed with skill and imagination according to an overall plan.

    Stay-Behind Measures
    A stay-behind measure is a planned method of retrograde in which a unit is left in position to
    conduct a specified mission while the remainder of the forces withdraw or retire from an area.
    Units are either assigned a stay-behind mission, are inserted to conduct a stay-behind mission, or
    default to a stay-behind mission because of enemy actions that result in their bypass. The force
    should consist of enough combat, combat support, and CSS elements to protect and sustain their
    fighting capability for the duration of the mission. Stay-behind measures are not suicide missions
    and occur only when the commander has reasonable confidence that the stay-behind force will
    rejoin the main body, extract itself in alternative ways, or that the main body will fight its way
    forward to linkup with them. Examples of short duration stay-behind missions include units
    continuing shaping actions in the security area of an area defense or units holding on to key terrain
    from strong points in a mobile defense.

    A stay-behind force’s main purpose is to destroy, disrupt, and deceive the enemy by attacking
    enemy combat forces and command and control, combat support, and CSS resources. The longer
    the mission, the greater the risk to the force because of the danger that they will be located,
    encircled, and destroyed by the enemy. Resupply and casualty evacuation also become extremely
    difficult as the length of time associated with the mission increases. Commanders consider these
    factors, and METT-T, when creating disengagement criteria or formally assigning this mission.

    Any type of force can conduct stay-behind operations depending on METT-T. Dismounted forces
    can be inserted via infiltration, air assault, or waterborne methods (a stay-behind operation is not a
    raid). The primary differences in the composition of a stay-behind force are terrain, logistic, and
    duration of the mission. A mounted force may remain behind, but its effectiveness will be limited
    by its ease of resupply. A dismounted force may have a comparatively smaller logistics
    requirement but will have survivability issues in open terrain.

    Stay-behind activities eventually require the force to reenter friendly lines or linkup with other
    elements, often in more than one location. The stay-behind force may have to conduct a breakout
    from encirclement to do so (see Chapter 19). The commander and staff must carefully coordinate
    reentry and linkups to prevent friendly fire incidents. The return routes for the stay-behind force
    are the best covered and concealed routes available.

                    CHAPTER 12.
               AMPHIBIOUS DEFENSE

An amphibious defense is a military operation to defeat an enemy amphibious operation. If the
joint force fails to defeat the enemy amphibious force enroute or during debarkation, then ground
units repel an amphibious assault through a counterlanding (part of an amphibious defense).

COUNTERLANDING

Counterlanding is a military operation that prevents the enemy from achieving amphibious
objectives through the buildup or projection of combat power ashore. It occurs once amphibious
defense and coastal defense has failed to prevent the enemy from being able to approach their
amphibious objective area and commence to land forces. Successful counterlanding operations
defeat enemy combat power ashore through ground-based multidomain combined arms
augmented by joint efforts to isolate the enemy's landings. Marine Corps forces employs two
counterlanding methods to support the larger amphibious defense:

  • Area defense that seeks to prevent an enemy lodgment.
  • Mobile defense that seeks to defeat an enemy lodgment.

Regardless of method chosen, commanders and staffs begin planning a counterlanding by
examining an enemy’s most dangerous and most likely COA. The choice of counterlanding
method is also guided by numerous factors such as the defenders’ available combat power, their
ability to contest and survive enemy fires, and their ability to act within periods of relative
advantage and disadvantage, etc.

Marine Corps units that opt to shape at the water’s edge and mount an area defense hold the ground
with dug-in positions and limited reserves to prevent the enemy from gaining a lodgment. This
COA is the costliest in terms of required personnel and resources but allows for the most detailed
preparation and would be the least susceptible to deception activities. However, nearly 70 percent
of all coastlines are suitable for landing when wheeled, tracked, heliborne, and air-cushioned
landing craft are used. Rarely will defenders have the resources to be strong everywhere; therefore,
there will be likely gaps an enemy can exploit in this method of counterlanding. Lastly, defenders
would need to mitigate and survive destructive enemy fires against known and prepared positions.

When the defenders hold enough maneuver space and relative maneuverability, they can choose a
mobile defense. Rather than attempting to predict the landing area, the defenders rely on joint and
naval fires to delay and disrupt an enemy landing. Those forward defenses are in the security area
and are used for shaping. The defender discerns the enemy’s main effort, then uses counterattacks
as its decisive action against the enemy’s main lodgment. The objective is to destroy the enemy


---

MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

    force vice holding ground. The advantage is that the defender’s forces are in the security area, not
    to defend terrain, but to sense. The security forces shape and delay through a combination of
    screen, guard, and cover missions, that set up the conditions for the decisive counterattack.
    Another advantage is, rather than trying to defend multiple shorelines and possibly hundreds of
    miles, manpower and resources are used more efficiently while complicating the enemy’s
    targeting efforts. However, the three biggest disadvantages are—

       • The attacker can gain a foothold that could be extremely difficult to reduce and destroy.
       • The counterattack force must have more mobility ashore then the attacker has from the sea

         and the initial lodgment.
       • The defender must correctly discern that the landing is the main effort and not a feint

         designed to draw them away from the main landing.

    The defender only needs to sufficiently defeat, delay, or disrupt the attacker at any one of these
    stages. Therefore, if facing a situation in which the enemy landing can’t be stopped by the larger
    joint and naval operation, the preferred course of action once the assault begins is shaping at the
    water’s edge followed by a decisive counterattack to destroy the lodgment (e.g., shaping and then
    executing a mobile defense).

   AREA DEFENSE METHOD

    The area defense at the water’s edge functions like any other method of the defense in its goal to
    attack and defeat the enemy landing to prevent the enemy from establishing itself ashore and
    forming a coherent lodgment. The area defense method of counterlanding is best when the
    defender is certain of the landing areas and is tactically located where the decisive battle is to be
    fought. In general, the focus of the area defense is to retain terrain for the purpose of defeating the
    enemy. In the case of an area defense in counterlanding, the purpose of retaining terrain forward
    in the landing area is to defeat the enemy's landing when the enemy is unable to land sufficient
    combat power to remain ashore and establish a lodgment. The area defense allows for depth and
    counterattacks—usually to retain terrain but not as the decisive action. In an area defense, the
    decisive action takes place in the engagement area. This type of an area defense uses one of the six
    defensive forms outlined in Chapter 8.

    The defenders can expect the enemy amphibious assault force to transit in a formation that allows
    minimal targeting opportunities until it nears the assault area, where it will transition into a
    formation that will allow projection of maximum power ashore via over-the-horizon techniques. To
    have the greatest effect on enemy surface transports, Marine forces, in conjunction with the joint
    force, conduct expeditionary strikes of the landing force’s surface and aerial targets as well as air
    assault and airborne assault forces conducting a vertical envelopment to support their landing.

    Should the defender fail in this initial effort, then the focus turns to enemy vulnerability. Enemy
    surface assault forces are most vulnerable when they have just left the landing craft and have their
    backs to the water, with no supplies except what they have carried ashore. Those attackers who
    assault via vertical envelopment are most vulnerable when the units and aircraft are in the LZ

                                                                        12-2


---

                                                                                  MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

landing and debarking troops. The defender shapes at the water’s edge and at any vertical
envelopment locations to try and prevent the attackers from lodging and linking up. See Chapter 9
for a discussion on an area defense and Chapter 18 for a discussion on vertical envelopment.

MOBILE DEFENSE METHOD

The mobile defense destroys the attacking enemy through maneuver and offensive action. It
allows the enemy forces to advance to a point where they are exposed to a decisive counterattack
by the reserve (the decisive action is the counterattack). Its goal is to attack and defeat the enemy
landing after it has established itself ashore in a lodgment. This type of counterlanding defense is
best when—

  • The defender is free to use terrain as maneuver space and has the battlespace depth for
     decisive maneuver through offensive counterattacks.

  • The enemy has a significant precision strike capability that makes sitting in a static
     defense untenable.

  • When the defender has equal or greater mobility than the enemy.

In a mobile defense the defender still shapes at the water’s edge and at any enemy vertical
envelopments. (See Chapter 18 and MCTP 3-01B for more information.) However, in this
method, the goal is to discern the main effort from any feints or demonstration and, most
importantly, determine when the enemy attack is most vulnerable to destruction through
maneuver and offensive action. The commander retains the bulk of the available combat power in
a reserve as the main effort—a major counterattack. In this mobile defense, the unit will bring
forward the mobile reserve forces to conduct a large-scale counterattack to prevent the enemy
from lodging and linking up—and ultimately to defeat the enemy. This will include waging heavy
firepower strikes against enemy positions to isolate them on the battlefield and sever their
connection with the sea and with adjacent units. The friendly force then focuses on destroying the
most threatening enemy units. See Chapter 5 for more details on attacks and Chapter 10 for more
details on a mobile defense to include organization, control measures, planning, preparing, and
executing the different types of attacks in conjunction with a mobile defense.

FORCE ORGANIZATION

Once a counterlanding method is chosen, the commander organizes the force accordingly. The
commander and staff may break down the counterlanding area into a sensing area, interdiction
area, maneuver area, and support area. Figure 12-1 depicts a notional counterlanding area. At the
operational level, planners conducting the tactical counterlanding efforts need to ensure close
coordination with higher and adjacent joint and naval units to ensure that the enemy cannot
exploit any seams between the execution of the counterlanding and the larger amphibious
defensive efforts. The enemy should face a continuous set of challenges to their attempts to enter
the amphibious objective area, project combat power ashore, and attempt to build and maintain
their lodgment.

Area Defense
There are two forms of area defense: defense in depth and forward defense. Both demonstrate that
area defenses are not merely static, but also employ all characteristics of the defense including
maneuver. Regardless of whether commanders choose a spatial- or purpose-based battlespace
framework, they organize the force into security, MBA, and reserve forces to execute the
defensive SOM. See Chapter 2 for discussion of battlespace frameworks and see Chapter 9 for a
thorough discussion on an area defense.

Mobile Defense
The mobile defense uses security, fixing, and reserve forces—the reserve, acting as the main
effort, may consist of one-half to two-thirds to the defender’s combat power. While the mobile
defense may be executed at any level, it is typically employed at the regiment-level and above
given the combat power requirements necessary to resource it. See Chapter 10 for a thorough
discussion on a mobile defense.

PLANNING A COUNTERLANDING

In planning for counterlanding in support of an amphibious defense, there are numerous
requirements that must occur to achieve success. Outlined below are the unique planning
requirements by warfighting area that are common to both area defense and mobile ground
defense counterlandings in support of the larger amphibious defense.

                                                                   12-4


---

                                                                                  MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

Command and Control
Unique counterlanding planning requirements for command and control include the following:

  • Use the pre-planned defense strength to create redundant and resilient command and control.
  • Ensure rehearsals and coordination across all ground defensive elements.
  • Prepare routes and positions and identify triggers for the reserve.
  • Prepare for defensive and offensive follow-on operations.

Fires
Unique counterlanding planning requirements for fires include the following:

  • In coordination with the joint and naval force—
      Understand and be prepared to support the larger joint and naval efforts to defeat the enemy’s
        attempts to shape the battlespace by seizing air, sea, and electromagnetic dominance.
      Conduct counterreconnaissance to contest enemy reconnaissance and collections
        throughout all domains.
      Conduct cyberattacks to gain access and manipulate enemy battle networks.
      Conduct electromagnetic attack on amphibious ships and the landing force to
        create confusion.
      Prioritize counter-space and counter-reconnaissance campaigns as critical.
      Lay mine barriers and obstacles to limit the enemy forces’ freedom of maneuver.

  • Plan and employ coastal artillery, coastal antiship missiles, torpedo boats, and aviation assets,
     to attack the enemy as it begins to transit ashore.

  • Identify enemy critical vulnerabilities that fires can affect, such as—
      At what depth are the amphibious ships and their assault craft most vulnerable?
      What are the vulnerabilities during movement, on landing beaches, ports, and landing
        zones to shape local or planned counterattacks?

  • Lay surf and land mines along likely assault beaches.
  • Reestablish minefields as enemy clears them (priority given to the surf zone).

Force Protection
Unique counterlanding planning requirements for force protection include the following:

  • Defend critical friendly capabilities such as command centers, air bases, and tactically
     significant points on the battlefield.

  • Prioritize engineering efforts (e.g., survivability, hardening, dug-in communication lines).
  • Support efforts to defeat of enemy efforts to establish a maritime blockade.
  • Contest the enemy's ability to use the air domain to create effects.
  • Create air defense and antiship employment triggers that balance risk against desired effects.

       • Use decoys and camouflage to protect US forces.

            course from convoy configurations to a formation to load out landing craft.

           Plan for manned and unmanned sensor operations.
           Plan requests to use space assets to develop an understanding of enemy’s deployments.

Logistics

Maneuver
Unique counterlanding planning requirements for maneuver include the following:

Chapters 8 and 9, commanders must plan—

      Plan for a combination of obstacles and massed fires to defeat the enemy while supporting

        forces, command and control, and logistics.

  • To prevent enemy consolidation and linkup by identifying key points within the defense that
     defenders should be focused on holding.

  • To evacuate civilians from the MBA to the rear area.

  • For the necessary resources (e.g., vehicle, assault support) required for the defender to gain
     and maintain relative mobility advantages over the enemy.

  • To limit the enemy’s mobility using obstacles, attrition, and suppression.

   PREPARING A COUNTERLANDING

    When preparing for counterlanding in support of an amphibious defense, numerous requirements
    must be met to achieve success. Outlined below are the unique preparation requirements by
    warfighting area that are common to both area defense and mobile ground defense
    counterlandings in support of the larger amphibious defense.

    Command and Control
    Unique counterlanding preparation requirements for command and control include the following:

       • Continue to develop redundant and resilient command and control, expecting C2 assets to
         be targeted.

       • Continue rehearsals and coordination across all ground defensive elements. This includes—
           Rehearsing triggers and movements for the reserve along planned routes and into positions.
          Continuing to prepare for defensive and offensive follow-on operations; rehearse as
            time permits.

    Fires
    Unique counterlanding preparation requirements for fires include the following:

       • In coordination with the joint and naval force—
           Understand and be prepared to support the larger joint and naval efforts to defeat the enemy’s
            attempts to shape the battlespace by seizing air, sea, and electromagnetic dominance.
           Conduct counterreconnaissance to contest enemy's reconnaissance and collections
            throughout all domains.
           Conduct cyberattacks to gain access and manipulate enemy battle networks.
           Conduct electromagnetic attack on amphibious ships and the landing force to
            create confusion.
           Prioritize counterspace and counterreconnaissance campaigns as critical.
           Lay mine barriers and obstacles to limit the enemy forces’ freedom of maneuver.

       • Plan and employ coastal artillery, coastal antiship missiles, torpedo boats, and aviation assets,
         to attack the enemy as it begins to transit ashore.

       • Lay surf and land mines along likely assault beaches.
       • Reestablish minefields as enemy clears them (priority given to the surf zone).

Force Protection
Unique counterlanding preparation requirements for force protection include the following:

  • Defend critical friendly capabilities such as command centers, air bases, and tactically
     significant points on the battlefield.

  • Defend against enemy air and missile attacks; avoid allowing the enemy to gain air
     superiority in the vicinity of assault areas and areas of defensive measures.

  • Continue supporting efforts to defeat enemy attempts to establish a maritime blockade.
  • Preserve multidomain targeting capabilities through concealment and deception in order to

     use those capabilities at key points in later phases.
  • Keep force concealed until ready to attack.

Information
Unique counterlanding preparation requirements for information include the following:

  • Conduct deception operations that suggest forces have less than actual capability to conduct
     multidomain denial operations during later phases in order to protect them from targeting.

  • Conduct military information support operations (MISO) seeking to foster doubt in enemy
     country’s population about the merits of enemy assault operations.

  • Create false networks and communications traffic correlated with physical and
     electromagnetic decoy operations to confuse enemy cyberspace-reconnaissance units.

Intelligence
Unique counterlanding preparation requirements for intelligence include the following:

  • Gain battlespace awareness throughout all domains.
  • Conduct a campaign of reconnaissance and counterreconnaissance.
  • Deny enemy attempts to collect reconnaissance on the force disposition.
  • Monitor the established intelligence network and early-warning system.
  • Conduct robust and in-depth air, surface, and subsurface maritime, cyberspace, and

     electromagnetic reconnaissance to develop a persistent understanding of enemy disposition
     and deployments. This includes—
      Conducting passive and, when advantageous, active sensing throughout all domains,

        including the electromagnetic spectrum and space.
      Geolocating entities of interest.
      Conducting manned and unmanned sensor operations.
      Conduct active sensing and jamming of electromagnetic emissions.
      Monitor the electromagnetic communications spectrum to support force protection and

        other information activity requirements.
      Use requested space assets to develop a persistent understanding of enemy deployments.
  • Employ human intelligence assets and capabilities.

EXECUTING A COUNTERLANDING

In executing a counterlanding in support of an amphibious defense, numerous requirements must
occur to achieve success. Outlined below are the unique execution requirements by warfighting
area that are common to area defense and mobile ground defense counterlandings in support of the
larger amphibious defense.

Command and Control
Unique counterlanding execution requirements for command and control include the following:

  • Continue to implement redundant and resilient command and control.
  • Continue to prepare for defensive and offensive follow-on operations; rehearse as time permits.

Fires
Unique counterlanding execution requirements for fires include the following:

  • Continuously attack the enemy to keep it from establishing a coherent beachhead.
  • Direct pre-planned fires on likely air assault landings.
  • Conduct electromagnetic attack on landing forces to ensure they cannot communicate with

     their supporting amphibious ships.
  • Separate landing forces from offshore support and follow-on echelons.
  • Continue surveillance of follow-on amphibious forces.
  • Separate landing forces from offshore support and follow-on echelons.
  • Destroy the first lodgment and follow that with the sequential destruction of other

     landing zones.
  • Focus fires on enemy command nodes and weapon emplacements during the landing.

Maneuver
Unique counterlanding execution requirements for maneuver are discussed in the following sections.

Area Defense. In addition to the maneuver considerations for the defense discussed in Chapters 8
and 9, commanders must consider the following:

  • Prevent enemy consolidation and linkup.
  • With an understanding of the enemy’s main direction and probable operational objectives,

     move forces to contest enemy’s advance.
  • Through a combination of firepower and maneuver, the defensive forces break apart the

     integrity of the enemy assault force to prevent enemy force linkup, put them on the defensive,
     and seize the initiative.
  • Commit the reserve to restore the situation, execute branch plans, and displace the main effort
     to supplementary and subsequent positions if—
      The enemy is taking unexpected actions, or
      Friendly shaping efforts fail to compel the enemy to maneuver in the desired manner.
  • If the reserve is committed, the defending force must—
      Deconflict traffic priorities.
      Establish control measures.
      Delineate command relationships.
      Mitigate battlespace geometry.
  • Gaps between defensive positions are kept under surveillance, covered by fire, or when
     necessary, covered by displacing units.
  • Units respond to enemy penetrations in their battle positions and sectors with local
     counterattacks or by repositioning to alternate positions.
  • A unit does not abandon a position unless it is in accordance with the defensive scheme of
     maneuver or a higher commander grants permission to do so.
  • Enemy gains that threaten the overall integrity of the defense should not be allowed to
     consolidate. The force can prevent this by—
      Destroying enemy forces either by committing the reserve directly against them or at

        exposed flanks that isolate the enemy penetrations for later defeat.
      The security force completing its reorganization and resupply and becoming available as a

        reconstituted reserve. The defensive force continues to attack the enemy throughout the
        depth of the AO.
  • Once the enemy main body is fixed, the defensive main effort executes its mission, massing
     combat power to defeat the enemy through local counterattacks to enhance the destructive
     effects of fires and information activities on the enemy.
  • With the focus on terrain retention, civil considerations will apply largely to the rear area.
