MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

    Mobile Defense. In addition to the maneuver considerations for the defense discussed in Chapters 8
    and 10, commanders must plan for the following:

       • Ensure countermobility assets support the fixing force while most of the mobility assets
          support the reserve.

       • Use situational obstacles—
           As economy-of-force measures to provide an advantage through the exploitation of enemy
            vulnerabilities.
           To take advantage of success—
              Through the separation of enemy follow-on forces.
              To provide flank protection.

       • After conducting shaping actions to disrupt and delay the enemy, the security force, or
         elements of them—
           Might withdraw back through the fixing force and reconstitute as an available maneuver
            force.
           Might remain in the security area continuing to disrupt and harass the enemy reserve,
            follow-on forces, logistic elements, and C2 assets.

       • Civil considerations include—
           Civilian status and movement are critical in the mobile defense, given its reliance on
            maneuver and tempo.
           Civilian attempts to avoid advancing enemy formations and locations where combat occurs
            can have immediate and negative impacts on the ground maneuver of defending units—
              Unless steps are taken to account for their presence.
              Unless they are provided alternative routes.
              Ideally, host-nation civilian or military organizations will provide civilian traffic
               regulation and immediate essential services along designated civilian evacuation routes.
              If the host nation cannot perform these tasks, the defending unit performs them.

    When defenders plan, prepare, and execute a counterlanding, they must consider that when an
    enemy conducts an amphibious assault, it must build up combat power on the beach from an
    initial zero while the attack is in progress. To establish an amphibious landing, the enemy must
    achieve a series of sequential victories against the larger joint and naval force. Once an enemy
    arrives at the objective area (having been subject to continuous disruption from the point of
    assembly to the objective), it must get ashore, resist counterattack, and force a decision before
    reaching the culminating point. Throughout this time, the enemy’s back is to the sea, and they are
    vulnerable to isolation. They also may have little cover and little to no organic ground indirect
    fires. As a defender, all that needs to be done, in conjunction with the joint and naval force is to
    defeat the attacker at any of these stages to be successful.

                        PART IV.
                 RECONNAISSANCE,
  COUNTERECONNAISSANCE, AND SECURITY

Commanders use reconnaissance, in any domain, with the full range of available detection
methods to obtain information about the activities and resources of an adversary. They also
employ counterreconnaissance to prevent the adversary from doing the same to us. Finally,
they conduct security operations to provide early and accurate warning of enemy operations,
to provide the force being protected with time and maneuver space within which to react to
the enemy, and to develop the situation to allow the commander to effectively use the
protected forces.


---



---

                    CHAPTER 13.
              RECONNAISSANCE AND
           COUNTERRECONNAISSANCE

Marines conduct reconnaissance missions to obtain, by visual observation or other detection
methods, information about the activities and resources of an enemy or adversary, or to secure
data concerning the meteorological, hydrographical, or geographical characteristics of a particular
area. They conduct counterreconnaissance measures to prevent hostile observation of a force,
area, or place. Reconnaissance, as it relates to ISR, primarily relies on the human dynamic rather
than technical means and is a focused collection effort. Units perform reconnaissance before,
during, and after operations to provide information for the IPB process and the staff to help
formulate, confirm, or modify a COA. The four types of reconnaissance missions are route, zone,
area, and force oriented.

Reconnaissance units identify terrain characteristics, enemy and friendly obstacles to movement,
and the disposition of enemy forces and the civilian population. Reconnaissance supports and
protects the force during movement and prior to the occupation of assembly areas. Reconnaissance
supports maneuver by keeping units free from contact as long as possible and allowing the
concentration of combat power at the decisive point in the offense and defense. Reconnaissance
enables commanders to understand the environment and potential adversaries.

The Marine Corps conducts reconnaissance to gain and maintain contact with the enemy while
preventing the enemy from affecting friendly forces. Although counterreconnaissance is
complimentary to security, security does not equate to conducting counterreconnaissance.
Rather, counterreconnaissance is a distinctive function that must be planned and resourced.
Reconnaissance focuses on sensing and seeing the enemy, counterreconnaissance focuses on
denying the enemy the ability to sense and see. In the multi-domain battlespace, these are not
separate activities, but dual aspects of the same action—collecting and concealing information.

RECONNAISSANCE OBJECTIVE

Commanders orient reconnaissance assets by providing them reconnaissance objectives.
Reconnaissance objectives result from the identification of priority information requirements
during IPB. Reconnaissance objectives may be a terrain feature, geographic area, enemy force,
adversary, or other mission or operational variable, such as specific civil considerations or the
trafficability of a specific area. The reconnaissance objective is tied directly to a reconnaissance
mission end state and represents the information that must be gathered.


---

MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

    The commander issues warning orders, FRAGORDs, and operation orders to create a framework
    for managing ISR assets during execution of the intelligence collection plan and throughout
    operations. This framework helps planners differentiate between surveillance requirements (i.e., the
    systematic observation of an area) and reconnaissance needs (i.e., a mission undertaken to obtain
    specific information). This framework also enables reconnaissance resources to act in concert,
    covering all the commander’s reconnaissance objectives, while acting according to their strengths.
    For example, air reconnaissance can surveil objectives beyond the range of ground reconnaissance.
    Conversely, ground reconnaissance units can conduct missions in weather that precludes aerial
    reconnaissance. Similarly, if a division G-2 uses technical sensors and human intelligence sources
    to determine that the enemy is not in an area and the terrain there appears to be trafficable, then
    reconnaissance units may be reprioritized to other missions within the framework.

   RECONNAISSANCE FUNDAMENTALS

    There are seven fundamentals of successful reconnaissance operations. Commanders and staff—

       • Ensure continuous reconnaissance.
       • Do not keep reconnaissance assets in reserve.
       • Focus on the reconnaissance objective.
       • Rapidly report information.
       • Retain freedom of maneuver.
       • Gain and maintain contact.
       • Rapidly develop the situation.

    Ensure Continuous Reconnaissance
    The unit conducts reconnaissance before, during, and after all operations. Before an operation,
    reconnaissance fills gaps in information about the enemy, the terrain, and civil considerations.
    During an operation, reconnaissance provides commanders with updated information that allows
    them to make decisions. This information could orient on the enemy, such as verifying disposition
    and intentions; civil considerations; or friendly activities, such as locations and status of units and
    resources during a CBRN event. After an operation, reconnaissance elements maintain contact
    with the enemy to determine the enemy’s next move and collect information, to include terrain
    and civil considerations necessary for planning subsequent operations.

    Operational pauses take place only when adjusting the pace of commitment or preparing for a
    planned, maximum effort. When current operational information is adequate, reconnaissance
    elements gather information for branches and sequels to current plans. Reconnaissance is
    continuously conducted as part of all security missions, including the conduct of local security for
    forces not in contact. As operations transition between the various offensive, defensive, and
    stabilization activities, the nature of information requirements may change.

                                                                        13-2


---

                                                                                  MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

Keep Reconnaissance Assets Committed
Reconnaissance assets, are never kept in reserve; however, reconnaissance elements may conduct
necessary administrative, training, and logistic actions to maintain their capability while
recovering from and planning for assigned missions. When committed, reconnaissance assets use
all their resources to conduct reconnaissance for the assigned missions. Commanders consider all
reconnaissance assets as committed assets with specific missions at all times. Exceptions to this
rule apply to unique assets, such as armored vehicles and LAR, that have numerous other potential
means of employment beyond reconnaissance missions.

Focus on the Reconnaissance Objective
The commander uses the reconnaissance objective to focus reconnaissance efforts, particularly
when time, unit limitations, or enemy actions prevent the unit from accomplishing all
reconnaissance tasks. Commanders of subordinate reconnaissance elements remain focused on
achieving the objective regardless of what their elements encounter during the mission.

Rapidly and Accurately Report Information
Because information—particularly tactical information—can quickly lose its value,
reconnaissance assets must rapidly and accurately collect and report information on the assigned
reconnaissance objective. Reconnaissance units report exactly what they see and, if applicable,
what they do not see. Seemingly unimportant data might be extremely important when combined
with other information. Reports such as no enemy activity are as important as reports of enemy
activity. The ability to report relies upon proper communications training and equipment.

Retain Freedom of Maneuver
Reconnaissance assets must retain battlespace mobility to successfully complete their missions.
The enemy attempts to find and destroy friendly reconnaissance assets. If these assets are
decisively engaged, reconnaissance stops and assets attempt to maintain relative mobility using
clear engagement criteria and SOPs, employing movement and reconnaissance techniques and
overwatching fires (to include indirect fire support). Stealth, initiative, and knowledge of the
terrain and the enemy reduce the likelihood of decisive engagement and help maintain freedom of
movement. When selecting routes, reconnaissance units use the IPB process to identify
anticipated areas of likely contact.

Gain and Maintain Contact
Once a unit conducting reconnaissance gains contact with the enemy, they maintain contact unless
the commander directing the reconnaissance orders otherwise or the survival of the unit is at risk.
This does not mean that individual scout and reconnaissance teams cannot break contact with the
enemy, but rather that the overall effort of the reconnaissance unit results in maintaining contact.
Although there are different types of contact, reconnaissance units primarily conduct surveillance
using stealth. Units conducting reconnaissance avoid combat unless it is necessary to gain
essential information, in which case the units use fire and maneuver to maintain contact while
avoiding decisive engagement.

Rapidly Develop the Situation
When a reconnaissance asset encounters an enemy force or an obstacle the nature of the threat
must be quickly determined as situations can rapidly change. When facing an enemy force,
reconnaissance assets must determine the enemy’s composition, disposition, activities, and

                                                                   13-3


---

MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

    movements and quickly assess the implications of that information. Reconnaissance assets must
    also determine the type and extent of an obstacle and whether it is protected by enemy fire
    support. Obstacles can provide the attacker with information concerning the location of enemy
    forces, weapon capabilities, and organization of fires. If a reconnaissance unit encounters the
    enemy, they typically conduct actions on contact while gathering information. See Chapter 3 for
    actions on contact.

   RECONNAISSANCE METHODS

    The reconnaissance methods include dismounted, mounted, aerial (manned and unmanned),
    and reconnaissance by fire. When deciding on which reconnaissance method to employ,
    commanders consider METT-T and the capabilities of their reconnaissance assets. When
    possible, commanders typically employ combinations of these methods to increase the
    reconnaissance operation’s effectiveness.

    Dismounted Reconnaissance
    Dismounted reconnaissance is the most time-consuming method ground units use. However, it
    permits the most detailed information collection about the enemy, terrain, civil considerations, and
    infrastructure. A commander considers using dismounted reconnaissance when—

       • Stealth is required, or security is the primary concern.
       • Time is available.
       • Detailed information is required.
       • The reconnaissance objective is a stationary threat, fixed site, or terrain feature.
       • Units expect, or has made, enemy contact through visual or electromagnetic means.
       • Environment conditions favor dismounted reconnaissance or hinder mounted reconnaissance.

         (For example, terrain is muddy or swampy and is easier to traverse on foot.)
       • The terrain or threat prevents using reconnaissance vehicles.
       • Vehicles are not available.
       • Terrain creates a visual dead space that prevents using optics or sensors.

    Mounted Reconnaissance
    The mounted reconnaissance method enables a more rapid tempo; however, it increases the
    potential compromise of reconnaissance operations. Mounted reconnaissance should take
    advantage of standoff capabilities provided by surveillance and weapon systems to observe and
    engage from increased ranges. A commander considers using mounted reconnaissance when—

       • Time is limited.
       • Distance to reconnaissance objective requires mounted movement.
       • Stealth and security are not primary concerns.
       • Detailed information is not required, or the mounted method affords the same scope as the

         dismounted method.

                                                                        13-4


---

                                                                                  MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

  • Environmental conditions permit this type of reconnaissance. (For example, the terrain is
     relatively flat and dry and tracked and wheeled vehicles can traverse with little difficulty.)

  • Enemy location is known.

Air Reconnaissance
Aerial reconnaissance units plan their missions in much the same way as ground units. They use
the same type of operations graphic control measures and consider the same critical tasks. Aerial
reconnaissance units organize aviation assets to accomplish missions by considering the same IPB
aspects as ground forces. Commanders focus on air hazards to navigation and anticipated enemy
air defense capabilities.

Air reconnaissance provides raw intelligence information to commanders and decision makers at
all levels, who then convert it into useful intelligence information to reduce uncertainties when
planning and executing operations. Intelligence gathered during air reconnaissance missions
provides the staff with a rapid means of acquiring visual, imagery, and electromagnetic
information on enemy activity and installations and the terrain. To execute air reconnaissance, the
Marine Corps relies on a complementary mix of organic, theater, and national air reconnaissance
sources to support its intelligence, planning, deployment, and operational phases. The G-2/S-2 and
G-3/S-3 are responsible for considering the full range of US air reconnaissance capabilities in
support of the assigned mission.

Marine aviation squadrons provide organic air reconnaissance support. They are designed to be
multi-mission capable and provide air reconnaissance information in support of the unit. Although
the Marine unmanned aerial vehicle squadron (also referred to as VMU) is the only dedicated air
reconnaissance squadron, all Marine aircraft squadrons are equipped and trained to perform
specific air reconnaissance operations (e.g., visual reconnaissance, photographic imager).

Manned Air Reconnaissance. Manned air reconnaissance assets of other Services within the
theater may support operations. Raw data collected by these platforms may be transmitted over
secondary imagery dissemination system networks for the unit to transform into actionable
intelligence through a systematic process. The products from these platforms range from detailed
imagery with precise global positioning system coordinates to verbal descriptions of an aircrew’s
visual reconnaissance. These assets may be requested to perform specific reconnaissance missions
for the unit. Additionally, these assets may collect imagery for other missions that might be useful
to MAGTF planners or units.

Unmanned Aircraft System Air Reconnaissance. Unmanned aircraft systems conduct air
reconnaissance, which is best suited for executing route, zone, and area reconnaissance.
Unmanned aircraft systems provide significant advantages over other reconnaissance assets.
The primary advantages being they typically do not put friendly personnel at risk and have a
relatively long loiter time. Both offer advantages to commanders, including the ability to—

  • Observe areas and objectives where terrain or a threat can hinder ground or manned aerial
     reconnaissance.

  • Operate at extended distances or extended durations, or both.
  • Maximize standoff distance to retain the element of surprise and increase force security.

                                                                   13-5


---

MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

    Units must have procedures to execute a battle handover between the UAS or small unmanned
    aircraft system (SUAS) and other reconnaissance assets or in case the data link between the UAS
    or SUAS and its operators is lost or corrupted. See MCTP 3-20G, Air Reconnaissance, for more
    information on UASs and SUASs.

    Reconnaissance by Fire
    Reconnaissance by fire is a reconnaissance method where a unit fires on a suspected enemy
    position to cause the enemy forces to disclose their presence. This technique is applicable when
    time is critical and stealthy maneuver is not possible. The fires may be either direct, indirect, or a
    combination. The advantage of indirect fire is that it does not give away friendly locations and
    usually causes enemy forces to displace from the impact area. However, reconnaissance by fire
    may not cause a seasoned or prepared enemy force to react.

   RECONNAISSANCE UNDER LIMITED-VISIBILITY CONDITIONS

    Battlefield obscuration, fog, rain, and snowfall reduce visibility. Generally, reconnaissance during
    limited visibility takes more time than during periods of clear visibility. However, limited-visibility
    conditions provide better stealth and increase the reconnaissance assets’ probability of survival.
    Units frequently employ dismounted reconnaissance patrols at night. These patrols use light
    amplification devices, thermal observation devices, and electromagnetic surveillance devices to
    compensate for limited-visibility conditions.

    Mounted reconnaissance typically focuses on road networks during limited-visibility conditions.
    Because of temperature inversion, an enemy force can detect engine and track noises of friendly
    mounted reconnaissance elements more clearly and over longer distances at night. This makes
    mounted reconnaissance elements susceptible to ambush. Strict noise and light discipline, along
    with masking sounds, such as artillery fires, help mounted reconnaissance forces avoid
    compromise or ambush. High winds, extreme temperature, loose topsoil, or sand can adversely
    affect aerial reconnaissance. See MCRP 2-10B.1 for more information on the effects of weather
    and atmospheric conditions.

   CHARACTERISTICS AND EMPLOYMENT OF RECONNAISSANCE ASSETS

    Ground reconnaissance elements are generally limited in the depth to which they can conduct
    reconnaissance. However, they can operate under weather conditions that prohibit air
    reconnaissance operations. Reconnaissance conducted by manned and unmanned aviation
    platforms complements ground reconnaissance by increasing the speed and depth at which
    reconnaissance operations can be conducted over an area. Air reconnaissance operates over terrain
    that hinders ground operations (e.g., swamps, extremely rugged terrain, deep snow). Aviation
    assets can operate at a considerable depth, far in advance of dedicated ground reconnaissance
    elements focused on the close fight.

                                                                        13-6

                                                   MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

All Marines and units have the implied task to report information about the terrain, civilian
activities, and friendly and enemy dispositions. Troops in contact report critical information about
their contact. Patrols observing hostile activity report information about that activity. Combat
service support elements conduct route reconnaissance, report enemy contact, and describe
changes in trafficability. Civil affairs teams report information on the local populace and decision
makers. However, the Marine Corps has units whose mission is to conduct reconnaissance—these
units are force reconnaissance, reconnaissance battalion, the ACE, LAR, and Marine Corps
special operations forces. While some occupational specialties, such as combat engineers and civil
affairs, perform specific reconnaissance tasks, commanders primarily use their organic or attached
reconnaissance elements—ground or air—and intelligence elements to conduct reconnaissance.

A command’s organization, equipment, training, and policy determines which ISR assets are
available to employ. leaders of reconnaissance assets are responsible for educating and advocating
for the proper employment of their units. Commanders and reconnaissance leaders should use all
available resources to satisfy information requirements, thereby ensuring ISR assets are not
overtasked or overextended. See Table 13-1 for available ISR assets.

                                             13-7


---

MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

   TYPES OF RECONNAISSANCE MISSIONS

    The five types of reconnaissance missions are—

       • Route reconnaissance.
       • Zone reconnaissance.
       • Area reconnaissance.
       • Force-oriented reconnaissance.
       • Special reconnaissance (only conducted by special operations forces).

    A reconnaissance in force is a method of attack that units can use to accomplish reconnaissance
    tasks in certain circumstances (see Chapter 5 for more information on methods of attack).

    Route Reconnaissance
    Route reconnaissance is a directed effort to obtain detailed information about a specified route and
    all terrain from which the enemy could influence movement along that route. Route
    reconnaissance provides new or updated information on route conditions, such as obstacles and
    bridge classifications, and enemy and civilian activity along the route. The commander typically
    assigns this mission when considering using a specific route for friendly movement.

    Force Organization. The commander assigns a route reconnaissance as a separate mission or as a
    specified task for a unit conducting a zone or area reconnaissance. A scout platoon conducts route
    reconnaissance over one route at a time. For larger organizations, the number of available
    reconnaissance units influences the number of routes that can be covered at one time. Integrating
    ground, air, and technical assets ensures a faster and more complete route reconnaissance—for
    example, air and technical assets can help focus ground efforts. However, a ground
    reconnaissance effort is essential if the mission is to conduct detailed route reconnaissance or
    clearing the enemy from the area around the route.

    When task-organizing reconnaissance units for route reconnaissance, commanders may augment
    the route reconnaissance element with technical specialists, such as combat engineers or CBRN
    personnel. Combat engineers in an engineer reconnaissance team can quantitatively evaluate
    critical points along the route (e.g., determine military load capacity of bridges) and assess
    obstacles and CBRN personnel can determine whether contaminated terrain is along the route.

    Control Measures. The minimum control measures necessary for a route reconnaissance are an
    AO, a start point, and a release point that define the section of the route on which the unit will
    collect detailed information. The AO should be wide enough and deep enough to allow the unit
    to conduct reconnaissance of all terrain from which the enemy could dominate the route. A line
    of departure and LOA create the rear and forward boundaries of the AO. The commander may
    add phase lines and checkpoints to coordinate reconnaissance, control movement, or designate
    critical points.

                                                                        13-8


---

                                                                                  MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

Tasks. The information requirements define the mission and reconnaissance objective. When a
commander selects a specific route to support maneuver, logistics, or both, units conduct route
reconnaissance. The information requirements will also affect the proposed purpose for the route
selection for the mission. The following are route reconnaissance tasks:

  • Use available capabilities to find, report, and—based on engagement criteria—clear all
     enemy forces that can influence movement along the route.

  • Determine if the route can support proposed usage requirements.
  • Reconnoiter all terrain that the enemy can use to dominate movement along the route, such as

     choke points, ambush sites, pickup zones (PZs), LZs, and DZs.
  • Reconnoiter all built up areas, contaminated areas, and lateral routes along the route.
  • Evaluate and classify (engineers conduct classification) all bridges, defiles, overpasses,

     underpasses, and culverts along the route.
  • Locate any fords, crossing sites, or bypasses for existing and reinforcing obstacles (including

     built up areas) along the route.
  • Locate all obstacles and create lanes as specified in execution orders.
  • Submit route-specific reports (e.g., bridge, tunnel, ford, ferry) to the unit that ordered the

     reconnaissance mission.

See MCRP 3-34.3, Engineer Reconnaissance, for additional information concerning route
reconnaissance and the DoD forms for recording and reporting reconnaissance results.

Zone Reconnaissance
Zone reconnaissance is a directed effort to obtain detailed information concerning all routes,
obstacles (including existing, reinforcing, and CBRN contamination), terrain, and enemy forces
within an AO. Commanders assign zone reconnaissance missions when—

  • They need additional information on a zone before conducting operations.
  • The enemy situation is vague.
  • They need information concerning cross-country trafficability.
  • Knowledge of terrain limited.
  • Combat operation have altered the terrain.

A zone reconnaissance may include several route or area reconnaissance missions assigned to
subordinate units. A zone reconnaissance is typically a deliberate, time consuming process,
conducted over extended distances. Typically, ground elements executing the zone reconnaissance
move alongside each other, with other ISR assets reinforcing their efforts and covering potential
gaps. When the reconnaissance objective is an enemy force, commanders may choose to forgo a
detailed sweep of the entire area and focus assets on NAIs within the zone that would reveal
enemy dispositions and intentions, and terrain likely to affect movement and maneuver.

Force Organization. General task organization considerations for organizing a zone
reconnaissance are the same as for organizing a route reconnaissance. The primary difference is in
size and scope. Given the large size of a zone and the detailed reconnaissance required, the

                                                                   13-9


---

MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

    mission is typically assigned to a single commander of a large unit, such as a battalion or a
    designated commander overseeing the actions of multiple, dedicated reconnaissance units. If the
    force conducting the zone reconnaissance expects to encounter significant enemy forces within
    the zone, the commander provides the force with a reserve. This reserve should have adequate
    combat power to extract elements of the reconnaissance force from decisive engagement. If a unit
    conducts a zone reconnaissance beyond supporting range of the main body, the commander
    ordering the zone reconnaissance provides the reconnaissance unit with adequate fire support
    assets that can move with the reconnaissance unit.

    Control Measures. The minimum control measure necessary for a zone reconnaissance is an AO.
    A line of departure and LOA create the rear and forward boundaries of the AO. The commander
    of the reconnaissance unit may subdivide the AO and employ control measures such as phase
    lines and contact points to coordinate the movement and actions of subordinate units. The
    commander may further designate the time that this physical contact takes place.

    Tasks. The requirement to conduct a zone reconnaissance is established when a commander lacks
    sufficient information regarding an area in terms of threat and terrain. These information
    requirements define the mission and reconnaissance objective. The following are zone
    reconnaissance tasks:

       • Use available capabilities to find, report, and—based on engagement criteria—clear all
          enemy forces within the zone.

       • Determine the trafficability of all terrain within the zone, including built up areas.
       • Locate and determine the extent of all contaminated areas in the zone.
       • Evaluate and classify (engineers conduct classification) all bridges, defiles, overpasses,

          underpasses, and culverts in the zone.
       • Locate any fords, crossing sites, or bypasses for existing and reinforcing obstacles (including

          built up areas) in the zone.
       • Locate all obstacles and create lanes as specified in execution orders.
       • Report the above information to the commander directing the zone reconnaissance to include

          providing a sketch map or overlay.

    Area Reconnaissance
    Area reconnaissance is “a directed effort to obtain detailed information concerning the terrain or
    enemy activity within a prescribed area such as a town, ridgeline, woods, or other features critical
    to operations” (USMC Dictionary). The area may consist of a single point, such as a bridge or an
    installation. There are two primary differences between an area reconnaissance and a zone
    reconnaissance. The first difference is size and scale—areas are smaller than zones and are not
    usually contiguous to other areas targeted for reconnaissance. The second difference is that units
    conducting an area reconnaissance first move to the area where the reconnaissance will take place,
    whereas units conducting a zone reconnaissance cross a line of departure and investigate the area
    in front of them. Additionally, an area reconnaissance typically takes less time to complete than a
    zone reconnaissance.

                                                                       13-10


---

                                                                                  MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

Force Organization. General considerations for organizing the area reconnaissance force are the
same as for organizing a zone reconnaissance. The primary difference is that larger forces are
unlikely to receive area reconnaissance missions.

Control Measures. The commander assigning an area reconnaissance specifies the area for
reconnaissance with a single continuous line to enclose the area to reconnoiter. Alternatively, the
commander may designate the area by using an AO. Commanders also designate a route into the
area and a route from the area—ideally separate. The commander of the unit conducting the
reconnaissance may use additional control measures to enable units to execute their assigned tasks.

Tasks. The tasks for an area reconnaissance are the same as for a zone reconnaissance.

Force-Oriented Reconnaissance
Force-oriented reconnaissance is a directed effort to obtain additional, timely intelligence on a
specific enemy or target unit. The ground reconnaissance element orients on that specific force,
moving when necessary to observe that unit and report all required information as well as any
other pertinent observed and collected information. The mobility of assigned ground
reconnaissance forces should match or exceed that of the target. Units assigned force-oriented
reconnaissance missions may act as subordinates within larger reconnaissance efforts, such as a
zone reconnaissance. Additionally, a force-oriented reconnaissance might employ several
different ground reconnaissance units, technical resources, and sensors, passing observation
responsibility from unit to unit as the target moves, enabling other units to reposition as necessary.
Enemy targets requiring such a focus likely have their own engagement criteria, and ground
reconnaissance units should have adequate fire support to engage such targets if engagement
criteria are met.

Force Organization. General considerations for organizing a force-oriented reconnaissance are the
same as for organizing a zone reconnaissance. The primary difference is the distribution and
maneuverability of assigned forces. Small forces focused on stealth and avoiding detection are
suitable for static enemy targets, while widely distributed, mobile reconnaissance units integrated
with extensive technical support and sensors are necessary for highly mobile targets. In such
situations, commanders focus their ground reconnaissance units on areas where other assets and
sensors are challenged (e.g., close or complex terrain) or contested (e.g., probable enemy contact,
enemy sensor location). Commanders assigned force-reconnaissance missions should maintain a
reserve that can extract elements of the reconnaissance force from decisive engagement or provide
cueing and mixing to target observation efforts.

Control Measures. The minimum control measure necessary for a force-oriented reconnaissance is
an AO. The commander of the reconnaissance unit may subdivide the AO and employ control
measures such as phase lines and contact points to coordinate the movement and actions of
subordinate units. However, overall control measures should be minimal to provide the
reconnoitering unit flexibility in the execution of their mission.

Tasks. A force-oriented reconnaissance is conducted when a commander and staff determine
there is a lack of sufficient information regarding a specific enemy force or unit. These

                                                                  13-11


---

MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

    information requirements define the mission and reconnaissance objective. The following are
    force-oriented reconnaissance tasks:

       • Determine the location, disposition, and depth of enemy forces.
       • Report patterns, readiness, and changes in status of targeted enemy units and forces.
       • Maintain constant observation to include movement.
       • Maintain the ability to engage, direct the engagement, or a combination of both when

         engagement criteria are met.

    Special Reconnaissance
    Special reconnaissance combines reconnaissance and surveillance actions as a special operation in
    hostile, denied, or diplomatically or politically sensitive environments to collect or verify
    information of strategic or operational significance, employing military capabilities not found in
    conventional Marine Corps units.

    Marine Corps ground reconnaissance units are not special operations forces, although they do
    share many of the same TTP, terms, and equipment. The clearest distinction between these units is
    who they work for and where they operate on the battlefield. In accordance with United States
    Code, Title 10, Armed Forces, subtitle A, part 1, chapter 6, section 167, Unified combatant
    command for special operations forces, additional units or forces may be designated as special
    operations forces by the Secretary of Defense.

    See JP 3-05, Special Operations, for detailed information relating to special operations forces and
    their organization. See MCRP 2-10A.6, Ground Reconnaissance Operations, and Army
    Techniques Publication (ATP) 3-18.4, Special Forces Special Reconnaissance, for additional
    information on special reconnaissance activities.

   PLANNING RECONNAISSANCE COLLECTION

    By integrating reconnaissance into the intelligence collection plan, the commander increases
    situational awareness of the battlespace. Reconnaissance planning ensures that reconnaissance assets
    are integrated, aggressively used, and support the commander’s decision-making requirements.

    Intelligence Collection Plan
    Using the MCPP, commanders and staffs determine and prioritize information requirements, and
    assign available ISR assets to fulfill those requirements. In terms of offensive and defensive
    tactics, such requirements may consist of reconnoitering avenues of approach that support friendly
    movement, investigating key terrain, locating obstacles, or finding exploitable enemy flanks.
    The requirements of the intelligence collection plan are the primary drivers of reconnaissance
    objectives, tasks, and all subsequent planning. See MCWP 5-10 and MCTP 2-10A, MAGTF
    Intelligence Collection, for more information on the MCPP and the intelligence collection plan.

                                                                       13-12


---

                                                                                  MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

Reconnaissance Pull versus Reconnaissance Push
The operations cycle of planning, executing, and assessing is continuous. While any particular
operation may begin with a deliberate planning and intelligence collection effort, as it unfolds,
continuous intelligence collection and reconnaissance efforts help assess the success of friendly
actions, identify enemy intentions and reactions, uncover opportunities to exploit, and identify
threats to avoid. Commanders use and interchange two reconnaissance methods to ensure that the
operations cycle outpaces the enemy’s ability to react.

Operations based on reconnaissance pull use information provided by reconnaissance forces to
guide friendly force activities. As commanders obtain combat information from available
reconnaissance assets, which drives COA selection and tactical choices. Reconnaissance pull is
preferred when the MAGTF can freely maneuver to exploit the enemy’s weaknesses and during
offensive operations as it takes advantage of the MAGTF’s inherent flexibility and reconnaissance
capabilities. MAGTF operations, such as operational maneuver from the sea, depend on
reconnaissance pull to determine enemy dispositions and find or create exploitable gaps while
avoiding obstacles and enemy strong points.

Operations based on reconnaissance push use information requirements of preplanned tactical
operations to guide reconnaissance force employment. As commanders prepare to execute an
operation or phase, they employ reconnaissance assets to determine specific information
requirements to support COA development. Reconnaissance push is often used when the MAGTF
is following a predetermined COA, targeting and destroying enemy forces is a priority, freedom of
maneuver is limited, and when conducting defense operations. For more information on
reconnaissance push and pull reference MCRP 2-10A.6.

Reconnaissance Guidance
Commanders provide reconnaissance guidance, which provides tasks, purpose, and objectives, to
ensure subordinate units can develop the situation and achieve the objectives within the required
timeframe. Commanders develop their planning guidance based on the RLT’s mission, timeline,
and intent to satisfy information requirements and identify opportunities to seize, retain, and
exploit the initiative. Commanders specify different reconnaissance guidance for each phase of an
operation and adjusts the components of their guidance as necessary. Commander’s guidance
consists of four elements—

  • Focus.
  • Tempo of reconnaissance.
  • Engagement/disengagement criteria, both lethal and nonlethal.
  • Displacement criteria.

Reconnaissance Focus. Reconnaissance focus defines the unit’s area of emphasis and includes four
categories: threat, infrastructure, terrain and weather effects, and society. The higher commander’s
intent as well as the commander’s initial assessment of information requirements and information
gaps guides the focus for reconnaissance tasks. Focus helps the unit narrow the scope of operations
to get the information most important to developing the situation for future operations.

                                                                  13-13


---

MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

    Commanders and staff can further focus reconnaissance efforts by assigning specific
    reconnaissance objectives. The objective should directly support the end state defined in the
    commander’s intent. For example, during offensive tasks an infantry regiment’s reconnaissance
    unit’s objective might be to locate an enemy’s security force, to include its composition,
    disposition, and capabilities. During that reconnaissance mission, the unit could also address
    information gaps concerning terrain—collecting information on key terrain features that might
    affect friendly forces, the enemy’s disposition, and the various COAs the regimental level staff
    might develop during planning. In stabilization tasks and activities, however, reconnaissance units
    might focus on locating improvised explosive device manufacturing sites. Planners use the
    information developed by terrain- or enemy-focused reconnaissance to update templated enemy
    COAs as part of a continuous assessment (through IPB) of the tactical situation and the
    operational environment.

    Additionally, a reconnaissance objective might include gaining an awareness of how the local
    population affects military operations and how military operations effect the population.
    Organizations might have to conduct reconnaissance to gather information on the size, location,
    composition, and political temperament of the population. Such reconnaissance focuses on
    developing an understanding of the cultural and human factors that affect friendly as well as
    adversarial perceptions and operations, such as religion, ethnicity, language, and political or
    tribal organizations. Civil considerations also address infrastructure—the systems that support
    a specific area’s inhabitants, economy, and government. Civil considerations that might be
    the focus of reconnaissance include areas, structures, capabilities, organizations, people, and
    events. Commanders use the reconnaissance objective to state the critical elements of the
    reconnaissance effort.

    Reconnaissance focus allows subordinate reconnaissance units and commanders to prioritize tasks
    to accomplish, and the assets used to accomplish them.

    Reconnaissance Tempo. Reconnaissance tempo refers to the level of detail and covertness
    required of the unit to best accomplish either reconnaissance tasks. Tempo is described by four
    terms: rapid, deliberate, stealthy, and forceful. “Rapid” and “deliberate” are levels of detail and
    cannot be applied at the same time. However, units can fluctuate between the two from phase to
    phase or even within sub-phases of an operation. “Stealthy” and “aggressive” indicates mutually
    exclusive levels of covertness.

    “Rapid” tempo dictates that the reconnaissance operation is limited to a certain prescribed list
    of tasks or priority intelligence requirements (PIRs). Rapid tempo is applicable when time is of
    the essence and only a limited number of information requirements are necessary to accomplish
    the mission.

    “Deliberate” tempo implies that units must accomplish all mission tasks to ensure mission
    success. Deliberate tempo allows the unit more time to answer all information requirements.
    Detailed and thorough reconnaissance and security tasks require time-intensive, comprehensive,
    and meticulous mounted and dismounted efforts to observe reconnaissance objectives and develop
    the situation.

                                                                       13-14


---

                                                                                  MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

“Stealthy” tempo includes restrictive engagement criteria to avoid detection and engagement.
Stealthy reconnaissance typically takes more time than aggressive reconnaissance and uses
dismounted scouts to take maximum advantage of cover and concealment to reduce signatures
that lead to compromise. Units use stealthy reconnaissance when they have time available, require
detailed reconnaissance, are likely to encounter enemy forces a specific area, encounter dangerous
areas, and when restrictive terrain limits effectiveness of mounted reconnaissance.

“Forceful” tempo rapidly develops the situation through action by employing air and ground
reconnaissance, technical means, and both direct and indirect fire systems. Forceful
reconnaissance requires firepower, aggressive exploitation of action on contact, operational
security, and training to survive and accomplish its mission. Forceful reconnaissance is applicable
when time is limited, detailed reconnaissance is not required, terrain is open, environmental
conditions allow for mounted reconnaissance, and when dismounted reconnaissance cannot
complete the mission within existing time constraints.

Reconnaissance Engagement and Disengagement Criteria. Engagement criteria are protocols that
specify those circumstances for initiating engagement with an enemy force. They can be either
restrictive or permissive. The commander and staff visualizes engagement criteria by analyzing
the mission, enemy, and troops and support available.

Commanders and staff must define the size or type of enemy force they expect subordinate units
to engage or avoid, which drives planning for direct and indirect fires, and establishes bypass
criteria. The commander and staff must consider information engagement and how the squadron
interacts and influences the local populace.

Engagement criteria should be defined using precise doctrinal terms. The squadron commander
issues specific planning guidance to define the engagement criteria. The staff and subordinate
commanders refine that guidance into specific execution information. Examples include—

  • Engagement criteria.
  • Guidance for actions on contact.
  • Bypass criteria.
  • Reconnaissance handover criteria.
  • Priority of fires.
  • ROE or rules for use of force.
  • FSCMs.
  • Weapons control status.

Reconnaissance Displacement Criteria. Displacement criteria define triggers for planned
withdrawal, passage of lines, or reconnaissance handover between units. The conditions
and parameters set out in displacement criteria integrate the commander’s intent with tactical
feasibility. Conditions are either event driven (e.g., associated PIR being met, threat contact
not expected in the area, and observed NAIs or avenues of approach denied to the enemy);
time driven (e.g., latest time information of value time triggers are met); or threat driven
(e.g., observation posts have been compromised).

                                                                  13-15


---

MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

    Reconnaissance Management
    The staff uses a mix of reconnaissance management methods, such as cueing, redundancy, and
    task-organizing to quickly collect the most critical information with the fewest assets.

    Cueing. Cueing is “external actions or inputs that cause a surveillance or target acquisition device
    to turn on and search a suspect area” (USMC Dictionary). Cueing uses technical assets to conduct
    wide-area surveillance, which focuses the efforts of limited ground reconnaissance assets. For
    example, airborne or electronic systems can identify portions of an enemy force or determine
    adversary or enemy C2 nodes. The commander can then dispatch ground reconnaissance to verify
    and develop the information. Similarly, ground reconnaissance units can cue other ISR assets.
    Commanders employ reconnaissance assets based on their capabilities and use the complementary
    capabilities of other ISR resources to verify and expand information to support decision-making.

    Redundancy. In intelligence collection, redundancy is a management method that uses several
    same-discipline assets to cover the same target and improves chances of collecting relevant
    information. Based on the information requirement’s priority, the commander must decide which,
    if any, NAI needs to be covered by more than one asset. For example, when more than one asset
    covers the same NAI, a backup is available if one asset cannot reach the NAI in time, suffers
    mechanical failure, or it is detected and engaged by the enemy.

    Task-Organizing. To increase a reconnaissance’s asset’s effectiveness and survivability the
    commander may task-organize additional assets under the unit’s control. For example, to conduct
    a long-range area reconnaissance of possible river crossing sites an LAR company might receive
    an engineer reconnaissance element, additional infantry, and a logistic element. The engineers
    provide additional technical information on proposed crossing sites, the infantry provides
    additional combat power and protection for the vehicles, and the logistic element brings additional
    fuel and a self-recovery capability.

   LOGISTICS

    Because METT-T drives how reconnaissance assets are employed and sustained, logistics
    planners must be flexible. Reconnaissance elements must either carry a large basic load, receive
    logistic assets as part of task organization, or a combination of both. Smaller reconnaissance
    elements, such as division reconnaissance teams, typically combine large basic loads with aerial
    resupply to extend their operating distances and durations. Larger elements, such as LAR, might
    require additional refueling and maintenance capabilities to extend their ability to operate. Both
    examples must also consider evacuation of personnel and equipment casualties. Combining
    logistic demands with operational capabilities is part of the reconnaissance planning necessary to
    support the intelligence collection plan.

   RECONNAISSANCE EMPLOYMENT

    Reconnaissance is characterized as either stealthy or aggressive. A key factor in reconnaissance
    execution is the time available to conduct the mission. The commander recognizes the increased risk
    to the reconnaissance element and the main body when accelerating the pace of reconnaissance. To

                                                                       13-16


---

                                                                                  MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

reduce risk, units can employ air reconnaissance assets and technical means to surveil terrain or
low-threat areas. Attack reconnaissance helicopters and other aerial platforms, as well as mounted
and dismounted ground reconnaissance assets, are characterized as either stealthy or aggressive
(depending on how they are employed).

Stealthy reconnaissance emphasizes avoiding enemy detection and engagement. It takes more
time than aggressive reconnaissance. Stealthy reconnaissance takes maximum advantage of cover
and concealment, limited visibility, and reduced battlespace signatures. However, because stealth
cannot be guaranteed units attempting to conduct stealthy reconnaissance (e.g., dismounted
scouts) must be trained to react if the enemy makes contact and have immediate access to
supporting fires.

Aggressive reconnaissance is characterized by the speed and way the reconnaissance force
develops the situation once they make contact with an enemy force. A unit conducting aggressive
reconnaissance uses both direct and indirect fire systems and movement to rapidly develop the
situation. A unit requires firepower, aggressive exploitation of actions on contact, OPSEC, and
training to increase chances of survival and accomplish the mission when conducting aggressive
reconnaissance. Mounted reconnaissance is typically characterized as aggressive. When
determining whether to conduct mounted or dismounted reconnaissance, commanders consider
METT-T. Specific conditions that might result in a decision to conduct mounted or aerial
reconnaissance include the following:

  • Time is limited.
  • Detailed reconnaissance is not required.
  • Air units are available to perform coordinated reconnaissance with the ground assets.
  • The IPB process has provided detailed information on the enemy.
  • Terrain is relatively open.
  • Environmental conditions permit this type of reconnaissance (deep snow and muddy or

     swampy terrain greatly hinder mounted reconnaissance).
  • Dismounted reconnaissance cannot complete the mission within existing time constraints.

The following conditions may cause a commander to direct a dismounted reconnaissance effort:

  • Time is available.
  • Detailed reconnaissance is required.
  • Stealth is required.
  • The IPB process indicates close proximity to enemy positions.
  • The reconnaissance force encounters danger areas.
  • Restrictive terrain limits the effectiveness of mounted reconnaissance.

In addition, see Reconnaissance Methods in this chapter for additional conditions to consider.
MCTP 3-01A provides further information on dismounted scouting, tracking, situational
awareness, and patrolling.

Typically, air reconnaissance units operate closely with ground reconnaissance units to maximize
redundancy and provide mutual security. Assault support aircraft can insert surveillance teams at
observation posts. Aircrews can observe, conduct electromagnetic surveillance, and provide

                                                                  13-17


---

MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

    security and responsive fire support. Although rarely carried out, aircrew members can dismount
    to evaluate bridges, fords, or crossing sites. Aircraft units conducting air reconnaissance plan their
    missions in much the same way as ground units, using the same graphics, considering the same
    tasks, and accounting for IPB. The ACE routinely participates in creating the intelligence
    collection plan, which is critical to employing aviation in support of reconnaissance.

   RECUPERATING, RECONSTITUTING, AND REORGANIZING RECONNAISSANCE ASSETS

    Commanders determine whether to reconstitute—by either regenerating or reorganizing—or
    recuperate reconnaissance units when they can no longer perform their primary missions.
    Recuperation—a short break for rest, resupply, and maintenance—is often sufficient to return
    units to effectiveness. Units can extend these recuperation periods to conduct refresher training,
    new equipment training, or any required specialized training for the next mission. Relieving units
    must complete a deliberate RIP to ensure continuous reconnaissance while maintaining contact
    with the enemy force.

    Regenerating a unit requires significant resources. The organization two echelons above the unit
    being regenerated directs the regeneration procedure and coordinates for the necessary personnel,
    equipment, and supplies. If that headquarters lacks the necessary personnel or sustainment assets,
    they coordinate with the appropriate theater sustainment command supporting organization. For
    example, a regiment can regenerate one of its reconnaissance platoons from the infantry battalion.
    In the regeneration process, the regiment could use a combination of weapon system replacement,
    battle damage assessment and repair, typical replacement operations, and medical returnees to
    provide the needed resources. Units could use these resources, combined with training, to
    regenerate the platoon’s degraded combat power. Alternatively, they could designate one of their
    maneuver companies to perform reconnaissance functions.

    Reorganization includes actions to shift resources within an attrited unit to increase unit combat
    effectiveness. Reorganization may be conducted when the operational tempo is such that the risk
    of removing a unit from the operation may jeopardize the mission. There are two types of
    reorganization operations: immediate and deliberate. The type of reorganization operation
    executed is based on mission and the operating environment. Reorganization may include such
    measures as—

       • Cross-leveling equipment and personnel.
       • Matching operational weapons and equipment with teams and units.
       • Forming composite units (joining two or more degraded units to form a single

         mission-capable unit).

    Immediate reorganization is the rapid and usually temporary restoration of attrited units to
    minimum levels of effectiveness. Typically, the commander implements immediate reorganization
    in the combat position or as close to that site as possible to meet near-term needs. Deliberate
    reorganization is conducted when more time and resources are available. It usually occurs farther
    away from hostile activity than immediate reorganization. Procedures are similar to those for
    immediate reorganization; however, some additional replacement resources may be available.
    Also, equipment repair is more intensive and more extensive cross-leveling is possible.

                                                                       13-18


---

                    CHAPTER 14.
                       SECURITY

Marines conduct security activities to protect the force from surprise and reduce unknowns. The
force being protected could also be the civilian population, civil institutions, and civilian
infrastructure within a unit’s AO. A unit can conduct security operations to the front, flanks, or
rear of the friendly force. The main difference between security operations and reconnaissance
operations is that security operations orient on the force or facility being protected, while
reconnaissance is enemy and terrain oriented. Security operations are shaping actions. As a
shaping action, economy of force is often a condition of security operations.

There are three types of security activities:

  • Screen is a type of security mission that provides early warning to the protected force.
     In a screen mission, Marines observe, identify, and report information, and only fight in
     self-protection.

  • Guard is a type of security mission that protects the main force by fighting to gain time while
     also observing and reporting information and preventing enemy ground from observing and
     directing fire against the main body.

  • Cover is a type of security mission that intercepts, engages, delays, disorganizes, and
     deceives the enemy to protect the covered force from surprise, develop the situation, and give
     the friendly unit time and space in which to respond to enemy actions.

Additionally, forces can be assigned rear area and local security missions:

  • Rear area security consists of the measures taken before, during, and after an enemy airborne
     attack, sabotage action, infiltration, guerrilla action, or initiation of psychological or
     propaganda warfare to minimize the effects thereof.

  • Local security are those security elements established near a unit, who are tasked to prevent
     surprise by the enemy and mitigate enemy actions.

The screen, guard, and cover, respectively, provide increasing levels of combat power and provide
increasing levels of security for the main body. However, more combat power in the security force
means less for the main body. Rear area security preserves the unit’s freedom to move reserves,
position fire support assets, provide for command and control, and conduct sustaining actions. Local
security is an inherent function of force protection; the responsibility of every leader; and consists of
immediate, organic, and self-protection measures (e.g., entry control points, perimeter security,
internal guard). The commander designates the security area wherein the security force operates.

         NOTE: With regard to security operations, the terms, “stationary” and “moving”
         describe the actions of the main body, not the security force.


---

MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

    All MAGTF elements conduct local security and rear area security. Although the ACE can
    conduct screens, the GCE is the one element of the MAGTF specifically capable of conducting all
    types of security operations. Unit SOPs and well-developed support relationships with
    attachments facilitate effective security activities.

   FUNDAMENTALS OF SECURITY OPERATIONS

    Successful security operations depend on five fundamentals:

       • Provide early and accurate warning.
       • Provide reaction time and maneuver space.
       • Orient on the force or facility to be secured.
       • Perform continuous reconnaissance.
       • Maintain enemy contact.

    Provide Early and Accurate Warning
    The security force provides early warning by quickly detecting the enemy force and reporting
    information to the main body commander. The security force operates at varying distances from
    the main body based on METT-T. At a minimum, they should operate far enough from the main
    body to prevent enemy ground forces from observing or engaging the main body with direct fires.
    The earlier the security force detects the enemy, the more time the main body has to assess and
    react to the changing situation. The security force is integrated with the main body’s ISR
    collection efforts.

    Provide Reaction Time and Maneuver Space
    The security force provides the main body with enough reaction time and maneuver space to
    effectively respond to enemy actions by operating at a distance from the main body and engaging
    enemy forces. The amount of reaction time and required maneuver space and the distance at
    which the security force must operate from the main body are based on METT-T analysis. The
    main body commander accepts prudent risk in balancing the security needs of the force against the
    combat power necessary to accomplish the primary mission.

    Orient on the Force or Facility to be Secured
    The security force focuses all actions on protecting and providing early warning to the secured
    force or facility. Because the security force’s movement is based on the main body’s movement,
    the security force commander must know the main body’s SOM to keep the security force
    between the main body and known or suspected enemy units. The value of terrain occupied by the
    security force hinges on the protection they provide to the main body commander.

    Perform Continuous Reconnaissance and Counterreconnaissance
    The security force aggressively and continuously seeks the enemy and reconnoiters terrain
    (including human factors). They conduct the reconnaissance missions, as required (see Chapter 13).
    The goal is to determine the enemy’s COA so that it can be mitigated or exploited by the main
    body. Security forces collect information on the terrain to determine its potential use by the enemy

                                                                        14-2


---

                                                                                  MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

or friendly force. Stationary security forces conduct reconnaissance by using observation posts,
aviation resources, patrols, intelligence collection assets, and battle positions. Moving security
forces conduct reconnaissance by using various reconnaissance missions along with observation
posts and battle positions.

The security force also conducts counterreconnaissance against enemy ISR assets to disrupt the
enemy force’s plan so friendly units can force enemy units to deploy into formations on the
ground of those commanders’ choosing. This also prevents the enemy from gaining intelligence
on the friendly forces main’ defensive force’s composition and disposition and forces the enemy
to attack into an unknown situation.

Maintain Enemy Contact
Once the security forces make enemy contact, they do not break contact unless directed by the
main force commander. Whether stationary or moving, the security force’s assigned security area
must be large enough to allow maneuver depth (in space and in time) sufficient to maintain
contact with the enemy while still providing the main body time and space to react.

PLANNING CONSIDERATIONS FOR SECURITY OPERATIONS

Control Measures
The minimum control measures for security operations are the boundaries necessary to create a
security area. When operating to the front of the main body, a security force’s lateral boundaries
are usually an extension of the main body’s lateral boundaries, and the rear boundary is typically
the handover line. When operating to the rear the main body, a security force’s lateral boundaries
are also extensions of the main body’s and the forward boundary is the main body’s rear boundary.
Boundaries for flank security depend on the SOM. Typically, the flank security force’s provides
security from the trail element of the advance security force or lead combat unit and to the lead
element of the rear security force or main body rear boundary.

Security force commanders can further subdivide the security area to coordinate the actions of
subordinate units, use battle positions and defensive sectors, and employ phase lines for screen or
delay lines, displacement triggers, or handover lines. Given likely maneuver requirements,
particularly for a moving security force, security force commanders typically employ internal
checkpoints and contact points.

Force Organization
In organizing the security force, the primary consideration is the nature of the force to secure. The
type of force being protected (moving or stationary) determines the limits of the security force’s
responsibilities, organizational requirements, and the amount of battlespace necessary to fulfill the
security functions. Table 14-1 shows the typical size of security forces at various echelons. Since
the security force must have equal or greater mobility than the force they are securing. Creating a
security force often places demands for additional resources on the parent command—for example,
an infantry company serving as an advance guard might require additional combat power and
mobility assets.
