Command and Control
Commanders place themselves where they can best direct the operation, often at most likely
points of friction, or where they can observe the most dangerous avenue of approach. Commander
placement, command post displacement, and combat train positioning are critical considerations
when conducting moving security operations. Ideally, the security force seeks to place C2 and
logistic assets behind masking terrain and along improved routes that provide lateral and
in-depth mobility.

Intelligence
Security operations are integrated into the intelligence warfighting function. The security force’s
observations can have an immediate impact on the main body’s intelligence picture. The main
body commander and staff should ensure that security forces can access higher intelligence
systems to increase situational awareness and reduce the risk of the security force having to wait
upon the main body for information. When main body commanders establish flank security, they
typically focus ISR collection efforts on that flank to identify threats and increase its effectiveness.
Organic and inorganic ISR resources (e.g., remote sensors, UAS platforms, electromagnetic
warfare) expand the area under surveillance and cue the security force. The ACE often serves as a
screening force because it can detect and report enemy forces at extended ranges. Integrating the

                                                   14-4


---

                                                                                  MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

security force into the intelligence collection plan and providing the force with ISR resources
enables the it to concentrate limited combat power against likely enemy threats, react to enemy
actions, and cover ISR gaps.

Maneuver
Security missions are usually time or event driven. The main body commander determines
the requirement for a security mission in advance to provide enough time for the security force
to establish themselves and prepare to execute the mission. The end of a security mission is
based on—

  • Actions by the main body (e.g., completing a specific mission).
  • A fixed time period (e.g., not allowing the enemy to penetrate a phase line for two hours).
  • Criteria based on the enemy force (e.g., size).

To terminate the security mission, the security force commander typically requires the permission
of the main body commander to withdraw behind the security area’s rear boundary.

The main body commander may impose special requirements or constraints, including engagement,
disengagement, and bypass criteria. The main body commander may order the security force not to
become decisively engaged or fall below a certain combat strength. The main body commander may
be willing to accept decreased security, which results from either the loss of more terrain or reduced
preparation time by the main body, to preserve the security force for later use.

Countermobility is critical in a security area. With integrated obstacles, the security force can
maintain a mobility advantage over the enemy and delay and disrupt the enemy’s plans. The
security force might initially mass engineer support in the security area and then shift support to the
MBA once those units are prepared to begin developing engagement areas. Engineering resources
also enhance the security force’s mobility by identifying repositioning routes and task-organizing
engineers to provide breaching capabilities.

Security Area. The main body commander determines the location, orientation, and depth of the
security area. The commander identifies specific avenues of approach and NAIs to be covered.
Depth in the security area provides the main body with time to react to approaching enemy ground
units. Occupying a deep security area allows the security force to destroy enemy reconnaissance
assets without compromising critical observation posts or positions. It also prevents the enemy
from penetrating the security area too easily and prevents gaps from occurring when observation
posts or units displace or are lost. The wider the security area, the less the security force can take
advantage of the increased depth. A shallow security area may require the commander to provide
the security force with additional resources to provide needed reaction time—for example, a
shallow security area may require the security force to guard the main body vice screen them.

After the security force analyzes the terrain in the security area, the commander—

  • Establishes the security force’s initial positions (usually a screen line) as far forward
     as possible.

  • Assigns responsibilities for the avenues of approach and designated NAIs.

                                                                   14-5


---

MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

    Next, the commander assigns responsibility for identified avenues of approach and designated
    NAIs. When conducting screen or guard operations, the initial screen line must be within
    supporting range of the main body while providing sufficient early warning.

    When deploying into the security area, the security force must quickly establish the security area
    to meet mission requirements and provide the necessary level of security.

    The security force moves into the security area using a tactical road march, movement to contact,
    or zone reconnaissance.

    Tactical Road March. The fastest but least secure method is a tactical road march from the rear
    boundary of the security area to the initial positions. The security force moves to a release point on
    the rear boundary where subordinate elements deploy to occupy initial positions. This method is
    appropriate when enemy contact is not expected, time is critical, or the ACE is conducting a zone
    reconnaissance forward of the ground element finds no enemy in the security area.

    Movement to Contact. The security force conducts a movement to contact from a line of departure
    (usually the rear boundary of the security area) to the initial positions. This method is slower but
    more secure than a tactical road march. It is used when enemy contact is likely, time is limited,
    terrain reconnaissance is not needed, or an aviation unit conducting zone reconnaissance forward
    of the ground element detects enemy forces in the security area.

    Zone Reconnaissance. The most secure method for moving to the initial positions is to conduct a
    zone reconnaissance from the security area rear boundary to the initial security line positions or
    the forward limit of the security area. Given adequate time, this method is preferred because it
    allows the security force to clear the security area and become familiar with the terrain that they
    may have to defend. The security force reconnoiters potential subsequent positions and fire
    support system firing positions as they move to initial positions. A zone reconnaissance is
    appropriate when time is available and information about the enemy or terrain is unknown.
    Although this method provides information on the enemy and terrain in the area, it can also be
    time consuming. Using air reconnaissance forward of the ground units increases the speed and
    security of the movement.

    Employment of the Aviation Combat Element. The ACE contribution is often critical to the success
    of the security mission. The ACE can—

       • Employ assault support assets to increase the mobility of ground forces.
       • Conduct screening operations in support of the main body and security forces.
       • Cover gaps and conduct reconnaissance of areas between ground maneuver units.
       • Assist in maintaining contact between the security force and the main body.
       • Assist in clearing the area between the flank security element and the main body during

          moving flank security missions.
       • Assist in disengaging ground units, particularly when conducting battle handover and passage

          of lines with the main body.
       • Monitor terrain that is hard to reach or would require too much time to cover with ground

          reconnaissance assets.

                                                                        14-6


---

                                                                                  MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

Observation Posts. An observation post is a communications position from which military
observations are made or fires directed and adjusted. They are occupied for a period of time to
conduct observation over a specifically assigned area. They will not likely be a permanent
concrete bunker. An infantry company could establish observation posts as part of an overnight
defense, and an LAR platoon might occupy an observation posts for only a few hours before leap
frogging ahead as the security force continues to move.

The security force commander and staff determine initial observation post locations along or
behind the screen line to ensure effective surveillance of the sector and designated NAIs. The unit
or asset that occupies each observation posts may shift its exact location to achieve the
commander’s intent. The staff may place more than one observation post along a high speed
avenue of approach to allow an enemy contact to be tracked from one observation post to another,
thus maintaining enemy contact without requiring security forces to displace. The security force
commander tasks subordinate units to perform reconnaissance and combat patrols to cover gaps
between observation posts. To prevent friendly fire incidents, the commander places a restrictive
FSCM around observation post locations.

Observation posts can be either mounted, dismounted, or airborne. Marines in a mounted
observation post use their vehicular optics and weapon systems, which facilitates rapid
displacement. However, an enemy can detect them more readily than dismounted observation
posts. Dismounted observation posts provide maximum stealth but lack the mounted
observation post’s speed. Two Marines should occupy an observation post for no more than
12 hours. Observation posts occupied for more than 12 hours should have a squad-sized
element to ensure continuous operation. In addition, units can use observation posts as listening
posts under limited-visibility conditions or in complex environments.

Conducting Moving Flank Security Operations. When conducting a moving flank, the security
force moves into and occupies a security area. The security force can—

  • Cross the line of departure separately from the main body and deploy to execute the mission.
  • Cross the line of departure separately from the main body while lead elements conduct a

     movement to contact
  • Cross the line of departure with the main body and conduct a zone reconnaissance outside the

     security area.

The security force then conducts a tactical road march, a movement to contact, or tactical
movements parallel to the main body and establishes observation posts or occupies battle positions
along the flank of the main body. This keeps the two forces from interfering with each other during
deployment. It is appropriate when another force penetrates the line of contact, the main body is not
in contact with the enemy and is moving quickly, the line of departure is uncontested, and the IPB
process indicates that enemy contact is not likely in the area through which the security force is
moving. It is the fastest but least secure form.

                                                                   14-7


---

MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

    In the second arrangement, the security force crosses the line of departure separately from the
    main body, and the lead elements conduct a movement to contact. Follow on elements occupy
    positions as they arrive. This form is applicable when the main body is moving slower than in the
    first method, the line of departure is uncontested, and the IPB process indicates possible enemy
    contact. It is slower than the previous form but provides better security.

    In the third arrangement, the security force crosses the line of departure with the main body and
    conducts a zone reconnaissance out to the far limit of the security area. This form is applicable
    when the line of departure is also the line of contact, the main body penetrates the enemy defenses
    along the line of contact, the main body is moving slowly, and the enemy situation is not clearly
    understood. The security force may follow the lead element of the main body through the gap and
    deploy when the situation permits. This form provides increased security for both the security
    force and the main body but is the most time consuming.

    Fires
    The main body provides fire support to screening and guarding forces. The main body allocates
    additional artillery to support a covering force, which operates independently of the main body.
    If the security force is assigned a wide AO, the commander may have to position ground fire
    support assets to cover only the most likely enemy avenues of approach. This is particularly
    important for a screen because the screening force often relies on indirect and aerial delivered fires
    to delay or disrupt the enemy. Providing adequate fire support to the security force may require the
    main body to position artillery well forward in the formation and may affect MAGTF
    prioritization of ACE missions.

   SCREEN

    The screening force’s primary tasks are to observe, identify, and report information; conduct
    counterreconnaissance; and fight only in self-protection. The screening force gains and maintains
    enemy contact consistent with the fundamentals of offense and destroys or repels enemy
    reconnaissance units by conducting counterreconnaissance. Typically, a screening force engages
    and destroys enemy reconnaissance elements within its capabilities—augmented by aviation and
    indirect fires—but otherwise fights only in self-defense. The screen has the minimum combat
    power necessary to provide early warning, which allows the main body to retain most of its combat
    power for commitment at the decisive place and time. A screen provides the least amount of
    protection of any security mission; and does not have the combat power to develop the situation.

    Security forces us a screen to cover gaps between forces, exposed flanks, or the rear of stationary
    and moving forces. A unit can typically screen an avenue of approach two echelons larger than
    itself, such as an LAR company screening a regimental-size avenue of approach. The commander
    can place a screen in front of a stationary formation when the likelihood of enemy action is small,
    the expected enemy force is small, or the main body needs only limited time (once they are
    warned) to react. Designed to provide minimum security with minimum forces, a screen is usually
    an economy of force operation based on prudent risk.

                                                                        14-8


---

                                                                                  MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

A security force typically conducts a screen by establishing a series of observation posts and
patrols to ensure adequate surveillance of the assigned area. The security force uses
reconnaissance patrols (e.g., mounted, dismounted, and aerial), relocates observation posts, and
employs technical assets to ensure continuous and overlapping surveillance.

Critical Tasks for a Screen
Units use screen tasks to—

  • Prevent enemy ground element from passing through the screen undetected and unreported.
  • Maintain continuous surveillance of all avenues of approach larger than a designated size into

     the area.
  • Conduct counterreconnaissance to destroy, defeat, or disrupt all enemy reconnaissance

     elements according to engagement criteria.
  • Locate the lead elements of each enemy advance guard and determine their direction of

     movement, when in the defense.
  • Maintain contact with enemy forces and report any activity in the AO.
  • Maintain contact with the main body and any security forces operating on the flanks.
  • Impede and harass the enemy.

Screening Force Organization
Units executing a screen mission employ a main body and small reserve. The main body provides
their own security, generally deploying into observation posts as determined by the number of
avenues of approach and NAIs they are responsible for. The reserve is deployed to allow other
security force elements to break contact with the enemy, extract units from endangered
observation posts, and take advantage of unexpected opportunities.

Control Measures
The control measures necessary to conduct a screen include phase lines, observation posts, named
areas of interest, handover lines, and contact points.

Executing a Stationary Screen
Although a screening force may execute their mission against enemy forces up to two echelons
above, a screening force covers operationally significant avenues of approach capable of use by
enemy forces one echelon smaller. For example, a company may conduct a screen against enemy
units up to a regiment in size but, when conducting IPB, the company will take into consideration
avenues of approach down to platoon size. Which avenues of approach the company observes
depends upon METT-T and the commander’s judgment.

After entering the security area, the screening force establishes screen lines consisting of
observation posts that, whenever possible, have overlapping fields of observation and integrate
with higher-echelon sensors and collection assets. The screening force establishes patrols to cover
areas that observation posts cannot observe. The commander positions the reserve force to
respond to the most dangerous enemy COAs and support the most vulnerable friendly positions.
When possible, the screening force establishes observations posts in depth on high speed avenues

                                                                   14-9


---

MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

    of approach. The commander and staff plan for egress routes between the initial and subsequent
    screen lines to facilitate rapid movement. The commander and staff establish disengagement
    criteria, and the unit rehearses displacement moves.

    The Marines at observation posts report the presence of enemy elements. Prompt, accurate
    reporting is essential to keep friendly forces manning the screen from being overrun or
    unknowingly bypassed. Once the enemy is detected, the observation post Marines employ fire
    support assets to engage the enemy at maximum range and either delay or prevent the enemy from
    penetrating the screen line. The screening force may destroy smaller enemy reconnaissance assets
    with direct fire, if fire support resources cannot accomplish this task.

    As enemy pressure threatens the security of the observation posts, subordinate units report and
    prepare to withdraw. The screening force commander might authorize some observation posts to
    withdraw while others stay in place to report enemy actions. The screening force uses a
    combination of requests and withdrawal criteria to manage retrogrades.

    As the screening force displaces from one screen line to another, they use rapid movement while
    maintaining contact with the enemy. The reserve remains in place as long as possible, ready to
    react and assist in the displacement of the main body. The commander may choose to divide the
    screening force and handoff observation and reserve duties among elements, using one of the
    methods discussed in Table 14-2. The screening force’s C2 and CSS elements displace as required
    to maintain control, keep from being overrun, and evacuate personnel and equipment casualties.
    The force repeats this procedure as often as necessary.

    As the screening force moves from one screen line to the next, the commander maintains
    communications with the main body. The main body commander decides whether the screening
    force can move behind a handover line and handoff the battle to the main body. When planning,
    the screening force commander develops branch plans that account for changes in mission—for
    example, transitioning from a screen operation to a guard operation to gain more time for the
    main body.

    Executing a Moving Screen
    A screening force may use several moving methods. Table 14-2 summarizes each method’s
    characteristics, advantages, and disadvantages.

    A screening force can maintain a moving screen along the flanks or rear of the protected force.
    The screen movement is keyed to time and distance factors associated with the main body’s
    movement. Responsibilities for a moving flank screen begin at the front of the main body’s lead
    combat element and end at the rear of the protected force. Responsibilities for a moving rear
    screen begin at the rear element of the main body.

    The commander and staff consider METT-T when deciding which movement method to employ.
    See Chapter 15 for more information on movement techniques.

Screening Operations During Limited Visibility
During limited visibility, the screening force uses all available night- and thermal-observation
devices and electronic surveillance devices. Although the screening force can use technical
ISR assets to offset limited visibility, they should also adjust techniques and procedures to
the conditions. For example, the screening force commander can establish more observation
posts—and listening posts—to cover avenues of approach that are masked in limited-visibility
conditions. Implementing rigorous noise and light discipline and using various warning devices
(e.g., trip flares) reduces the likelihood of compromise and increases the likelihood of enemy
reconnaissance forces bypassing the observation posts.

GUARD

Unlike a screen, the guarding force is expected to fight to accomplish the mission. A guarding
force’s primary task is to protect the main force by fighting to gain time while also observing and
reporting information. They routinely engage enemy forces with direct and indirect fires, using
uses all available means including decisive engagement, to prevent the enemy from observing and
engaging the main body. A guarding force operates within the range of the main body’s fire
support weapons, deploying over a narrower front than a screening force to permit the
concentration of combat power. The three methods of conducting guard operations are advance,
flank, and rear guard.

                                                                  14-11


---

MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

    A commander employs a guard when the significance of expected enemy contact requires
    additional security beyond that provided by a screen. The multiple requirements of the guard
    operation are often performed simultaneously over relatively large areas. The guarding force’s
    exact size is determined by METT-T; however, Table 14-1 provides general guidance on the size
    of an echelon’s guarding force.

    Critical Tasks for a Guard
    Units use guard tasks to—

       • Destroy the enemy advance guard.
       • Maintain contact with enemy forces and report activity in the AO.
       • Conduct counterreconnaissance to destroy or defeat all enemy reconnaissance elements

         according to engagement criteria. Must prevent ground observation and direct fire against the
         main body.
       • Continuously surveil avenues of approach into the AO.
       • Impede and harass the enemy while displacing.
       • Cause the enemy main body to deploy and then report the direction of travel.
       • Prevent enemy ground elements from passing through the security area undetected and
         unreported.
       • Destroy or cause the withdrawal of all enemy reconnaissance patrols.
       • Maintain contact with the main body and any other security forces operating on the flanks.

    Guarding Force Organization
    The guarding force typically executes the guard task by employing an area defense, a delay, a zone
    reconnaissance, or a movement to contact within the security area.

    Control Measures
    The guard force employs the control measures associated with the method they are employing in
    the security area. The guarding force may choose to combine and employ multiple types of
    security activities, such as having a subordinate element conduct a screen to the guard force’s
    front. Consequently, the guarding force commander may subdivide the security area into multiple
    AOs to support the selected SOM.

    Advance Guard
    An advance guard for a stationary or retrograding force operates defensively. They defend or
    delay in accordance with the main body commander’s intent. An advance guard for a moving
    force operates offensively. The advance guard develops the situation so that the main body can use
    their combat power to the greatest effect.

    An advance guard for a moving force typically conducts a movement to contact clearing enemy
    elements from the axis of advance or designated portions of the AO. Ground subordinate elements
    of a guarding force typically deploy to cover the axis of advance or the main body’s AO.
    This enables the main body to move unimpeded, avoid delays, and defer deployment for as long
    as possible.

                                                                       14-12


---

                                                                                  MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

The advance guard can operate behind the security force of a higher echelon. For example, a
division may use a reinforced LAR battalion as an offensive covering force, while each subordinate
regimental column organizes one of the battalion task forces into an advance guard. In these
situations, the higher-echelon security force initially develops the situation. The lower-echelon
advance guards may—

  • Coordinate and conduct the rearward passage of lines of the covering force.
  • Reduce obstacles to create lanes or improve existing lanes as required to support the main

     body’s maneuver.
  • Eliminate enemy forces bypassed by the covering force.
  • Coordinate and conduct a forward passage of lines through the covering force and fix enemy

     forces in the enemy’s main defensive positions to allow the friendly main body to maneuver.

The movement of multiple security forces and the handoff of surveilling a detected enemy force
from the higher echelon security force to the lower echelon security force are controlled using
checkpoints, contact points, phase lines, handover lines, and disengagement criteria, in addition to
other graphic control measures. At a minimum, the covering force’s rear boundary is also the
advance guard’s forward boundary.

The advance guard engages in offensive and defensive operations. For example, in the offense the
guarding force may conduct hasty attacks if they have sufficient combat power or may use a hasty
defense on an exposed flank until relieved by the advance of the main body or flank security.
Whereas in the defense, the guarding force may use counterattacks to exploit enemy weaknesses
or various other defensive methods to disrupt and delay enemy advance.

Flank Guard
A flank guard is “a security element operating to the flank of a moving or stationary force to protect
them from enemy ground observation, direct fire, and surprise attack” (USMC Dictionary). A flank
guard protects an exposed flank of the main body. A flank guard is like a flank screen except that
the staff plans defensive positions in addition to observation posts.

The main body’s commander designates the general location of the flank guard’s positions. The
commander assigns an AO to each flank guard that is sufficiently deep to provide early warning
and reaction time. However, each flank guard must remain within supporting range of the main
body. To determine the guarding force’s initial positions, the flank guard commander considers the
front and rear of the flank of the main body, the axis taken by the main body, the enemy’s
capabilities, and the available avenues of approach. Once the flank guard makes contact with the
enemy, it strives to defeat the enemy by attacking or defending, conduct a delay to develop the
situation, or fix the enemy for destruction by the main body.

The flank guard moves to its initial positions using one of the movement techniques (refer to
Chapter 15). Once the flank guard reaches their initial positions, it occupies defensive positions
in assigned battle positions or within the assigned AO and establishes a screening element
forward of these positions. In situations when knowledge about the enemy is vague, the flank
guard maintains a large reserve.

                                                                  14-13


---

MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

    When conducting a moving flank guard, a unit occupies a series of battle positions that cover
    potential enemy avenues of approach. The lead element of the moving flank guard does not
    reconnoiter battle positions or occupy them unless required when making contact. Instead, they
    maintain contact with the protected force’s main body, reconnoiter the area between that main
    body and the flank guard’s routes of advance, and reconnoiter the flank guard’s route. They
    perform these tasks by conducting a zone reconnaissance (see Chapter 13). The fundamental
    factors that affect the flank guard’s lead element are their mobility, the pace of the main body, and
    the width of the security area as measured from the main body’s boundary to the flank guard’s
    screen line. The size and combat power of the flank guard’s lead element is based upon this width.

    The rest of the flank guard marches along the route of advance and occupies battle positions as
    necessary. Engagement criteria for the route are the same as in a moving flank screen. The flank
    guard’s commander designates battle positions parallel to the axis of the main body. The flank
    guard commander places these battle positions outside the flank guard’s route of advance and
    along avenues of approach into the flank guard. The flank guard occupies observation posts along
    a screen line forward of these battle positions.

    Because the flank guard is moving in one direction and orienting on providing protection to the
    secured force in another direction, the flank guard staff plans control measures for a moving flank
    are typically the same as a moving screen, and they include phase lines that facilitate this dual
    orientation. These control measures are typically associated with the moving screen, as well as
    phase lines that run parallel to the main body’s movement. If the enemy attacks the protected
    flank, the guarding force uses these phase lines to control the delay or defense. The main body
    commander may also assign the flank guard an objective that secures the flank for the main body’s
    objective or otherwise serves to orient the security efforts.

    The flank guard regulates movement along the route of advance by the pace of the main body, the
    distance to the objective, and the enemy situation. The three techniques of movement are
    traveling, traveling overwatch, and bounding overwatch (see Chapter 15). If the main body stops,
    the flank guard occupies blocking positions. As the pace of the main body changes, the flank
    guard changes movement techniques. The guarding force must not allow the flank guard to fall
    behind the main body or present a lucrative target by remaining stationary along the route. If the
    flank guard becomes overextended, the guarding force commander recommends one of the
    following COAs to the main body commander:

       • Reinforce the flank guard.
       • Reduce the size of the flank guard’s AO.
       • Screen a portion of the area and guard the rest.

    Rear Guard
    The rear guard consists of the rearmost elements of an advancing or a withdrawing force. They
    have the following functions:

       • Protect the rear of a column from hostile forces.
       • Delay the enemy during the withdrawal.
       • Keep supply routes open during the advance.

                                                                       14-14


---

                                                                                  MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

The rear guard may consist of a security detachment to inform and cover the moving ground force.
This occurs during offensive operations when the main body breaks contact with friendly forces
defending the flanks or during a retrograde The rear guard for a moving force displaces to
successive battle positions along phase lines or delay lines in depth as the main body moves. The
nature of enemy contact determines the exact movement method or combination of methods used
in the displacement (successive bounds, alternate bounds, or continuous marching).

During a retrograde, the rear guard accomplishes their defensive mission in the same way as any
other guard operation after the main body clears the security area. As the main body moves, the
rear guard moves to subsequent phase lines in depth. Contact with the enemy force could
eventually be lost if the enemy does not pursue the retrograding friendly force. Conducting a
defense or a delay is necessary if the enemy detects the retrograde movement and attacks. See
Chapter 11 for retrograde operations.

COVER

A covering force operates independently from the main body to intercept, engage, delay,
disorganize, and deceive the enemy before the enemy can attack the main body. They prevent
surprise during the advance, protect the covered force, and develop the situation. They are usually
a task-organized, independent maneuver force that operates beyond the range of indirect fires
positioned with the main body. They have the necessary aviation, combat support, and logistic
resources to operate as a self-sufficient unit and decisively engage the enemy. A covering force
develops the situation earlier than a screening or guarding force, fights longer and more often, and
engages larger enemy forces.

The covering force’s distance from the main body depends on the main body commander’s
intentions and instructions, the terrain, the enemy location and strength, and the rates of march.
The covering force’s AO should be as wide or as long (depending on whether the force is covering
to the front, rear, or flank) as the main body’s AO. The covering force generally operates in the
area forward of the FEBA.

Although a covering force provides more security and more tactical options than a screening or
guarding force, they also require more resources. Before assigning a cover mission, the main body
commander must weigh and validate mission requirements by balancing the combat power
necessary to accomplish the decisive action against the combat power necessary for the covering
force to operate. When the commander lacks the resources to support both, the main body
commander must assign the security force a less resource intensive security operation (i.e., screen
or guard).

Critical Tasks for a Cover
A covering force performs all the tasks of screening and guarding forces. A covering force for a
stationary force performs a defensive mission, while a covering force for a moving force generally
conducts offensive actions. A covering force typically operates forward of the main body in the
offense or defense, or to the rear for a retrograde operation.

                                                                  14-15


---

MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

    Covering Force Organization
    The covering force typically executes its task by employing an area defense, a delay, a zone
    reconnaissance, or a movement to contact within the security area. The covering force commander
    employs and tasks subordinate forces and uses the control measures associated with the missions
    of area defense, a delay, a zone reconnaissance, or a movement to contact within the security area.
    In addition, the covering force prepares to conduct a passage of lines as part of the mission and
    maintains a sizable reserve to account for uncertain conditions. See Chapter 17 for more
    information on forward or rearward passage of lines.
    Although a commander can organize and resource any force to serve as a covering force, covering
    forces are typically established at the battalion-level and above who have the necessary
    capabilities and C2 structure to cover the area typically assigned a covering force. A covering
    force is usually allocated combat support (e.g., artillery, information capabilities and combat
    engineers) and CSS (e.g., a specifically task-organized logistic detachment) beyond that typically
    given to a force of its size because they are operating beyond the main body’s supporting range
    (MAGTFs are often ideal covering forces). The covering force also relies on the ACE to extend
    the force’s ability to observe, cover gaps, and react to events. The covering force’s mobility must
    equal, and preferably exceed, that of both the main body and the enemy. Depending on METT-T,
    using assault support assets can assist in achieving that mobility.
    Offensive Cover
    In the offense, the covering force (Figure 14-1) typically seeks to seize the initiative and shape the
    battlespace for the main body’s decisive actions. Offensive cover tasks include—

       • Performing zone reconnaissance along the main body’s axis of advance or within the AO.
       • Clearing or bypassing enemy forces within the AO.
       • Denying the enemy information about the main body’s strength, composition, and objective.
       • Conducting counterreconnaissance to destroy or defeat all enemy reconnaissance elements.
       • Preventing enemy ground observation of and direct fire against the main body.

                                                                  Covering Force

                                                                   Main Body

                                                      Figure 14-1. Cover Force.

                                                                       14-16


---

                                                                                  MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

Covering tasks against a defending enemy include—

  • Penetrating the enemy’s security area to locate enemy main defensive positions.
  • Determining enemy strengths and dispositions.
  • Locating gaps or weaknesses in the enemy’s defensive scheme.
  • Defeating or repelling enemy forces as directed by the higher commander.
  • Deceiving the enemy into thinking the main body has been committed and causing the enemy

     to launch counterattacks prematurely.
  • Fixing enemy forces to allow the main body to maneuver around enemy strengths or

     through weaknesses.

In a meeting engagement, covering tasks include—

  • Destroying enemy’s reconnaissance, advance guard, and lead elements of the main body.
  • Determining the location of enemy assailable flanks.
  • Fixing enemy forces to allow the main body to maneuver around enemy strongholds or

     through weakened defenses.

The covering force executing offensive operations typically employs either a zone reconnaissance
or a movement to contact. When developing the situation for the main body, the covering force
can plan on either the main body passing through or maneuvering around their position. Because
there is an inherent uncertainty involved in executing the cover task, the covering force maintains
a large reserve to either exploit or recover the situation.

The covering force advances on a broad front, typically alongside their subordinate ground
maneuver elements (except for the reserve). This force clears the enemy’s security area, penetrates
the enemy defenses, and fixes the enemy’s main force in place for defeat by the main body. Unlike
screening or guarding forces, the covering force does not bypass enemy forces unless ordered to
do so by the main body commander.

If the covering force discovers a gap in the enemy’s defenses, they prepare to exploit the weakness
and disrupt its integrity. The covering force commander immediately reports this to the main body
commander, so the main body commander can divert follow on forces to support the penetration.
The main body commander synchronizes the covering force’s penetration with the other arriving
maneuver units, combat support, and CSS to prevent counterattacking enemy forces from
isolating and destroying the penetrating elements of the covering force.

When the covering force cannot advance, they defend and prepare to assist the forward passage of
lines of main body units. They continue to perform reconnaissance of enemy positions to locate
gaps or assailable flanks. The covering force may guide main body units as they attack through or
around the covering force. If the covering force has accomplished its mission, the main body
attacks the enemy’s weak point with previously uncommitted main body forces.

                                                                  14-17


---

MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

    Flank Cover
    When the main body commander perceives a significant threat to a flank, the main body
    commander can establish a flank covering force. That force conducts their mission in much the
    same way as a flank guard. The primary differences between the two missions are the scope of
    operations and the expectation that the covering force will defeat an enemy assault, not just delay
    or disrupt them. The force covering the main body flank remains in contact with the main body;
    however, covering forces are still required to independently operate.

    Defensive Cover
    In the defense, the covering force seeks to prevent the enemy from exercising the initiative which
    enables friendly forces to attack at a time of their choosing. Defensive cover gains time for the
    main body, enabling them to deploy, move, or prepare defenses in the MBA. Defensive cover
    accomplishes this by disrupting the enemy’s attack, contesting the enemy’s ability to keep the
    initiative, and establishing the conditions for friendly decisive actions. The covering force makes
    the enemy repeatedly deploy to fight through the covering force’s position and commit their
    reserves and follow-on forces early to try to sustain momentum.

    Defensive cover tasks include—

       • Preventing the enemy from surprising and engaging main body.
       • Defeating enemy advance guard formations.
       • Maintaining continuous surveillance of high speed avenues of approach into the security area.
       • Conducting counterreconnaissance to destroy or defeat all enemy reconnaissance elements.
       • Preventing enemy ground observation of the main body.
       • Causing the enemy’s main body to deploy.
       • Determining the size, strength, composition, and direction of the enemy’s main effort.
       • Destroying, defeating, or attriting enemy forces.
       • Depriving the enemy of fire support and air defense umbrellas or requiring the enemy to

         displace these systems before attacking into the friendly MBA.
       • Deceiving the enemy regarding the location of main body and main defensive positions.
       • Avoiding being bypassed.

    The defensive covering force defends, delays, and counterattacks, as required. If the covering
    force’s AO has not previously been occupied, the force may have to reconnoiter and clear the area
    before establishing the cover. As in offensive operations, the support of the ACE is necessary to
    extend the covered area. Aviation units can screen less threatened areas, rapidly deliver fires to
    seize opportunities to engage the enemy or support of the covering force, provide mobility to
    elements of the covering force, and support logistics.

    There is an inherent expectation then that at some point, the covering force will hand the battle
    over to friendly units in the MBA by conducting a rearward passage of lines. The covering force
    can handover the battle in stages depending on the battle. As they complete the battle handover,
    the covering force will either assume positions in the MBA, assume security responsibilities for
    the main body’s flanks or rear, fall through the MBA to conduct reconstitution, or become part of
    the reserve. See Part III for more information on the defense.

                                                                       14-18


---

                                                                                  MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

REAR AREA SECURITY

Rear area security is conducted in all military operations, focusing on securing the installations and
functions necessary to continue operations; controlling and protecting the population (whether
friendly, neutral, or hostile); and protecting other agencies and forces conducting stabilization
tasks. Military forces assigned to support civil authority perform activities related to the concept of
rear area security. Protected forces range from higher headquarters through artillery and echelon
reserves to the logistic base. Protected installations can be part of the logistic base or part of the
area’s infrastructure. Areas to secure range from specific points (e.g., bridges and tunnels) and
terrain features (e.g., ridgelines, hills) to large civilian population centers and their adjacent areas.

Any MAGTF element, except the command element (which is still responsible for local security),
can conduct rear area security functions. Depending on METT-T, the LCE and ACE may require
augmentation from the GCE to undertake responsibility for rear area security. During traditional
warfare, rear area security is typically an economy of force measure to ensure the continued conduct
of logistics in support of military action. All rear area security operations incorporate and take
advantage of the basic local security activities of all units regardless of their location within the AO.

Since civilians are usually present within any given AO, units executing rear area security can use
different ROE than the rest of the force, requiring control measures that delineate between rear
and forward areas, superb discipline and leadership, and continual training. When addressing
these considerations, commanders must remember their primary responsibility remains the
protection of the force.

LOCAL SECURITY

Local security is continuous, an inherent responsibility of command, and applies to all operations.
It includes any local measure taken by units to prevent surprise, maintain the initiative, and
mitigate enemy actions. It involves avoiding enemy detection or deceiving the enemy about
friendly positions and intentions. It also includes finding any enemy forces in the vicinity and
collecting information about their positions and intentions.

Units use both active and passive measures to provide local security. Active measures include—

  • Using observation posts and patrols.
  • Establishing specific levels of alert within the unit. The commander adjusts those levels based

     on METT-T analysis.
  • Establishing stand to times.
  • Actively training to maintain proficiency, avoid complacency, and reinforce rules on the use

     of force if necessary.

                                                                  14-19


---

MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

    Passive local security measures include—
       • Using camouflage, movement control, noise and light discipline, and proper
         communications procedures.
       • Employing available ground sensors, night vision devices, and daylight sights to maintain
         surveillance over the area surrounding the unit.

   COMBAT OUTPOSTS

    A combat outpost is a reinforced observation post where Marines can conduct limited combat,
    stabilization, or other activities. During defensive or stationary operations, the commander at the
    regimental level can establish a combat post as an additional security measure. Using combat
    outposts is a technique for employing security forces in restrictive terrain that precludes mounted
    security forces from covering the area. They are also used when smaller observation posts are in
    danger of being overrun by enemy forces infiltrating the security area. Marines use combat
    outposts to extend the depth of the security area and to support and protect smaller observation
    posts. Both mounted and dismounted forces can employ combat outposts.
    Planners use METT-T analysis to determine the size, location, and number of combat outposts a
    unit establishes, although their size typically ranges from squad to platoon level. A combat
    outpost must have sufficient resources to accomplish the missions, but not so much as to deplete
    the strength of the main body or create a significant support burden. It is usually located far
    enough forward of the protected force to prevent enemy ground reconnaissance elements from
    observing the protected force’s actions.
    The commander organizes a combat outpost to provide an all around defense against a superior
    enemy force. When the enemy has significant armored capability, the commander may give a
    combat outpost more than the standard allocation of antitank weapons. Forces occupying combat
    outposts can conduct aggressive patrolling, engage and destroy enemy reconnaissance elements,
    and engage the enemy main body prior to their extraction. The staff plans to extract friendly forces
    from the outpost before they are overrun by the enemy.

                                                                       14-20


---

                        PART V.
               ENABLING ACTIVITIES

Enabling activities connect offensive and defensive operations with stabilization activities. On their
own, they are not decisive, but they help set conditions for the execution of all operations. They
require either a deliberate planning effort or a well-developed and understood SOP to execute.


---



---

                    CHAPTER 15.
                 TROOP MOVEMENT

Troop movement is shifting troops from one place to another by any available means. Successful
movement places troops and equipment at the proper place, at the proper time, ready for combat.
The commander’s ability to employ a force depends on its ability to move. The battlespace tempo
dictates a unit’s ability to conduct rapid and orderly movement to concentrate combat power at
decisive points and times.

METHODS OF TROOP MOVEMENT

Troop movements are made by dismounted and mounted marches using—

  • Organic combat and tactical vehicles.
  • Motor transport.
  • Air.
  • Rail.
  • Water.

The method employed depends on the situation, the size and composition of the moving unit, the
distance the unit must cover, the urgency of execution, and the condition of the troops. It also
depends on the availability and capacity of the different modes of transportation. When necessary,
dismounted, and mounted marches can be hurried by conducting a forced march.

Dismounted March
Dismounted marches are typically by foot, with limited vehicle support. Dismounted marches
increase the unit’s maneuver options. Advantages include combat readiness (all personnel can
immediately respond to enemy attack without the need to dismount), ease of control, adaptability
to terrain, and independence from the existing road network. Their limitations include a slow
movement rate and increased personnel fatigue—personnel become tired carrying heavy loads
over long distances or large changes in elevation. A unit conducts a dismounted march when the
situation requires stealth, the distance of travel is short, transport or fuel is limited, or the situation
or terrain precludes using many vehicles.

Mounted March
A mounted march is conducted by combat and tactical vehicles. Mechanized and motorized units
routinely conduct mounted marches. The speed of the march and the increased amounts of
supplies that can accompany the unit characterize this march method. Heavy and motorized
maneuver units are typically self sufficient to conduct mounted marches over short distances.


---

MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

    Light maneuver units and most combat support and CSS units require assistance from
    transportation elements to conduct mounted marches. Considerations for mounted marches over
    extended distances include—

       • The ability of the route network to support the number, size, and weight of the tactical and
         combat vehicles assigned to or supporting the unit making the move.

       • Available refueling and maintenance sites and crew rest areas.
       • The need for recovery and evacuation assets.

    Air Movement
    Air movement is a continual, progressive operation that transports successive elements of the
    deploying force to the objective area. Units conduct air movements to move troops and
    equipment; emplace systems; and transport ammunition, fuel, and other high value supplies. Units
    can employ air movements as a substitute for ground tactical movements. Air movements are
    generally faster than ground tactical moves. The same general considerations that apply to air
    assault operations also apply to air movements. See Chapter 18 and MCTP 3-01B for more
    information on air assaults.

    Rail Movement
    Operating forces can use available railways to conduct troop movement. Railways can provide
    flexibility by freeing other modes of transport for other missions. Their use usually involves
    military and commercial assets, such as defense freight railway interchange railcars pulled by
    privately owned diesel-electric engines to transport heavy equipment and supplies along railroad
    right of ways from one rail terminus to another. Responsibility for coordinating the use of
    railroads lies within the theater logistics command.

    Using rail transportation is contingent upon commanders and staff understanding rail’s potential
    capabilities. Rail operations are limited to fixed routes that traverse areas outside the non-contiguous
    operational environment protected by combat forces. Establishing rail in a theater is based on initial
    planning that includes assessing the host nation’s rail capabilities and infrastructure. The Marine
    Corps relies on the US Army’s expeditionary railway center to provide this assessment as well as a
    feasibility study on the host nation rail capability. The expeditionary railway center can also advise
    on how to employ those rail capabilities. For additional information on rail operations and the
    expeditionary railway center, refer to ATP 4-14, Expeditionary Railway Center Operations.

    Water Movement
    Operating forces can also use available inland waterways to free other modes of transport for
    concurrent missions. As with rail movement, responsibility for coordinating the use of waterways
    and commercial assistance lies within the theater logistics command.

    The waterway or sea mode of transport consists of assets such as ships, boats, and barges that
    transport commodities and personnel over a body of water like a lake, canal, or river. Army and
    Navy watercraft platforms primarily conduct water transport operational maneuvers and the
    intra-theater sealift of units, equipment, and supplies. They support marine-terminal and sea-based
    operations to conduct force closure and execute distributed support and sustainment of employed

                                                                        15-2


---

                                                                                  MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

forces. Operating as part of the joint force, these watercrafts and their organizations provide
critical capability in mitigating an adversary’s anti-access strategy and in overcoming area denial
challenges present in the theater of operations.

To meet land maneuver requirements, watercraft have the following core competencies—

  • Intra-Theater Lift. Watercraft are designed to perform missions related to intra-theater
     movement of combat power and sustainment. Although capable of deploying over strategic
     distances, watercraft are not strategic-lift platforms; rather, they are a critical link between
     strategic lift and land oriented tactical maneuver operations. This capability provides
     flexibility so units can tactically position and support the scheme of maneuver, with speed
     and magnitude.

  • Logistics over the Shore. Lighters transport cargo from ship to shore or seabase to shore,
     reducing operational footprint ashore and provide an alternative to using piers and austere ports.

  • Anti-Access/Port Denial. Circumvent enemy anti-access strategies by providing alternative
     water transport means for achieving combat power throughput when strategic and tactical
     ports are unavailable.

  • Surface Infiltration. Watercraft are distinctly suitable as secure staging bases for various types
     of special operations, infiltration, and exfiltration operations.

Watercraft flexibility complements land maneuver forces’ inherent speed and agility by
allowing forces to be positioned close to the objective, but out of direct contact with enemy
resistance. Further, the vessel’s command, control, communications, computers, intelligence,
surveillance, and reconnaissance enhance maneuver units’ situational awareness while on the
move and provides the capability to conduct mission planning and rehearsal while enroute to
the objective. For additional information on watercraft and watercraft operations see, Army
Doctrine Publication 4-0, Sustainment, and ATP 4-15, Army Watercraft Operations.

Forced March
Mounted or dismounted units can accelerate their rate of movement by conducting a forced
march. Forced marches require speed, exertion, and an increase in the number of hours marched
or traveled by vehicles each day beyond typical standards. Personnel and vehicles cannot sustain
forced marches for more than a short period. In a forced march, a unit might not halt as often or
for as long as recommended for maintenance, rest, feeding, and fuel. The commander must
understand that immediately following a forced march, personnel and vehicles experience a
temporary deterioration in their physical condition. The combat effectiveness and cohesion of the
unit also temporarily decreases. The movement plan must accommodate the presence of stragglers
and address increased maintenance failures.

Administrative Movement
Administrative movement is movement when there is little or no likelihood of enemy contact. It
may use both military and civilian vehicles and places the priority on maximizing use of available
vehicles and their cargo capacities. Units only conduct administrative movements in secure areas.
Examples of administrative movements overseas include movements in secure rear areas and
aboard secured forward operating bases. Although Marine Corps units do not conduct offensive
and defensive operations inside the continental United States, rail and highway movement as well

                                                                   15-3


---

MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

    as convoy operations within the continental United States are other examples of administrative
    movements. Since these types of moves are not tactical, the echelon logistic officer (G-4/S-4)
    usually supervises them. Once units deploy into a theater of war, commanders do not usually
    employ administrative movements.

   TACTICAL ROAD MARCH

    A tactical road march is used to relocate units within the combat zone to prepare for combat
    operations. The primary consideration is the relative speed of movement. Although units
    executing tactical road marches do not expect to encounter significant enemy ground forces, they
    conduct local security measures, maintain security against enemy air attack, and prepare to take
    immediate action against an enemy ambush (see Figure 15-1). Units expecting contact with
    significant enemy forces use other techniques, such as approach marches (see Chapter 4), combat
    formations, and movement techniques.

                                Reconnaissance Element
                                                     Advance Party

                                                                              Main Body

                                                                                                   Rear Body

                                                 Figure 15-1. Tactical Road March.
    Organization for a Tactical Road March
    The organization for a tactical road march is the march column. A march column is a group of
    two-to-five units using the same route for a single movement, organized under a single
    commander for planning, regulating, and controlling. A march column has four elements:
    reconnaissance, advance party, main body, and rear body. An RLT conducting a tactical road
    march is an example of a march column. A march column’s subordinate elements are a march
    serial and a march unit.

                                                                        15-4


---

                                                                                  MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

A march serial is a subdivision of a march column organized under a single commander. An
example is a battalion serial formed from an RLT size march column. A march unit is the smallest
subdivision of a march column; typically, a group of no more than 25 vehicles using the same
route for a single movement organized under a single commander. An example of a march unit is
a company from a battalion size march serial.

A march column provides excellent speed, control, and flexibility but limited flank security. It
provides the ability to deploy forces to the front of the column. Units use a march column when
speed is essential and enemy contact is unlikely. However, they space combat support resources,
such as air defense and engineers, throughout the column to protect and support the movement.
Reconnaissance elements augmented by engineer, CBRN, and other resources, conduct a route
reconnaissance of the march routes. This reconnaissance confirms and supplements the IPB
conducted by the commander’s staff.

The MAGTF commander establishes a task-organized advance party that consists of personnel
designated to form the nucleus of the arrival and assembly organizations. The primary tasks of
the advance party are to arrange for the reception of the main body and provide force protection.
They also coordinate the convoy’s arrival at the destination. They might initially move with the
main body but must arrive at the destination ahead of the main body. A unit’s advance party
usually accompanies the route reconnaissance effort to the designated assembly area. Unit
SOPs establish the exact composition of the advance party and the transportation, security,
communications equipment needs, and specific duties—an advance party is not the same as a
forward command post. The advance party secures, reconnoiters, and organizes an area for the
main body’s arrival and occupation. They typically reconnoiter and confirm the tentative locations
selected by the commander of the parent element, based on a map reconnaissance. When
necessary, the advance party changes previously assigned unit locations within the assembly area.
The advance party guides the main body into position from the release point to precise locations
within the assembly area.

The main body of the march column consists of the remainder of the unit, including attachments
other than the rear body. The rear body is the last march unit in a march column and typically
consists of maintenance elements. They maintain communications with the main body. The
function of the rear body is to recover disabled vehicles or control stragglers in a foot march. If the
rear body cannot immediately repair a disabled vehicle, they tow the disabled vehicle and move
the crew and passengers to a unit maintenance collection point located at a secure area near the
movement route.

During extended road marches, halts are necessary to rest personnel, service vehicles, and adjust
movement schedules. The march order or unit SOP regulates when to take halts. In motor
movements, the leaders schedule short halts for every 2–3 hours of movement and halts may last
up to an hour. Long halts occur on marches that exceed 24 hours and last no more than 2 hours.
Long halts are not scheduled at night, which allows maximum time for night movement. During
halts, each unit typically clears the march route and moves to a previously selected assembly area
to prevent route congestion and avoid being a target. Units establish security and take other
measures to protect the force. Unit leaders promptly notify commanders of the time and
approximate length of unscheduled halts.

                                                                   15-5


---

MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

    The commander must emphasize security during halts. Once a unit stops moving, there is a natural
    inclination for personnel to relax their vigilance. The commander addresses this by defining in the
    SOP unit actions for various types of halts, such as maintenance halts, security halts, and
    unexpected halts.

    Graphic Control Measures
    The commander directing a tactical road march often uses a strip map or overlay to graphically
    depict critical information about the route to subordinates. The overlay or strip map should show
    the route of march, start points, release points, checkpoints, critical points (e.g., bridges), light
    line, and traffic control posts (TCPs). Other graphic control measures for a tactical road march
    include assembly areas and phase lines.

    The start point is a location on a route where the marching elements fall under the control of a
    designated march commander. All routes have a designated start point that is easily recognizable
    on the map and on the ground, such as a road junction. The start point is far enough from the
    assembly area to allow units to organize and be moving at the prescribed speed and interval as
    they cross it.

    A release point is a well-defined point on a route at which the elements composing a column
    return under the authority of their respective commanders, each one of these elements continuing
    their movement toward their respective destination. Each start point must have a corresponding
    release point, which must also be easily recognizable on the ground. As marching units move
    through the release point, unit guides meet each march unit and lead them to assembly areas.

    The commander designates checkpoints along the route to assist marching units in complying
    with the timetable. The movement overlay identifies critical points along the route where
    interference with movement might occur. The commander positions TCPs along the route to
    prevent congestion and confusion. The TCPs can be staffed by military police or unit personnel.
    These personnel report to the appropriate area movement control organization when each convoy,
    march column, and march serial arrives at and completes passage of their location.

    A light line is a designated phase line beyond which vehicles must use blackout lights during
    periods of reduced visibility. Commanders at MEF and division levels establish light lines based
    on the risk that the enemy might detect moving vehicles using white light. A light line is a
    designated line forward of which vehicles are required to use blackout lights during periods of
    limited visibility.

    A movement corridor is a designated area established to protect and enable ground movement
    along a route. Units establish a movement corridor to set the conditions to protect and enable
    movement of traffic along a designated surface route. Units conduct synchronized operations
    within the movement corridor such as reconnaissance, security, mobility, information activities
    (for forces that require additional command and control), force protection, and support to enable
    their movement. A commander might establish a movement corridor to facilitate the movement of
    a single element or the movement of several elements along a route. The AO commander might
    establish a movement corridor within an AO along an established MSR or a route designated for a
    unit’s movement. The movement corridor typically includes the airspace above it to allow the
    establishing unit to conduct aerial reconnaissance and fires.

                                                                        15-6


---

                                                                                  MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

Forms of Tactical Marches
Units conducting tactical road marches employ three different forms: open column, close column,
and infiltration. Each of these forms uses scheduled halts to control and sustain the road march.
The METT-T analysis requires adjustments in the standard distances between individual Marines
or vehicles. During movement, elements within a column might encounter many different types of
routes and obstacles simultaneously. Consequently, parts of the column may be moving at
different speeds that can produce an undesirable accordion like effect. The movement order
establishes the order of march, rate of march, interval or time gaps between units, column gap, and
maximum catch up speed for vehicles. March units report when they have crossed each control
point. Throughout the movement, the units have air and ground security.

Open Column. Open column is typically used during daylight marches. It can be used at night
with infrared lights and night vision equipment. Using an open column roughly doubles the
column’s length and thereby doubles the time it takes to clear a point when compared to a close
column moving at the same speed. The open column is the most common form of movement
because it offers the most security while still providing the commander with a reasonable degree
of control.

Vehicle Distance. The distance between vehicles varies, depending on road conditions and weather,
but is typically 50–100 meters with a vehicle density of 15–20 vehicles per kilometer. See
MCTP 3-40F, Distribution and Transportation Operations, for more detail on vehicle distances.

Dismounted Distance. The distance between dismounted personnel varies from 2–5 meters to
allow for dispersion and space for marching comfort. Any distance that exceeds 5 meters between
dismounted Marines increases the length of the column and hinders control. A single infantry
company, with intervals between the platoons, occupies roughly one kilometer of road or trail.

Close Column. The commander typically employs a close column for marches during darkness
under blackout driving conditions or for marches in restricted terrain. This form of marching takes
maximum advantage of the traffic capacity of a route but provides little dispersion. Marches under
limited-visibility conditions are characterized by close formations, difficult command and control
and reconnaissance, a slow rate of march, and good concealment from enemy observation and
air attack.

Vehicle Distance. In a close column, the unit spaces vehicles about 20–25 meters apart with a
vehicle density of 40–50 vehicles per kilometer. At night, vehicles are spaced so each driver can
see the two lights in the blackout marker of the vehicle ahead.

Dismounted Distance. The dismounted equivalent to the close column is a limited-visibility
march. The distance between individuals is reduced to 1–3 meters to help maintain contact and
facilitate control.

Infiltration. The infiltration form of a tactical road march should not be confused with infiltration
as a form of maneuver as discussed in Chapter 3. Infiltration provides passive defense against
enemy observation and attack. It is suited for tactical road marches when there is enough time and
road space and when the commander desires the maximum security, deception, and dispersion.
The commander dispatches vehicles and personnel in small groups, or at irregular intervals, at a
rate that keeps the traffic density down and prevents undue massing of vehicles or personnel. The

                                                                   15-7


---

MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

    disadvantages of an infiltration are that more time is required to complete the move, column
    control is nearly impossible, and recovery of vehicles or stragglers by the rear body is more
    protracted. Additionally, unit integrity is not restored until the last vehicle or individual arrives
    at the destination, complicating the unit’s onward deployment.

MOVEMENT TECHNIQUES

A tactical road march is used to position units in the battlespace and focuses on rapid movement.
When the emphasis of movement is on security and readiness for contact, units use the combat
formations described in Chapter 3 in conjunction with three movement techniques: traveling,
traveling overwatch, and bounding overwatch. Table 15-1 describes when a unit is most likely to
use each technique.

                     Table 15-1. Movement Techniques.

                      Likelihood of        Movement
                     Enemy Contact         Technique

                     Not likely      Traveling
                     Possible        Traveling Overwatch
                     Expected        Bounding Overwatch

Movement techniques limit the unit’s exposure to enemy fire and position them to react to enemy
contact. The commander and staff select the movement technique based on the chance of enemy
contact. While moving, individuals and vehicles use the terrain to protect themselves when enemy
contact is possible or expected. They use natural cover and concealment to avoid enemy fires. The
following rules apply—

• Do not present a silhouette against the skyline.

• Cross open areas quickly.

• Do not move directly forward from a concealed firing position.

• Avoid possible kill zones because it is easier to cross difficult terrain than fight the enemy on
  unfavorable terms.

• Avoid large, open areas, particularly when they are dominated by high ground or by terrain
  that can cover and conceal the enemy.

• Take active countermeasures, such as using smoke and direct and indirect fire, to suppress or
  obscure suspected enemy positions.

Traveling
Units use the traveling movement technique when speed is necessary and contact with enemy
forces is not likely. All elements of the unit move simultaneously. Trailing elements may move in
parallel columns to shorten the column and reaction time. For example, a company traveling in a
wedge formation could have its platoons use the traveling technique.

                                     15-8


---

                                                                                  MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

Traveling Overwatch
Units use the traveling overwatch movement technique when contact with enemy forces is
possible, but speed is important. The lead element and trailing element are separated by a short
distance which varies with the terrain. The trailing element moves at variable speeds and may
pause for short periods to overwatch the lead element. The trailing element keys their movement
to terrain and the lead element. The trailing element overwatches at such a distance that, should
the enemy engage the lead element, it will not prevent the trailing element from firing or moving
to support the lead element (see Figure 15-2).

                                            Figure 15-2. Traveling Overwatch.
Bounding Overwatch
Bounding overwatch is a movement technique used when contact with enemy forces is expected.
The unit moves by bounds with one element always halted in position to overwatch another
element while they move. The overwatching element is positioned to support the moving unit by
fire or fire and movement. Units use the bounding overwatch movement technique when
expecting to make contact with enemy forces. There are two types of this technique: alternate
bounds and successive bounds. The successive bound form is more deliberate and offers more
security. In both cases, the overwatching elements cover the bounding elements from covered and
concealed positions with good observation and fields of fire against possible enemy positions. The
length of any given bound is based on the terrain and the range of overwatching weapons.
When using alternate bounds, the lead element moves forward, halts, and then occupies a
support-by-fire position that is always covered by the rear overwatching element (see Figure 15-3).
The former rear overwatching element advances past the former lead element and takes an
overwatch position. The initial lead element then advances past the initial trail element and occupies
a new support-by-fire position. One element moves at a time. This method is usually more rapid
than successive bounds.
