---

                                                                                  MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

DEFENDING ENCIRCLED FORCES

Encirclement of a friendly force is likely to occur during highly mobile and fluid operations, when
operating in restrictive terrain, or because of a deliberate tactical decision to mislead the enemy.
Examples include encirclement because of offensive action or as a DLIC ordered to defend a
strong point or tasked as a stay-behind force. Once encircled, the force has four choices: defend,
breakout, exfiltrate, or attack deeper into enemy controlled territory. The commander’s decision
depends on the mission of the higher headquarters, METT-T, whether preparations for
encirclement were completed (e.g., a strong point defense), whether resupply and casualty
evacuation can be accomplished, and on the levels of the force’s morale and fighting capacity.

As it becomes obvious that the unit is about to be encircled, the commander must quickly decide
what assets stay and what assets to leave. In the confusion, it may be difficult to determine what
units are being encircled or to identify the senior commander. However, the senior commander
within an encirclement is quickly identified and assumes command over all encircled forces,
taking immediate action to protect them. The commander immediately informs higher
headquarters of the situation while the encircled units—

  • Establish security.
  • Reestablish a chain of command.
  • Establish a viable defense.
  • Maintain morale.

If the force is encircled, but not within contact of the enemy, the commander positions security
elements as far forward as possible to reestablish contact with the enemy, create maneuver room,
and provide early warning. Each unit clears their position to ensure no enemy forces remain
within the perimeter and begin immediate, vigorous patrolling. The commander reorganizes
fragmented units and stragglers under the control of other units, changes task organization across
the force if necessary, and reestablishes communication with units outside the encirclement. In
situations where encirclement was not prepared for or was unexpected, the survival of the force is
dependent on rapidly organizing and hardening itself prior to undertaking any other actions.

Organization of Forces for an Encircled Defender
The encircled force establishes a perimeter defense maximizing the capabilities of the available
forces. Forward units establish mutually supporting positions around the perimeter and in depth
along principal avenues of approach. Units occupy the best available defensible terrain. It might
be necessary to attack to seize key terrain, so that it is incorporated within the perimeter defense.
Commanders establish a reserve force that is centrally located, uses interior lines, and mobile
enough to react rapidly to anywhere on the perimeter. Once the commander assigns defensive
AOs and battle positions, preparations are the same as in the defense. Encircled units make their
defensive positions as strong as possible given time and resource constraints. The commander
anticipates that the enemy will attempt to split the defenses of the encircled force and defeat them
in detail. See Chapter 8 for information on the conduct of perimeter defenses.

                                                                   19-7


---

MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

    Considerations for an Encircled Defender
    Establishing command and control in unplanned or unexpected encirclements is a critical factor to
    the survivability of the force. In the case of strong points, combat outposts, and stay-behind
    forces, maintaining command and control while encircled has already been planned and prepared
    for. Beyond the basic functions of command and control however, coherent and reliable command
    is instrumental to the morale and well-being of the force.

    As the situation stabilizes, the encircled unit must anticipate enemy attempts to reduce the pocket
    while locating enemy weaknesses that can be exploited either in a breakout or a linkup with
    friendly relief forces. This requires employing the encircled force’s ISR assets. Reconnaissance
    assets are organic to every unit, and the commander employs these Marines to aggressively
    maintain contact with the enemy and seek to discover their intentions. Encircled units must
    reestablish communications with units outside the encirclement to gain access to other ISR assets
    and awareness of enemy actions.

    The commander centralizes control of fire support systems, such as artillery, to rapidly shift and
    mass fires along threatened portions of the perimeter and conduct counterbattery fires. Friendly
    and enemy forces typically use massed and synchronized fires to reduce a trapped force.
    Commanders might choose to control the mortars of various units in the same manner, particularly
    if the encircled force lacks artillery and is beyond the support of other friendly units. Similarly, the
    ACE is a central component of the MAGTF’s defense, and it is retained within the perimeter until
    either enemy artillery can range the airfields or enemy air and air defense action makes support
    and survivability from within the perimeter untenable.

    The encircled force prioritizes countermobility, survivability, and mobility. Countermobility is
    essential to supporting the encircled force’s perimeter defense and the force’s survival.
    Survivability is a close second in prioritization because the enemy is likely to try and use massed
    and synchronized fires to reduce the friendly pocket, and it is difficult to disperse within a perimeter
    type defense. Attaining mobility is the logical result of succeeding in the first two priorities.

    Because encircled units must monitor their logistic resources commanders conserve and centrally
    control available resources. This control applies to casualty and mortuary affairs as well.
    Commanders evacuate casualties whenever possible for humanitarian reasons and to reduce the
    logistical burden on the force. The commander might direct units on the perimeter to cease all
    vehicle movement to allocate remaining fuel assets to the reserve force. When possible, the
    commander positions CSS units and resources in protected and concealed locations. When CSS
    elements can no longer perform their functions—such as maintenance personnel with no parts or
    tools—the commander might choose to employ them as maneuver units.

   BREAKOUT FROM AN ENCIRCLEMENT

    An encircled force conducts a breakout to regain freedom of movement or contact with friendly
    units. It differs from other attacks because other areas of the perimeter must be maintained. A
    breakout contains elements of the offense and the defense.

                                                                        19-8


---

                                                                                  MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

An encircled force typically attempts to conduct breakout operations when one of the following
four conditions exist:

  • The breakout falls within the intent of a higher commander.
  • The encircled force does not have sufficient combat power to defend itself.
  • The encircled force does not have adequate terrain available to conduct their defense.
  • The encircled force cannot sustain itself long enough to be relieved.

Organization of Forces for a Breakout
The commander organizes the force to conduct rupture, follow and assume, main body, and
rear-guard tasks. The focus is on tasks because the encircled force may lack the strength to resource
separate forces and, therefore, subordinate units are likely to receive multiple missions—such as
the main body being prepared to conduct tasks associated with both follow-and-assume and the rear
guard. If sufficient forces exist within the encirclement, the commander organizes a reserve and a
diversionary force. Regardless, the priority of combat power is to the force with the rupture
mission. The encircled force maintains the momentum of the breakout attack; otherwise, they are
more vulnerable to destruction than before. Forces located outside the encirclement assist the
breakout by conducting shaping actions.

The encircled force attacks using the rupture forces, which varies in size from one-third to two-thirds
of the total force, to penetrate the enemy defensive positions in at least one location. The rupture
force is the decisive action. The rupture force penetrates the enemy’s encirclement, widens the gap,
and holds the shoulders of the gap open until all other encircled forces can move through. The
rupture force must have sufficient strength to accomplish these tasks; therefore, it receives most of
the combat power. See Chapter 3 for discussion of the penetration form of maneuver.

The follow and assume forces follow the rupture force, seize objectives beyond the rupture, and
maintain the momentum of the attack. They do so by opening and improving the passage from the
rupture toward friendly forces. It is often the force that conducts the linkup with relief forces.
In tasking and resourcing the follow-and-assume force, the commander must weigh the need to
open up the passage to friendly forces over other tasks such as clearing and improving routes or
fixing bypassed enemy forces. If these types of tasks are essential to the success of the breakout,
the staff must resource the follow-and-assume force appropriately or create another task force for
this purpose.

The main body consists of the main command post, most of the encircled logistic assets, the unit’s
casualties, and combat support assets. The main body contains only the combat forces necessary
for immediate security—typically, a flank security force that deploys once the main body passes
through the rupture. The rear guard consists of units, such as diversionary forces, and equipment
on the perimeter, which provide protection for the rupture and any shaping actions. Forces left in
contact must conduct a vigorous delay operation on the perimeter, so that no portion of the rear
guard gets cut off. Under a single commander, the rear guard, which remains on the perimeter of
the rupture, protects the main body from attack. In addition to providing security, the rear guard
deceives the enemy about the intentions of the encircled force, simulating its activities until the
main body clears the gap.

                                                                   19-9


---

MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

    The reserve force’s primary purpose is to retain flexibility through offensive action. The
    commander attempts to keep a small portion of the encircled force uncommitted, employing them
    at the decisive moment to ensure the breakout’s success. The commander may be unable to
    establish a reserve force because of the need to resource either the rupture force, the follow and
    assume force, or the rear guard. In this event, the commander assigns and prioritizes various
    contingency missions to the follow and assume force.

    Control Measures for a Breakout
    A commander controls and synchronizes a breakout using, at a minimum, a line of departure or
    line of contact, time of the attack, phase lines, axis of advance or direction of attack, objectives,
    and a LOA assist in the linkup with friendly forces (see Chapters 2 and 3).

    Planning a Breakout
    Commanders conduct hasty planning to execute a breakout as quickly as possible after the
    encirclement while the enemy is still disorganized and friendly forces can exploit. It is unlikely
    that an encircled force has accurate information on enemy dispositions and capabilities, but it
    still seeks to capitalize on the fluid nature of the moment and the difficulty the enemy will have in
    executing a coordinated response to the breakout. Units patrol and employ ISR assets to discover
    exploitable gaps in the enemy force, using the reconnaissance pull method to guide planning
    and execution.

    Conversely, commanders conduct deliberate planning to execute a breakout in conjunction with
    the actions of a strong relief force. In this case, both the encircled force and relief force combine
    ISR assets to provide the commander greater situational awareness of the enemy’s tactical
    disposition, intentions, and capabilities.

    Commanders seek to capitalize on routes and terrain the enemy is unlikely to defend or expect
    friendly forces to use. The commander must weigh the risks in choosing a slower but stealthier
    movement over a faster but more obvious movement, directing limited information collection
    capabilities to provide the information necessary to make a decision. The commander applies
    similar consideration in choosing whether to move during limited-visibility conditions.

    Employing information assets in the breakout is as important, if not more important, then the
    employment of other fires. Military and tactical deception are instrumental in misleading the
    enemy about the intentions of the encircled force, the location of the breakout attempt, and in
    the actual conduct of the breakout attempt itself—such as assisting the rear guard in maintaining
    the appearance of normal operations along the perimeter. Other information capabilities can assist
    in introducing hesitation or delay into the enemy’s decision-making cycle as they try to react to
    the breakout.

    Information activities are coordinated and synchronized with maneuver and other fires. Shaping
    actions, such as diversionary attacks from either the encircled or relief forces, divert enemy
    attention and resources away from the rupture effort. Such diversions must be credible and present
    a threat to the enemy—such as directing them at places where the enemy might expect a breakout
    attempt to occur. Diversionary forces from the encircled force are as mobile as available vehicles,
    fuel stocks, and trafficability allow, repositioning to support the breakout or maneuver.

                                                                       19-10


---

                                                                                  MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

The success of a breakout attempt increases when synchronized with the actions of a relief force.
If the situation or METT-T factors preclude an immediate breakout attempt, then the success of
the breakout primarily relies on actions external to the encircled force. In this case, primary
planning is done by the higher headquarters conducting command and control for both the
encircled and relief forces. The relief force’s actions support the larger plan.

The force organizes the breakout attempt around the available combat support and CSS assets.
For example, fuel and parts scarcity might mean the force can only move a limited number of
vehicles. Priority of vehicles in this case may be limited to the rupture force and the rear guard,
with the remaining force keeping only sufficient transportation assets to move the wounded and
critical assets and supplies. The breakout plan outlines the commander’s destruction criteria for
equipment or supplies left behind. All vehicles, critical munitions, supplies, and equipment
(except medical supplies) that cannot be moved should be destroyed as soon as possible.

Executing a Breakout
The unit should deceive the enemy about the location of the decisive action. Destruction of
equipment comes at the last possible moment or is done mechanically to avoid alerting the enemy.
Preparing to evacuate casualties, critical assets, and similar items blends with the daily movement
of the force to mask the preparations from the enemy. As much as possible, units remain on their
portion of the perimeter, limiting the RIPs that will take place as the encircled force reorganizes
for the breakout. The rear-guard conducts preparations. If the perimeter must be held or shortened
to generate combat power for the rupture force, the rear guard uses DLICs to deceive the enemy
(see Chapter 11). Simultaneously, the rupture force assembles and occupies their attack positions,
minimizing movement and visibility.

The encircled force and any other friendly forces, such as a relief force, begin conducting shaping
actions such as feints and demonstrations, mobility and countermobility operations, suppressing
enemy positions, and isolating the battlespace. When the conditions are set, the encircled force
generates overwhelming combat power at the point(s) of penetration in support of the rupture force.
The rupture force attacks and conducts a penetration, rapidly overwhelming enemy positions and
expanding the penetration (see Chapters 3 and 5). If not already in position, the follow-and-assume
force moves from the perimeter, advancing through the point(s) of penetration. The commander
may accept risk in preparedness in favor of deception by having elements of the encircled force
remain on the perimeter until the last moment before leaving and committing directly to their
assigned tasks. Elements of the main body destroy equipment as necessary, assemble in their order
of march, and establish flank security. The rear guard continues to deceive the enemy as long as
possible, and then begins conducting security operations in support of the breakout.

The rupture force holds the shoulders of the penetration open and the follow-and-assume
force moves through the penetration to exploit the success. In cases when the rupture force
encounters weak or little enemy resistance, the commander may order the rupture force to
transition to a movement to contact and the follow-and-assume force remains in trace.
Otherwise the follow-and-assume force rapidly moves to secure objectives beyond the
penetration, using available engineer assets to conduct route improvement and establish
countermobility obstacles to the flanks. In addition to providing CAS, the ACE screens the
flanks of the follow-and-assume force.

                                                                  19-11


---

MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

    As the rupture force completes their mission and the follow-and-assume force advances, the main
    body moves in trace. The rear guard and any diversionary forces disengage from the enemy and
    conduct security operations to the rear of the encircled force. If engineering assets are available,
    they assist the rear guard in establishing countermobility obstacles to delay and disrupt enemy
    pursuit. If the rear guard is destroyed, it is immediately reconstituted out of other forces. Artillery
    and mortars begin echeloning forward, providing continuous fire support to various elements. As
    the breakout progresses, the commander retains centralized control of fires, shifting priorities to
    various elements as needed. The ACE is employed in the same manner, aggressively attacking
    enemy threats.

    The main body rapidly moves on multiple routes in an approach or road march formation
    immediately behind the follow and assume force, using available combat power to provide flank
    security. The follow-and-assume force advances until it either conducts a linkup with friendly
    forces or is in a position to pass the main body. As the linkup occurs, the breakout force begins
    withdrawing its defenses and security.

    The main body passes through and into friendly forces, moving directly to assembly areas in the
    rear. The breakout force then conducts a series of battle handovers to allow friendly forces to follow
    in trace and reach friendly lines. The commander maintains centralized control of combat support
    assets (e.g., artillery, engineers) throughout the process—moving their priorities as needed. The
    rear guard evacuates the perimeter, handing off both the duties and additional combat power to the
    rupture force, still holding open the shoulders of the penetration. The original rear guard moves
    directly through the follow-and-assume force, reenters friendly lines, and moves in trace of the
    main body to designated assembly areas. The former rupture force now assumes the duties of rear
    guard, delaying the enemy as they retrograde while receiving priority of available support.

    As they reach the follow-and-assume force, another battle handover occurs. The follow-and-assume
    force becomes the last elements of the breakout force, allowing the rupture force to pass through,
    reenter friendly lines, and then move to designated assembly areas. The follow-and-assume force
    assumes rear guard responsibilities, and conducts delaying and security operations until it hands
    the battle over to relief forces before rejoining the rest of the breakout force in designated
    assembly areas.

    Usually, the rear guard initially conducts a withdrawal to break contact with the enemy forces
    around the perimeter. It contracts the perimeter as it delays behind the main body. If the enemy
    closely pursues the breakout force, the efforts of the rear guard may become the decisive action
    for the encircled force. The commander should position the reserve where they can also support
    the rear guard.

   EXFILTRATION

    If the success of a breakout attack appears questionable or if it fails, and a relief operation is not
    planned, one way to preserve a portion of the force is through organized exfiltration (see
    Appendix C).

                                                                       19-12


---

                                                                                  MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

ATTACKING DEEPER INTO ENEMY TERRITORY

Attacking deeper into enemy territory is a COA that the enemy is unlikely to expect, although
friendly forces prepare for such an action when they encircle an enemy force. The encircled force
may execute such a COA for several reasons:

  • The encircled force occupies a strong point or combat outpost, or they are a stay-behind force
     executing an assigned mission.

  • The encircled force can move to a more defensible location or to a place where they can be
     extracted by ground, naval, or air forces.

  • The encircled force is executing an offensive action and deliberately continues forward to the
     objectives, or attacks in a new direction. Similarly, by attacking deeper into enemy territory
     the encircled force can create conditions favorable for a linkup with friendly forces by
     disrupting enemy plans through attacks against their rear areas and LOCs, or by attacking to
     support the offensive action of other friendly forces.

Attacking deeper into enemy territory is an offensive action (see Chapter 3). It is only feasible if a
unit can sustain itself while isolated, although those logistics can come from aerial resupply and
enemy supply stocks.

CORDON

A cordon is a tactical operation in which a unit prevents withdrawal from or reinforcement to a
position (see Appendix C). Commanders employ cordons as shaping actions to enable other actions
to occur, such as a search, meeting, detainee release, etc. Commanders also provide additional
guidance on what should occur within the cordon or what effect they would like generated. A
company might be tasked with conducting a cordon around a city block to isolate the area,
receiving appropriate support to execute that isolation. Similarly, the same company might
establish the cordon as part of an operation to fix an adversary or enemy in place so that host-nation
forces can reduce adversary or enemy forces. The cordon force must establish security outward (to
prevent reinforcement and support) and establish security inward (to prevent withdrawal).

The headquarters ordering the cordon establishes—

  • The purpose and intent of the cordon.
  • Command relationships with other elements participating in, supporting, or conducting

     actions within the cordon.
  • Coordination of fires and information support.
  • Coordinating instructions to include control measures and linkup procedures.
  • Operations to conduct following the cordon.

                                                                  19-13


---

MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

    Organization of Forces for a Cordon
    The commander of the cordon force organizes forces into inner and outer cordon elements, and a
    reserve (though this may be provided by higher headquarters). Each is prioritized according to
    METT-T, though the inner cordon element typically receives greater priority as it most directly
    supports actions within the cordon. The inner cordon element prevents withdrawal of the enemy
    or adversary, or provides overwatch for ongoing activities such as food distribution, and receives
    tasks such as contain, fix, provide security, etc. The outer cordon element prevents external
    interference with actions within the cordon, such as reinforcement or relief, and receives tasks
    such as block, deny, or interdict.

    Cordon Control Measures
    The minimum control measures for a cordon are an assembly area, line of departure, and objective
    area. Commanders may also employ control measures such as routes, checkpoints, phase lines,
    rally points, and release points. The fundamental risk that a unit must mitigate is the battlespace
    geometry and coordination between the inner cordon element of the cordon force, and friendly
    forces conducting actions within the cordon. During small scale operations, such as the company
    and below, the inner cordon will physically tie-in with forces within the cordon, deconflicting
    positions and fires appropriately. During larger operations, units use NFAs and RFLs to allow the
    inner cordon element to prevent enemy withdrawal without endangering friendly forces operating
    within the cordon.

    Cordon Planning Considerations
    The cordon is an operation that frequently occurs throughout the competition continuum. The
    most significant planning factor for the cordon is the environment in which it will occur. Most
    often, the cordon force will serve as an element within a larger operation. There are four
    fundamental planning considerations for cordons:

       • Purpose. What actions are occurring within the cordon and how is the cordon force
          supporting them?

       • Threat. What is the nature of the threat and its capabilities? If the enemy can react with armor
         or mechanized vehicles, that changes the posture and tactics of the outer cordon. If actions
         within the cordon are likely to generate reactions from the civilian population, that
         complicates the mission of the inner cordon.

       • Time. The cordon is a temporary operation. Depending on threat and purpose, how long the
         cordon force must provide security for actions in the objective area effects tactical
         dispositions and sustainment. Typically, cordons that exceed 24 hours in duration should be
         considered bypasses or encirclements.

       • Movement. How will the cordon force move into the objective area, establish inner and outer
         cordons, and deconflict movement with other friendly forces.

    The cordon force can enter and depart the objective area through single or multiple routes;
    however, the cordon force typically plans to depart on different routes than the routes used to
    deploy. The commander weighs speed, trafficability, the employment of surprise, and the
    likelihood of enemy contact when selecting routes. The commander determines if the cordon force
    should occupy the inner and outer cordons sequentially or simultaneously. The terrain is a primary
    factor in this decision—determining when, where, and how the cordon force can move. The

                                                                       19-14


---

                                                                                  MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

commander also considers the threat when comparing the surprise associated with simultaneously
establishing inner and outer cordons, versus a more deliberate sequential occupation. If the cordon
force faces or is likely to face significant resistance, it conducts an encirclement.

When the enemy threat is significant, the cordon force plans to execute accordingly, conducting
the priority of work associated with the defense to include employing obstacles. The cordon force
must receive the combat support and CSS resources required for this environment, to include
planning for obstacle removal at the end of the operation. When the enemy threat is minimal, then
the cordon force still establishes local security and prevents reinforcement of, or withdrawal from,
the objective area. This may still require combat support and CSS resources necessary to set up
TCPs and to control the movement of the population. Contingent on METT-T, commanders might
employ any combination of observation posts, patrols, and static positions to conduct the cordon.

Cordon Execution
The cordon force occupies an assembly area and begins planning in conjunction with higher
headquarters and elements associated with the operation. The cordon force departs the assembly
area, crosses the line of departure (or passes through friendly lines), and follows the designated
route. The cordon force is typically the lead element, and has most of the combat power, given
their tactical requirements. As the lead element, they typically serve as the security element,
conducting screen and guard missions to the front and flanks.

After reaching the objective area, the cordon force conducts either a simultaneous or sequential
occupation of the inner and outer cordons. The cordon force executes priorities of work focused
on establishing immediate control of likely avenues of approach and escape, improving positions,
setting up observation posts and patrol routes, and establishing a reserve that can react to threats.
Depending on the higher headquarters plan, actions might begin with the cordon or wait for the
cordon force to establish the cordon.

While actions occur on the objective, the cordon force continues to maintain inner and outer
security. Depending on the threat and the length of time the cordon is to exist, this may consist of
completely blocking off traffic routes, or merely observing them while preserving the capability to
react to threats. The inner cordon maintains constant coordination with friendly forces within the
cordon. The cordon commander should either collocate with friendly forces within the cordon or
allow the commander of the inner cordon element to do so.

When actions are complete within the cordon, the cordon force remains in place until friendly
forces depart the objective area. Using either sequential or simultaneous methods, the cordon
force terminates the cordon. When moving away from the objective area, the cordon force follows
in trace of friendly forces, serving as a rear security element executing screen and guard missions,
while also providing overwatch for stragglers and vehicle casualties. Because the cordon force
typically has most of the combat power, it might be tasked with providing all-around security on
ingress and egress from the objective area.

                    CHAPTER 20.
                      DECEPTION

The Marine Corps plans and conducts tactical deception and deception in support of operations
security (DISO), which can directly lead to achieving surprise and enhancing security. Joint
military deception (MILDEC) is a joint activity, conducted under combatant command authority,
which Marine Corps component commands and Fleet Marine Forces contribute to.

Effective deception relies on two complementary functions: concealing facts (hiding the truth)
and revealing fiction (portraying falsehoods). Friendly forces combine these functions to
misdirect the enemy decision maker’s understanding of the battlespace, causing the enemy to
make decisions that are detrimental to achieving the objective. For more information on, refer to
MCTP 3-32F, Deception.

DECEPTION GOAL

Friendly forces use deception is to gain or preserve an advantage. The deception goal is the
“commander’s statement of the purpose of military deception as it contributes to the successful
accomplishment of the assigned mission” (DoD Dictionary). It is usually stated as a positive
friendly advantage or condition such as “successful deception creates a decisive combat power
advantage for the main effort attack along AXIS MONTEZUMA.”

Deception is not an end to itself; the success is measured by its direct contribution to mission
accomplishment. Deception often requires substantial investments in effort and resources that
would otherwise be applied against the adversary in a more direct fashion. Consequently, the
commander should first envision the deception goal in terms of its specific contribution to
accomplishing the designated mission.

DECEPTION TARGET (ADVERSARY DECISION-MAKER)

The deception target is “the adversary decision maker with the authority to make the decision that
will achieve the deception objective” (DoD Dictionary). To achieve friendly force objectives, the
friendly force affects the target’s mental state using desired perceptions. Friendly forces should
select the target(s) after reviewing the deception goal and objective and analyzing the enemy’s
doctrine, current battlespace situation, and future actions.

In DISO, the deception target is a foreign intelligence entity (FIE), not the adversary decision
maker. The intent of targeting FIE is obfuscate the true purpose, intention, or indications and
warning of a friendly force. A thorough understanding of the intelligence collection streams
available to an enemy is required to ensure that the maximum number of indicators are concealed
through deception.


---

MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

   DECEPTION METHODOLOGY

    Deception operations unfold as a “SEE-THINK-DO” methodology:
       • Friendly forces present deceptive executions that are observable to enemy intelligence
         collection (“SEE”).
       • Enemy decision-makers form perceptions of the operational environment influenced by that
         collection (“THINK”).
       • Enemy decision makes make a decision to take an action or inaction detrimental to their own
         objective(s) (“DO”).

    A deception operation is planned, however, in a reverse sequence as a “DO-THINK-SEE:”
       • What potential action or inaction take that would enhance the friendly force’s ability to
         achieve their objective (“DO”)?
       • What enemy perceptions of the operational environment need to shift, change, be re-enforced,
         or created in order to come to that conclusion (“THINK”)?
       • What friendly force indicators will an enemy’s intelligence collection apparatus need to
         observe to generate those perceptions (“SEE”)?

    Deception Objective (“Do”)
    The deception objective is “the desired result of a deception operation expressed in terms of what
    the adversary is to do or not to do at the critical time and/or location” (DoD Dictionary). For
    example, a deception objective could be “the enemy commander does not commit the armored
    reserve along AXIS MONTEZUMA through D+36 hours.”

    Desired Perceptions and the Deception Story (“Think”)
    Desired perceptions lead the deception target to make decisions that achieve the deception
    objective. They can include personal conclusions, official estimates, or assumptions formed from
    both objective (observation and analysis) and subjective (intuition and experience) approaches.
    Perceptions are affected by biases, preconceptions, predispositions, and filters applied in the
    collection, analysis, delivery, and reception of information. This is why most successful
    deceptions reinforce existing perceptions; it is far more challenging to change or create a
    perception than reinforce one.

    Marine commanders must understand the enemy’s baseline perceptions (i.e., what would an enemy
    commander reasonably conclude based on recent actions and the overall intelligence collection and
    analysis capabilities). From this baseline, Marine commanders must determine the desired
    perceptions an enemy commander would need to take the action or inaction of the deception
    objective. The transition from baseline to desire perceptions can be completed by changing,
    shifting, or creating new perceptions that have no baseline or by re-enforcing current—but
    inaccurate—perceptions (see Table 20-1).

                                                                        20-2


---

                                               MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

Table 20-1. Transitions from Baseline to Desired Perception.

                                    Method

                                   Change

                                               The Marines will not attack.

                                   Shift

                                                                 The Marines will attack
                                                              from the southeast or south.

Marines will attack from the east  Create

                                               It is a different unit that will
                                                 attack from the north.

                                                                Re-enforce

                                                                                          The Marines will definitely attack from
                                                                                       the east and will initiate movement at 1300.

People use narratives to process information; therefore, deception is fundamentally a process of
communication. A deception story, which is created using a narrative, is “a scenario that outlines
the friendly actions that will be portrayed to cause the deception target to adopt the desired
deception perception” (DoD Dictionary). The deception story must be believable, verifiable,
consistent, and executable. It is primarily communicated to the target through indirect means,
which lets individuals see pieces of information and create their own narrative (e.g., the target
“sees” indications that Marine rifle platoon is preparing to conduct movement and “thinks” the
whole Marine rifle company is preparing to conduct movement for an attack).

                                                                   20-3


---

MCWP 3-01, Offensive and Defensive Tactics

    Deception Executions and Observables (“See”)
    Deception executions create convincing observables for an adversary’s intelligence collection
    apparatus that provide indicators, that in aggregate, form the basis of a believable deception story.
    They are conducted through three categories of means: physical, technical, and administrative. A
    single execution may have multiple means (e.g., a decoy system that produces a physical signature
    of the object to observation and a technical signature that corroborates its authenticity through
    adversary direction finding). See MCTP 3-32F for a full description.

    Physical Means. Physical means include information or signatures conveyed through direct
    observation or sensors. For example, a decoy that imitates a real LAV is a physical means because
    its value is in observation by the enemy. Examples include movement of forces, real or decoy
    equipment, conducting rehearsals, etc.

    Technical Means. Technical means include manipulated cyber, electromagnetic, or acoustic
    information. Forces can apply technical means alone, with corresponding physical means, or
    integrated with other technical aspects to replicate something physical that is absent from direct
    visual observation. For example, establishing communications networks and interactive
    transmissions that replicate a specific unit type, size, or activity.

    Administrative Means. Administrative means include manipulated written, oral, pictorial, or
    signature information. They typically portray information and indicators associated with
    ongoing or planned military activity. For example, administratively clearing the airspace over
    a specific area when the enemy expects an attack would indicate pending indirect fires or
    deliberate OPSEC-violations that convey unclassified indicators to an enemy.

   DECEPTION TACTICS

    Marine Corps deception activities apply the three deception means to conduct four basic tactics
    categories (feints, demonstrations, display, ruse). Planners consider the time, place, and adversary
    when selecting which deception tactic to use. To conduct a deception, some materiel and manpower
    might not be available for other actions. For example, when conducting a display, the work party
    conducting the display needs available transportation, fuel, food, water, and other systems required
    to sustain themselves and re-join the main force.

    Feint
    A feint is designed to mislead the adversary regarding friendly dispositions and concentrations. A
    series of feints can condition the adversary to react ineffectively to a future main attack in the
    same area. Feints are characterized by direct fire contact (see Figure 20-1).

Enemy Perception                       Friendly Concept

A demonstration in military deception is, “a show of force similar to a feint without actual contact
with the adversary, in an area where a decision is not sought that is made to deceive an adversary”
(DoD Dictionary). A demonstration’s intent is to cause the enemy to select a COA favorable to
friendly goals (see Figure 20-2).

Display

Displays (Figure 20-3) include the simulating, disguising, or portraying friendly objects, units, or
capabilities. They are designed to mislead the enemy’s assessment of friendly force capabilities
(e.g., thinking there is less Marine combat power available for a given action than what exists).

Ruse
A ruse in military deception is, “an action designed to deceive the adversary, usually involving the
deliberate exposure of false information to the adversary’s intelligence collection system” (DoD
Dictionary). A ruse deceives the enemy to obtain a friendly advantage. A ruse in deception
generally contributes to a larger deception plan.

DECEPTION IN SUPPORT OF OPERATIONS SECURITY

A DISO is used to obfuscate indicators of a friendly operation that remain visible to an enemy’s
intelligence collection assets despite an OPSEC plan. Unit commanders employ DISO to create
multiple false indicators that confuse enemy forces operating in the unit’s area of operations by
targeting the enemy’s intelligence apparatus, making unit intentions harder to interpret. A DISO
uses controlled information about friendly force capabilities, activities, and intentions to shape

    perceptions. The intent of targeting the enemy’s intelligence apparatus is more general, focusing
    on interposing deceptive indicators between the intelligence collection method and the real

INFORMATION PATHWAYS

Marine commanders need to analyze conduits to determine the information pathway to the enemy
decision maker. Understanding the flow of information from the sensor collecting the information
through the enemy’s nodes and filters to their decision maker is paramount to determining which
executions and OPSEC countermeasures are required to convey the deception story.

The deception planner chooses, and deconflicts access to, specific conduits to provide a
synchronized portrayal of selected information and indicators. Typically, an individual conduit
contains a sensor that registers a signature, a transmission means from the sensor to an
intermediate node or nodes that might act or aggregate the information in various ways, and
delivery to the deception target(s).

Conduits comprise systems, organizations, and individuals through which information reaches the
target. Selecting appropriate conduits is a critical part of developing a successful deception plan.
A filter is a node within a conduit that aggregates, synthesizes, or applies bias to the observable on
its path to the deception target. To develop an effective deception story, planners must understand
each conduit’s construct, filtering, and estimated function time; the relationships and redundancy
with other conduits; and their comparative value as perceived by the target.
